## Khuddaka Nikāya
## Cūḷaniddesa Pāḷi
## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## Pārāyanavagga
## Vatthugāthā

The Brahmin (Bāvarī), who had reached the far shore of the three Vedas and desired the state of possessionlessness (ākiñcañña), went from the delightful city of Sāvatthī of the Kosalans to the region of Dakkhiṇāpatha.

That Brahmin Bāvarī dwelt on the banks of the Godhāvarī River, in a place close to the borders of King Assaka's territory and King Muḷaka's territory, subsisting on gleaned alms and fruits.

Depending on that very riverbank, a large village arose. With the revenue obtained from that village, he performed a great sacrifice.

Having performed the great sacrifice, he returned to his hermitage. After he had returned, another Brahmin arrived.

That Brahmin had feet injured from travel, was parched with thirst, had stained teeth, and a head covered in dust. Approaching Brahmin Bāvarī, he begged for five hundred pieces of money.

Seeing that Brahmin, Bāvarī invited him to a seat, asked if he was well and free from illness, and spoke these words:

"Whatever gift-objects I had, I have already given them all away. O Brahmin, I no longer have five hundred pieces of money; please forgive me for this."
2:
“If you do not give to me who is begging, O Brahmin, may your head split into seven pieces on the seventh day.”

That deceitful Brahmin, having fabricated these terrifying words, spoke them. Upon hearing his words, Brahmin Bāvarī became distressed and fell into suffering.

Afflicted by the thorn of grief, he remained withered, unable to eat. Furthermore, with a mind thus troubled, Bāvarī’s heart found no delight in meditation (jhāna).

Seeing Bāvarī trembling with fear and suffering, a deity who desired his welfare approached him and spoke these words:

“That Brahmin does not know the head. He is merely a deceiver who desires wealth. He has no knowledge regarding the head or the splitting of the head.”

“O deity, if you know, please tell me, who am asking you, about the head and the splitting of the head. Let us hear your words.”

“I too do not know the head and the splitting of the head. I have no knowledge regarding this head and the splitting of the head. Indeed, only the Buddhas have the vision that can see the head and the splitting of the head.”

“O deity, if that is so, then tell me who on this earth knows the head and the splitting of the head.”

“In former times, there was a Sakyan prince, an offspring of King Okkāka, a leader of the world, a bringer of light, who departed from the city of Kapilavatthu.

O Brahmin, that Fully Enlightened One has reached the far shore of all phenomena (dhammas). He has attained the power of all higher knowledges (abhiññā) and possesses the eye of wisdom that sees into all dhammas. He has reached the end of all kamma and is liberated in Nibbāna, the end of the bases of existence (upadhi).

That Blessed Buddha in this world, the one with five eyes, teaches the Dhamma. Go to Him and ask; He will explain that splitting of the head to you.”

Hearing the word “Buddha,” Bāvarī became uplifted in mind. His grief diminished, and he attained abundant joy (pīti).
3:
That Brahmin Bāvarī, with a delighted and uplifted mind, being filled with inspiration, asked the deity: "In which village, or in which market town, or in which province does the Protector of the World dwell? Where should we go to behold the Fully Enlightened One, the Supreme among bipeds?"

"The Victorious One is in Sāvatthī, the capital of the Kosalan King. That Buddha is of great wisdom, of vast intelligence like the earth. That Sakyan prince is one who has abandoned the enemy of defilements and is free from taints (āsavas). He is the best among men, knowing the matter of the head and the splitting of the head."

Thereupon, Bāvarī addressed his students, the Brahmins who had reached the far shore of the Vedas: "Come, young men, I shall speak; listen to my words.

The appearance of such a one in the world is rare to obtain constantly. That one, renowned as the Fully Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha), has now appeared in the world. Go quickly to Sāvatthī and behold the Supreme among bipeds."

"O Brahmin, how shall we know, upon seeing Him, that He is the Buddha? Tell us, who do not know, how we may recognize Him."

"The thirty-two marks of a Great Man are found in the Vedic texts. They have been explained in full and in order.

For one who has these marks of a Great Man on his body, only two destinies are possible; a third does not exist.

If he lives the household life, he will conquer this earth and rule by Dhamma, without punishment or weapons.

But if he goes forth from the household life into homelessness, he will become a Fully Enlightened One, an Arahant, the Unsurpassed One, who has removed the veil of defilements.

Ask Him only in your mind about my birth, clan, and marks, and about the Vedas you have learned, as well as about the head and the splitting of the head.

If He is indeed a Buddha who sees all without obstruction, He will verbally answer the questions asked in your mind."
4:
Upon hearing the words of the Brahmin Bāvarī, the sixteen brahmin disciples—Ajita, Tissa Metteyya, Puṇṇaka, Mettegū, Dhotaka, Upasīva, Nanda, Hemaka, Todeyya and Kappa (the two), the wise Jatukaṇṇī, Bhadrāvudha, Udaya, the brahmin Posāla, the wise Mogharāja, and the great sage Piṅgiya—set out on their journey. All of them were leaders of their own groups, renowned throughout the world, practitioners of meditation (jhāna) who delighted in it, wise, and imbued with the tendencies of their past practices. Having respectfully paid homage to the Brahmin Bāvarī and performed the circumambulation, they all departed toward the north, wearing matted hair and antelope skins.

They passed through Patiṭṭhāna, the seat of King Muḷaka; then to Māhissati, Ujjeni, Gonaddha, Vedisa, and the city named Vanasavhaya. From there, they proceeded to Kosambī, Sāketa, and Sāvatthī, the most excellent of cities; then through Setabya, Kapilavatthu, Kusinārā, Pāvā, Bhoganagara, Vesālī, and the capital of Magadha (Rājagaha). They then ascended the delightful and heart-pleasing Pāsāṇaka Cetiya. Just as a thirsty man longs for cool water, as a merchant longs for great profit, or as one scorched by the sun longs for shade, they hurriedly climbed the mountain, eager to see the Blessed One.

At that time, the Blessed One, surrounded by the community of monks, was preaching the Dhamma to the monks, roaring like a lion in the forest. Ajita saw the Buddha, who was as radiant as the sun with all its rays, and as beautiful as the full moon on the fifteenth day. Then, seeing the perfect marks on the Blessed One's body, he stood joyfully to one side and mentally asked these questions: "Speak of Bāvarī's birth, speak of his lineage and his marks. Speak of his mastery of the Vedas, and how many disciples does that brahmin teach?"
5:
"The Brahmin Bāvarī is one hundred and twenty years of age; his lineage is Bāvarī. There are three marks on his body, and he has reached the end of the three Vedas. In the science of marks, in the Itihāsa (history) along with the Nighaṇḍu (lexicon) and Keṭubha (ritual), and in his own three Vedas, he has reached perfection and teaches five hundred disciples."

"O Supreme among men, please detail the three marks on the body of the Brahmin Bāvarī. O Cutter of Doubts, please reveal them so that we may have no more uncertainty."

"Young man, that Brahmin Bāvarī can cover his face with his tongue; he has hair between his eyebrows (uṇṇā); and his male organ is ensheathed. Know it to be so."

Although they did not hear any audible questions, upon hearing the problems thus answered, all the people were filled with joy and, with joined palms, they thought: "Who is this—a deva, a Brahmā, or Sakka, the lord of Sujā? Who is it that answers questions asked only in the mind?"

"Bāvarī asks about the 'head' and the 'splitting of the head.' O Blessed One, please explain this; O Sage, dispel our doubts."

"Know that ignorance (avijjā) is the 'head,' and knowledge (vijjā) is the 'splitter of the head,' when combined with faith, mindfulness, concentration, desire, and energy."

Then, with great joy, the young man Ajita composed himself, placed his antelope skin over one shoulder, and prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet. "O Venerable One, the Brahmin Bāvarī, together with his disciples, with a joyful and happy mind, pays homage to your feet, O One with Vision."

"May the Brahmin Bāvarī be happy together with his disciples. And may you also be happy, young man; may you live long. I grant permission to Bāvarī, to you, and to all to ask whatever doubt you have in your minds."

Having been granted permission by the Fully Enlightened One, Ajita sat with joined palms and asked the first question to the Tathāgata right there.

## The Introductory Verses are finished.
6:
## 1. The Questions of the Young Man Ajita
The Venerable Ajita asked thus:
"By what is the world enveloped? Why does it not shine? What do you say is its smear? What is its great fear?"

(The Blessed One replied:)
"Ajita, the world is enveloped by ignorance (avijjā). It does not shine because of avarice and negligence. I say craving (jappā) is its smear, and suffering (dukkha) is its great fear."

The Venerable Ajita asked thus:
"The streams flow everywhere. What is the restraint for the streams? Tell me the protection for the streams. By what are the streams closed?"

(The Blessed One replied:)
"Whatever streams there are in the world, mindfulness (sati) is their restraint. I say mindfulness is the protection for the streams. They are closed by wisdom (paññā)."

The Venerable Ajita asked thus:
"O Venerable One, there are wisdom, mindfulness, and also name-and-form. Tell me this when I ask: where do these things cease without remainder?"

(The Blessed One replied:)
"Ajita, I shall answer the question you ask. Where name-and-form cease without remainder—by the cessation of consciousness (viññāṇa), they cease there (in Nibbāna)."

The Venerable Ajita asked thus:
"There are those who have understood the Dhamma (Arahants) and many who are still training (sekhas) here. O Wise One, please tell me their conduct when I ask."

(The Blessed One replied:)
"He should not be greedy for sensual pleasures; his mind should be undisturbed. Skilled in all things, the mindful bhikkhu should wander, destroying the defilements."

## The Questions of the Young Man Ajita is finished.
7:
## 2. Tissametteyya-māṇava-pucchā
Venerable Tissametteyya asked: "Who in this world is well-stilled? For whom are there no tremors (of craving and views)? Who, having known the two ends through higher knowledge, is not smeared by wisdom in the middle? Whom do you call a Great Man? Who in this world has transcended the seamstress (craving)?"

The Blessed One replied: "Metteyya, the monk who leads a holy life among sensual pleasures, who is free from craving, always mindful, and cooled through reflection—he is well-stilled; for that monk, there are no tremors.

He, having known the two ends through higher knowledge, is not smeared by wisdom in the middle. I call that monk a Great Man; he has transcended the seamstress in this world."

## Tissametteyya-māṇava-pucchā is second.

## 3. Puṇṇaka-māṇava-pucchā
Venerable Puṇṇaka asked: "I have come with a question to the one who is without agitation and who sees the root. Dependent on what do sages, humans, nobles, and brahmins in this world offer many sacrifices to the deities? O Blessed One, please tell me this."

The Blessed One replied: "Puṇṇaka, all those sages, humans, nobles, and brahmins in this world who offer many sacrifices to the deities do so because they long for existence as humans and so forth. Dependent on aging, they offer sacrifices."
8:
Venerable Puṇṇaka asked: "O Blessed One, all those sages, humans, nobles, and brahmins in this world offer many sacrifices to the deities. O Venerable Sir, are they diligent in the path of sacrifice and have they crossed over birth and aging? O Blessed One, please tell me this."

The Blessed One replied: "Puṇṇaka, they long, they praise, they pray, and they sacrifice. Dependent on gain, they long for sensual pleasures. Those who are engaged in sacrifice, being attached to the passion for existence, have not crossed over birth and aging, I declare."

Venerable Puṇṇaka asked: "O Venerable Sir, if those engaged in sacrifice have not crossed over birth and aging through their sacrifices, then who in the world of gods and humans has crossed over birth and aging? O Blessed One, please tell me this."

The Blessed One replied: "Puṇṇaka, having reflected with wisdom on the high and low states in this world, he for whom there is no tremor anywhere in the world, who is peaceful, smokeless, untroubled, and without desire—he has crossed over birth and aging, I declare."

## Puṇṇaka-māṇava-pucchā is third.

## 4. Mettagū-māṇava-pucchā
Venerable Mettagū asked: "O Blessed One, I ask you this; please tell it to me. I consider you a master of knowledge with a developed self. From where have these many forms of suffering in the world arisen?"
9:
The Blessed One replied: "Mettagū, you have indeed asked me about the origin of suffering. As one who knows, I shall tell you the cause of that suffering. There are many various forms of suffering in the world. These sufferings arise because of acquisitions (upadhi) as the cause.

Indeed, the ignorant one who, without knowing, creates acquisitions, undergoes suffering again and again. Therefore, one who observes the birth and origin of suffering, seeing the nature of conditioned things, should not create acquisitions."

Venerable Mettagū said: "O Blessed One, you have well-answered what we asked. Now we wish to ask another matter; please tell us that. 'How do the wise cross over the flood, as well as birth, aging, sorrow, and lamentation?' O Sage, please explain this well to me, for this Dhamma is known by you in such a manner."

The Blessed One replied: "Mettagū, I will teach you the Dhamma, realized in this very life and not based on hearsay, knowing which and wandering mindfully, one may cross over the entanglement (craving) in the world."

Venerable Mettagū said: "O Great Seer, I greatly delight in that supreme Dhamma, knowing which and wandering mindfully, one may cross over the entanglement in the world."

The Blessed One replied: "Mettagū, whatever you know—above, below, across, and in the middle—having dispelled delight, attachment, and consciousness in those things, one should not stand in existence.

A monk living thus, mindful and diligent, wandering and having given up 'mine-making,' being wise, would abandon birth, aging, sorrow, and lamentation, and abandon suffering in this very life."
10:
"O Great Seer, I delight in these words of yours. O Gotama, you have well-explained the state without acquisitions. Surely the Blessed One has abandoned suffering, for this Dhamma is known by you in such a manner.

Those whom you, O Sage, would constantly admonish, they too would surely abandon suffering. O Great Hero, I pay homage to you having approached. May the Blessed One also constantly admonish me."

"The Brahmin whom one should know as a master of knowledge, possessing nothing and unattached to sensual existence—he has surely crossed this flood. Having reached the far shore, he is without barrenness and without doubt.

And the man who is a master of knowledge here, having let go of this attachment to various existences, free from craving, untroubled, and without desire—he has crossed over birth and aging, I declare."

## Mettagū-māṇava-pucchā is fourth.

## 5. Dhotaka-māṇava-pucchā
The long-lived Dhotaka asked thus:
"O Blessed One, I ask you; please tell me that answer. O Great Seer, I long for your words. Having heard your voice, I will train for my own Nibbāna."

The Blessed One spoke thus:
"Dhotaka, if that is so, you should exert yourself, being wise and mindful right here in this dispensation. Having heard the sound of Dhamma from my mouth, train for your own Nibbāna."

"O Blessed One, I see in the world of gods and humans a Brahmin wandering without possessions. O All-Seeing One, I pay homage to you. O Sakyan, please release me from my doubts."
11:
“Dhotaka, I am not able to set free anyone in the world who has doubts. Having known the supreme Dhamma, in this way, you shall cross this flood.”

“O Blessed One, please instruct me out of compassion so that I may know the Dhamma of seclusion (Nibbāna). I shall practice, being peaceful and detached (from craving and views) even in this very Dispensation, without hindrance like the sky.”

“Dhotaka, I will proclaim to you that peace (Nibbāna) which is to be realized for oneself in this very life, without relying on hearsay; knowing which, and wandering mindfully, one can cross over the craving that clings to the world.”

“O Great Seeker of the supreme benefit, I greatly delight in that supreme peace; knowing which, and wandering mindfully, one can cross over the craving that clings to the world.”

“Dhotaka, whatever you know—above, below, across, and in the middle—having known that as a bond in the world, do not create craving for various states of existence.”

## The Questions of the Youth Dhotaka (Fifth).

## 6. The Questions of the Youth Upasīva

“O Sakyan, I alone, without support, am unable to cross the great flood. O All-Seeing One, please tell me the support relying on which I may cross this flood.”
12:
“Upasīva, mindfully looking upon the sphere of nothingness, cross the flood by relying on the thought ‘there is nothing.’ Abandoning sensual pleasures, being free from various talks (doubts), look specifically at Nibbāna, the destruction of craving, day and night,” said the Blessed One.

“One who is free from passion for all sensual pleasures, relying on the sphere of nothingness, having abandoned conceit (the lower states), and is intensely devoted to the supreme liberation through perception—does such a person stay there without following along (to other realms)?” asked the venerable Upasīva.

“One who is free from passion for all sensual pleasures, relying on the sphere of nothingness, having abandoned conceit (the lower states), and is intensely devoted to the supreme liberation through perception—such a person would stay there without following along,” said the Blessed One.

“O All-Seeing One, if that person stays there without following along for many years, would he be cooled and liberated right there? Or would the consciousness of such a person cease?”

“Just as a flame struck by a gust of wind goes out and cannot be defined by name, even so, the sage, liberated from the name-group (nāmakāya), goes out and cannot be defined by name,” said the Blessed One.

“Has he reached an end and no longer exists, or is he safe because he is eternal? O Sage, please explain this matter well to me, for this Dhamma is known by you in such a way.”

“For one who has reached the end, there is no measure (such as form, etc.). That by which one might speak of him does not exist for him. When all phenomena are removed, all pathways of speech are also removed,” said the Blessed One.

## The Questions of the Youth Upasīva (Sixth).
13:
## 7. The Questions of the Youth Nanda
The venerable Nanda asked thus:
“People say that there are sages in the world; how is this so? Do they call one a sage because he is endowed with the knowledge of attainments, or because he is endowed with a frugal life?”

“Nanda, the wise ones in this Dispensation do not say one is pure by means of views, or by hearing, or by the knowledge of attainments. Those who, having destroyed the groups (of defilements), wander without oppression such as passion and are free from desire—them I call sages.”

The venerable Nanda asked again:
“Whatever recluses and brahmins say that purity is by seeing and hearing, or say that purity is by virtue and ritual, or say that purity is by many other ways—O Friend, the Blessed One, can they cross over birth and aging while they are practicing and guarding their own views? O Blessed One, I ask this matter; please preach this matter to me.”

The Blessed One, addressing him as “Nanda,” replied thus:
“Whatever recluses and brahmins say that purity is by seeing and hearing, or say that purity is by virtue and ritual, or say that purity is by many other ways—even if they are practicing and guarding their own views, I say they cannot transcend birth and aging.”

The venerable Nanda asked again:
“Whatever recluses and brahmins say that purity is by seeing and hearing, or say that purity is by virtue and ritual, or say that purity is by many other ways—O Great Sage, if you say they are unable to cross the flood, then who in the world of devas and humans crosses over birth and aging? O Blessed One, I ask this matter; please preach this matter to me.”
14:
The Blessed One said, "Nanda, I do not say that all ascetics and brahmins are shrouded by birth and aging. Those in this world who have abandoned all that is seen, heard, or sensed, or all precepts and vows, and have also abandoned all the various [omens], and who, having understood craving through the three full understandings, live without taints—those men, I say, have indeed crossed the fourfold flood."

Ven. Nanda said, "O Blessed One, the Ven. Gotama has well-proclaimed Nibbāna. I greatly rejoice in these words of the Blessed One. Those in this teaching who have abandoned all that is seen, heard, or sensed, or all precepts and vows, and have also abandoned all the various noisy omens, and who, having known craving through full understanding, are without taints—I also say those people have crossed the fourfold flood. (As you have said), O Blessed One, I greatly rejoice in these words spoken by the Blessed One."

## The Questions of the Young Man Nanda is finished.

## 8. Hemakamaṇavapucchā

Ven. Hemaka said, "Those former teachers outside the teaching of Ven. Gotama explained their views to me, saying, 'It was thus in the past, it will be so in the future.' All those words were just hearsay, and because all of it only increased speculation, I did not find delight in the views of those teachers. O Sage, who is more noble than the four types of brave ones, please tell me the Dhamma that destroys craving, knowing which, and practicing mindfully, one may cross over the entanglement in the world."

The Blessed One replied, "Hemaka, the removal of desire and lust for those pleasant things that are seen, heard, sensed, and cognized in this world is the undying state of Nibbāna. Those who, knowing this Nibbāna, are endowed with mindfulness and have become cooled in this very life, they are always at peace and have crossed over the entanglement in the world."

## The Questions of the Young Man Hemaka is finished.
15:
## 9. Todeyya-māṇava-pucchā

'In whom sensual pleasures do not dwell and do not cling,
In whom craving does not exist,
And who has crossed over doubt—what is the liberation (vimokkha) of such a person?' (Thus Venerable Todeyya asked.)

'Todeyya, in whom sensual pleasures do not dwell,
In whom craving does not exist,
And who has crossed over doubt—for that person, there is no other liberation.' (Thus the Blessed One said.)

'Is that person free from lustful attachment, or is there still longing? Is that person wise, or is he still planning with intellect?
O Sakyan, who has the eye that sees all around, please preach to me so that I may understand the nature of that Sage (muni).'

'That Sage is free from attachment; he has no longing. That Sage is wise; he has no speculative thinking (views) through intellect.
Todeyya, know such a person, who is without attachment in the realm of sensual pleasures and free from anxiety, as a Sage.' (Thus He said.)

## The Questions of the Young Man Todeyya, the ninth, is finished.

## 10. Kappa-māṇava-pucchā

'Venerable Sir, for those standing in the middle of the lake of Saṃsāra where the floods of great danger have arisen,
For those oppressed by aging and death, please tell me of an island of refuge.
O Noble One, please preach to me of this island of refuge where these sufferings of aging and death shall not occur again.' (Thus Venerable Kappa asked.)

'Kappa, for those standing in the middle of the lake of Saṃsāra where the floods of great danger have arisen,
For those oppressed by aging and death, I shall tell you of the island that is a refuge.'
16:
'Kappa, that island is without attachment (kiñcana), without grasping through craving and views, and without another rival; it is the end of aging and death. I call that island Nibbāna.'

'Those who, knowing that island of Nibbāna and being mindful, have extinguished the heat of defilements in this very life, do not follow the will of Māra; they do not become the servants of Māra.'

## The Questions of the Young Man Kappa, the tenth, is finished.

## 11. Jatukaṇṇi-māṇava-pucchā

'O Blessed One of great effort, having heard of the virtues of the Blessed One who does not desire sensual pleasures, I have come to the Blessed One who has crossed the flood and is free from desire. O Blessed One who has the eye of omniscience, please preach the Dhamma of peace, which is Nibbāna. O Blessed One, please preach that Nibbāna to me as it truly is.'

'Just as the powerful sun stands pervading the earth with its radiance, so the Blessed One stands having overcome sensual pleasures. O Blessed One of vast wisdom, I wish to know the Dhamma; please preach to me, who has little wisdom, that Dhamma which is the absence of rebirth and aging in this Dispensation.'

'Jatukaṇṇi, having seen the practice leading to Nibbāna as secure, remove greed for sensual pleasures. Abandon that which is grasped through craving and views, as well as the sense bases that should not be craved; let there be no attachment (kiñcana) such as lust in you.'

'Dry up the aggregates that occurred in the past. Let there be no mass of defilements for you in the future. If you do not grasp in the present either, you will live in peace.'

'O Brahmin, for one who is free from greed in every way regarding name-and-form (nāma-rūpa), those taints (āsava) by which one goes to the realm of death do not exist.'

## The Questions of the Young Man Jatukaṇṇi, the eleventh, is finished.
17:
## 12. Bhadrāvudhamāṇavapucchā
Venerable Bhadrāvudha spoke thus: "I entreat the Wise One, who has abandoned the flood, cut off craving, is passionless, has abandoned delight, crossed the flood, is liberated, has abandoned the stains of doubt, and possesses excellent wisdom. By hearing the words of the Exalted One, doubts will be dispelled from here."

"O Hero, people from various regions have gathered, greatly longing for your words. Please explain the Dhamma well to them, for this Dhamma is known to you thus."

The Blessed One said: "Bhadrāvudha, one should remove all craving for clinging—above in the future, below in the past, across in the present, and in the middle. Whatever people cling to in the world, by that very clinging, Death follows the creature."

"Therefore, knowing this, a mindful monk should not cling to anything in the whole world, seeing these creatures who are attached to clinging, stuck in the realm of Death."

## Bhadrāvudhamāṇavapucchā is the twelfth.

## 13. Udayamāṇavapucchā
Venerable Udaya spoke thus: "I have come with a question to the one who is meditative, free from the dust of passion, seated, who has done what was to be done, is free from taints, and has reached the far shore of all dhammas. Please tell me the liberation through final knowledge, the breaker of ignorance."

The Blessed One said: "Udaya, I speak of the abandoning of both sensual desires and grief, the dispelling of sloth and torpor, and the prevention of remorse."
18:
"I speak of the liberation through final knowledge, the breaker of ignorance, which is purified by equanimity and mindfulness, and preceded by thinking about the Dhamma."

"With what is the world fettered? What is its wandering? By the abandoning of what is it called Nibbāna?"

"The world is fettered by delight (craving); thought is its wandering and investigating the world's objects; by the abandoning of craving, it is called Nibbāna."

"For one living mindfully in what way does consciousness cease? We have come to ask the Blessed One; let us hear your words."

"For one who does not delight in feeling, both internally and externally, living thus mindfully, consciousness ceases."

## Udayamāṇavapucchā is the thirteenth.

## 14. Posālamāṇavapucchā
"I have come with a question to the one who points out past lives, who is passionless, has cut off doubt, and has reached the far shore of all dhammas."

"I ask the Sakyan about the knowledge of one whose perception of form has disappeared, who has abandoned the whole material body, and who sees internally and externally that 'there is nothing.' How is such a person to be known?"

"Posāla, the Tathāgata, knowing all the stations of consciousness, knows this person standing there, the liberated one who is intent on the sphere of nothingness."

"Knowing the craving that gives rise to the sphere of nothingness as the 'fetter of delight,' and having specially known that sphere of nothingness, he then practices insight therein. Such is the true knowledge of that brahmin who has lived the life."

## Posālamāṇavapucchā is the fourteenth.
19:
## 15. Mogharājamāṇavapucchā
Venerable Mogharāja spoke thus: "O Sakyan, although I have asked twice, the Visionary One did not answer me. I have heard that the Divine Seer answers on the third time."

"This world, the other world, the Brahma world together with the world of devas, do not know the view of the famous Gotama."

"I have come with a question to the one of such excellent vision. How should one look upon the world so that the King of Death does not see him?"

The Blessed One said: "Mogharāja, always mindful, look upon the world as empty. Having uprooted the view of self, one would thus be a crosser of death. The King of Death does not see one who looks upon the world in this way."

## Mogharājamāṇavapucchā is the fifteenth.

## 16. Piṅgiyamāṇavapucchā
Venerable Piṅgiya spoke thus: "I am old, weak, and my complexion has faded. My eyes are not clear, and my hearing is not good. May I not perish while still confused in the interval. Teach me the Dhamma that I may understand, the abandoning of birth and aging in this life."

The Blessed One said: "Piṅgiya, seeing people suffering in forms, heedless people are afflicted because of forms. Therefore, Piṅgiya, being diligent, abandon form for the sake of non-becoming."
20:
Venerable Piṅgiya continued to speak: "In the four directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below—in these ten directions, there is nothing in the world not seen, heard, sensed, or known by you. Teach me the Dhamma that I may understand, the abandoning of birth and aging in this life."

The Blessed One said: "Piṅgiya, seeing people overcome by craving, born of distress, and oppressed by aging; therefore, Piṅgiya, being diligent, abandon craving for the sake of non-becoming."

## Piṅgiyamāṇavapucchā is the sixteenth.

(Summary of Pārāyanavagga)
The Blessed One taught this Pārāyana Sutta while staying at the Pāsāṇaka Shrine in the Magadha country to the sixteen brahmin disciples who were attendants of the brahmin Bāvarī. At their request, he answered the questions they asked. One should understand the meaning of each question, understand the Pali text, and practice the path in accordance with the supramundane Dhamma. One who practices thus will surely reach Nibbāna, the far shore of aging and death. Because these teachings are suitable for going to Nibbāna, this Dhamma teaching is named "Pārāyana" (The Way to the Far Shore). The disciples were Ajita, Tissa Metteyya, Puṇṇaka, Mettagū, Dhotaka, Upasīva, Nanda, Hemaka, Todeyya and Kappa (the two), Jatukaṇṇī, Bhadrāvudha, Udaya, Posāla, and Mogharāja.
21: Due to predominance condition, a state arises: dependent on unwholesome aggregates, mind-produced matter arises. Dependent on an unwholesome state, unwholesome and indeterminate states arise due to predominance condition: dependent on one unwholesome aggregate, three aggregates and mind-produced matter arise; dependent on three aggregates, one aggregate and mind-produced matter arise; dependent on two aggregates, two aggregates and mind-produced matter arise. (3) Dependent on an indeterminate state, an indeterminate state arises due to predominance condition: dependent on one resultant indeterminate or functional indeterminate aggregate, three aggregates and mind-produced matter arise; dependent on three aggregates, one aggregate and mind-produced matter arise; dependent on two aggregates, two aggregates and mind-produced matter arise; dependent on one great essential, three great essentials arise; dependent on three great essentials, one great essential arises; dependent on two great essentials, two great essentials arise; dependent on the great essentials, mind-produced matter and derived matter arise. (1) Dependent on a wholesome state and an indeterminate state, an indeterminate state arises due to predominance condition: dependent on wholesome aggregates and the great essentials, mind-produced matter arises. (1) Dependent on an unwholesome state and an indeterminate state, an indeterminate state arises due to predominance condition: dependent on unwholesome aggregates and the great essentials, mind-produced matter arises. 22:
"O teacher brahmin, I have approached the Buddha, who dispels darkness, who has the eye of all-around vision, who has reached the end of the world, who has transcended all existences, who is taintless, who has abandoned all suffering, and who has a name that is true. Just as a bird leaves a forest with little fruit and dwells in a forest with much fruit, even so, I have left those of little vision and have reached the Buddha, like a swan reaching the great ocean. In the past, outside the teaching of Gotama, there were those who taught, 'It has been thus, it will be thus.' All that was mere hearsay and only increased speculation. Only the Buddha Gotama, the dispeller of darkness, the powerful, the light-maker, the one of vast knowledge, the one of vast wisdom, dispels the darkness of defilements. That Blessed One has taught me the Dhamma that is visible here and now, timeless, the destruction of craving, free from danger, and incomparable to anything."

"Piṅgiya, why do you stay away even for a moment from that Buddha Gotama, who is of vast knowledge and vast wisdom? Why do you stay away from that Buddha who taught you the Dhamma that is visible here and now, timeless, the destruction of craving, free from danger, and incomparable to anything?" asked the brahmin Bāvarī.

"O teacher brahmin, I do not stay away even for a moment from that Buddha Gotama, who is of vast knowledge and vast wisdom. That Blessed One has taught me the Dhamma that is visible here and now, timeless, the destruction of craving, free from danger, and incomparable to anything. O teacher brahmin, without negligence, I see that Blessed One with my mind as if seeing with my eyes, day and night. I spend the night in worship; therefore, I consider that there is no staying away."
23:
Faith, joy, mind, and mindfulness do not depart from the teaching of the Buddha Gotama for me.
In whichever direction the Buddha of vast wisdom goes, I am always bowed towards that direction.

Brahmin, my body is old and weak; because of that weakness, it cannot go to where the Venerable Gotama is.
However, I go there constantly by means of thought. For, brahmin, my mind is always joined with that Buddha.

Lying in the mud of sensuality and trembling, I drifted from one island to another.
While so drifting, I saw the Buddha who has crossed the flood and is taintless.

Just as the Elder Vakkali, the Elder Bhadrāvudha, and Āḷavi-Gotama were released from defilements by putting faith foremost,
Even so, Piṅgiya, you too should release your faith; you will reach the far shore of the realm of death, which is Saṃsāra.

Having heard the words of the Sage, the Buddha, I am even more inspired.
The Buddha is the one who has opened the veil of defilements, who is free from the thorns of defilements, and who is endowed with courageous wisdom.

The Buddha, having known with higher knowledge the truths that excel those of the devas, knows all the high and low states of others and himself.
The Buddha, the Teacher, puts an end to the collection of questions of those who have doubts while professing themselves.

I will certainly reach that Nibbāna, which is incomparable to anything, which cannot be disturbed by defilements, and which is indestructible.
In this matter, I have no doubt. Venerable Sir, please regard me as one whose mind is directed towards Nibbāna with faith.

## The Pārayanānugītigāthā is finished.

25:
"What is its great fear?" means what is the fear, the great fear, the oppression, the impact, the affliction, and the entanglement of the world? This is the question. Therefore, that brahmin Ajita spoke thus:

"By what, O Lord, is the world enveloped?
By what does it not shine?
What do you say is its smearing?
What is its great fear?"

The Blessed One replied thus:

"Ajita, the world is enveloped by ignorance (avijjā).
Because of stinginess (vevicchā) and negligence (pamāda), it does not shine.
I say craving (jappā) is its smearing.
Suffering (dukkha) is its great fear."

In the phrase "the world is enveloped by ignorance," ignorance (avijjā) means non-knowledge regarding the truth of suffering, non-knowledge regarding the truth of the origin of suffering, non-knowledge regarding the truth of the cessation of suffering, non-knowledge regarding the truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering, non-knowledge regarding the past, non-knowledge regarding the future, non-knowledge regarding both the past and the future, and non-knowledge regarding the phenomena of dependent origination. Such non-knowledge, lack of vision, non-realization, non-awakening, non-enlightenment, non-penetration, non-comprehension, non-immersion, non-examination, non-reflection, the act of non-reflection, lack of wisdom, foolishness, lack of clear comprehension, delusion, intense delusion, complete delusion, ignorance, the flood of ignorance, the yoke of ignorance, the latent tendency of ignorance, the obsession of ignorance, the barrier of ignorance, delusion, and the root of unwholesomeness—this is called ignorance.

"World" (loka) refers to the hell realm, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, the human world, the deva world, the world of aggregates, the world of elements, the world of sense bases, this present world, the world beyond, the brahma world, and the deva world. Because this world of beings is obstructed, enveloped, shrouded from below, closed from above, hidden, and concealed by this ignorance, it is said that "the world is enveloped by ignorance."

"Ajita" is the name by which the Blessed One addresses that brahmin. "Bhagavā" (Blessed One) is a title of reverence. Furthermore, he is called Bhagavā because he has broken (bhagga) lust (rāga); he is called Bhagavā because he has broken hatred (dosa).
26:
He is called Bhagavā because he has destroyed delusion. He is called Bhagavā because he has destroyed conceit. He is called Bhagavā because he has destroyed wrong view. He is called Bhagavā because he has destroyed the thorns of defilements. He is called Bhagavā because he has destroyed defilements. He is called Bhagavā because he has analyzed, specifically analyzed, and extensively analyzed the Treasure of the Dhamma. He is called Bhagavā because he has made an end to the three types of existence. He is called Bhagavā because he possesses a developed body, developed virtue, developed mind, and developed wisdom.

Or else, the Blessed One is called Bhagavā because he frequents remote lodgings such as forests and groves, which are quiet, free from noise, secluded from people, suitable for privacy, and conducive to seclusion.

Or else, the Blessed One is called Bhagavā because he is a partaker of the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal supports for the sick. Or else, the Blessed One is called Bhagavā because he is a partaker of the taste of the meaning, the taste of the Dhamma, the taste of liberation, higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom. Or else, the Blessed One is called Bhagavā because he is a partaker of the four jhānas, the four immeasurables (appamaññā), and the four formless attainments (arūpa-samāpatti). Or else, the Blessed One is called Bhagavā because he is a partaker of the eight liberations (vimokkha), the eight bases of transcendence (abhibhāyatana), and the nine successive attainments (anupubba-samāpatti). Or else, the Blessed One is called Bhagavā because he is a partaker of the ten developments of perception (saññā-bhāvanā), the ten kasiṇa attainments, the concentration of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati-samādhi), and the attainment of foulness (asubha-samāpatti). Or else, the Blessed One is called Bhagavā because he is a partaker of the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), the four right efforts (sammappadhāna), the four bases of psychic power (iddhipāda), the five faculties (indriya), the five powers (bala), the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), and the Noble Eightfold Path. Or else, the Blessed One is called Bhagavā because he is a partaker of the ten powers of a Tathāgata (tathāgatabala), the four kinds of intrepidity (vesārajja), the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), the six supernormal powers (abhiññā), and the six qualities of a Buddha (buddhadhamma).

This name 'Bhagavā' was not given by his mother, nor by his father, nor by his brothers, nor by his sisters, nor by his friends and colleagues, nor by his relatives and kinsmen, nor by recluses and brahmins, nor by deities. This name 'Bhagavā' of the Blessed Buddhas is a designation realized at the end of liberation, together with the attainment of omniscience at the foot of the Bodhi tree. Ajita, thus he is called Bhagavā.

In the phrase 'vevicchā pamādā nappakasati', 'veviccha' refers to the five kinds of stinginess: stinginess regarding lodgings (āvāsa-macchariya), stinginess regarding families (kula-macchariya), stinginess regarding gains (lābha-macchariya), stinginess regarding praise (vaṇṇa-macchariya), and stinginess regarding the Dhamma (dhamma-macchariya). Such stinginess, the act of being stingy, the state of being stingy, the state of desiring various things, the state of being miserly, the state of shrinking the mind, the state of the mind's lack of clarity—this is called stinginess (macchariya). Furthermore, stinginess regarding the aggregates (khandha), stinginess regarding the elements (dhātu), and stinginess regarding the sense bases (āyatana) are also called stinginess. Grasping is also called stinginess. Negligence (pamāda) is spoken of. Whether in bodily misconduct or in verbal misconduct...
27:
Negligence (pamāda) is the letting go of the mind, or the repeated letting go of the mind, in mental misconduct or in the five strands of sensual pleasure; it is the lack of thoroughness, the lack of perseverance, the lack of steadfastness in the development of wholesome states; it is sluggishness, the relinquishing of desire, the relinquishing of the task, the non-cultivation, non-development, non-repetition, non-determination, and non-application of the mind. Such negligence, the act of being negligent, the state of being negligent—this is called negligence. In the phrase 'The world is not illumined because of stinginess (veviccha) and negligence (pamāda),' it means that because of this stinginess and this negligence, the world of beings is not illumined, does not shine, does not glow, does not radiate, is not known, and is not manifest. Thus, 'The world is not illumined because of stinginess and negligence.'

In the phrase 'I say craving (jappā) is the smearing (abhilepana),' what is called 'jappā' is craving (taṇhā). That which is lust (rāga), intense lust (sarāga), compliance (anunaya), non-opposition (anurodha), delight (nandī), delight and lust (nandirāga), intense lust of the mind, desire (icchā), infatuation (mucchā), total immersion (ajjhosāna), greed (gedha), intense greed (paligedha), attachment (saṅga), mire (paṅka), agitation (ejā), deceit (māyā), the progenitress (janikā), the producer (sañjananī), the seamstress (sibbini), the net (jālini), the flowing stream (saritā), the entangler (visattikā), the thread (sutta), the widespread (visaṭa), the stirrer (āyūhanī), the companion (dutiyā), aspiration (paṇidhi), the guide to becoming (bhavanetti), the forest (vana), the underbrush (vanatha), intimacy (santhava), affection (sineha), regard (apekkā), the bond (paṭibandhu), longing (āsā), the act of longing (āsīsanā), the state of longing (āsīsitatta), longing for forms, longing for sounds, longing for smells, longing for tastes, longing for tangibles, longing for gains, longing for greed (visamalobha), attachment (nikanti), desiring (nikāmanā), aspiration (patthanā), yearning (pihanā), strong aspiration (sampatthanā), craving for sensual pleasures (kāma-taṇhā), craving for craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for smells, craving for tastes, craving for tangibles, craving for mental objects, the flood (ogha), the yoke (yoga), the knot (gantha), clinging (upādāna), the obstruction (āvaraṇa), the hindrance (nīvaraṇa), the covering (chadana), the bond (bandhana), the defilement (upakkilesa), the underlying tendency (anusaya), the obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna), the creeper (latā), various desires (veviccha), the root of suffering (dukkhamūla), the cause of suffering (dukkhanidāna), the source of suffering (dukkhappabhava), the snare of Māra (mārapāsa), the fish-hook of Māra (mārabalisa), the bait of Māra (mārāmisa), the domain of Māra (māravisaya), the dwelling of Māra (māranivāsa), the pasturage of Māra (māragocara), the bond of Māra (mārabandhana), the river of craving, the net of craving, the leash of craving (taṇhāgaddula), the ocean of craving, covetousness (abhijjhā), greed (lobha), the unwholesome root—this is called craving (jappā). By this craving, which is the smearing, the attachment, the binding, and the defiling of the world, the world of beings is smeared, thoroughly smeared, closely smeared, defiled, thoroughly defiled, anointed, associated, attached, stuck by way of being placed on an object, and constantly bound to the object—thus I say, I declare, I teach, I establish, I reveal, I analyze, I clarify, and I manifest. Therefore, it is said: 'I say craving is the smearing.'
28:
In the phrase 'Suffering is its great peril (dukkhamassa mahabbhayaṃ)': Suffering (dukkha) means the suffering of birth, the suffering of aging, the suffering of sickness, the suffering of death, the suffering of sorrow, lamentation, physical pain, grief, and despair. It is the suffering experienced in hell, the suffering in the animal realm, the suffering in the realm of hungry ghosts (petas), the suffering in the human realm, the suffering rooted in descending into the womb, the suffering rooted in staying in the womb, the suffering rooted in emerging from the womb, the suffering of a newborn such as being bathed, the suffering of a newborn caused by the efforts of others, the suffering caused by one's own actions, the suffering of formations (saṅkhāra-dukkha), and the suffering of change (vipariṇāma-dukkha). It includes eye disease, ear disease, nose disease, tongue disease, body disease, head disease, ear-lobe disease, mouth disease, tooth disease, cough, asthma, catarrh, burning sensation, fever, stomach ache, fainting, dysentery, piercing pain, diarrhea, leprosy, boils, eczema, consumption, epilepsy, ringworm, itch, scabies, rashes, shingles, jaundice, diabetes, shoulder pain, abscesses, and fistula. It includes illnesses arising from bile, illnesses arising from phlegm, illnesses arising from wind, illnesses arising from the conflict of the three humors, illnesses produced by change of season, illnesses produced by improper care, illnesses produced by external exertion, and illnesses produced by the result of kamma. It includes suffering from cold, heat, hunger, thirst, defecation, urination, and the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things. It includes the suffering of a mother's death, a father's death, a brother's death, a sister's death, a son's death, a daughter's death, the suffering of the loss of relatives, the suffering of the onset of disease, the suffering of the loss of wealth, the suffering of the failure of virtue, and the suffering of the failure of right view. For whatever states their initial arising is manifest, their cessation through destruction is also manifest. There is result (vipāka) dependent on kamma, and kamma dependent on result; there is form (rūpa) dependent on name (nāma), and name dependent on form. It is followed by birth, pursued by aging, overwhelmed by sickness, struck down by death. It is established in suffering, without protection, without shelter, without refuge, and unable to provide refuge—this is called suffering. This suffering is the fear of the world, the great fear, the oppression, the affliction, the calamity, and the misfortune. Thus, 'Suffering is its great peril.' Therefore, the Blessed One said:

'The world is shrouded by ignorance, [O Ajita,] it is not illumined because of stinginess and negligence. I say craving is its smearing, and suffering is its great peril.'
29:
The Venerable Ajita addressed [the Buddha] thus:
"The streams flow in all sense bases (āyatana). What is the dharma that obstructs and hinders those streams? Please tell me the dharma that restrains and obstructs those streams; by what dharma are those streams shut off?"

In the phrase "The streams flow in all sense bases," 'streams' (sota) refers to the stream of craving (taṇhā), the stream of views (diṭṭhi), the stream of defilements (kilesa), the stream of misconduct (duccarita), and the stream of ignorance (avijjā). "In all sense bases" means in all the [six] sense bases. "Flow" means they flow, they repeatedly arise and flow, they run, they proceed. They flow and repeatedly arise and flow from the eye towards forms. They flow from the ear towards sounds... [pe]... from the nose towards smells, from the tongue towards tastes, from the body towards tangibles, and from the mind towards mental objects; they flow, repeatedly arise and flow, run, and proceed. Craving for forms flows and repeatedly arises and flows from the eye. Craving for sounds flows from the ear, craving for smells from the nose, craving for tastes from the tongue, craving for tangibles from the body, and craving for mental objects flows and repeatedly arises and flows from the mind. This is the meaning of the phrase "The streams flow in all sense bases."

In the phrase "The long-lived Ajita [addressed thus]," the word "Iccā" is a word-connection (padasandhi). It is a word that follows the preceding word. This is the meaning of the phrase "The long-lived Ajita [addressed thus]."

In the phrase "What is the dharma that obstructs and hinders those streams?" it is a question asking: what is the dharma that obstructs, hinders, restrains, preserves, and guards the streams? This is the meaning of the phrase "What is the dharma that obstructs and hinders those streams?"

In the phrase "Please tell me the dharma that restrains and obstructs those streams," it means: please tell, inform, teach, prescribe, establish, reveal, analyze, clarify, and manifest the dharma that obstructs, hinders, restrains, preserves, and guards the streams. This is the meaning of the phrase "Please tell me the dharma that restrains and obstructs those streams."

In the phrase "By what dharma are those streams shut off?" it is a question asking: by what dharma are the streams shut off, by what dharma are those streams cut off so that they no longer flow, overflow, run, or proceed? This is the meaning of the phrase "By what dharma are those streams shut off?"

Therefore, that Brahmin Ajita addressed [the Buddha] thus:
"The streams flow in all sense bases,
What is the restraint for the streams?
Tell me the restraint for the streams; by what are the streams shut off?"
30:
Whatever streams [of craving, etc.] flow in the world, [Ajita, the Blessed One said,] mindfulness is the restraint for those streams. I tell you the restraint for those streams; they are shut off by wisdom.

Regarding "Whatever streams there are in the world": those streams which have been praised, specifically praised, told, taught, prescribed, established, revealed, analyzed, clarified, and manifested by me—namely, the stream of craving, the stream of views, the stream of defilements, the stream of misconduct, and the stream of ignorance. "In the world" means in the world of misery (apāya-loka), the human world, the deva world, the world of aggregates (khandha-loka), the world of elements (dhātu-loka), and the world of sense bases (āyatana-loka). Thus, it is said, "Whatever streams there are in the world." "Ajita" is the name by which the Blessed One addressed that Brahmin.

Regarding "Mindfulness is their restraint": 'Mindfulness' (sati) refers to that which is mindfulness, recollection, constant mindfulness, the state of remembering, bearing in mind, non-superficiality, non-forgetfulness, the faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, right mindfulness, the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, and the one-way path (ekāyana-magga). This is called mindfulness. 'Restraint' (nivāraṇa) means obstructing, hindering, restraining, preserving, and guarding. Thus, it is said, "Mindfulness is their restraint."

Regarding "I tell you the restraint for the streams": I tell, I inform... [pe]... I clarify, and I manifest the obstruction, hindrance, restraint, preservation, and guarding of the streams. Thus, it is said, "I tell you the restraint for the streams."

Regarding "They are shut off by wisdom": 'Wisdom' (paññā) refers to that which is wisdom, understanding... [pe]... non-delusion, investigation of states (dhamma-vicaya), and right view (sammā-diṭṭhi). "They are shut off by wisdom" means that by wisdom those streams are shut off, cut off, they do not arise, they do not arise even up to the peak of existence, they do not flow, and they do not repeatedly flow. For one who knows and sees that "All conditioned things are impermanent," those streams are shut off by wisdom, cut off, they do not arise, they do not arise even up to the peak of existence, they do not flow, and they do not repeatedly flow. For one who knows and sees that "All conditioned things are suffering," those streams are shut off by wisdom, cut off, they do not arise, they do not arise even up to the peak of existence, they do not flow, and they do not repeatedly flow. For one who knows and sees that "All things are non-self (anatta)," those streams are shut off by wisdom, cut off, they do not arise, they do not arise even up to the peak of existence, they do not flow, and they do not repeatedly flow. For one who knows and sees that "Conditioned by ignorance, formations arise," those streams are shut off by wisdom...
31: (Those streams) are cut off; they do not arise; they do not arise up to the peak of existence; they do not flow; they do not flow repeatedly. "With formations as condition, consciousness arises" ... "With consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises" ... "With name-and-form as condition, the six bases arise" ... "With the six bases as condition, contact arises" ... "With contact as condition, feeling arises" ... "With feeling as condition, craving arises" ... "With craving as condition, clinging arises" ... "With clinging as condition, existence arises" ... "With existence as condition, birth arises" ... "With birth as condition, aging and death arise." For one who knows and sees thus, these streams are closed by wisdom, they are cut off, they do not arise, they do not arise up to the peak of existence, they do not flow, they do not flow repeatedly. "With the cessation of ignorance, formations cease" ... "With the cessation of formations, consciousness ceases" ... "With the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases" ... "With the cessation of name-and-form, the six bases cease" ... "With the cessation of the six bases, contact ceases" ... "With the cessation of contact, feeling ceases" ... "With the cessation of feeling, craving ceases" ... "With the cessation of craving, clinging ceases" ... "With the cessation of clinging, existence ceases" ... "With the cessation of existence, birth ceases" ... "With the cessation of birth, aging and death cease." For one who knows and sees thus, these streams are closed by wisdom, they are cut off, they do not arise, they do not arise up to the stage of Gotrabhū, they do not flow, they do not flow repeatedly. "This is the Noble Truth of Suffering" ... "This is the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering" ... "This is the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering" ... "This is the practice leading to Nibbāna, the cessation of suffering." For one who knows and sees thus, these streams are closed by wisdom, they are cut off, they do not arise, they do not arise up to the stage of Gotrabhū, they do not flow, they do not flow repeatedly. "These states are the taints (āsavas)" ... "This is the cause of the taints" ... "This is Nibbāna, the cessation of the taints" ... "This is the practice leading to Nibbāna, the cessation of the taints." For one who knows and sees thus, these streams are closed by wisdom, they are cut off, they do not arise, they do not arise up to the stage of Gotrabhū, they do not flow, they do not flow repeatedly. "These states should be known with higher knowledge" ... "These states should be fully understood" ... "These states should be abandoned" ... "These states should be developed" ... "These states should be realized." For one who knows and sees thus, these streams are closed by wisdom, they are cut off, they do not arise, they do not arise up to the stage of Gotrabhū, they do not flow, they do not flow repeatedly. For one who knows and sees the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the six bases of contact... For one who knows and sees the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the five aggregates of clinging... For one who knows and sees the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the four great elements... For one who knows and sees that "Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease," these streams are closed by wisdom, they are cut off, they do not arise, they do not...
32: It is said that those streams do not flow, do not spread, and do not arise repeatedly. Those streams are closed by wisdom. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Whatever streams there are in the world, O Ajita," said the Blessed One, "mindfulness is their restraint. I say the restraint of the streams; they are closed by wisdom." "Wisdom and mindfulness, and name-and-form, dear sir; tell me this when asked: where does this cease completely?" In the phrase "Wisdom and mindfulness": Wisdom means that which is understanding, knowing in a particular way, searching, discrimination, investigation of states, marking, closely marking, repeatedly marking, sagacity, proficiency, skill, analysis, reflection, examination, breadth, prudence, guidance, insight, clear comprehension, the goad, wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the sword of wisdom, the palace of wisdom, the light of wisdom, the radiance of wisdom, the lamp of wisdom, the treasure of wisdom, non-delusion, investigation of states, right view. Mindfulness means that which is mindfulness, recollection... (p) ... right mindfulness. Thus, "Wisdom and mindfulness," the venerable Ajita asked. In the phrase "and name-and-form, dear sir": Name means the four immaterial aggregates. Form means the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements. "Dear sir" (mārisa) is a term of endearment, a term of weight, a term of respect and reverence. Thus, "and name-and-form, dear sir," is what is meant. In the phrase "tell me this when asked": "This me" (etaṃ me) means that which I ask, request, urge, and clarify. "Asked" (puṭṭho) means the Blessed One who is asked, requested, urged, and clarified. "Tell" (pabrūhi) means speak, tell, teach, prescribe, establish, open, analyze, make clear, and manifest. In the phrase "where does this cease": it means where does this cease, where is it appeased, where does it disappear, where is it completely stilled. Therefore, that brahmin said this.
33:
The Venerable Ajita said: "Venerable Sir, where do wisdom, mindfulness, and name-and-form cease? Please tell me, who asks this."

"Ajita, I shall tell you the answer to the question you asked. In that (Nibbāna) where name and form cease without remainder. Through the cessation of consciousness, these (wisdom, mindfulness, name-and-form) cease in this (Nibbāna)."

"Yametaṃ pañhaṃ apucchi" means: you ask, request, urge, and clarify this question regarding wisdom, mindfulness, and name-and-form.

In the phrase "Ajita taṃ vadāmi te," the Blessed One addresses that young brahmin by the name "Ajita." "Taṃ" refers to wisdom, mindfulness, and name-and-form. "Vadāmi" means I speak, tell, teach, prescribe, establish, open, analyze, clarify, and reveal.

In the phrase "Yattha nāmañca rūpañca asesaṃ uparujjhati," "Nāma" (name) refers to the four immaterial aggregates. "Rūpa" (form) refers to the four great elements and the derived form (upādāya-rūpa) based on the four great elements. "Asesaṃ" means entirely, in every way, without remainder, completely; it is a word for totality. "Uparujjhati" means it ceases, is extinguished, comes to an end, and is further stilled.

In the phrase "Viññāṇassa nirodhena etthetaṃ uparujjhati," by abandoning the volitional consciousness (abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa) through the knowledge of the path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga-ñāṇa), leaving aside seven births, the name and form that would arise in the beginningless saṃsāra cease, are extinguished, come to an end, and are further stilled in this (path-knowledge). By abandoning the volitional consciousness through the knowledge of the path of Once-returning (sakadāgāmi-magga-ñāṇa), leaving aside two births, the name and form that would arise in five births cease, are extinguished, come to an end, and are further stilled in this (path-knowledge). By abandoning the volitional consciousness through the knowledge of the path of Non-returning (anāgāmi-magga-ñāṇa), leaving aside one birth, the name and form that would arise in the fine-material realm or the immaterial realm cease, are extinguished, come to an end, and are further stilled in this (path-knowledge). By abandoning the volitional consciousness through the knowledge of the path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga-ñāṇa), the name and form that would arise cease, are extinguished, come to an end...
34:
...and are further stilled. Through the cessation of the final consciousness of an Arahant who attains Parinibbāna in the Nibbāna element without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu), wisdom, mindfulness, name, and form cease, are extinguished, come to an end, and are further stilled in this (attainment of Parinibbāna). Through the cessation of consciousness, this (name-and-form) ceases in this (attainment of Parinibbāna). Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"Ajita, I shall tell you the answer to the question you asked,
In that (Nibbāna) where name and form cease without remainder,
Through the cessation of consciousness, these (name-and-form) cease in this (Nibbāna)."

There are those who are Saṅkhātadhamma (Arahants) and many who are Sekha (Learners) in this world. O Wise One, being asked, please tell me of their conduct and behavior.

'Ye ca saṅkhātadhammāse' means: Arahants whose taints are destroyed are called Saṅkhātadhamma. Why are Arahants whose taints are destroyed called Saṅkhātadhamma? Those Arahants have known the Dhamma, weighed the Dhamma, investigated the Dhamma, clarified the Dhamma, and developed the Dhamma. They have known, weighed, investigated, clarified, and developed the Dhamma that "All formations are impermanent." They have known the Dhamma that "All formations are suffering." ...pe... They have known the Dhamma that "All phenomena are non-self." ... They have known the Dhamma that "Formations arise because of ignorance." ... They have known, weighed, investigated, clarified, and developed the Dhamma that "Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease."

Alternatively, for those Arahants, the five aggregates are known, the eighteen elements are known, the twelve sense bases are known, the five destinations are known, the rebirths (upapatti) are known, the relinking (paṭisandhi) is known, the nine existences are known, the cycle of birth (saṃsāra) is known, and the three rounds (vaṭṭa) are known. Alternatively, those Arahants stand at the end of the aggregates, the end of the elements, the end of the sense bases, the end of the destinations, the end of rebirth, the end of relinking, the end of existence, the end of the cycle of birth, the end of the rounds; they stand in their final existence, in their final physical form, and are Arahants bearing their final body.

This body of those Arahants is the last; this occurrence of the body is the last;
For those Arahants, there is no cycle of birth and death, nor is there further existence.

For that reason, Arahants whose taints are destroyed are called Saṅkhātadhamma. In the phrase "Ye ca saṅkhātadhammāse, ye ca sekhā puthū idha" — why are Learners called Sekha?
35:
Why are they called trainees (sekhas)? They are called trainees because they are training. In what do they train? They train in higher virtue (adhisīla), they train in higher mind (adhicitta), and they train in higher wisdom (adhipaññā).

What is the training in higher virtue? Here, a monk is virtuous, dwelling restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults; having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. The aggregate of virtue is a great aggregate of virtue; it is the foundation, the beginning, the footing, restraint, protection, the gateway, and the precursor to the attainment of wholesome states—this is the training in higher virtue.

What is the training in higher mind? Here, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures... [pe] ...enters and dwells in the first jhāna, the second jhāna, the third jhāna, and the fourth jhāna—this is the training in higher mind.

What is the training in higher wisdom? Here, a monk is wise, possessed of wisdom regarding rise and fall, which is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. He understands as it really is: 'This is suffering'; he understands as it really is: 'This is the origin of suffering'... [pe] ...'This is the cessation of suffering'; 'This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.' He understands as it really is: 'These are the taints (āsavas)'... [pe] ...'This is the origin of the taints'; 'This is the cessation of the taints'; 'This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints.' This is the training in higher wisdom.

Reflecting upon these three trainings, they train; knowing, they train; seeing, they train; resolving the mind, they train; being convinced through faith, they train; exerting energy, they train; establishing mindfulness, they train; concentrating the mind, they train; understanding with wisdom, they train; knowing what should be known through direct knowledge, they train; fully understanding what should be fully understood, they train; abandoning what should be abandoned, they train; developing what should be developed, they train; realizing what should be realized, they train; they practice repeatedly, they practice well, they practice having undertaken them. For that reason, they are called trainees (sekhas).

'Puthu' means many. These trainees are: those who are Stream-enterers and those practicing for the realization of the fruit of Stream-entry; Once-returners and those practicing for the realization of the fruit of Once-returning; Non-returners and those practicing for the realization of the fruit of Non-returning; Arahants and those practicing for the realization of the fruit of Arahantship. 'Here' (idha) means: in this view, in this patience, in this preference, in this taking up, in this Dhamma, in this Vinaya, in this Dhamma-Vinaya, in this word of the Buddha, in this holy life, in this teaching of the Teacher, in this personality, in this world of humans—whichever many trainees are here in this teaching.
36:
Venerable Sir, you who are wise, please tell me the conduct of those who have understood the Dhamma and of the trainees, as I have asked. 'You' means you who are 'nipaka'—wise, learned, intelligent, sagacious, knowledgeable, and discerning. 'Of those who have understood the Dhamma and of the trainees' refers to the conduct (iriyaṃ), behavior, way of life, occurrence, practice, resort, dwelling, and path of the Arahants and the trainees. 'Asked' (puṭṭho) means questioned, requested, invited, and entreated. 'Tell' (pabrūhi) means speak, inform, teach, point out, establish, reveal, analyze, clarify, and manifest. 'Mārisā' is a term of endearment, a term of respect, and a term of reverence and honor. Because of the meaning 'Please tell me the conduct of those who have understood the Dhamma and of the trainees, as I have asked,' that brahmin spoke thus:

'Those who have understood the Dhamma, and the many trainees here; tell me their conduct, O wise one, when asked, O dear sir.'

One should not be greedy for sensual pleasures; one should be undisturbed in mind; skilled in all things, a mindful monk should wander.

In the phrase 'One should not be greedy for sensual pleasures' (kāmesu nābhigijjhေyya), sensual pleasures (kāma) are twofold in brief: objective sensuality (vatthukāma) and defilement sensuality (kilesakāma).

What are objective sensualities? Pleasing sights, pleasing sounds, pleasing smells, pleasing tastes, pleasing touches; rugs, clothing, female and male slaves, goats and sheep, fowl and pigs, elephants, cattle, horses and mares, fields, land, silver, gold, villages, towns, royal capitals, kingdoms, countries, treasuries, and storehouses—whatever object is capable of causing attachment is called objective sensuality.

Furthermore, past sensual pleasures, future sensual pleasures, present sensual pleasures; internal, external, and internal-external sensual pleasures; inferior, middling, and superior sensual pleasures; those of the states of deprivation, those of the human world, and those of the celestial worlds; those that are present, those that are created, and those created by others; those that are possessed and those not possessed; those that are cherished as 'mine' and those not cherished as 'mine'; all states of the sense sphere, all states of the fine-material sphere, all states of the immaterial sphere—in the sense of being the basis for craving, the object of craving, in the sense of being desirable, attachable, intoxicating, and delightful—these are called sensual pleasures. These are called objective sensualities.

What are defilement sensualities? Desire is sensuality, lust is sensuality, desire-and-lust is sensuality, thought is sensuality, lust is sensuality, thought-and-lust is sensuality; whatever sensual desire, sensual lust, sensual delight, and sensual craving there is for sensual pleasures.
37: Attachment to sensuality 'kāmasineha', thirst for sensuality 'kāmapipāsā', fever of sensuality 'kāmapariḷāha', greed for sensuality 'kāmagedha', infatuation with sensuality 'kāmamucchā', obsession with sensuality 'kāmajjhosāna', the flood of sensuality 'kāmogha', the yoke of sensuality 'kāmayoga', the clinging to sensuality 'kāmupādāna', and the hindrance of sensual desire 'kāmacchandanīvaraṇa' which obstructs the mind. ## I have seen your root, O Lust; you are born from thought. I will not think of you; thus, O Lust, you will not be. These are called defilement-lusts (kilesakāma). Greed (gedha) is called craving (taṇhā). Whatever lust, intense lust ... covetousness 'abhijjhā', greed for objects 'lobha'—these are the unwholesome roots. 'One should not be greedy for sensual pleasures' means one should not be greedy for objective-lusts (vatthukāma) through defilement-lust (kilesakāma), should not be repeatedly attached, should be one who is not greedy, not infatuated, not heedless, and not transgressing. Having abandoned the nature of greed, being free from greed, having relinquished greed, having vomited greed, being released from greed, having discarded greed, having renounced greed, being free from passion, being without passion, having relinquished passion, having vomited passion, being released from passion, having discarded passion, having renounced passion, being without thirst, being quenched, being cooled, experiencing happiness, one should dwell with a mind that has become noble. This is the meaning of 'one should not be greedy for sensual pleasures'. In the phrase 'one should be undisturbed in mind', 'mind' (mana) refers to that which is the diverse mind, the mind that cognizes objects, the mind that compares, the heart, the pure mind, the sense base of mind, the faculty of mind, consciousness, the aggregate of consciousness, and the mind-consciousness element arising accordingly. Because of bodily misconduct, the mind is disturbed, agitated, stirred, struck, shaken, violently moved, and unpeaceful. Because of verbal misconduct ... because of mental misconduct, because of lust, hatred, delusion, anger (kodha), malice (upanāha), hypocrisy (makkha), spite (paḷāsa), envy (issā), stinginess (macchariya), deceit (māyā), treachery (sāṭheyya), stubbornness (thambha), impetuosity (sārambha), pride (māna), arrogance (atimāna), intoxication (mada), negligence (pamāda), all defilements, all misconduct, all fevers, all distresses, all torments, and all unwholesome volitional formations, the mind is disturbed, agitated, stirred, struck, shaken, violently moved, and unpeaceful. 'One should be undisturbed in mind' means one should be undisturbed in mind—not agitated, not stirred, not struck, not shaken, not violently moved, and peaceful. One should abandon, fully abandon, dispel, eliminate, and bring to non-existence the defilements that cause disturbance. One should be one who stays far away from, especially avoids, repeatedly avoids, escapes from, relinquishes, and is well-released from the defilements that cause disturbance. One should dwell with a mind that is boundless. This is the meaning of 'one should be undisturbed in mind'.
38: 'Skilled in all things' means being skilled in all things as 'all conditioned things are impermanent', being skilled in all things as 'all conditioned things are suffering', being skilled in all things as 'all things are non-self', being skilled in all things as 'conditioned by ignorance, volitional formations arise' ... being skilled in all things as 'whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease'. In this way, too, one is skilled in all things. Alternatively, one is skilled in all things by way of impermanence, by way of suffering ... by way of disease, by way of a boil, by way of a thorn, by way of a calamity, by way of an affliction, by way of an alien, by way of disintegration, by way of a plague, by way of a disaster, by way of a terror, by way of an obstacle, by way of instability, by way of perishability, by way of being non-permanent, by way of being without protection, by way of being no shelter, by way of being no refuge, by way of being no resort for those who seek refuge, by way of being empty, by way of being vain, by way of being void of a master, by way of being non-self, by way of being a danger, by way of being subject to change, by way of being coreless, by way of being the root of calamity, by way of being a killer, by way of being a destroyer, by way of being the object of taints, by way of being conditioned, by way of being the bait of Māra, by way of being subject to birth, by way of being subject to aging, by way of being subject to sickness, by way of being subject to death, by way of being subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, by way of being the basis for defilements that corrupt, by way of arising from a cause, by way of being subject to cessation, by way of being a cause for gratification, by way of being a danger, and by way of being the escape. In this way, too, one is skilled in all things. Alternatively, one is skilled in the aggregates, skilled in the elements, skilled in the sense bases, skilled in dependent origination, skilled in the foundations of mindfulness, skilled in the right efforts, skilled in the bases of power, skilled in the faculties, skilled in the powers, skilled in the factors of enlightenment, skilled in the path, skilled in the fruits, and skilled in Nibbāna. In this way, too, one is skilled in all things. Alternatively, 'all things' refers to the twelve sense bases—eye and forms, ear and sounds, nose and odors, tongue and tastes, body and tangibles, mind and mental objects. When, in regard to internal and external sense bases, sensual desire (chandarāga) is abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, and made such that it is not subject to future arising—by this much of abandoning, one is called 'skilled in all things'. The monk should wander being mindful. 'Being mindful' means being mindful through four reasons: being mindful while developing the foundation of mindfulness of contemplating the body in the body, in feelings...
39:
He is mindful by developing the foundation of mindfulness of feelings, dwelling contemplating feelings in feelings; he is mindful by developing the foundation of mindfulness of the mind, dwelling contemplating the mind in the mind; he is mindful by developing the foundation of mindfulness of mental objects, dwelling contemplating mental objects in mental objects.

He is also mindful for four other reasons: he is mindful because of avoiding those who lack mindfulness; he is mindful because of performing those things that should be done with mindfulness; he is mindful because of having destroyed those things that are obstacles to mindfulness; he is mindful because of not forgetting those things that are the causes of mindfulness.

He is also mindful for four other reasons: he is mindful because of being endowed with mindfulness; he is mindful because of having attained mastery in mindfulness; he is mindful because of being endowed with proficiency in mindfulness; he is mindful because of not falling away from mindfulness.

He is also mindful for four other reasons: he is mindful because of being endowed with mindfulness; he is mindful because of being peaceful; he is mindful because of the subsiding of defilements; he is mindful because of being endowed with the peaceful Dhamma.
