He is mindful through the repeated recollection of the Buddha (buddhānussati); he is mindful through the repeated recollection of the Dhamma (dhammānussati); he is mindful through the repeated recollection of the Saṅgha (saṅghānussati); he is mindful through the repeated recollection of virtue (sīlānussati); he is mindful through the repeated recollection of generosity (cāgānussati); he is mindful through the repeated recollection of the deities (devatānussati); he is mindful through the repeated recollection of breathing (ānāpānassati); he is mindful through the repeated recollection of death (maraṇassati); he is mindful through the repeated recollection of mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati); he is mindful through the repeated recollection of peace (upasamānussati). That which is mindfulness, recollection... (and so on) right mindfulness, the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, the one-way path leading to Nibbāna—this Dhamma is called mindfulness. One who is endowed with, fully endowed with, approached by, fully approached by, possessed of, fully possessed of, and accompanied by this mindfulness is called mindful (sato).

A bhikkhu is so called because he has destroyed seven things: identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) is destroyed, doubt (vicikicchā) is destroyed, adherence to rites and rituals (sīlabbataparāmāsa) is destroyed, lust (rāga) is destroyed, hatred (dosa) is destroyed, delusion (moha) is destroyed, and conceit (māna) is destroyed. Evil unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and leading to future birth, aging, and death are destroyed.

[The Blessed One said to Sabhiya:]
"Sabhiya, he who has reached Parinibbāna by the path he himself developed, who has crossed over doubt, who has abandoned both non-existence and existence, who has lived the life, and for whom renewed existence is exhausted—he is a bhikkhu."
40:
A monk should live being mindful. He should walk mindfully, stand mindfully, sit mindfully, lie down mindfully, move forward mindfully, move backward mindfully, look straight ahead mindfully, look aside mindfully, bend his limbs mindfully, stretch them mindfully, and carry his outer robe, bowl, and robes mindfully; he should practice, dwell, maintain his postures, follow the training, protect, sustain, and maintain his life mindfully—thus, a monk should live being mindful. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“One should not be intensely greedy for sensual pleasures; the mind should be undisturbed. Skilled in all Dhammas, a monk should live being mindful.”

At the end of the verse, for the many thousands of beings who shared the same desire, the same effort, the same intention, and the same disposition as the young man Ajita, the dustless and stainless Dhamma-eye arose: “Whatever is subject to origination is all subject to cessation.” The mind of that young man Ajita was also liberated from the taints (āsavas) without clinging. Simultaneously with the attainment of Arahantship, the antelope skin, the matted hair, the bark garment, the triple staff, the water pot, and the hair and beard disappeared. Shaven-headed, wearing the dyed cloth, carrying the outer robe, bowl, and robes, and having the practice directed towards the goal of Nibbāna, he sat with hands joined in reverence, paying homage to the Blessed One, saying: “Venerable sir, the Blessed One is my teacher; I am the disciple.”

## 1. The Exposition of the Question of the Young Man Ajita is Finished.

## 2. The Exposition of the Question of the Young Man Tissa Metteyya

The Venerable Tissa Metteyya asked this:
“Who in this world is well-contented? For whom do no agitations (of craving) exist? Who, having known the two extremes through wisdom, is not smeared in the middle by wisdom? Whom do you call a Great Man (Mahāpurisa)? Who in this world has transcended the seamstress (craving)?”

“Who in this world is well-contented?” means who in this world is pleased, well-contented, joyful, and has fulfilled intentions?
41:
In the phrase “Iccāyasmā Tissametteyyo,” the word “Iccā” is a word-junction, a word-combination, a word-completion, a combination of letters, a smoothness of consonants, and a word-sequence. “Āyasmā” is a term of endearment, a term of respect, and a designation accompanied by reverence and deference. “Tissa” is the name, designation, appellation, concept, conventional term, name, naming, name-giving, expression, consonant, and utterance of that brahmin. “Metteyya” is the clan, designation, appellation, concept, and conventional term of that brahmin. Thus, it is said: “Iccāyasmā Tissametteyyo.”

“Kassa no santi iñjitā” refers to the agitation of craving, the agitation of views, the agitation of conceit, the agitation of defilements, and the agitation of sensuality. For whom do these agitations not exist, are not found, are not obtained, are abandoned, are completely cut off, are calmed, are subsided, are incapable of arising, and are burnt by the fire of knowledge? Thus, it is said: “Kassa no santi iñjitā.”

“Ko ubhantamabhiññāya” means: who, having fully known both ends, having known, weighed, investigated, clarified, and made them manifest? Thus, it is said: “Ko ubhantamabhiññāya.”

“Majjhe mantā na lippati” means: in the middle (practice), one is not smeared by wisdom, is not attached, is especially not attached, has gone out, has escaped, is especially released, and dwells with a mind that is especially dissociated and free from boundaries. Thus, it is said: “Majjhe mantā na lippati.”

In the phrase “Kaṃ brūsi mahāpuriso,” “mahāpuriso” means the foremost man, the praised man, the especially praised man, the leader, the especially noble man, the chief man, and the most excellent man. “Kaṃ brūsi” means: whom do you speak of, whom do you tell of, whom do you consider, whom do you recite, whom do you see, and whom do you name? Thus, it is said: “Kaṃ brūsi mahāpuriso.”

“Ko idha sibbinimaccagā” means: who here in this world of beings has transcended the “seamstress” (craving), has gone beyond, has well transcended, and has especially transcended? Thus, it is said: “Ko idha sibbinimaccagā.” Therefore, that brahmin said:

“Who in this world is well-contented? [Thus said the Venerable Tissa Metteyya]
For whom do agitations not exist?
Who, having fully known both ends by wisdom, is not smeared in the middle?
Whom do you speak of as a Great Man? Who here has transcended the seamstress?”
42:
“One who leads the holy life among sensual pleasures, O Metteyya (thus said the Blessed One), who is always mindful and free from craving, a monk who is cooled after reflecting—for him, agitations do not exist.”

“Kāmesu brahmacariyavā” means: Sensual pleasures (kāma) are briefly of two kinds—objective sensuality (vatthu-kāma) and subjective sensuality (kilesa-kāma). ... These are called objective sensuality. ... These are called subjective sensuality. “Brahmacariya” (the holy life) refers to abstinence, refraining, further refraining, avoidance, non-action, non-doing, non-transgression, and not crossing the boundary of the unwholesome. Alternatively, in the direct sense, the Noble Eightfold Path is called the holy life, namely: Right View, Right Intention, Right Speech, Right Action, Right Livelihood, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, and Right Concentration. One who is endowed with this Noble Eightfold Path is called “brahmacariyavā.” Just as one is called “dhanavā” by having wealth, “bhogavā” by having possessions, “yasavā” by having fame, “sippavā” by having skills, “sīlavā” by having virtue, “vīriyavā” by having energy, “panyavā” by having wisdom, and “vijjavā” by having knowledge—in the same way, one who is endowed with this Noble Eightfold Path is called “brahmacariyavā.” This is the meaning of the phrase “Kāmesu brahmacariyavā.”

“Metteyyāti bhagavā” means: The Blessed One addresses that brahmin by his clan name, Metteyya. “Bhagavā” is a term of respect. It is a designation based on realization. This is the meaning of the phrase “Metteyyāti bhagavā.”

“Vītatāṇha sadā sato” means: Craving (taṇhā) ranges from craving for forms to craving for mental objects. For whom this craving is abandoned, cut off at the root, calmed, subsided, made incapable of arising, and burnt by the fire of knowledge, he is called “vītatāṇha” (free from craving), one who has relinquished craving, vomited it, released it, abandoned it, and given it up; one who is free from lust, has relinquished lust, vomited it, released it, abandoned it, and given it up; one who is free from hunger, cooled, tranquil, experiencing happiness, and dwelling with a mind that has become sublime. “Sadā” means always, at all times, at every moment, perpetually, constantly, continuously, without interruption, as a single whole, unmixed, like a wave, incessantly, connectedly, and in contact; occurring before meals, after meals, in the first watch, the middle watch, the last watch, the waning moon, the waxing moon, the rainy season, the winter, the summer, the first stage of life, the middle stage of life, and the last stage of life. “Sato” means being mindful through four reasons: being mindful while developing the mindfulness of the body (kāyānupassanā satipaṭṭhāna) in the body; in feelings...
43: (Mindfulness is maintained) continuously and without interruption like the waves of the sea, during the time before the meal, the time after the meal, the first watch, the middle watch, the last watch, the waning moon, the waxing moon, the rainy season, the winter season, the summer season, the first stage of life, the middle stage of life, and the last stage of life. "One who is mindful" refers to one who is mindful through four reasons: one who is mindful by developing the foundation of mindfulness of contemplation of the body in the body, one who is mindful by developing the foundation of mindfulness of contemplation of feelings in feelings, one who is mindful by developing the foundation of mindfulness of contemplation of the mind in the mind, one who is mindful by developing the foundation of mindfulness of contemplation of phenomena in phenomena... [pe]... such a person is called "one who is mindful." Being free from craving, he is always mindful. ## "The bhikkhu who is quenched through reflection" In the phrase "the bhikkhu who is quenched through reflection," "saṅkhā" refers to knowledge. It is that wisdom, knowing, investigation, scrutiny... [pe]... non-delusion, investigation of states, right view. "Having reflected" (saṅkhāya) means having reflected, known, weighed, investigated, developed, and made manifest. It means having reflected, known, weighed, investigated, developed, and made manifest that "all conditioned things are impermanent," that "all conditioned things are suffering," ... [pe] ... that "all phenomena are non-self," that "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be," that "whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease." Or otherwise, it means having reflected, known, weighed, investigated, developed, and made manifest as impermanent... [pe]... as suffering, as a disease, as a boil, as a dart... [pe]... as an escape. "Quenched" (nibbuto) means quenched because of the extinguishing of greed, quenched because of the extinguishing of hatred, quenched because of the extinguishing of delusion, anger, enmity, disparaging, malice, envy, stinginess, deceit, craftiness, obstinacy, impetuosity, conceit, arrogance, intoxication, negligence, all defilements, all misconduct, all distress, all internal fevers, all burning, and all unwholesome formations. "Bhikkhu" means a bhikkhu because of having broken the seven things [such as identity view]... [pe]... he who has lived the holy life and whose rebirth is exhausted is a bhikkhu. Thus, he is a bhikkhu who is quenched through reflection. ## "For him, there are no stirrings" In the phrase "for him, there are no stirrings," "for him" refers to the Arahant, the one whose taints are destroyed. "Stirrings" (iñjitā) refers to stirrings of craving, stirrings of views, stirrings of conceit, stirrings of defilements, and stirrings of sensuality. For that (Arahant, these stirrings):
44: For that bhikkhu, the stirrings such as stirrings due to views, stirrings due to conceit, stirrings due to defilements, and stirrings due to sensuality do not exist, are not present, are not found, are not obtained; they are abandoned, uprooted, calmed, stilled, incapable of arising again, and burnt by the fire of knowledge. For him, there are no stirrings. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "One who practices the holy life among sensual pleasures, [Metteyya, said the Blessed One,] Free from craving, always mindful, The bhikkhu quenched through reflection, for him there are no stirrings." "Having known both ends through higher knowledge, he is not smeared in the middle by wisdom; him I call a Great Man, he has here overcome the seamstress (craving)." In the phrase "Having known both ends through higher knowledge, he is not smeared in the middle by wisdom," "ends" (antā) means: contact is one end, the origin of contact is the second end, and the cessation of contact is the middle. The past is one end, the future is the second end, and the present is the middle. Pleasant feeling is one end, painful feeling is the second end, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is the middle. Name is one end, form is the second end, and consciousness is the middle. The six internal sense bases are one end, the six external sense bases are the second end, and consciousness is the middle. Identity (sakkāya) is one end, the origin of identity is the second end, and the cessation of identity is the middle. Wisdom is called "mantā"—that knowing, knowing specifically... non-delusion, investigation of states, right view (sammādiṭṭhi) are called "mantā." "Smearing" (lepa) is of two kinds: craving-smearing and view-smearing. What is craving-smearing? It is the extent of making boundaries, making limits, making ends, grasping, and possessiveness known as craving—"This is mine, that is mine, this much is mine; to this extent, these forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, rugs, cloaks, female and male slaves, goats and sheep, poultry and pigs, elephants, cattle, horses and mares, fields, lands, silver, gold, villages, towns, royal cities, kingdoms, countries, treasuries, and storehouses are mine." He regards even the whole great earth as "mine" through the power of craving. Whatever the 108-fold movement of craving is—this is craving-smearing.
45:
What is the smearing of views (diṭṭhilepa)? The self-identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) with twenty bases, the wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) with ten bases, the view of holding to an extreme (antaggāhikadiṭṭhi) with ten bases; such a view, the thicket of views, the wilderness of views, the contortion of views, the vacillation of views, the fetter of views, grasping, adhering, dogmatic belief, misinterpretation, the wrong path, the false way, falsity, the sectarian landing-place, the perverted grasp, the inverted grasp, the distorted grasp, the wrong grasp, the grasp of what is not the case as being the case, as many as the sixty-two types of views—this is called the smearing of views.

'Having known both ends through direct knowledge, he is not smeared by wisdom in the middle' means: that monk, having known both ends and the middle through wisdom, having known, weighed, investigated, clarified, and made them manifest, he is not smeared, not stained, not defiled. Being unsmeared, unstained, undefiled, having departed, escaped, and being liberated, detached, he dwells with a mind that has made an end to boundaries. Thus, 'Having known both ends through direct knowledge, he is not smeared by wisdom in the middle.'

'I call him a Great Man (mahāpurisa)' means: a Great Man, a supreme man, a noble man, an excellent man, a foremost man, a highest man, an exalted man. 'I call him' means I say, I speak, I point out, I declare.

The Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Blessed One: 'Venerable Sir, it is said, "A Great Man, a Great Man." To what extent, Venerable Sir, is one a Great Man?' 'Sāriputta, I say one is a Great Man because of having a mind liberated from the taints (āsavas); I say one is not a Great Man because of not having a mind liberated from the taints.'

'And how, Sāriputta, is one's mind liberated from the taints? Here, Sāriputta, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. As he dwells contemplating the body in the body, his mind becomes dispassionate and is liberated from the taints through non-clinging. ... in feelings ... in the mind ... in phenomena (dhammas), he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. As he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, his mind becomes dispassionate and is liberated from the taints through non-clinging. In this way, Sāriputta, a monk is one with a liberated mind. Sāriputta, because of having a mind liberated from the taints, I truly...'
46:
...say "a Great Man." Because of not having a mind liberated from the taints, I say "not a Great Man." I call him a "Great Man."

'He has here overcome the seamstress'—in this statement, 'seamstress' (sibbinī) refers to craving (taṇhā). Whatever lust, infatuation... covetousness, greed, the unwholesome root; for whomsoever this seamstress craving has been abandoned, cut off, calmed, stilled, made incapable of arising, and burnt by the fire of knowledge. He has overcome, transcended, surpassed, gone beyond the seamstress craving. Therefore, it is said: 'He has here overcome the seamstress.' Thus the Blessed One said:

'Having known both ends through direct knowledge, he is not smeared by wisdom in the middle;
I call him a Great Man, he has here overcome the seamstress.'

At the conclusion of the verse, for many thousands of beings who shared the same desire, effort, intention, and disposition as the Brahmin Tissa Metteyya, there arose the dustless, stainless Dhamma-eye: 'Whatever is subject to origination is all subject to cessation.' The mind of that Brahmin was also liberated from the taints through non-clinging. Simultaneously with the attainment of Arahantship, the antelope skin, matted hair, bark garments, triple-staff, water-pot, hair, and beard disappeared. Wearing the shaven-headed appearance and saffron robes, carrying the outer robe, bowl, and inner robe, and possessing the practice consistent with the goal, he sat with palms joined in reverence to the Blessed One, saying: 'Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is my teacher, I am the disciple.'

## The Exposition of the Question of the Youth Tissa Metteyya, Part Two, is finished.

## 3. The Exposition of the Question of the Youth Puṇṇaka

The Venerable Puṇṇaka spoke thus:
'I have come with a question to the one who is unshaken and sees the root.
On what basis did the seers, men, nobles, and brahmins in this world offer sacrifices to the deities?
I ask you, Blessed One, please tell me this.'

'Unshaken and seeing the root'—in this phrase, 'shaking' (ejā) refers to craving. Whatever lust, infatuation... covetousness, greed, the unwholesome root—that shaking craving has been abandoned by the Buddha, the Blessed One, cut off, made like a palm stump, made non-existent, and is of a nature not to arise in the future. Therefore, the Blessed One is called 'unshaken' (aneja) because craving has been abandoned. The Blessed One is not shaken, not moved, not stirred by gain or loss, fame or disrepute, praise or blame, pleasure or pain. This is the meaning of 'unshaken.' 'Seeing the root' (mūladassāvī) means the Blessed One sees the root-cause, the reason, the source, the origin, the genesis, the starting point, the nutriment, the object, the condition, and the origination. Greed is an unwholesome root, hatred is an unwholesome root, delusion is..."
47:
That craving (ejā) which causes agitation has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, and is not subject to future arising. Therefore, the Buddha is called 'Aneja' (one free from the agitation of craving). Because he has abandoned craving (ejā), he is called 'Aneja'. The Blessed One is not shaken by gain, nor is he shaken by loss; he is not shaken by fame, nor is he shaken by disrepute; he is not shaken by praise, nor is he shaken by blame; he is not shaken by pleasure, nor is he shaken by pain. Because he does not move, does not shake, and is not severely shaken, he is called 'Aneja'. 'Mūladassāvī' means the Blessed One sees the root cause, he sees the reason (hetu), he sees the origin (nidāna), he sees the source (sambhava), he sees the genesis (pabhava), he sees the origination (samuṭṭhāna), he sees the nutriment (āhāra), he sees the object (ārammaṇa), he sees the condition (paccaya), and he sees the cause of arising (samudaya).

The three unwholesome roots are: the unwholesome root of greed (lobha), the unwholesome root of hatred (dosa), and the unwholesome root of delusion (moha).

This was indeed spoken by the Blessed One: "Monks, there are these three origins for the arising of kamma. Which three? Greed is an origin for the arising of kamma, hatred is an origin for the arising of kamma, and delusion is an origin for the arising of kamma. Monks, by kamma born of greed, by kamma born of hatred, and by kamma born of delusion, devas are not known, humans are not known, nor are any other happy destinations (sugati) known. Rather, monks, by kamma born of greed, by kamma born of hatred, and by kamma born of delusion, hell is known, the animal realm is known, the realm of hungry ghosts (peta) is known, or any other miserable destinations (duggati) for the manifestation of individual existence in hell, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts are known." The Blessed One knows and sees that these three are the unwholesome roots. In this way, the Blessed One is called Mūladassāvī... pe... Samudayadassāvī.

The three wholesome roots are: the wholesome root of non-greed (alobha), the wholesome root of non-hatred (adosa), and the wholesome root of non-delusion (amoha).

This was indeed spoken by the Blessed One: "These three... pe... Monks, by kamma born of non-greed, by kamma born of non-hatred, and by kamma born of non-delusion, hell is not known, the animal realm is not known, the realm of hungry ghosts is not known, nor are any other miserable destinations known. Rather, monks, by kamma born of non-greed, by kamma born of non-hatred, and by kamma born of non-delusion, devas are known, humans are known, or any other happy destinations for the manifestation of individual existence in the worlds of devas and humans are known." The Blessed One knows and sees that these three are the wholesome roots. In this way, the Blessed One is called Mūladassāvī... pe... Samudayadassāvī.
48:
This was indeed spoken by the Blessed One: "Monks, whatever states are unwholesome, partaking of the unwholesome, or on the side of the unwholesome, all those are rooted in ignorance (avijjā), converge in ignorance, and by the uprooting of ignorance, all those states reach destruction." Thus the Blessed One knows and sees. In this way, the Blessed One is the one who sees the root... the one who sees the cause of arising.

This was indeed spoken by the Blessed One: "Monks, whatever states are wholesome, partaking of the wholesome, or on the side of the wholesome, all those are rooted in heedfulness (appamāda) and converge in heedfulness. Of those states, heedfulness is declared to be the foremost." Thus the Blessed One knows and sees. In this way, the Blessed One is the one who sees the root... the one who sees the cause of arising.

Alternatively, the Blessed One knows and sees: "Ignorance is the root of volitional formations; volitional formations are the root of consciousness; consciousness is the root of name-and-form; name-and-form is the root of the six sense bases; the six sense bases are the root of contact; contact is the root of feeling; feeling is the root of craving; craving is the root of clinging; clinging is the root of existence; existence is the root of birth; birth is the root of aging and death." Thus the Blessed One knows and sees. In this way, the Blessed One is the one who sees the root... the one who sees the cause of arising.

Alternatively, the Blessed One knows and sees: "The eye is the root of eye diseases; the ear is the root of ear diseases; the nose is the root of nose diseases; the tongue is the root of tongue diseases; the body is the root of body diseases; the mind is the root of mental sufferings." Thus the Blessed One knows and sees. In this way, the Blessed One is the one who sees the root, the one who sees the reason, the one who sees the origin, the one who sees the source, the one who sees the genesis, the one who sees the origination, the one who sees the nutriment, the one who sees the object, the one who sees the condition, and the one who sees the cause of arising. He is the one who sees the root, free from craving.

In the phrase "Iccāyasmā puṇṇako", "Iccā" is a word-junction... Venerable Puṇṇaka.

"Atthi pañhena āgamaṃ" means: I have come with a desire for a question; I have come as one wishing to ask a question; I have come as one wishing to hear a question. In this way also, it is said "Atthi pañhena āgamaṃ". Alternatively, it means: there is the coming, the approaching, the drawing near, and the attending of those who desire a question, who wish to ask a question, and who wish to hear a question. In this way also, it is said "Atthi pañhena āgamaṃ". Alternatively, it means: "There is the arrival of a question for you; you are capable and competent. Please bear this burden of preaching and answering the question I have asked." In this way also, it is said "Atthi pañhena āgamaṃ".
49:
On what do the hermits and humans depend? On what do they rely? To what have they approached? To what are they deeply attached? In what do they have settled faith? 'Isayo' refers to all those named hermits who have gone forth in the renunciation of a hermit, such as Ājīvakas, Nigaṇṭhas, Jaṭilas (matted-hair ascetics), and Tāpasas (ascetics). 'Manujā' refers to humans. (Therefore) on what do the hermits and humans depend?

Nobles and Brahmins (offer sacrifices) to the deities. 'Khattiyā' refers to all those of the noble/warrior caste. 'Brāhmaṇā' refers to all those who are called 'Bho-sayers' (Brahmins). 'Devatānaṃ' means: for the disciples of Ājīvakas, the Ājīvakas are the deities; for the disciples of Nigaṇṭhas, the Nigaṇṭhas are the deities; for the disciples of matted-hair ascetics, the matted-hair ascetics are the deities; for the disciples of wandering ascetics (Paribbājakas), the wandering ascetics are the deities; for the disciples of Aviruddhakas, the Aviruddhakas are the deities; for those with the elephant-vow, elephants are the deities; for those with the horse-vow, horses are the deities; for those with the cow-vow, cows are the deities; for those with the dog-vow, dogs are the deities; for those with the crow-vow, crows are the deities; for those with the Vāsudeva-vow, Vāsudeva is the deity; for those with the Baladeva-vow, Baladeva is the deity; for those with the Puṇṇabhadda-vow, Puṇṇabhadda is the deity; for those with the Maṇibhadda-vow, Maṇibhadda is the deity; for those who worship fire, fire is the deity; for those with the Nāga-vow, Nāgas are the deities; for those with the Supaṇṇa-vow, Supaṇṇas (Garudas) are the deities; for those with the Yakkha-vow, Yakkhas are the deities; for those with the Asura-vow, Asuras are the deities; for those with the Gandhabba-vow, Gandhabbas are the deities; for those with the Mahārāja-vow, the Mahārājas (Great Kings) are the deities; for those with the Moon-vow, the Moon is the deity; for those with the Sun-vow, the Sun is the deity; for those with the Indra-vow, Indra is the deity; for those with the Brahmā-vow, Brahmā is the deity; for those with the Deva-vow, the Deva is the deity; for those who respectfully practice the vow of the directions, the directions are the deities. Whoever are the worthy recipients (dakkhiṇeyya) for certain people, those are the deities for them. (Therefore) nobles and Brahmins (offer sacrifices) to the deities.

Many in this world have prepared a sacrifice. 'Yajña' (sacrifice) refers to the objects of offering, namely: robes, alms-food, lodgings, medicinal requisites for the sick, food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes, ointments, beds, dwellings, and lamps. 'Yajñamakappayiṃsu' means: those who seek these objects of offering such as robes, alms-food, lodgings, medicinal requisites, food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes, ointments, beds, dwellings, and lamps; those who seek with the mind, those who seek with effort, those who seek by various means—they too prepare the sacrifice. Those who prepare and arrange food, drink, etc.—they too prepare the sacrifice. Those who give, offer, and relinquish robes, alms-food, lodgings, medicinal requisites, food, drink, etc...
50:
...beds, dwellings, and lamps (they seek); they too prepare the sacrifice (offering). 'Puthū' (many) means these offerings are many, or these sacrificers are many, or these worthy recipients are many.

How are these offerings many? These offerings—robes, alms-food, lodgings, medicinal requisites, food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes, ointments, beds, dwellings, and lamps—are very numerous. In this way, these offerings are many.

How are these sacrificers many? These sacrificers—nobles, Brahmins, merchants (Vessas), laborers (Suddas), householders, renunciants, devas, and humans—are very numerous. In this way, these sacrificers are many.

How are these worthy recipients many? These worthy recipients—ascetics (Samaṇas), Brahmins, the destitute, wayfarers, vagrants, and beggars—are very numerous. In this way, these worthy recipients are many. 'In this world' means in the world of humans. 'Many in this world have prepared a sacrifice' is the meaning.

In the phrase "I ask you, Blessed One, tell me this," there are three types of 'Pucchā' (questions). They are: a question to illuminate what is not yet seen or known (Aditthajotanā pucchā), a question to compare or confirm what is already seen or known (Ditthasaṃsandanā pucchā), and a question to cut off doubt (Vimaticchedanā pucchā).

What kind of question is the one to illuminate what is not yet seen or known (Aditthajotanā pucchā)? It is when a characteristic is naturally unknown, unseen, unweighed, unexamined, unmanifested, and undeveloped. One asks a question for the sake of knowing, seeing, weighing, examining, manifesting, and developing that unknown truth. This is called Aditthajotanā pucchā.

What kind of question is the one to compare what is already seen or known (Ditthasaṃsandanā pucchā)? It is when a characteristic is naturally known, seen, weighed, examined, manifested, and developed. One asks a question for the sake of comparing and discussing it with other wise people. This is called Ditthasaṃsandanā pucchā.

What kind of question is the one to cut off doubt (Vimaticchedanā pucchā)? It is when one naturally falls into doubt, falls into uncertainty, and is of two minds, thinking: "Is it thus, or is it not thus? What is it? How is it?" That person asks a question for the sake of cutting off doubt. This is called Vimaticchedanā pucchā. These are the three types of questions.

There are also another three types of questions: questions by humans (Manussapucchā), questions by non-humans (Amanussapucchā), and questions by created beings (Nimmitapucchā). What kind of question is the one by humans (Manussapucchā)? It is when humans approach the Blessed Buddha and ask; when monks ask, when nuns ask, when laymen (upāsakas) ask, and when laywomen (upāsikās) ask.
51:
Kings ask, Khattiyas ask, Brahmins ask, Vessas ask, Suddas ask, householders ask, monastics ask—this is called human questioning (manussa-pucchā).

What is non-human questioning (amanussa-pucchā)? Non-human beings approach the Blessed One and ask questions. Nāgas ask, Supaṇṇas ask, Yakkhas ask, Asuras ask, Gandhabbas ask, Great Kings ask, Indras ask, Brahmās ask, deities ask—this is called non-human questioning (amanussa-pucchā).

What is created questioning (nimmita-pucchā)? The Blessed One creates a mind-made form, complete in all its parts and limbs, with unimpaired faculties. That created form approaches the Blessed One and asks a question; the Blessed One answers—this is called created questioning (nimmita-pucchā). These are the three kinds of questioning.

Other sets of three questionings are: questioning for one's own benefit, questioning for another's benefit, and questioning for the benefit of both. Other sets of three questionings are: questioning for benefit to be experienced in the present life, questioning for benefit to be experienced in a future life, and questioning for the ultimate benefit. Other sets of three questionings are: questioning for blameless benefit, questioning for benefit free from defilements, and questioning for pure benefit. Other sets of three questionings are: questioning related to the past, questioning related to the future, and questioning related to the present. Other sets of three questionings are: questioning related to internal phenomena, questioning related to external phenomena, and questioning related to both internal and external phenomena. Other sets of three questionings are: questioning about wholesome states, questioning about unwholesome states, and questioning about indeterminate states. Other sets of three questionings are: questioning about the aggregates (khandha), questioning about the elements (dhātu), and questioning about the sense bases (āyatana). Other sets of three questionings are: questioning about the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), questioning about the right efforts (sammappadhāna), and questioning about the bases of power (iddhipāda). Other sets of three questionings are: questioning about the faculties (indriya), questioning about the powers (bala), and questioning about the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga). Other sets of three questionings are: questioning about the path (magga), questioning about the fruit (phala), and questioning about Nibbāna.

"Pucchāmi taṃ" means: I ask you, I entreat you, I urge you, I seek your favor, saying "Please tell me," I ask you. "Bhagavā" is a term of respect... the name "Bhagavā" is a designation realized through personal experience. "Brūhi metantaṃ" means: please tell me this matter, preach it, designate it, establish it, open it, analyze it, make it clear, and reveal it—may the Blessed One tell me this question. Therefore, that Brahmin Puṇṇaka spoke thus:

"O one free from craving, seer of the root, [thus spoke the venerable Puṇṇaka]
I have come with a question.
On what basis do the many sages, humans, Khattiyas, and Brahmins in this world offer sacrifices to deities?
O Blessed One, please tell me that matter."
52:
"Puṇṇaka, whatever sages, humans, Khattiyas, and Brahmins in this world offer many sacrifices intended for the deities; they offer those sacrifices longing for rewards in this state of existence and dependent on [the fear of] old age," said the Blessed One. Regarding the words "Ye kecime isayo manujā": "Ye keci" is an inclusive term meaning all, without exception, and in every way. "Isayo" refers to all those who have gone forth in the sage's renunciation, such as Ājīvakas, Nigaṇṭhas, Jaṭilas, and Tāpasas. "Manujā" means humans. Thus, the Blessed One said, "Puṇṇaka, whatever sages and humans in this world..."

Regarding the words "Khattiyā brāhmaṇā devatānaṃ": "Khattiyā" refers to all those of the warrior-noble class. "Brāhmaṇā" refers to all those who are speakers of 'bho' (Brahmins). "Devatānaṃ" means that just as for the disciples of Ājīvakas, the Ājīvakas are their deities (objects of worship), or for those who worship the quarters, the quarters are their deities; whoever are worthy of offerings are the deities of the donors. Thus, it means "Khattiyas and Brahmins [offer sacrifices] to the deities."

Regarding the words "Yaññamakappayiṃsu puthūdha loke": "Yañña" (sacrifice/offering) refers to the objects to be given, such as robes, alms-food, lodgings, medicines and provisions for the sick, food, drink... bedding, dwellings, and lamps. "Yaññamakappayiṃsu" means those who seek, search for, and collect those offerings; they are said to perform a sacrifice. "Puthū" means that these sacrifices, the sacrificers, and the recipients of the offerings are numerous. "Idha loke" means in the human world.

Regarding the words "Āsīsamānā puṇṇaka itthattaṃ": "Āsīsamānā" means longing to obtain visual forms, longing to obtain sounds, smells, tastes, and touches; longing to obtain sons, longing to obtain wives, longing to obtain wealth, fame, and sovereignty; and longing to obtain a rebirth in the families of great Khattiyas.
53:
Aspiring to obtain an individual existence in a wealthy Brahmin family, aspiring to obtain an individual existence in a wealthy householder family, aspiring to obtain an individual existence among the Cātumahārājika devas, aspiring to obtain an individual existence among the Tāvatiṃsa devas, the Yāma devas, the Tusita devas, the Nimmānarati devas, the Paranimmitavasavattī devas, and the Brahmakāyika devas—because they desire, enjoy, long for, wish for, and intensely crave it, it is said 'aspiring'.

'Puṇṇaka, in this state of being' means aspiring to the arising of an individual existence in this state of being as a human, aspiring to the arising of an individual existence in this wealthy Khattiya family... pe... because they desire, enjoy, long for, wish for, and intensely crave the arising of an individual existence among these Brahmakāyika devas, it is said 'aspiring, Puṇṇaka, in this state of being'.

'Dependent on aging, they performed sacrifices' means they are dependent on aging, dependent on sickness, dependent on death, and dependent on sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Those who are dependent on birth are the very ones dependent on aging. Those who are dependent on aging are the very ones dependent on sickness. Those who are dependent on sickness are the very ones dependent on death. Those who are dependent on death are the very ones dependent on sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Those who are dependent on sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are the very ones dependent on their destination (gati). Those who are dependent on their destination are the very ones dependent on rebirth (upapatti). Those who are dependent on rebirth are the very ones dependent on conception (paṭisandhi). Those who are dependent on conception are the very ones dependent on existence (bhava). Those who are dependent on existence are the very ones dependent on saṃsāra. Those who are dependent on saṃsāra are the very ones dependent on the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa); they are attached to it, they have approached it, they are deeply immersed in it, and they are intent upon it. Therefore, it is said, 'Dependent on aging, they performed sacrifices.' For that reason, the Blessed One said:

"Whatever hermits, men, [Puṇṇaka, the Blessed One said]
nobles, and Brahmins in this world,
performed many sacrifices to the deities, aspiring for results in this state of being, Puṇṇaka;
dependent on aging, they performed sacrifices."
54:
"Venerable Puṇṇaka, in this world, whatever human seers, nobles, and brahmins have offered many sacrifices to the gods—O Blessed One, are those who offered sacrifices diligent in the path of sacrifice? O Dear Sir, do they cross over birth and old age? I ask the Blessed One this; please tell me."

In the phrase 'Ye kecime isayo manujā', 'ye keci' means all... and so on.

In the phrase 'Kaccisu te bhagavā yaññapathe appamattā', 'kaccisu' is a question arising from doubt, inquiry, indecision, and uncertainty, such as 'Is it thus? Is it not thus? How is it? In what way?'. 'Te' refers to those who offer sacrifices. 'Bhagavā' is a title used with respect and reverence, a designation realized [by the Buddha]. In 'yaññapathe appamattā', the sacrifice itself is called the 'path of sacrifice' (yaññapatha). Just as the Noble Path is called 'ariyapatha', the Divine Path 'devapatha', and the Brahma Path 'brahmapatha', so too the sacrifice is called the 'path of sacrifice'. 'Appamattā' means being diligent in the path of sacrifice, acting with respect, acting continuously, acting firmly, developing without shrinking back, having unflagging desire, having unflagging energy, practicing only that sacrifice, being frequent in it, giving it weight, inclining towards it, leaning towards it, entering into it, and making it predominant. They are those who are diligent in the path of sacrifice.

Those who respectfully seek robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, food, drink... and so on, such as beds, dwellings, and lamps—they too are diligent in the path of sacrifice.

Those who respectfully prepare robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, food, drink... and so on, such as beds, dwellings, and lamps—they too are diligent in the path of sacrifice.

Those who respectfully give, offer, and relinquish robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, food, drink... and so on, such as beds, dwellings, and lamps—they too are diligent in the path of sacrifice.

'Atāruṃ jātiñca jarañca mārisa' means they have crossed over, transcended, and well-surpassed birth and old age. 'Mārisa' is a term of endearment, a term of respect, and a title used with reverence.
55:
‘I ask you’ means I ask you, I entreat you, I request you, I propitiate you, please tell me—thus ‘pucchāmi taṃ’. ‘Bhagavā’ is a designation of reverence ... (etc.) ... it is a designation based on realization—namely, ‘Bhagavā’. ‘Tell me this’ means tell, inform, teach, designate, establish, reveal, analyze, make clear, and proclaim—thus ‘brūhi metaṃ’. 

Therefore, that Brahmin Punnaka addressed [the Buddha] thus:
“I ask you, O Blessed One, tell me this: Whoever these sages, men, Khattiyas, and Brahmins are who offered sacrifices to deities here in the world—O Blessed One, were they diligent in the path of sacrifice? Did they cross over birth and aging, O Venerable Sir? I ask you, O Blessed One, tell me this.”

The Blessed One said this:
“Punnaka, they long for, they praise, they pray, and they sacrifice. They pray for sensual pleasures because of gain. Those devoted to sacrifice, enamored with the lust for existence, do not cross over birth and aging, I say.”

Among the words ‘āsīsanti, thomayanti, abhijappanti, juhanti’: ‘Āsīsanti’ means they long for the acquisition of sights, they long for the acquisition of sounds, they long for the acquisition of smells, tastes, and touches; they long for the acquisition of sons, wives, wealth, fame, and power; they long for the acquisition of a new existence in the family of a great Khattiya, a great Brahmin ... (etc.) ... a great householder; they long for the acquisition of a new existence among the gods of the Four Great Kings ... (etc.) ... among the Brahma-kayika gods. They desire, they enjoy, they long for, and they cherish—thus ‘āsīsanti’.

‘Thomayanti’ means they praise either the sacrifice, the result, or the recipients of the gift. How do they praise the sacrifice? They praise it saying: ‘It is given purely, it is given pleasingly, it is given excellently,’
56:
‘It is given at the right time, it is given as allowable, it is given after choosing, it is given blamelessly, it is given constantly, the mind is cleared while giving’—thus they praise, they celebrate, they extol, and they commend. In this way, they praise the sacrifice.

How do they praise the result? They praise, celebrate, extol, and commend, saying: ‘From this cause, there will be the acquisition of sights in the celestial realm ... (etc.) ... there will be the acquisition of a new existence among the Brahma-kayika gods.’ In this way, they praise the result.

How do they praise the recipients? They praise, celebrate, extol, and commend, saying: ‘The recipients are endowed with [high] birth, endowed with [noble] lineage, they are reciters of the Vedas, masters of the mantras, they have reached the end of the three Vedas with the Nighaṇḍu and Keṭubha, the phonology, and the histories as the fifth; they are experts in the words and grammar, fully proficient in the Lokāyata and the marks of a Great Man (Mahāpurisalakkhaṇa)’; or they say: ‘They are free from lust or practicing for the removal of lust, free from hatred or practicing for the removal of hatred, free from delusion or practicing for the removal of delusion; they are endowed with faith, virtue, concentration, wisdom, the fruit of Arahantship, and the knowledge of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa).’ In this way, they praise the recipients; thus it is said ‘they long for, they praise’.

‘Abhijappanti’ means they repeatedly long for the acquisition of sights, they repeatedly long for the acquisition of sounds, smells, tastes ... (etc.) ... they repeatedly long for the acquisition of a new existence among the Brahma-kayika gods; thus it is said ‘they long for, they praise, they pray’.

‘Juhanti’ means they sacrifice, they give, they offer, they relinquish robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites; they give food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, beds, dwellings, and lamps—thus the Blessed One told Punnaka. In this way, they long for, they praise, they pray, and they sacrifice.

‘They pray for sensual pleasures because of gain’ means they pray intensely for sensual pleasures based on the acquisition of sights, they repeatedly long for sensual pleasures based on the acquisition of sounds ... (etc.) ... they pray intensely and repeatedly for sensual pleasures based on the acquisition of a new existence among the Brahma-kayika gods. This is the meaning of ‘kāmābhijappanti paṭicca lābhaṃ’.

Those who perform the sacrifice are called ‘te’. ‘Yājayogā’ means those who are devoted to sacrifice, especially devoted, closely devoted, well devoted, habituated to that sacrifice, frequently performing that sacrifice, valuing that sacrifice, leaning towards it, sloping towards it, inclining towards it, focused on it, and dominated by that sacrifice. This is the meaning of ‘te yājayogā’. In the phrase ‘bhavarāgarattā’, ‘bhavarāga’ refers to the desire for existence, the lust for existence.
57:
There is delight in existence, craving for existence, affection for existence, fever for existence, infatuation with existence, and excessive obsession with existence. Those who are attached to existences through lust for existence, who are greedy, intensely lustful, infatuated, deeply obsessed, stuck, entangled, and repeatedly obstructed, are called those devoted to sacrifice who are attached to lust for existence.

"I say that those devoted to sacrifice who are attached to lust for existence cannot transcend birth and aging." This means that those devoted to sacrifice who are attached to lust for existence cannot transcend birth, aging, and death; they cannot cross over, cannot get beyond, cannot overcome, and cannot surpass them. They cannot escape from birth, aging, and death; they cannot be liberated from them, cannot transcend them, cannot overcome them, and cannot surpass them. They merely revolve within birth, aging, and death; they revolve within the path of saṃsāra. Birth follows them, aging is pervasive, sickness overcomes them, and death oppresses them. They are without protection, without shelter, without refuge, and have become those without a savior. Thus, I speak, I inform, I teach, I establish, I reveal, I analyze, I clarify, and I manifest. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"Puṇṇaka, they long for, they praise, they pray, and they sacrifice. [The Blessed One said:]
They pray for sensual pleasures because of gain. Those devoted to sacrifice who are attached to lust for existence,
I say, have not transcended birth and aging."

[The Venerable Puṇṇaka said:]
"If those devoted to sacrifice have not transcended birth and aging through sacrifices, O Noble Sir,
Then who in the world of gods and humans has transcended birth and aging, O Noble Sir?
I ask this of the Blessed One; please tell this to me."

"If those devoted to sacrifice have not transcended" means that those who perform sacrifices and are devoted to sacrifice, being attached through lust for existence, cannot transcend birth, aging, and death; they cannot cross over, cannot get beyond, cannot overcome, and cannot surpass them. They cannot escape from birth, aging, and death; they cannot be free from them, cannot transcend them, cannot overcome them, and cannot surpass them. They merely revolve within birth, aging, and death; they revolve within the path of saṃsāra. They are followed by birth, pervaded by aging, overcome by sickness, and oppressed by death. They are without protection, without shelter, without refuge, and do not become a refuge for those who take refuge in them. Thus, I speak, I inform, I teach, I establish, I reveal, I analyze, I clarify, and I manifest.

"The Venerable Puṇṇaka" is... (a conjunction of words)... the Venerable Puṇṇaka.
58:
In the phrase "yannyehi jātiñca jarañca mārisā," "yannyehi" means by means of many sacrifices, various sacrifices, and abundant sacrifices. "Mārisa" is a term of endearment, a term of respect, and a term spoken with reverence and deference. "Yannyehi jātiñca jarañca mārisa" means "O friend... (can one transcend) birth and aging through sacrifices?"

"Atha ko carahi devamanussaloke, atāri jātiñca jarañca mārisā" means: If they cannot transcend (through sacrifices), then who in this world of opportunities—including the six heavens of the sensual realm, the Vasavatti realm, and the Brahma realm—and among the world of beings—including recluses, brahmins, gods, and humans—has transcended birth, aging, and death? Who has crossed over, got beyond, overcome, and surpassed them? "Mārisa" is a term of endearment, a term of respect, and a term spoken with reverence and deference. "Atha ko carahi devamanussaloke, atāri jātiñca jarañca mārisa" means "O friend... if that is so, who in the world of gods and humans has transcended birth and aging?"

In the phrase "pucchāmi taṃ bhagavā brūhi metanti," "pucchāmi taṃ" means I ask about that matter, I entreat you, I urge you, I have faith in you; please preach that matter to me. "Bhagavā" is a title of respect... (and so on)... it is a designation realized through direct experience. "Brūhi metanti" means please tell, preach, inform, establish, reveal, analyze, clarify, and manifest that matter. Therefore, that Brahmin Puṇṇaka asked thus:

"O friend... if those devoted to sacrifice
Cannot transcend birth and aging through sacrifices,
O friend... if that is so, who in the world of gods and humans has transcended birth and aging?
O Blessed One... I ask about that matter; please preach it to me."

The Blessed One replied thus:
"Puṇṇaka, having discerned the things of this world, such as one's own and others' individual existence, with wisdom,
He for whom there is no commotion (craving) anywhere in the world,
Who is peaceful, smokeless (free from the smoke of defilements), free from affliction (such as lust), and desireless,
I say that he has transcended birth and aging."

In the phrase "saṅkhāya lokasmi paroparānīti," "saṅkhā" refers to knowledge. It is the wisdom that knows analytically, the wisdom that knows through modes... (and so on)... the wisdom that knows without delusion, the wisdom that investigates the Four Noble Truths, and the wisdom of right view (sammā-diṭṭhi). In the phrase "paroparānīti," "ora" refers to one's own individual existence (attabhāva), and "para" refers to the individual existence of others. One's own form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are called "ora," while the form, feeling, perception, and mental formations of others... (the text breaks off).
59:
Consciousness is called 'this side' (ora), the six internal sense bases are called 'this side', and the six external sense bases are called 'the other side' (para). The human world is called 'this side', and the deva world is called 'the other side'. The sensual element (kāmadhātu) is called 'this side', while the fine-material element (rūpadhātu) and the immaterial element (arūpadhātu) are called 'the other side'. The sensual element and the fine-material element are called 'this side', and the immaterial element is called 'the other side'.

'Saṅkhāya lokasmi paroparāni' means: having considered 'this side' and 'the other side' in the world by means of wisdom as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a boil... as an escape; having known, weighed, judged, developed, and made them clear.

'Puṇṇakāti bhagavā' means: the Blessed One addressed that young man Puṇṇaka by name. 'Bhagavā' is a term of respect... this is the phrase 'Puṇṇakāti bhagavā'.

'Yassiñjitaṃ natthi kuhiñci loke' means: 'Yassa' refers to the Arahant whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava). 'Iñjitaṃ' refers to the agitation caused by craving, the agitation caused by views, the agitation caused by conceit, the agitation caused by defilements, and the agitation caused by sensual desires. For that Arahant, these agitations do not exist, are not found, have been abandoned, uprooted, calmed, completely stilled, are incapable of arising again, and have been burnt by the fire of knowledge. 'Kuhiñci' means anywhere: internally, externally, or both internally and externally. 'Loke' means in the world of misery... in the world of sense bases. This is the phrase 'Yassiñjitaṃ natthi kuhiñci loke'.

'Santo vidhūmo anīgho nirāso, atāri so jātijaranti brူmi' means: 'Santo' is called 'peaceful' (santa) because of the calming of lust (rāga). Because of the calming, stilling, complete quieting, extinguishing, quenching, vanishing, and total tranquility of hatred... delusion, anger, malice, disparaging, and all unwholesome formations (akusalābhisaṅkhāra), he is called 'peaceful' (santa), 'stilled' (upasanta), 'tranquil' (vūpasanta), 'quenched' (nibbuta), and 'allayed' (paṭipassaddha).

'Vidhūmo' (smokeless) means: bodily misconduct has been destroyed, dried up, and eliminated. Verbal misconduct... mental misconduct has been destroyed, dried up, and eliminated. Lust, hatred, and delusion have been destroyed, dried up, and eliminated. Anger, malice, disparaging, rivalry, envy, stinginess, deceit, craftiness, stubbornness, impetuosity, conceit, arrogance, intoxication, negligence, all defilements, all misconduct, all distress, all fever, all burning, and all unwholesome formations have been destroyed, dried up, and eliminated. Alternatively, anger (kodha) is called 'smoke' (dhūma).
60:
Brahmin, your pride is a burdensome yoke, anger is smoke, and false speech is ashes. The tongue is the sacrificial ladle, the heart is the place where the fire is established, and the well-tamed self is the (wisdom) fire of a man.

Furthermore, anger arises in ten ways: 'He did me harm,' thus anger arises. 'He is doing me harm,' thus anger arises. 'He will do me harm,' thus anger arises. 'He did harm to one who is dear and pleasing to me,' 'He is doing harm,' 'He will do harm,' thus anger arises. 'He did a benefit to one who is not dear and not pleasing to me,' 'He is doing a benefit,' 'He will do a benefit,' thus anger arises. Or else, anger arises groundlessly.

Such resentment of the mind, repeated resentment, the state of repeated resentment, opposition, destruction, particular destruction, extreme destruction, ruin, particular ruin, extreme ruin, the state of the mind being discordant, the destruction of the mind, anger, the state of being angry, the condition of one who is angry, corruption, the state of being corrupted, the condition of one who is corrupt, the state of abandoning the natural state, the act of abandoning, the condition of one who abandons the natural state, opposition, repeated opposition, the state of a harsh person, incomplete speech, the state of the mind being displeased—this is called anger (kodha).

Furthermore, the greatness or smallness of anger should be understood. At some times, anger is merely a disturbance of the mind, but at that time, the contortion of the face has not yet occurred. At some times, anger is merely the contortion of the face, but at that time, the trembling of the jaw has not yet occurred. At some times, anger is merely the trembling of the jaw, but at that time, the uttering of harsh words has not yet occurred. At some times, anger is merely the uttering of harsh words, but at that time, the looking around in all directions has not yet occurred. At some times, anger is merely the looking around in all directions, but at that time, the seizing of sticks and weapons has not yet occurred. At some times, anger is merely the seizing of sticks and weapons, but at that time, the raising of sticks and weapons has not yet occurred. At some times, anger is merely the raising of sticks and weapons, but at that time, the striking and hacking with sticks and weapons has not yet occurred. At some times, anger is merely the striking and hacking with sticks and weapons, but at that time, the cutting into pieces has not yet occurred. At some times, anger is merely the cutting into pieces,
61: Anger, in the beginning, does not yet have the nature of crushing and pulverizing. At one time, anger is merely the raising of a stick or weapon, but not yet striking, beating, or hacking. At one time, anger is merely striking, beating, or hacking, but not yet cutting into pieces. At one time, anger is merely cutting into pieces, but not yet crushing and pulverizing. At one time, anger is merely crushing and pulverizing, but not yet dragging the limbs. At one time, anger is merely dragging the limbs, but not yet taking life (killing). At one time, anger is merely taking life, but not yet being established in the total sacrifice of one's own life. When anger kills another person and then kills oneself, at that point, anger has reached its peak of intensity and its greatest abundance. He for whom that anger is abandoned, cut off at the root, calmed, stilled, made incapable of arising again, and consumed by the fire of knowledge, is called 'Vidhūma' (smokeless). He is called 'Vidhūma' because anger is abandoned. He is called 'Vidhūma' because the basis of anger is fully understood. He is called 'Vidhūma' because the cause of anger is fully understood. He is called 'Vidhūma' because the cause of anger is cut off. 'Anīgha' means: lust is an affliction (nīgha), hatred is an affliction, delusion is an affliction, anger is an affliction, malice is an affliction... [pe]... all unwholesome formations are afflictions. He for whom these afflictions are abandoned, cut off at the root, calmed, stilled, made incapable of arising again, and burnt by the fire of knowledge, is called 'Anīgha' (free from affliction). 'Nirāsa' means: longing (āsā) is called craving (taṇhā). That lust, infatuation... [pe]... covetousness, greed, the unwholesome root which is craving exists. He for whom that craving with its longing is abandoned, cut off at the root, calmed, stilled, made incapable of arising again, and consumed by the fire of knowledge, is called 'Nirāsa' (free from longing). 'Birth' (jāti) means: the birth, being born, descent, arising, appearance of the aggregates, and acquisition of the sense bases of various beings in various categories of beings. 'Old age' (jarā) means: the aging, decrepitude, broken teeth, graying hair, wrinkling skin, decline of life, and ripening of the faculties of various beings in various categories of beings. 'The one who is peaceful, smokeless, free from affliction, and free from longing has crossed over birth and old age'—so I declare, I teach, I make known, I establish, I reveal, I analyze, I clarify, I proclaim. Therefore, it is said: 'The one who is peaceful, smokeless, free from affliction, and free from longing has crossed over birth and old age.' Thus the Blessed One said:
62:
"Having discerned with wisdom the high and low in the world, [Punnaka, the Blessed One said this:]
For whom there is no agitation of craving anywhere in the world,
Who is peaceful, free from the smoke of defilements, free from suffering, and without longing—that person, I declare, has crossed over birth and aging."

At the conclusion of the verse... he remained sitting, paying homage to the Blessed One with joined palms, saying: "Venerable sir, the Blessed One is my teacher, I am a disciple."

## The Exposition of the Question of the Youth Punnaka, the Third, is finished.

## 4. The Exposition of the Question of the Youth Mettagū

"I ask you, Blessed One, please tell me this, [the venerable Mettagū said this:]
I consider you to be one who has reached knowledge (vedagū) and is of developed self (bhāvitatta);
From where have these many forms of suffering (dukkha) arisen in the world?
I ask you, Blessed One, please tell me this."

Regarding "I ask you": there are three kinds of questions (pucchā)—a question to clarify what is unknown and unseen (adiṭṭhajotanā pucchā), a question to compare and verify what is already known and seen (diṭṭhasandandanā pucchā), and a question to cut off doubt (vimaticchedanā pucchā). What is a question to clarify what is unknown and unseen? If a characteristic is naturally unknown, unseen, unweighed, unexamined, unmanifested, and undeveloped. For the sake of knowing, seeing, weighing, examining, manifesting, and developing that truth, one asks a question—this is called a question to clarify what is unknown and unseen (adiṭṭhajotanā pucchā).

What is a question to compare and verify what is already known and seen? If a characteristic is naturally known, seen, weighed, examined, manifested, and developed. For the sake of comparing it with other wise people, one asks a question—this is called a question to compare and verify what is already known and seen (diṭṭhasandandanā pucchā).

What is a question to cut off doubt? If one is naturally fallen into doubt, fallen into uncertainty, and is of two minds, thinking: "Is it thus? Is it not thus? What is it? How is it?" For the sake of cutting off that doubt, one asks a question—this is called a question to cut off doubt (vimaticchedanā pucchā). These are the three kinds of questions.

There are also another three kinds of questions—questions by humans (manussapucchā), questions by non-humans (amanussapucchā), and questions by created beings (nimmitapucchā). What are questions by humans? Humans approach the Blessed One and ask questions; monks ask, nuns ask, laymen (upāsaka) ask, laywomen (upāsikā) ask, kings ask...
63:
Khattiyas ask, Brahmins ask, Vessas ask, Suddas ask, householders ask, monastics ask—this is called the human questioning (manussa-pucchā).

What is the non-human questioning (amanussa-pucchā)? Non-humans approach the Buddha, the Blessed One, and ask questions; Nagas ask, Supannas ask, Yakkhas ask, Asuras ask, Gandhabbas ask, the Great Kings ask, Indras ask, Brahmas ask, Devas ask—this is called the non-human questioning (amanussa-pucchā).

What is the questioning by a created form (nimmita-pucchā)? The Blessed One creates a mind-made form, complete in all its limbs and parts, with faculties unimpaired. That created (nimmita) Buddha approaches the Buddha, the Blessed One, and asks a question. The Blessed One answers. This is called the questioning by a created form (nimmita-pucchā). These are the three types of questioning.

There are also other sets of three questionings—questioning for one's own benefit, questioning for another's benefit, questioning for the benefit of both... ... There are also other sets of three questionings—questioning for benefit in the present life, questioning for benefit in the future life, questioning for the ultimate benefit... There are also other sets of three questionings—questioning for blameless benefit, questioning for stainless benefit, questioning for pure benefit... There are also other sets of three questionings—questioning about the past, questioning about the future, questioning about the present... There are also other sets of three questionings—questioning about internal things, questioning about external things, questioning about both internal and external things... There are also other sets of three questionings—questioning about the wholesome, questioning about the unwholesome, questioning about the indeterminate (avyākata)... There are also other sets of three questionings—questioning about the aggregates (khandha), questioning about the elements (dhātu), questioning about the sense bases (āyatana)... There are also other sets of three questionings—questioning about the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), questioning about the right efforts (sammappadhāna), questioning about the bases of power (iddhipāda)... There are also other sets of three questionings—questioning about the faculties (indriya), questioning about the powers (bala), questioning about the enlightenment factors (bojjhaṅga)... There are also other sets of three questionings—questioning about the path (magga), questioning about the fruit (phala), questioning about Nibbāna.

'Pucchāmi taṃ' means: I ask you about that problem, I entreat you about it, I urge you about it, I show devotion to you regarding it; "Please preach to me," thus I ask you about it. 'Bhagavā' is a term of respect... ... the designation realized is 'the Blessed One' (Bhagavā). 'Brūhi me taṃ' means: please tell me, preach to me, show me, make me know, establish it, open it, analyze it, make it clear, and manifest it—thus, I ask you, Blessed One, tell me this.

'Iccāyasmā mettagū'—'Icca' is a word-conjunction... ... the venerable Mettagū spoke thus.

'Maññāmi taṃ vedagū bhāvitattaṃ' means: I consider you a Vedagū (one who has reached the end of knowledge), I consider you a Bhāvitatta (one of developed self); thus I know, thus I perceive, thus I recognize, thus I penetrate. In the phrase 'Vedagū bhāvitatto', in what way is the Blessed One a Vedagū? Knowledge, wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom... ... the enlightenment factor of investigation of states (dhamma-vicaya-sambojjhaṅga) occurring in the four paths are called 'Veda'.
64:
Investigation (vīmaṃsā), insight (vipassanā), and right view (sammādiṭṭhi) are called 'Veda'. Through these Vedas (path-knowledge), the Blessed One has reached the end of birth, aging, and death; he has reached the summit, reached the limit, reached the conclusion, reached the boundary, reached the completion, reached the refuge, reached the shelter, reached the safety, reached the security, reached the unshakable, reached the deathless, reached Nibbāna. He is a 'Vedagū' because he has reached the end of the Vedas, or because he has reached the end through the Vedas, or because he has known the seven things. He has known identity view (sakkāya-diṭṭhi), he has known doubt (vicikicchā), he has known adherence to rules and rituals (sīlabbata-parāmāsa), he has known lust, hatred, delusion, and pride. The Blessed One has known those low, unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and causing birth, aging, and death in the future.

Having investigated all Vedas (dhamma) through the path,
Having known the things that exist in this world for both recluses and brahmins,
Being free from lust in all feelings,
Having transcended all Veda, he is called a 'Vedagū'.

In this way, the Blessed One is a Vedagū.

How is the Blessed One a 'Bhāvitatta' (one of developed self)? The Blessed One is one of developed body, developed virtue, developed mind, and developed wisdom. He is one of developed foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of power, faculties, powers, enlightenment factors, and the path. He has abandoned the defilements, penetrated the unshakeable [fruition], and realized cessation. By that Blessed One, suffering (dukkha-sacca) has been fully understood, the origin (samudaya-sacca) has been abandoned, the path (magga-sacca) has been developed, and cessation (nirodha-sacca) has been realized. He has known what should be known through higher knowledge, he has fully understood what should be fully understood, he has abandoned what should be abandoned, he has developed what should be developed, and he has realized what should be realized. The Blessed One possesses wisdom that is not small (great), vast, deep, immeasurable, difficult to fathom, and like the ocean containing many jewels. He is endowed with the six-factored equanimity (chaḷaṅgupekkhā).

Having seen a form with the eye, he is neither glad nor sad, but dwells with equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending. Having heard a sound with the ear, having smelled an odor with the nose, having tasted a flavor with the tongue, having touched a tangible object with the body, having [cognized a mental object] with the mind...
65:
Having known a mental object, he is neither glad nor sad; he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending.

Having seen a form with the eye, he does not lust after a pleasant form, does not rejoice in it, and does not give rise to passion (rāga). The body of that Blessed One is steady, and his mind is well-settled within, well-established, and well-liberated (by the five kinds of liberation). Indeed, having seen an unpleasant form with the eye, he is not dejected; with an unperturbed mind, he is not downcast, and his mind is free from ill-will. The body of that Blessed One is steady, and his mind is well-settled within, well-established, and well-liberated. Having heard a sound with the ear... having smelled an odor with the nose... having tasted a flavor with the tongue... having touched a tangible object with the body... having known a mental object with the mind, he does not lust after a pleasant object, does not rejoice in it, and does not give rise to passion. The body of that Blessed One is steady, and his mind is well-settled within, well-established, and well-liberated. Indeed, having known a mental object with the mind, he is not dejected; with an unestablished mind, he is not downcast, and his mind is free from ill-will. The body of that Blessed One is steady, and his mind is well-settled within, well-established, and well-liberated.

Having seen a form with the eye, his body is steady regarding both pleasant and unpleasant forms, and his mind is well-settled within, well-established, and well-liberated. Having heard a sound with the ear... having known a mental object with the mind, his body is steady regarding both pleasant and unpleasant mental objects, and his mind is well-settled within, well-established, and well-liberated.

Having seen a form with the eye, he does not lust after what is lust-inducing, does not feel aversion toward what is aversion-inducing, is not deluded by what is delusion-inducing, does not get angry at what is anger-inducing, is not intoxicated by what is intoxicating, and is not defiled by what is defiling. Having heard a sound with the ear... having known a mental object with the mind, he does not lust after what is lust-inducing, does not feel aversion toward what is aversion-inducing, is not deluded by what is delusion-inducing, does not get angry at what is anger-inducing, is not intoxicated by what is intoxicating, and is not defiled by what is defiling.

In the seen, there is only the seen; in the heard, there is only the heard; in the sensed, there is only the sensed; in the cognized, there is only the cognized. He is not smeared (by craving and views) in the seen, not smeared in the heard, not smeared in the sensed, and not smeared in the cognized. He is detached from the seen, has a mind free from ill-will, and does not rely on (craving and views)...
66:
One who is unattached, well-liberated, and disconnected dwells with a mind that has made away with boundaries. Regarding the heard... the sensed... the cognized, he is detached, free from ill-will, not relying on (craving and views), unattached, well-liberated, and disconnected, dwelling with a mind that has made away with boundaries.

The Blessed One has an eye; the Blessed One sees a form with the eye, but the Blessed One has no desire and lust; the Blessed One has a well-liberated mind. The Blessed One has an ear; the Blessed One hears a sound with the ear, but the Blessed One has no desire and lust; the Blessed One has a well-liberated mind. The Blessed One has a nose; the Blessed One smells an odor with the nose, but the Blessed One has no desire and lust; the Blessed One has a well-liberated mind. The Blessed One has a tongue; the Blessed One tastes a flavor with the tongue, but the Blessed One has no desire and lust; the Blessed One has a well-liberated mind. The Blessed One has a body; the Blessed One touches a tangible object with the body, but the Blessed One has no desire and lust; the Blessed One has a well-liberated mind. The Blessed One has a mind; the Blessed One cognizes a mental object with the mind, but the Blessed One has no desire and lust; the Blessed One has a well-liberated mind.

The eye delights in forms, rejoices in forms, and is gladdened by forms; that eye is tamed, guarded, protected, and restrained for the Blessed One, and he teaches the Dhamma for its restraint. The ear delights in sounds, rejoices in sounds... the nose delights in odors, rejoices in odors... the tongue delights in flavors, rejoices in flavors, and is gladdened by flavors; that tongue is tamed, guarded, protected, and restrained for the Blessed One, and he teaches the Dhamma for its restraint. The body delights in tangible objects, rejoices in tangible objects, and is gladdened by tangible objects... the mind delights in mental objects, rejoices in mental objects, and is gladdened by mental objects; that mind is tamed, guarded, protected, and restrained for the Blessed One, and he teaches the Dhamma for its restraint—

"The tamed they lead to the assembly; the king mounts the tamed. Among humans, the tamed is best, he who endures abusive words."

"Excellent are the tamed mules, and the noble Sindhu horses, and the great elephants of the Kuñjara breed; but more excellent than those is the one who has tamed himself."

"For not by these vehicles could one go to the unreached region (Nibbāna), as one who is well-tamed goes to it by his tamed self."
67:
They do not tremble in the three modes [of conceit]; they are liberated from renewed existence. Having reached the stage of the tamed, the Fruit of Arahantship, those Arahants are conquerors [of Māra] in the world.

For whom the faculties are developed, both internally and externally in the whole world; having understood this world and the next with penetrating knowledge, he who is tamed and has a developed mind awaits his time [of passing away].

Thus, the Blessed One has a developed mind.

"I regard you, O Blessed One, as a Vedagū (knower of the four truths) with a developed mind. From where have these sufferings arisen?" "From where?" (Kuto nu) is a question asked out of doubt, uncertainty, or hesitation—"Is it thus, or is it not thus? How is it? Why is it?" "Sufferings" (Dukkhā) refers to the suffering of birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, physical pain, mental grief, and despair; suffering due to ruin, suffering in hell, suffering in the animal realm, suffering in the realm of hungry ghosts, suffering in the human realm; suffering rooted in conception in the womb, staying in the womb, and emerging from the womb; suffering of being bound or oppressed after birth; suffering connected with others, suffering due to one's own effort, suffering due to others' effort; the suffering of pain (dukkha-dukkha), the suffering of formations (saṅkhāra-dukkha), and the suffering of change (vipariṇāma-dukkha).

[Diseases include]: Eye disease, ear disease, nose disease, tongue disease, body disease, head disease, ear-lobe disease, mouth disease, tooth disease, cough, asthma, catarrh, burning sensation, fever, stomach ache, fainting, dysentery, sharp pain, cholera, leprosy, boils, eczema, consumption, epilepsy, ringworm, itch, scabies, rashes, vitiligo, jaundice, diabetes, piles, pustules, fistula; diseases arising from bile, phlegm, or wind; diseases resulting from the conflict of the humors, from change of seasons, from improper care, from external attacks, or from the result of kamma.

[Other sufferings include]: Suffering from cold, heat, hunger, thirst, defecation, and urination; suffering from the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and reptiles; suffering from the death of a mother, father, brother, sister, son, or daughter; suffering from the loss of relatives, from disease, from the loss of wealth, from the loss of virtue, and from the loss of right view. The first appearance of these phenomena is evident, and their cessation through destruction is evident. Resultant (vipāka) arises depending on kamma; kamma arises depending on resultant. Form (rūpa) arises depending on mind (nāma).
68:
Mind arises depending on form. Birth follows; aging spreads; sickness overcomes; death oppresses. It stands in suffering; it is without protection, without shelter, without refuge, and cannot provide refuge—these are called sufferings. From where do these sufferings constantly arise? From where are they born? From where are they produced? Why do they arise through sense-objects? Why do they manifest? Why do they appear? What is their cause? What is their origin? What is their birth? What is their source? Thus he asks about the basis of these sufferings, their productive cause, their origin, their place of arising, their source, their cause of manifestation, their sustaining cause, their object, their condition, and their origin. He asks repeatedly, requests, urges, and expresses devotion—"From where have these sufferings arisen?"

In the phrase "Whatever various forms of suffering there are in the world": "Whatever" is a term that includes everything entirely, in every way, without exception, and exhaustively. "In the world" means in the world of hell, the human world, the deva world, the world of aggregates (khandha), the world of elements (dhātu), and the world of sense-bases (āyatana). "Various forms" means sufferings of many kinds and various aspects. Therefore, that brahmin Mettagū said this:

"I ask you, O Blessed One, please tell me this, [thus said the Venerable Mettagū]
I regard you as a Vedagū with a developed mind;
From where have these various forms of suffering in the world arisen?"

"Mettagū, you certainly ask me about the source of suffering, [thus said the Blessed One]
I will tell you that cause as I know it;
Whatever various forms of suffering there are in the world, they arise having acquisitions (upadhi) as their cause."

In the phrase "You certainly ask me about the source of suffering": "Of suffering" refers to the suffering of birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, physical pain, mental grief, and despair. "Ask about the source" means he asks about the basis of suffering, its productive cause, its manifesting cause, its origin, its source, its place of arising, its sustaining cause, its object, its condition, and its origin. He requests, urges, and expresses devotion. "Mettagū" is how the Blessed One addresses the brahmin by name.
69:
The name "Bhagavā" is a term of respect. ... By the name "Bhagavā," which is a designation realized [by him], the Blessed One addressed [himself] as "Mettagū."
