In the phrase "Taṃ te pavakkhāmi yathā pajānaṃ," "Taṃ" (that) refers to: I shall proclaim to you the root of suffering, I shall proclaim the cause, I shall proclaim the origin, I shall proclaim the source, I shall proclaim the beginning, I shall proclaim the starting point, I shall proclaim the nutriment, I shall proclaim the object, I shall proclaim the condition, I shall proclaim the arising; I shall tell, I shall teach, I shall describe, I shall establish, I shall reveal, I shall analyze, I shall make plain, I shall manifest—"Taṃ te pavakkhāmi" (I shall proclaim that to you).

"Yathā pajānaṃ" means knowing distinctly, knowing by way of perceiving the object, knowing specially, knowing again specially, as if knowing through penetration. I shall speak of that Dhamma which is not by hearsay, not by tradition, not by lineage, not by accordance with scriptures, not by logical reasoning, not by inference, not by reflecting on reasons, not by agreement through pondering views, but is self-known, self-realized, and personally witnessed.

In the phrase "Upadhinidānā pabhavanti dukkhā," there are ten acquisitions (upadhi). They are: the acquisition of craving (taṇhūpadhi), the acquisition of views (diṭṭhūpadhi), the acquisition of defilements (kilesūpadhi), the acquisition of kamma (kammūpadhi), the acquisition of misconduct (duccaritūpadhi), the acquisition of nutriment (āhārūpadhi), the acquisition of aversion (paṭighūpadhi), the four elements of clinging (upādinnadhātu), the six internal sense bases (ajjhattika āyatana), and the six classes of consciousness (viññāṇakāya). All suffering, in the sense of being painful, is also called upadhi. These are called the ten acquisitions. Suffering (dukkhā) refers to the suffering of birth, the suffering of aging, the suffering of sickness, the suffering of death, the suffering of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, the suffering of hell... the suffering due to the ruin of views. Those phenomena whose arising is known from the beginning, whose cessation through passing away is known, where result (vipāka) is dependent on kamma, kamma is dependent on result, matter (rūpa) is dependent on mind (nāma), mind is dependent on matter, followed by birth, pursued by aging, overwhelmed by sickness, struck by death, established in suffering, without protection, without shelter, without refuge, and unable to provide refuge—these are called sufferings. These sufferings have acquisitions as their source, acquisitions as their cause, acquisitions as their condition, and acquisitions as their reason; they arise, they appear, they are produced, they are born, they are generated, they are manifested—"Upadhinidānā pabhavanti dukkhā."

In the phrase "Ye keci lokasmiṃ anekarūpā," "Ye keci" is a term that includes everything in every way, without exception or remainder. "Lokasmiṃ" (in the world) means in the world of miserable realms, the human world, the deva world, the world of aggregates (khandha-loka),
70:
in the world of elements (dhātu-loka), and in the world of sense bases (āyatana-loka). "Anekarūpā" means many, of various kinds, and diverse sufferings—"Ye keci lokasmiṃ anekarūpā." Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"O Mettagū, you have indeed asked me about the origin of suffering.
I shall proclaim it to you as one who knows.
Whatever various forms of suffering there are in the world,
They arise with acquisitions (upadhi) as their source.
The ignorant one who creates acquisitions,
That dull-witted one undergoes suffering again and again.
Therefore, one who understands, seeing the birth and origin of suffering,
Should not create acquisitions."

Regarding "Yo ve avidvā upadhiṃ karoti": "Yo" refers to anyone, of such nature, appropriately joined, of such manner, of such kind, reached such a state, endowed with such qualities, whether a noble (khattiya), a brahmin, a merchant (vessa), a worker (sudda), a householder, a renunciant, a deva, or a human. "Avidvā" means one who is possessed of ignorance, lacking knowledge, lacking clear vision, and of weak wisdom. "Upadhiṃ karoti" means he creates the acquisition of craving, creates the acquisition of views, creates the acquisition of defilements, creates the acquisition of kamma, creates the acquisition of misconduct, creates the acquisition of nutriment, creates the acquisition of aversion, makes the four elements of clinging into acquisitions, makes the six internal sense bases into acquisitions, makes the six classes of consciousness into acquisitions; he generates, well-generates, produces, and specifically produces them—thus, "the ignorant one creates acquisitions."

Regarding "Punappunaṃ dukkhamupeti mando": "Punappunaṃ" means again and again. He undergoes, fully undergoes, approaches, takes up, wrongly touches, and repeatedly clings to the suffering of birth, the suffering of aging, the suffering of sickness, the suffering of death, and the suffering of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. "Mando" means one who is of weak wisdom, bewildered, ignorant, possessed of ignorance, lacking knowledge, lacking clear vision, and of weak wisdom. Thus, "the dull-witted one undergoes suffering again and again."

Regarding "Tasmā pajānaṃ upadhiṃ na kayirā": "Tasmā" means because of that reason, because of that cause, because of that condition, because of that source, seeing this danger in acquisitions—thus "tasmā." "Pajānaṃ" means knowing distinctly, knowing thoroughly, knowing specially, knowing again specially, knowing through penetration; knowing distinctly that "all conditioned things are impermanent (sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā)," knowing thoroughly, knowing specially, knowing again specially, knowing through penetration...
71:
One who understands through penetrating knowledge (paṭivijjanto) realizes: 'All formations are impermanent... All formations are suffering... All phenomena are non-self (anatta)... Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease.' By knowing through distinguishing, knowing completely, knowing specially, knowing specially once more, and knowing through penetration, one is 'one who penetrates' (paṭivijjanto).

'One should not create acquisitions (upadhi)' means one should not create the acquisition of craving, the acquisition of views, the acquisition of defilements, the acquisition of misconduct, the acquisition of nutriment, the acquisition of aversion, the acquisition of the four primary elements born of kamma, the acquisition of the six internal sense bases, or the acquisition of the six classes of consciousness. It means one should not generate, produce, or bring them into existence repeatedly. Therefore, one who understands should not create acquisitions.

'Suffering' (dukkha) refers to the suffering of birth, the suffering of aging, the suffering of sickness, the suffering of death, and the suffering of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. 'Contemplating the origin' (pabhavānupassī) means one who constantly contemplates the root cause, the reason, the source, the origin, the excessive cause, the place of arising, the conveyor, the object, the condition, and the emergence of suffering. This contemplation (anupassanā) is called wisdom (paññā). One who is endowed with this wisdom, clear understanding, non-delusion, investigation of states, and right view (sammā-diṭṭhi) is called 'one who contemplates the origin of the birth of suffering' (dukkhassa jātippabhavānupassī). Therefore, the Blessed One said:

'The ignorant one who, without knowing, creates acquisitions,
That fool encounters suffering again and again.
Therefore, one who understands, contemplating the origin of the birth of suffering,
Should not create acquisitions.'

'That matter which we asked about, you have explained to us; we ask you something else, please tell us that: How do the wise cross the flood, and birth, aging, sorrow, and lamentation? O Sage, please explain that well to me, for this Dhamma is known to you.'

'You have explained to us what we asked' means what we requested, entreated, and asked with devotion. 'Explained to us' means it has been told, declared, and taught to us.
72:
It has been made known, established, opened, analyzed, made clear, and manifested—this refers to: 'That matter which we asked about, you have explained to us.'

'We ask you something else, please tell us that' means we ask another matter, we entreat another matter, we request another matter, we seek another matter with devotion, we ask a further matter. 'Tadiṅgha brūhi' means: I entreat you, please speak, tell, teach, make known, establish, open, analyze, make clear, and manifest that matter. Thus: 'We ask you something else, please tell us that.'

'How do the wise cross the flood, and birth, aging, sorrow, and lamentation?' 'How' (kathaṃ nu) is a question of doubt, a question of uncertainty, a question of being at a crossroads, or a question of indecision—asking 'Is it thus?', 'Is it not so?', 'What is it?', 'How is it?'. 'The wise' (dhīrā) refers to those who are steadfast in the face of suffering, who are not heedless or elated by happiness, who seek the welfare of both the present and the future, who know their own benefit and the benefit of others, who penetrate deep meanings, who illuminate difficult causes and effects, and who are wise, pure, and balanced like a scale, free from defilements. 'The flood' (oghaṃ) refers to the flood of sensuality, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance. 'Birth' (jāti) refers to the birth, production, descent, arising, and repeated arising of various beings in various classes of beings, the manifestation of the aggregates (khandha), and the acquisition of the sense bases (āyatana). 'Aging' (jarā) refers to the aging, decrepitude, broken teeth, graying hair, wrinkling of skin, decline of life, and the ripening of the faculties of various beings in various classes of beings. 'Sorrow' (soko) refers to the sorrow, the act of sorrowing, the state of sorrowing, inner sorrow, inner intense sorrow, inner burning, inner intense burning, the distress of mind, grief, and the dart of sorrow in one who is touched by the loss of relatives, loss of wealth, affliction of disease, loss of virtue, loss of right view, or any other kind of loss or painful state. 'Lamentation' (paridevo) refers to the crying, wailing, the act of crying, the act of wailing, the state of crying and wailing, the speech of lamentation, useless talk, distorted talk, repeated wailing, the act of repeated wailing, and the state of repeated wailing in one who is touched by the loss of relatives, loss of wealth, affliction of disease, loss of virtue, loss of right view, or any other kind of loss or painful state.

'How do the wise cross the flood, and birth, aging, sorrow, and lamentation?' means: How do the wise cross over, get beyond, or transcend the flood, birth, aging, sorrow, and lamentation? Or, how do they transcend them by means of the Path of Stream-entry, the Path of Once-returning, the Path of Non-returning, and the Path of Arahatship?
73:
"Samatikkamanti" means they transcend or surmount. How do the wise transcend the flood [of saṃsāra], as well as birth, aging, sorrow, and lamentation?

O Sage (Muni), please explain this matter well to me. "Taṃ" refers to that which I ask, request, urge, and express confidence in. "Muni" refers to the wisdom called "mona". That wisdom is the act of knowing... (pe)... non-delusion, investigation of states (dhammavicaya), and right view (sammādiṭṭhi). The Blessed One is a Muni because he is endowed with that knowledge; he has attained sagehood (mona). There are three kinds of sagehood (moneyya): bodily sagehood, verbal sagehood, and mental sagehood.

What is bodily sagehood (kāyamoneyya)? The abandoning of the three types of bodily misconduct is bodily sagehood. The three types of bodily good conduct, knowledge having the body as its object, the full understanding of the body (kāyapariññā), the path associated with full understanding, the abandoning of desire and lust for the body, and the attainment of the fourth jhāna where bodily formations (in-breath and out-breath) cease—these are called bodily sagehood. This is bodily sagehood.

What is verbal sagehood (vacīmoneyya)? The abandoning of the four types of verbal misconduct is verbal sagehood. The four types of verbal good conduct, knowledge having speech as its object, the full understanding of speech (vācāpariññā), the path associated with full understanding, the abandoning of desire and lust for speech, and the attainment of the second jhāna where verbal formations (initial and sustained thought) cease—these are called verbal sagehood. This is verbal sagehood.

What is mental sagehood (manomoneyya)? The abandoning of the three types of mental misconduct is mental sagehood. The three types of mental good conduct, knowledge having the mind as its object, the full understanding of the mind (cittapariññā), the path associated with full understanding, the abandoning of desire and lust for the mind, and the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpatti) where mental formations (feeling and perception) cease—these are called mental sagehood. This is mental sagehood.

A sage of body, a sage of speech, a sage of mind free from taints,
Endowed with sagehood and having abandoned everything—him they call a sage.
A sage of body, a sage of speech, a sage of mind free from taints,
Endowed with sagehood and having washed away all evil—him they call a sage.
74:
There are six types of sages (munis) endowed with these three qualities of sagehood. They are: the householder sage (agāramuni), the homeless sage (anagāramuni), the sage in training (sekhamuni), the sage beyond training (asekhamuni), the solitary sage (paccekamuni), and the sage of sages (munimuni). 

What is a householder sage? Those householders who have seen the state [of Nibbāna] and understood the teaching (the three trainings)—these are householder sages. 

What is a homeless sage? Those who have gone forth (monks) who have seen the state and understood the teaching—these are homeless sages. 

The seven types of persons in training are sages in training (sekhamunis). 

Arahants are sages beyond training (asekhamunis). 

Paccekabuddhas are solitary sages (paccekamunis). 

Tathāgatas, Arahants, Fully Enlightened Buddhas are sages of sages (munimunis). 

Not by silence alone does one become a sage, if one is foolish and ignorant. 
But the wise man who, as if holding a scale, takes what is noble and avoids evils, 
By that avoidance, he is a sage; for that reason, he is a sage. 
He who knows both worlds is called a sage for that reason. 

Having known the states of the wicked and the states of the virtuous, internally and externally in the whole world, 
Transcending the net of craving and remaining firm, that sage is worthy of worship by gods and humans. 

"Explain well" means: please tell, teach, describe, establish, open, analyze, clarify, and manifest that matter. 

"For this Dhamma is known by you" means: this Dhamma has been known, weighed, investigated, manifested, and developed by you. 

Therefore, that brahmin said: 
'What we asked, you have told us; we ask another, please speak. How do the wise transcend the flood [of saṃsāra], as well as birth, aging, sorrow, and lamentation? O Sage, please explain this matter well to me, for this Dhamma is known by you in such a way.'
75:
Mettagū, I shall proclaim to you the Dhamma visible in this very life, not based on hearsay (but personally realized). Knowing which, one who wanders mindfully may cross over the craving that clings to the world.

'I shall proclaim to you the Dhamma' means— 'Dhamma' refers to the holy life (brahmacariya) that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, complete in meaning and phrasing, entirely perfect and pure; the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the Noble Eightfold Path, Nibbāna, and the practice leading to Nibbāna. I shall proclaim, tell, teach, make known, establish, open, analyze, clarify, and manifest it. This is the meaning of 'I shall proclaim to you the Dhamma.'

'Mettagū' is the Blessed One addressing that brahmin by name.

'Visible in this very life, not based on hearsay' means— 'Visible in this very life' refers to the Dhamma that is seen, known, weighed, investigated, manifested, and developed in the present—that 'all formations are impermanent' ... 'whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease.' In this way, I shall proclaim the Dhamma visible in this very life. Alternatively, when suffering is seen, I shall proclaim suffering; when the origin is seen, I shall proclaim the origin; when the path is seen, I shall proclaim the path; when cessation is seen, I shall proclaim cessation. In this way also, I shall proclaim the Dhamma visible in this very life. Alternatively, I shall proclaim the Dhamma that is visible (sandiṭṭhika), immediate (akālika), inviting one to come and see (ehipassika), worthy of application (opaneyyika), to be personally realized by the wise (paccattaṃ veditabbo viññūhi). This is the meaning of 'visible in this very life.'

'Not based on hearsay' means not by oral tradition, not by lineage of teaching, not by hearsay, not by collection of scriptures, not by logical reasoning, not by inference, not by reflection on appearances, not by acceptance of a view after pondering, but the Dhamma that is personally known and self-realized. I shall proclaim that—this is 'visible in this very life, not based on hearsay.'

'Knowing which, one who wanders mindfully' means— having known, weighed, investigated, developed, and manifested that Dhamma; having known, weighed, investigated, developed, and manifested that 'all formations are impermanent'; having known... that 'all formations are suffering' ... 'all phenomena are non-self' ... 'whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease.'

'Mindfully' means being mindful through four causes—developing the foundation of mindfulness of the body in the body... such a person is called mindful.
76:
Caraṃ (wandering) means practicing, living, moving, protecting, sustaining, and maintaining one's life. 'Knowing which, one who wanders mindfully' refers to this kind of practicing and living.

'May cross over the craving (visattikā) in the world': Craving is called visattikā. That craving is lust, intense lust, covetousness, greed, the unwholesome root. For what reason is it called visattikā? Because it spreads; because it is vast; because it is diffused; because it is uneven; because it moves about; because it brings suffering; because it is deceptive; because it is the basis of kamma that leads to suffering; because it yields painful results; because it is a poisonous enjoyment.

Alternatively, that craving is called visattikā because it spreads and expands through forms, sounds, smells, tastes, touches; through family, group, dwelling, gain, fame, praise, happiness, robes, alms-food, lodging, medicinal requisites; through the sense element, the fine-material element, the immaterial element; through the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, the sphere of perception, the sphere of non-perception, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the sphere of one constituent, the sphere of four constituents, the sphere of five constituents; through the past, future, and present; and through things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized.

'World' refers to the world of misery, the human world, the deva world, the world of aggregates, the world of elements, and the world of sense bases. 'May cross over the craving (visattikā) in the world' means that a mindful person should cross over, transcend, surmount, well-overcome, and specifically transcend that visattikā craving which exists in the world. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

'Mettagū, I shall proclaim to you the Dhamma visible in this very life, not based on hearsay. Knowing which, one who wanders mindfully may cross over the craving in the world.'

'I rejoice in that supreme Dhamma, O Great Seer (Mahesī), knowing which, one who wanders mindfully may cross over the craving in the world.'

'I rejoice in that Dhamma' means— 'that' refers to your words, speech, teaching, instruction, and advice. 'I rejoice' means I delight in, approve of, desire, enjoy, request, long for, cherish, and intensely aspire to.

In the phrase 'Mahesi dhammamuttamaṃ,' 'Mahesī' means the Blessed One is called a Great Seer because he seeks the great aggregate of virtue, and because he seeks benefits. He is called a Great Seer because he knows and seeks the aggregates of virtue, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. He is called a Great Seer because he seeks the knowledge (vijjā) that destroys ignorance (avijjā), and because he seeks the destruction of defilements through the insight of the Four Noble Truths.
77:
In the phrase "Mahesi dhamm-m-uttamaṃ," what is meant by "Mahesi"? The Blessed One is called "Mahesi" because he sought, searched, and repeatedly looked for the great aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha). He is called "Mahesi" because he sought, searched, and repeatedly looked for the great aggregate of concentration... the great aggregate of wisdom... the great aggregate of liberation... the great aggregate of knowledge and vision of liberation.

He is called "Mahesi" because he sought, searched, and repeatedly looked for the breaking of the great mass of darkness (ignorance). He is called "Mahesi" because he sought, searched, and repeatedly looked for the destruction of great perversion. He is called "Mahesi" because he sought, searched, and repeatedly looked for the removal of the great dart of craving. He is called "Mahesi" because he sought, searched, and repeatedly looked for the disentangling of the great mass of views. He is called "Mahesi" because he sought, searched, and repeatedly looked for the casting down of the great banner of conceit. He is called "Mahesi" because he sought, searched, and repeatedly looked for the calming of great volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra). He is called "Mahesi" because he sought, searched, and repeatedly looked for the crossing of the great flood (ogha). He is called "Mahesi" because he sought, searched, and repeatedly looked for the laying down of the great burden. He is called "Mahesi" because he sought, searched, and repeatedly looked for the cutting off of the great cycle of saṃsāra. He is called "Mahesi" because he sought, searched, and repeatedly looked for the extinguishing of the great heat. He is called "Mahesi" because he sought, searched, and repeatedly looked for the complete calming of the great fever. He is called "Mahesi" because he sought, searched, and repeatedly looked for the raising of the great banner of Dhamma.

He is called "Mahesi" because he sought, searched, and repeatedly looked for the great foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna)... the great right efforts (sammappadhāna)... the great bases of power (iddhipāda)... the great faculties (indriya)... the great powers (bala)... the great factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga)... the great Noble Eightfold Path... the great ultimate reality, the deathless Nibbāna. Alternatively, he is called "Mahesi" because he is sought, searched, and repeatedly looked for by beings of great power, who ask: "Where is the Buddha? Where is the Blessed One? Where is the God of gods? Where is the Bull among men?"

"Dhamma-m-uttamaṃ" refers to the deathless Nibbāna. That Dhamma is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna. "Uttamaṃ" means the highest, the most excellent, the specially noble, the foremost, the supreme Dhamma; thus it is said, "Mahesi dhamma-m-uttamaṃ."

"Yaṃ viditvā sato caranti" means having known, weighed, investigated, developed, and made manifest (that Dhamma). Having known, weighed, investigated, developed, and made manifest that "all formations are impermanent"; having known, weighed, investigated, developed, and made manifest that "all formations are suffering"... "all dhammas are non-self"... "whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease." "Sato" means being mindful through four causes: in the body...
78:
One who is mindful while developing the mindfulness of the body (kāyānupassanā satipaṭṭhāna), one who is mindful while developing the mindfulness of feelings... of the mind... of dhammas, is called "sato" (mindful). "Caranti" means practicing, living, maintaining the postures, guarding, sustaining, and continuing. "Yaṃ viditvā sato caranti" means practicing with mindfulness after knowing that Dhamma.

"Visattikā" refers to craving (taṇhā). It is that lust, intense greed... covetousness, the unwholesome root of greed. Why is it called "visattikā"? It is called "visattikā" because it is pervasive (visata) and extensive (vitthata). "Loke" refers to the world, from the world of woe to the world of sense bases. "Tare loke visattikaṃ" means that one should cross over this craving in the world while being mindful; one should cross over by the path of stream-entry, by the path of once-returning, by the path of non-returning, and by the path of arahantship. Therefore, that Brahmin said:

"O Great Seeker, I greatly delight in that supreme Dhamma,
Knowing which, and practicing with mindfulness, one can cross over craving in the world."

The Blessed One said:
"Mettagū, you know all things well in the upper, lower, and middle.
Having dispelled delight and attachment in those things, and also consciousness, one should not remain in existence."

"Yaṃ kiñci sampajānāsi" means knowing all things generally, knowing thoroughly, knowing specifically, and knowing penetratively. The Blessed One addressed that Brahmin by name as "Mettagū." "Bhagavā" is a term of respect... it is a realized designation, namely "Bhagavā."

"Uddhaṃ adho tiriyañcāpi majjhe": "Uddhaṃ" (above) refers to the future; "adho" (below) refers to the past; "tiriyañcāpi majjhe" (across and in the middle) refers to the present. "Uddhaṃ" is the deva world; "adho" is the hell world; "tiriyañcāpi majjhe" is the human world. Alternatively, "uddhaṃ" refers to wholesome dhammas; "adho" refers to unwholesome dhammas; "tiriyañcāpi majjhe" refers to indeterminate (abyākata) dhammas. "Uddhaṃ" is the formless realm (arūpadhātu); "adho" is the sense realm (kāmadhātu); "tiriyañcāpi majjhe" is the fine-material realm (rūpadhātu). "Uddhaṃ" is pleasant feeling; "adho" is painful feeling; "tiriyañcāpi majjhe" is neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling. "Uddhaṃ" also means upwards from the soles of the feet.
79:
"Below" means the part below the tips of the hair. "In the middle" means the center. These are the meanings of above, below, and in the middle (everywhere).

In the phrase "In these, having dispelled delight and settling, let consciousness not stand in existence," "in these" (etesu) refers to the dhammas that have been taught, shown, declared, established, opened, analyzed, clarified, and made manifest. "Delight" (nandī) is said to be craving (taṇhā). It refers to the unwholesome root of greed, such as lust, passion, covetousness, and greed. "Settling" (nivesana) is of two kinds: settling through craving (taṇhā-nivesana) and settling through views (diṭṭhi-nivesana). Settling through craving is the mental adherence and attachment known as craving. Settling through views is the wrong view such as the self-identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) consisting of twenty bases, and so forth.

"Dispelling consciousness" (panujja viññāṇaṃ) refers to consciousness associated with meritorious formations, consciousness associated with demeritorious formations, and consciousness associated with imperturbable formations. In those dhammas, one should dispel, thoroughly dispel, pluck out, abandon, remove, eliminate, and bring to non-existence craving, views, and consciousness associated with volitional formations. Thus, it is said: "In these, having dispelled delight and settling, let consciousness [not stand in existence]."

In the phrase "Let it not stand in existence" (bhave na tiṭṭhe), existence is of two kinds: action-existence (kammabhava) and rebirth-existence (punabbhava). What is action-existence? Meritorious formations, demeritorious formations, and imperturbable formations—this is action-existence. What is rebirth-existence? The form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness that arise at rebirth—this is rebirth-existence. Because one abandons, removes, eliminates, and brings to non-existence craving, views, consciousness associated with volitional formations, action-existence, and rebirth-existence, one would not stand in action-existence, nor stand or remain in rebirth-existence. Thus, it is said: "Having dispelled consciousness, let it not stand in existence." Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"Whatever you cognize, [Mettagū, said the Blessed One,]
Above, below, and in the middle,
In these, having dispelled delight and settling,
Let consciousness not stand in existence."

Dwelling thus, mindful, and heedful,
A monk, wandering, having given up possessiveness,
Understanding birth, aging, sorrow, and lamentation,
Should abandon suffering right here in this life.

"Dwelling thus" (evaṃvihārī) refers to one who dwells abandoning and removing craving, views, consciousness associated with volitional formations, action-existence, and rebirth-existence. "Mindful" (sato) refers to one who is mindful through the four foundations of mindfulness, one who develops the foundation of mindfulness regarding contemplation of the body. "Heedful" (appamatto) refers to one who acts constantly, respectfully, firmly, and without shrinking in wholesome states; one who fulfills the unfulfilled aggregate of virtue, and the fulfilled aggregate of virtue...
80:
Dwelling thus, being mindful, and being heedful means: "One who dwells thus" refers to one who dwells abandoning, removing, eliminating, and bringing to non-existence craving, views, consciousness associated with volitional formations, action-existence, and rebirth-existence. "Mindful" refers to one who is mindful through four reasons, such as developing the foundation of mindfulness regarding contemplation of the body; such a person is called mindful. "Heedful" refers to one who acts respectfully, constantly, and firmly, with unshrinking conduct, unflagging desire, and unrelaxed effort in wholesome states. Thinking, "How shall I fulfill the unfulfilled aggregate of virtue? How shall I support the fulfilled aggregate of virtue with wisdom in various places?" the desire, effort, exertion, intense endeavor, perseverance, mindfulness, clear comprehension, ardor, prominence, resolution, and application that arise therein are called "heedfulness" (appamāda) in wholesome states. Thinking, "How shall I fulfill the unfulfilled aggregate of concentration... aggregate of wisdom... aggregate of liberation... aggregate of knowledge and vision of liberation? How shall I support the fulfilled aggregate of knowledge and vision of liberation with wisdom in various places?" the desire, effort, exertion, intense endeavor, perseverance, mindfulness, clear comprehension, ardor, prominence, resolution, and application that arise therein are called "heedfulness" in wholesome states. Thinking, "How shall I fully understand the Truth of Suffering which is not yet fully understood? How shall I abandon the defilements which are not yet abandoned? How shall I develop the Path which is not yet developed? How shall I realize the Truth of Cessation which is not yet realized?" the desire, effort, exertion, intense endeavor, perseverance, mindfulness, clear comprehension, ardor, prominence, resolution, and application that arise therein are called "heedfulness" in wholesome states. Thus, one is a person who dwells thus, is mindful, and is heedful.

"A monk, wandering, having given up possessiveness" means: "Monk" refers to a virtuous ordinary person or a trainee monk (sekha). "Wandering" means living, moving, proceeding, maintaining, and sustaining. "Possessiveness" (mamatā) is of two kinds: craving-possessiveness and view-possessiveness... this is craving-possessiveness... this is view-possessiveness. Having abandoned craving-possessiveness, having relinquished view-possessiveness, having given up, let go of, abandoned, removed, eliminated, and brought to non-existence all forms of possessiveness—this is the meaning of "A monk, wandering, having given up possessiveness."
81:
The wise one should abandon birth, aging, sorrow, and lamentation even in this Dispensation; he should abandon suffering. 'Birth' (jāti) means the birth of various beings... etc. 'Aging' (jarā) means the aging of various beings... etc. 'Sorrow' (soka) means the sorrow of one touched by the loss of relatives, etc... etc. 'Lamentation' (parideva) means the crying out of one touched by the loss of relatives, etc... etc. 'Here' (idha) means in this view... etc., in this human world. 'The wise one' (vidvā) means one who has attained knowledge, one who is wise, discerning, and intelligent. 'Suffering' (dukkha) means the suffering of birth... etc., the suffering of displeasure and despair. The one who has attained knowledge, who is wise, discerning, and intelligent, should abandon, dispel, eliminate, and bring to non-existence birth, aging, sorrow, lamentation, and suffering even in this Dispensation. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

'A bhikkhu living thus, mindful and diligent, wandering and having abandoned possessiveness, would abandon birth, aging, sorrow, and lamentation; even here, the wise one would abandon suffering.'

'I greatly rejoice in these words of the Great Seer, well-proclaimed by Gotama, leading to the end of acquisitions. Indeed, the Blessed One has abandoned suffering, for thus this Dhamma is known by you.'

'Etābhinandāmi vaco mahesino' means: I rejoice, greatly rejoice, delight, appreciate, desire, enjoy, long for, cherish, and speak with longing for these words, utterances, teachings, instructions, and advice of yours. 'Mahesino': Why is the Blessed One called 'Mahesi'? He sought, searched for, and pursued the great aggregate of virtue... etc. Where is the Bull among men? Thus he is sought; therefore, he is called 'Mahesi'. This is the meaning of the phrase 'Etābhinandāmi vaco mahesino'.

'Sukittitaṃ gotamanūpadhikaṃ': 'Sukittitaṃ' means well-proclaimed, well-told, well-taught, well-appointed, well-established, well-opened, well-analyzed, well-clarified, and well-manifested. In the phrase 'gotamanūpadhikaṃ', 'acquisitions' (upadhi) refers to defilements, aggregates, and volitional formations. O Gotama, O Blessed One, you have well-proclaimed the deathless Nibbāna, which is the abandoning of acquisitions, the stilling of acquisitions, the relinquishing of acquisitions, and the complete tranquilizing of acquisitions.
82:
'Indeed, the Blessed One has abandoned suffering' means: The word 'addhā' is a word of certainty, a word of no doubt, a word of no hesitation, a word of no ambiguity, a word of no duality, a word of excluding other doubts, a word of determination, and a word of permanent establishment. 'Bhagavā' is a term of respect... the realization-based designation is 'Bhagavā'. 'Has abandoned suffering' means he has abandoned, relinquished, dispelled, eliminated, and brought to non-existence the suffering of birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair. Therefore, it is said, 'Indeed, the Blessed One has abandoned suffering.'

'For thus this Dhamma is known by you' means: It is true; in that way (by which you have made us know), you have known, weighed, investigated, clarified, and developed this Dhamma. Therefore, it is said, 'For thus this Dhamma is known by you.' Thus that brahmin addressed the Buddha:

'I greatly rejoice in these words of the Great Seer; Gotama has well-proclaimed the Dhamma of Nibbāna, free from acquisitions.
Indeed, the Blessed One has abandoned suffering, for thus this Dhamma is known by you.
O Sage, those whom you would respectfully advise, they too would surely abandon suffering.
O Noble One (Nāga) who has conquered the enemies, I approach and pay homage to you; may the Blessed One also respectfully advise me.'

'They too would surely abandon suffering' means: 'They too' refers to nobles, brahmins, merchants, workers, householders, monastics, devas, and humans. 'Would abandon suffering' means they would relinquish, dispel, eliminate, and bring to non-existence the suffering of birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair. Therefore, it is said, 'They too would surely abandon suffering.'

'Those whom you would respectfully advise' means: 'Those whom' refers to nobles, brahmins, merchants, workers, householders, monastics, devas, and humans. 'You' refers to the Blessed One. 'Muni': Knowledge is called 'mona'... because he has transcended the net of craving and views, he is called a 'Muni'. 'Would respectfully advise' means would advise with respect, would advise with honor, would advise continuously, would advise repeatedly, and would instruct. Therefore, it is said, 'Those whom you would respectfully advise.'

'O Noble One who has conquered the enemies, I approach and pay homage to you' means: 'To you' refers to the Blessed One. 'I pay homage' means I pay homage with the body, with speech, with the mind, with practice that follows the goal, and with practice in accordance with the supramundane Dhamma; I respect, honor, and cherish.
83:
I worship [the Buddha] with practice that follows the benefit, and with practice that is in accordance with the Supramundane Dhamma. I pay respect, I revere, I honor, and I offer puja. 'Sameticca' means having known and understood, having penetrated and realized, having reached and approached closely, I worship that Blessed One in His presence. 'Nāga' means: He is called 'Nāga' because the Blessed One does not commit evil; He is called 'Nāga' because He does not go [to wrong paths]; He is called 'Nāga' because He does not return [to abandoned defilements].

How is the Blessed One called 'Nāga' because He does not commit evil? Evil, unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, causing distress, resulting in suffering, and leading to future birth, aging, and death are called 'āgu'.

(Sabhīya, the Blessed One)
Does not commit even a slight evil in the world,
Having released the bonds in all yokes,
He is not attached to anything, being liberated,
Because He is such and possesses such qualities, He is called 'Nāga'.

In this way, the Blessed One is called 'Nāga' because He does not commit evil.

How is the Blessed One called 'Nāga' because He does not go? The Blessed One does not go to the path of desire (chandāgati), He does not go to the path of hatred (dosāgati), He does not go to the path of delusion (mohāgati), He does not go to the path of fear (bhayāgati). He does not go by the power of lust, He does not go by the power of hatred, He does not go by the power of delusion, He does not go by the power of conceit, He does not go by the power of views, He does not go by the power of restlessness, He does not go by the power of doubt, He does not go by the power of underlying tendencies. He is not pulled, led, carried away, or swept away by partisan states. In this way, the Blessed One is called 'Nāga' because He does not go.

How is the Blessed One called 'Nāga' because He does not return? Those defilements which have been abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry, He does not go back to them, does not approach them, does not return to them. Those defilements which have been abandoned by the Path of Once-returner... the Path of Non-returner... the Path of Arahantship, He does not go back to them, does not approach them, does not return to them. In this way, the Blessed One is called 'Nāga' because He does not return. I worship that Blessed One, the 'Nāga', in His presence.

May the Blessed One surely admonish me while I am steadfast; may He admonish me respectfully; may He admonish me constantly; may He admonish and give me advice again and again. Therefore, that brahmin said—
84:
“Those whom you, O Sage, would admonish while they are steadfast, they would surely abandon suffering. I approach and worship that Nāga (the Noble One); may the Blessed One also admonish me, who am steadfast.”

“The Brāhmaṇa whom one should know as a Vedagū (one who has reached the end of knowledge), as one without impediments, and as one unattached to the realm of sensual existence—he has indeed crossed over this flood; having reached the other shore, he is without harshness and without doubt.”

In the phrase, “The Brāhmaṇa whom one should know as a Vedagū”: He is called a Brāhmaṇa because he has cast away seven things. Self-view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) is cast away, doubt (vicikicchā) is cast away, adherence to rites and rituals (sīlabbataparāmāsa) is cast away, lust is cast away, hatred is cast away, delusion is cast away, and conceit is cast away. For him, evil, unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, causing distress, resulting in suffering, and leading to future birth, aging, and death are cast away.

The Blessed One said: “Sabhīya, one who has cast away all evils, who is stainless, whose mind is well-concentrated and who is self-steadfast, who has transcended the round of rebirths and has completed all tasks, who is unattached to craving and views, and who is endowed with the quality of suchness—he is called a Brāhmaṇa.”

Regarding 'Vedagū': Knowledge in the four paths is called 'Veda'. ... He is called 'Vedagū' because he stands having transcended all Vedas. 'Abhijaññā' means to know thoroughly, to understand, to distinguish, to know repeatedly, and to penetrate.

In the phrase, “One without impediments and unattached to the realm of sensual existence”: 'Akiñcana' refers to one who is without the 'impediments' (kiñcana) of lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, views, defilements, and misconduct. For whom these impediments are abandoned, cut off at the root, calmed, tranquilized, made incapable of arising again, and burnt by the fire of knowledge—he is called 'Akiñcana' (one without impediments). Sensual pleasures (kāma) are of two kinds in brief: objective sensuality (vatthukāma) and defilement sensuality (kilesakāma). ... These are called objective sensuality. ... These are called defilement sensuality. Existences (bhava) are of two kinds: existence as action (kamma-bhava) and existence as rebirth (paṭisandhika-bhava).
85:
Renewed existence (punabbhava) means... this is the renewed existence that involves rebirth. "One who is without possessions and unattached in the realm of sensual existence" means a person who has no possessions in the realm of sensual existence, who is not clinging, not particularly attached, not repeatedly bound, who has emerged, is released, is liberated in various ways, is well-detached, and lives with a mind that has no boundaries—thus, he is one who is without possessions and unattached in the realm of sensual existence.

"He has indeed crossed over this flood"—here, "addhā" is a word expressing certainty. (p). This word "addhā" is a word expressing established permanence. "Flood" (ogha) refers to the flood of sensuality, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance. "Crossed over" means he has transcended by the first path, transcended by the path of Once-returning, transcended by the path of Non-returning, and transcended by the path of Arahantship—thus, he has indeed crossed over this flood.

"One who has crossed over, reached the far shore, is free from thorns, and free from doubt"—here, "one who has crossed over" means he has crossed the flood of sensuality by the path of Arahantship, crossed the flood of existence by the path of Non-returning, crossed the journey of views by the path of Stream-entry, crossed the flood of ignorance by the path of Arahantship, and crossed the journey of the continuous occurrence of the aggregates and elements known as saṃsāra by the path of Arahantship; he has crossed over by the path of Stream-entry, crossed over by the path of Once-returning, transcended by the path of Non-returning, well-transcended by the path of Arahantship, and completely transcended by the path of Arahantship. He is one who has lived the holy life, completed the conduct, finished the journey, reached the destination, reached the end, guarded the holy life, attained the supreme view, developed the path, abandoned the defilements, realized the unshakable fruition, and realized Nibbāna. For him, suffering has been fully understood, the origin has been abandoned, the path has been developed, and cessation has been realized. What should be known by higher knowledge has been known; what should be fully understood has been understood; what should be abandoned has been abandoned; what should be developed has been developed; and what should be realized has been realized.

He is one who has lifted the crossbar, filled the trench of unmixed sensual requisites, pulled up the pillar of craving, unbolted the door of the noble path, is a noble one (ariya) who is pure due to the absence of defilements, has lowered the banner of conceit, has laid down the burden of the aggregates, is detached from defilements, has abandoned the five factors such as sensual desire, is endowed with the six factors, has the single guard of supreme mindfulness, has the four supports such as reflection through wisdom, has dispelled individual truths, has well-relinquished longing and searching, has pure thoughts, has calmed bodily formations, has a mind well-liberated from defilements, has good wisdom liberated from defilements, is consummate in all qualities of a virtuous person, has lived the supreme holy life, is a supreme person, a great man, and has reached the attainment of Arahantship which is the supreme benefit. He neither accumulates nor diminishes the results of wholesome and unwholesome deeds; he stands having diminished them. He neither abandons nor clings to defilements; he stands having abandoned them. He does not scatter through defilements nor gather through pride; he stands having scattered them. He neither extinguishes nor kindles the fire of defilements; he stands having extinguished it. He stands because he is endowed with the aggregate of virtue of an adept (asekha). He stands because he is endowed with the aggregate of concentration... (p)... the aggregate of wisdom... the aggregate of liberation... and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation of an adept. He stands having well-fulfilled the Four Noble Truths. He stands having well-transcended the agitation of craving. He stands having extinguished the fire of defilements. He stands in the state of not returning. How does he stand having well-taken [his stand]? He stands by means of enjoying the attainment of fruition, being liberated from defilements.
86:
He stands firm. He is established in purity through loving-kindness. He is established in purity through compassion... sympathetic joy... equanimity. He is established by reaching the end of ultimate purity. He is established in purity through non-identification (freedom from craving and conceit). He is established by being liberated. He is established by being content. He is established at the end of the aggregates. He is established at the end of the elements. He is established at the end of the sense bases. He is established at the end of the destinations. He is established at the end of rebirth. He is established at the end of conception. He is established at the end of existence. He is established at the end of the round of rebirths. He is established at the end of the cycle. He is established in his final existence. He is established in his final body. He is an Arahant bearing his last body.

For this Arahant, this is the last birth, this is the final body; for him who has ended the round of birth and death, there is no further becoming.

In the phrase "Crossed over to the other shore" (Tiṇṇo ca pāraṃ), "the other shore" (pāra) refers to the deathless Nibbāna. That Nibbāna is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, and cessation. He has gone to the other shore, reached the other shore, gone to the end, reached the end, gone to the summit, reached the summit, gone to the limit, reached the limit, gone to the finish, reached the finish, gone to safety, reached safety, gone to the shelter, reached the shelter, gone to the refuge, reached the refuge, gone to the fearless state, reached the fearless state, gone to the unshakable, reached the unshakable, gone to the deathless, reached the deathless, gone to Nibbāna, reached Nibbāna. He is one who has lived the life, whose conduct is perfected... (ellipsis)... for him who has ended the round of birth and death, there is no further becoming—this is the meaning of "crossed over to the other shore."

"Free from thorns" (Akhilo) means the absence of the thorn of lust, the thorn of hatred, the thorn of delusion, the thorn of anger, the thorn of malice... and all unwholesome volitional formations which are thorns. He for whom these thorns are abandoned, cut off at the root, calmed, tranquilized, made incapable of arising, and burnt by the fire of knowledge, is called "free from thorns."

"Free from doubt" (Akaṅkho) means the absence of doubt regarding the truth of suffering, doubt regarding the origin of suffering, doubt regarding the cessation of suffering, doubt regarding the path leading to the cessation of suffering, doubt regarding the past, doubt regarding the future, doubt regarding both the past and the future, and doubt regarding states that are dependently arisen through specific conditionality. Such doubt, the act of doubting, the state of being doubtful, perplexity, skepticism, indecision, a fork in the road, uncertainty, taking various views, wavering, mental agitation, inability to penetrate with knowledge, trembling of the mind, and mental scratching—he for whom these doubts are abandoned, cut off at the root, calmed, tranquilized, made incapable of arising, and burnt by the fire of knowledge...
87:
...is called "one free from doubt" (akaṅkho). Thus he is: "Crossed over to the other shore, free from thorns, free from doubt." Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“The Brahmin who is known as a Vedagū, who has nothing, unattached to the world of sense-desires and existence; he has indeed crossed this flood, crossed to the other shore, free from thorns, free from doubt.”

“The wise man who is a Vedagū here, having abandoned this bond (agitation) in existence great and small, is free from craving, free from distress, free from longing; I say he has crossed birth and aging.”

In the phrase “The wise man who is a Vedagū here”: “Wise” (vidvā) means one who possesses clear vision, is knowledgeable, discerning, and wise. “Who” (yo) refers to any person... whether human (or celestial). “Vedagū” refers to the knowledge, wisdom, faculty of wisdom, power of wisdom, investigation of states enlightenment factor, scrutiny, insight, and right view regarding the four paths, which are called “Vedas.” One who, through these “Vedas” (knowledges), has gone to the end of birth, aging, and death, reached the summit, reached the limit, reached the finish, reached safety, reached the shelter, reached the refuge, reached the fearless state, reached the unshakable (Nibbāna), reached the deathless, and reached Nibbāna.

Alternatively, he is a “Vedagū” because he has reached the end of the Vedas, or because he has reached the end (of suffering) through the Vedas (knowledges), or because seven things are known (vidita) by him. Personality belief (sakkāya-diṭṭhi) is known by him; doubt, wrong grasp of rules and observances, lust, hatred, delusion, and conceit are known by him. Evil, unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and leading to birth, aging, and death in the future, are known by him.

The Blessed One said in the Sabhiya Sutta: “Having investigated all the Vedas (knowable things) of recluses and brahmins that exist here; free from passion for all feelings, having transcended all Vedas (knowable things), he is a Vedagū.”
88:
"Naro" means a being, a man, a male, a person, a living being, a creature, a human. "Idha" means in this doctrine... in this world of humans. The meaning is: "In this Dispensation, there is a wise person, a knower (vedagū)."

"Bhavābhave saṅgamimaṃ visajja" means having abandoned this attachment in various states of existence, both great and small. "Bhavābhave" means in various states of existence, both great and small; kamma-existence and rebirth-existence; in the sense sphere, kamma-existence and rebirth-existence; in the fine-material sphere, kamma-existence and rebirth-existence; in the immaterial sphere, kamma-existence and rebirth-existence; repeated existence, repeated destiny, repeated rebirth, repeated conception, and the repeated arising of selfhood. "Saṅgā" refers to the seven attachments: the attachment of lust, the attachment of hatred, the attachment of delusion, the attachment of pride, the attachment of views, the attachment of defilements, and the attachment of misconduct. "Visajja" means having thoroughly abandoned or released the attachments. Alternatively, it means having severed or released the bonds known as attachment, fetters, close bonds, various bonds, clinging, and firm ties. For example, just as one prepares or dismantles a vehicle, a carriage, a chariot, a cart, or a palanquin, even so, having thoroughly abandoned or released those attachments; or having severed the bonds of attachment, fetters, close bonds, various bonds, clinging, and firm ties—this is the meaning of "Abandon this attachment in various states of existence."

In the phrase "He is free from craving, free from distress, free from longing; I say he has crossed over birth and old age," "Taṇhā" (craving) refers to craving for forms and so on, up to craving for mental objects. For whomsoever this craving is abandoned, uprooted, calmed, extinguished, made incapable of arising again, and consumed by the fire of knowledge, he is called one who is free from craving, one who has gone beyond craving, one who has relinquished craving, one who has vomited craving, one who is liberated from craving, one who has abandoned craving, one who has cast away craving, one who is free from lust, one who has relinquished lust, one who has abandoned lust, one who has cast away lust, one who is without hunger, one who is extinguished, one who has become cool, one who experiences happiness, and one who dwells with a mind that has become sublime. Thus, "He is free from craving."

"Anīgho" means: lust is distress (nīgha), hatred is distress, delusion is distress, anger is distress, enmity is distress... all unwholesome formations are distresses. For whomsoever these distresses are abandoned, uprooted, calmed, extinguished, made incapable of arising again, and consumed by the fire of knowledge, he is called "free from distress" (anīgha).

"Nirāso": Craving is called "āsā" (longing). Whatever lust, intense passion... covetousness (abhijjhā), greed, or unwholesome root exists—for whomsoever this longing of craving is abandoned, uprooted, calmed, extinguished, made incapable of arising again, and consumed by the fire of knowledge, he is called "free from longing" (nirāsa).

"Jāti" means the obtaining of the sense bases... of various beings. "Jarā" means of those various...
89:
Of beings ... there is also the maturation of the faculties. This is called old age. That person who is free from craving, free from suffering, free from longing, has crossed over birth and old age, I say—this means: whoever is free from craving, and is free from the distress and suffering of passion and so forth, and is free from longing, that person has indeed crossed over birth, old age, and death; has transcended, has gone beyond, has overcome. I say, I declare, I teach, I describe, I establish, I reveal, I analyze, I clarify, I manifest—this is what is meant. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'The man who is wise, a master of knowledge (vedagū) here, having abandoned this attachment to existence and non-existence, he is free from craving, free from suffering, free from longing; he, I say, has crossed over birth and old age.' At the end of the verse ... 'Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is my teacher, I am the disciple,' he said.

## Exposition of the Questions of the Young Man Mettagū is finished. (Fourth)

## 5. Exposition of the Questions of the Young Man Dhotaka

Blessed One, I ask you, please tell me this, [thus the venerable Dhotaka spoke]: I long for your words, O Great Seer (Mahesi). Having heard your voice, I would train for my own Nibbāna.

'I ask you, please tell me this'—'I ask' refers to the three kinds of questions: the question to clarify what is unknown, the question to compare what is seen, and the question to cut off doubt... these three... the question about Nibbāna. 'I ask you' means I question you, I entreat you, I urge you, I place my faith in you; please speak to me—this is what is meant. 'Bhagavā' is a title of respect... it is a designation realized [by him]. 'Please tell me this' means tell me, declare to me, teach me, describe to me, establish for me, reveal to me, analyze for me, clarify for me, manifest to me.

'Thus the venerable Dhotaka'—'Iccā' is a conjunction of words... 'Āyasmā' is a term of endearment, a term of respect, a designation used with reverence and deference. 'Dhotaka' is the name, appellation, designation, description, expression, name, naming, naming-process, utterance, making, and speaking of that brahmin.
90:
In the phrase "Iccāyasmā Dhotako", "icca" is a conjunction of words. "Āyasmā" is a term of endearment, honor, and respect. The name, appellation, designation, common usage, naming, philology, expression, and utterance of that Brahmin is "Dhotaka".

"Vācābhikaṅkhāmi mahesi tuyhaṃ" means: I long for, greatly long for, desire, take pleasure in, yearn for, love, and intensely seek your word, utterance, teaching, instruction, and advice. Why is the Blessed One called "Mahesi"? Because the Blessed One seeks, searches for, and explores the great aggregate of virtue and other qualities, He is called "Mahesi". ... Because He is sought after as the best among men, He is called "Mahesi". "Vācābhikaṅkhāmi mahesi tuyhaṃ" means I long for your word.

"Tava sutvāna nigghosaṃ" means: having heard, listened to with the ear-consciousness, well-grasped, firmly retained, and well-noted your word, utterance, teaching, instruction, and advice.

In the phrase "Sikkhe nibbānamattano", "sikkhā" refers to the three trainings: the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā), the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā), and the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā). ... This is the training in higher wisdom. "Nibbānamattano" means for the quenching of one's own lust, for the quenching of hatred, for the quenching of delusion, for the quenching of anger, for the quenching of malice ... for the calming, the complete calming, the cessation, the quenching, the relinquishing, and the tranquility of all unwholesome formations (saṅkhāra), one should train in higher virtue, one should train in higher mind, and one should train in higher wisdom. One should train while reflecting on these three trainings, while knowing, while seeing, while contemplating, while exerting the mind, while being resolved with faith, while upholding energy, while establishing mindfulness, while concentrating the mind, while understanding with wisdom, while fully knowing what should be fully known, while comprehending what should be comprehended, while abandoning what should be abandoned, while developing what should be developed, while realizing what should be realized; one should practice, follow, and undertake them.

Therefore, that young Brahmin Dhotaka said:
"I ask you, O Blessed One, tell me this, [thus said the venerable Dhotaka],
I long for your speech, O Great Seer;
Having heard your sound, I shall train for my own quenching."
91:
Dhotaka, if that is so, then exert yourself;
Being wise and mindful right here in this Dispensation,
Having heard the voice of the Buddha, one should train for one's own quenching of defilements.

'Tena hātappaṃ karohi' means: make an effort that burns up defilements, exert yourself, strive vigorously, apply strength, be firm in endeavor, put forth energy, generate desire, produce it well, make it manifest, bring it into being, produce it, bring it forth fully.

'Dhotakāti Bhagavā' means the Blessed One addresses that brahmin by name. 'Bhagavā' is a title of supreme respect... the name 'Bhagavā' is a designation realized [by him].

'Idheva nipako sato'—'Idha' (here) means in this view, in this patience, in this choice, in this grasp, in this Dhamma, in this Vinaya, in this Dhamma-Vinaya, in this Word of the Buddha, in this holy life, in this teaching of the Teacher, in this personality, in this world of humans. 'Nipako' means wise, one who accumulates the two benefits (of the present and the future), unshakable in welfare, entering into the known benefit, shining in difficult and profound matters, a pure and true sage. 'Sato' means being mindful through four causes, developing the foundation of mindfulness regarding the body (kāyānupassanā satipaṭṭhāna).

'Ito sutvāna nigghosaṃ' means having heard, learned, attended to, and constantly noted the words, the teaching, the instruction, and the repeated advice of the Buddha.

'Sikkhe nibbānamattano'—'Sikkhā' refers to the three trainings: the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā), the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā), and the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā). 'Nibbānamattano' means for the quenching of one's own lust, for the quenching of hatred, for the quenching of delusion, for the quenching of anger, for the quenching of resentment... for the calming, the ceasing, the subsiding, the quenching, the relinquishing, and the tranquility of all unwholesome formations (abhisaṅkhāra), one should train in higher virtue, train in higher mind, and train in higher wisdom. One should train while reflecting on these three trainings, knowing them, observing what is seen, establishing the reflecting mind unshakably, entering with faith, exerting effort, making mindfulness manifest, composing the mind well, knowing with wisdom, fully knowing what should be fully known, comprehending what should be comprehended, abandoning what should be abandoned, developing what should be developed, and realizing what should be realized.
92:
For the sake of one's own quenching of defilements, one should learn the practice in accordance with the training, and practice it well; one should undertake and practice it. Because of the meaning that one should practice for one's own Nibbāna (quenching of defilements), the Blessed One said this:

“Dhotaka, if that is so, strive then in this very Dispensation, being wise and mindful. Having heard the sound of my Dhamma from this Dispensation, one should train for the sake of one's own quenching of defilements (Nibbāna).”

I see in the world of gods and men, a Brahmin who has discarded evil, living without possessions. O All-Seer, I pay homage to You. O Sakyan, release me from my doubts.

In the phrase “Passāmahaṃ devamānussaloke,” “Devā” refers to three kinds of gods: conventional gods (sammuti-deva), gods by rebirth (upapatti-deva), and gods by purity (visuddhi-deva). What are conventional gods? Kings, princes, and queens are called conventional gods. These are called conventional gods. What are gods by rebirth? The gods of the Four Great Kings, the gods of the Thirty-three, the Yāma gods, the Tusita gods, the gods who delight in creation, the gods who wield power over others' creations, the gods of the Brahma-group, and those gods who are higher than those are called gods by rebirth. These are called gods by rebirth. What are gods by purity? The Arahants, the disciples of the Tathāgata whose taints are exhausted, and the Paccekabuddhas are called gods by purity. These noble ones are called gods by purity.

The Blessed One is a god superior to conventional gods, gods by rebirth, and gods by purity; He is the supreme god, the god beyond gods, the lion among lions, the noble among the noble, the leader among leaders, the sage among sages, and the king among kings. In the phrase “Passāmahaṃ devamānussaloke,” it means: I see the god (the noble one who is a conventional or rebirth god) in the world of men; I see the supreme god (the noble one who is a god by purity); I see the god beyond gods; I behold, I look upon, I contemplate, I observe. Thus, it is said, “Passāmahaṃ devamānussaloke.”

In the phrase “Akiñcanaṃ brāhmaṇamiriyamānaṃ,” “Akiñcana” (possessionless) refers to the impediments of greed, the impediments of hatred, the impediments of delusion, the impediments of conceit, the impediments of views, the impediments of defilements, and the impediments of misconduct. These impediments have been abandoned by the Buddha, the Blessed One, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, and are of a nature not to arise again in the future. Therefore, the Buddha is called “Akiñcana.”

Regarding “Brāhmaṇa,” the Blessed One is called a Brahmin because He has cast out seven things. Self-identity view (sakkāya-diṭṭhi) has been cast out, doubt (vicikicchā) has been cast out, adherence to rites and rituals (sīlabbata-parāmāsa) has been cast out, greed has been cast out, hatred...
93:
...delusion has been cast out, conceit has been cast out. For that Blessed One, the evil unwholesome states—which are defiling, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and leading to future birth, aging, and death—have been cast out.

The Blessed One addressed him as "Sabhiya": "One who has discarded all evil deeds, who is stainless, well-concentrated with the concentration of the fruit of Arahantship, of firm mind, who has crossed over the round of rebirths, who is complete in all tasks, who is unattached to craving and views, and who is unshaken by the worldly conditions—he is called a Brahma."

“Iriyamānaṃ” means living, behaving, occurring, protecting, maintaining, or sustaining the Brahmin who is without possessions (akiñcana).

In the phrase “Taṃ taṃ namassāmi samantacakkhu,” “Taṃ” refers to that Blessed One. “Namassāmi” means I pay homage, I show respect, I revere, I honor and worship through body, speech, mind, practice in accordance with the goal, or practice in accordance with the supramundane Dhamma. “Samantacakkhu” refers to Omniscient Knowledge. The Blessed One is fully endowed with, possessed of, and has attained Omniscient Knowledge.

“In this world, there is nothing unseen by that Blessed One; furthermore, there is nothing in the past that is unknown, nor anything in the future that is to be known. He has known through direct knowledge all that is to be known (neyya-dhamma); therefore, the Tathāgata is called the All-Seer (Samantacakkhu).” I pay homage to that All-Seer.

In the phrase “Pamuñca maṃ sakka kathaṃkathāhi,” “Sakka” means the Blessed One is called Sakka because He went forth from the Sakyan clan. Alternatively, He is called Sakka because He is wealthy and possesses great riches in the form of the Dhamma. For that Blessed One, there are these treasures: the treasure of faith, the treasure of virtue, the treasure of moral shame, the treasure of moral dread, the treasure of learning, the treasure of generosity, the treasure of wisdom, the treasure of the foundations of mindfulness, the treasure of right efforts, the treasure of the bases of power, the treasure of the faculties, the treasure of the powers, the treasure of the factors of enlightenment, the treasure of the path, the treasure of the fruit, and the treasure of Nibbāna. Because He is wealthy and possesses such various treasures of Dhamma-gems, He is called Sakka. Alternatively, Sakka means He is capable, powerful, competent, brave, heroic, courageous, fearless, undaunted, not terrified, not fleeing, having abandoned fear and dread, and being free from horripilation.
94:
Sakka means being wealthy, possessing great wealth, and being endowed with wealth in the form of these treasures of the Dhamma. Alternatively, being of the Sakyan clan, he is called 'Sakka' because he is capable of conquering enemies, sufficient for victory, brave, firm, possessing supreme energy, fearless, without dread, unshakable, and not fleeing; and because he has abandoned fears and terrors and is free from horripilation. Doubt is called 'kathaṃkathā' (perplexity). There is doubt regarding the truth of suffering, doubt regarding the origin of suffering, doubt regarding the cessation of suffering in Nibbāna, doubt regarding the path leading to the cessation of suffering in Nibbāna, doubt regarding the past, doubt regarding the future, doubt regarding both the past and the future, and doubt regarding things that arise through specific conditionality and dependent origination. Such doubt, the state of being doubtful, uncertainty, perplexity, duality, a forked path, hesitation, multiple grasping, wavering, mental agitation, inability to plunge in, trembling of the mind, and mental scratching are called 'kathaṃkathā'.

'Sakka, release me from doubts' means: O Sakyan Prince, may you release me from the dart of doubt, release me completely, release me through action, release me by distinguishing various aspects, lift me out of saṃsāra and place me in Nibbāna, lift me well out of saṃsāra and place me in Nibbāna, and make me rise up from doubt. Therefore, that Brahmin Dhotaka said:

"I see in the world of gods and humans a Brahmin who lives without any possessions. I pay homage to you, the All-Seeing One; Sakka, release me from my doubts."

"Dhotaka, I am not able to release anyone in the world who has doubts. When you know the supreme Dhamma, thus you will cross this flood."

'I am not able to release' means: I am not able to release you from the dart of doubt, to release you completely, to release you through action, to release you by distinguishing various aspects, to lift you out of saṃsāra and place you in Nibbāna, to lift you well out of saṃsāra and place you in Nibbāna, or to make you rise up free from doubt. Alternatively, it means: I do not desire, I do not strive, I do not exert, I do not struggle, I do not make an effort, I do not strive vigorously, I do not apply strength, I do not be firm in exertion, I do not put forth energy, I do not generate desire, I do not produce it, I do not bring it into being, or bring it forth fully to teach the Dhamma to persons who are faithless in the Triple Gem, without desire for the fruit of the path, lazy, lacking energy, and not practicing. Thus also, 'I am not able to release'. Alternatively, there is no one else who can release those who do not yet have faith in the Triple Gem from doubt. Such persons can be released by their own strength, power, energy, and effort; by their own manly strength, manly power, manly energy, and manly effort; and by themselves following the good practice, the practice in accordance with the Dhamma, and the practice that is unopposed.
95:
By practicing the right way, the practice in accordance with the Dhamma, the non-opposing practice, the practice according to the meaning, and the practice in accordance with the supramundane Dhamma, they may be released (from doubt). Even so, I cannot release (another).

For the Blessed One has said: 'Cunda, it is impossible that one who is himself sunk in the mud should pull out another who is sunk in the mud. Cunda, it is impossible that one who is himself untamed, undisciplined, and unextinguished should tame another, discipline another, or help another to become extinguished.' Even so, I cannot release another.

For the Blessed One has also said:
'By oneself is evil done, by oneself is one defiled;
By oneself is evil left undone, by oneself is one purified.
Purity and impurity are personal; no one can purify another.'
Even so, I cannot release another.

For the Blessed One has also said: 'Brahmin, in the same way, Nibbāna exists, the path leading to Nibbāna exists, and I exist as the one who encourages and instructs. However, although my disciples are thus exhorted and repeatedly instructed by me, some attain Nibbāna, the ultimate goal, while others do not. Brahmin, what can I do in this matter? The Tathāgata, Brahmin, is only the shower of the path.' The Buddha points out the path. Only by practicing it themselves can they be released. Even so, I cannot release another.

'Kathaṃkathiṃ Dhotaka kañci loke' means: 'Dhotaka, anyone in the world who has doubt' refers to a person who has doubt, who has uncertainty, who has the dart (of doubt), who is double-minded, and who has skeptical doubt. 'Kañci' means any person—whether a Khattiya, a Brahmin, a Vessa, a Sudda, a householder, a renunciant, a god, or a human. 'Loke' refers to the world, from the world of suffering (apāya-loka) to the world of the sense bases (āyatana-loka).

'Dhammañca seṭṭhaṃ ājānamāno' means: 'The supreme Dhamma' refers to the deathless Nibbāna. That Dhamma is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna. 'Seṭṭhaṃ' means the foremost, the most praised, the specially praised, the chief, the supreme, the excellent. 'Ājānamāno' means knowing, understanding, fully realizing, and penetrating that Dhamma.
96:
In this way, 'you cross this flood' means that in this way, one should cross, should cross over, should cross through, should fully transcend, and should specially transcend the flood of sensuality, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance. Thus, you cross this flood. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

'Dhotaka, I am not able to release anyone in the world who is doubtful; only by knowing the supreme Dhamma will you be able to cross this flood.'

O Noble One, out of compassion, please teach me the Dhamma of seclusion that I may know it. May I, being peaceful and unattached, practice in this very Dispensation, without anxiety, just like the sky.

'Anusāsa brahme karuṇāyamāno' means: O Noble One, please teach me, instruct me, and have compassion for me. 'Karuṇāyamāno' means being compassionate, being kind, being protective, being helpful, and being sympathetic.

In the phrase 'Vivekadhammaṃ yamahaṃ vijaññaṃ': The Deathless, Nibbāna, is called the Dhamma of seclusion. That Dhamma which is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna. 'Yamahaṃ vijaññaṃ' means that I may know that Dhamma of Nibbāna, that I may perceive it, specially know it, repeatedly know it, penetrate it, reach it, touch it, and realize it.

'Yathāhaṃ ākāsova abyāpajjamāno' means: Just as the sky has no anxiety, does not grasp any object, is not bound by any object, and is not firmly bound by any object; in the same way, I shall practice without anxiety, without grasping, without being bound, and without being firmly bound. Thus should the meaning of 'ākāsova abyāpajjamāno' be understood. Furthermore, just as the sky is not stained by lac, or by turmeric, or by blue dye, or by crimson dye; in the same way, I shall practice without being stained by lust, without being corrupted by hate, without being bewildered by delusion, and without being defiled. Thus should the meaning of 'ākāsova abyāpajjamāno' be understood. Just as the sky...
97:
...does not get angry, does not reach the state of anger, does not remain in anger, and is without oppression; in the same way, living without getting angry, without reaching anger, without remaining in anger, without being oppressed, and without being struck—this is being without anxiety like the sky. 

'Right here, being peaceful and unattached, I shall practice' means: 'Idheva santo' means being right here, being in this very body, sitting in this very seat, sitting in this very assembly. Alternatively, 'idheva santo' means being calmed, fully calmed, extinguished, tranquil, and at peace. 

'Unattached' (Asito) means: There are two supports—the support of craving and the support of views. Having abandoned the support of craving and having relinquished the support of views, one does not depend on the eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, or the mind. One does not depend on forms, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, or mental objects; nor on family, group, dwelling, gain, fame, praise, or pleasure; nor on robes, almsfood, lodging, or medicinal requisites for the sick; nor on the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere, or the immaterial sphere; nor on sense-existence, fine-material existence, immaterial existence, existence with perception, existence without perception, existence with neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one-constituent existence, four-constituent existence, or five-constituent existence; nor on the past, future, or present; nor on things seen, heard, sensed, or cognized. Without depending, without clinging, without approaching, without being obsessed, without being intent upon, having emerged, having been released, being specially liberated, being dissociated, one shall practice with a mind that has made no boundaries. 

'Careyyaṃ' means I shall practice, dwell, move, proceed, maintain, and subsist. This is the meaning of 'Right here, being peaceful and unattached, I shall practice.' 

Therefore, that brahmin said: 'O Noble One, out of compassion, please teach me the Dhamma of seclusion that I may know it. May I, being peaceful and unattached, practice in this very life, without anxiety, just like the sky.' 

The Blessed One said: 'Dhotaka, I will teach you the peace that is visible in this very life, not based on hearsay. Knowing this and wandering mindfully, one may cross over the attachment in the world.'
98:
I will proclaim to you the peace of greed, the peace of hatred, the peace of delusion, the peace of anger, the peace of malice... the peace of denigration... of rivalry... of envy... of stinginess... of deceit... of treachery... of stubbornness... of impetuosity... of conceit... of arrogance... of intoxication... of negligence... of all defilements... of all misconduct... of all distress... of all fever... of all burning... I will proclaim, announce, point out, teach, describe, establish, reveal, analyze, clarify, and manifest the peace, the tranquility, the calming, the extinguishment, the subsiding of all unwholesome formations—this is what is meant by 'I will proclaim to you peace.'

'Dhotaka,' said the Blessed One. The Blessed One addresses that Brahmin by name. 'Bhagavā' (the Blessed One) is a term of respect... 'Bhagavā' is a designation realized by himself. Thus, it is said, 'Dhotaka, said the Blessed One.'

'In this visible world' (diṭṭhe dhamme) means the Dhamma seen, known, weighed, investigated, manifested, and developed in this very life. 'All formations are impermanent'... 'Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease.' Thus, in this visible world, in the Dhamma that is known, weighed, investigated, developed, and manifested, it is said 'in this visible world.'
