Alternatively, it means: when suffering is seen, I will speak of suffering; when the origin is seen, I will speak of the origin; when the path is seen, I will speak of the path; when cessation is seen, I will speak of cessation. Thus also, it is said 'in this visible world.' Alternatively, it means: I will teach the Dhamma that is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onwards, to be realized by the wise for themselves. Thus also, it is said 'in this visible world.' 'Anītiham' (not based on hearsay) means not by tradition, not by report, not by lineage, not by the authority of scriptures, not by logical reasoning, not by inference, not by reasoned reflection, not by acceptance of a view after deliberation; rather, I will teach the Dhamma that is known by oneself, directly realized by oneself. This is what is meant by 'in this visible world, not based on hearsay.'

'Knowing which, they wander mindful' means having known, weighed, investigated, developed, and manifested [the Dhamma]. Having known, weighed, investigated, developed, and manifested that 'All formations are impermanent'; having known, weighed, investigated, developed, and manifested that 'All formations are suffering'... 'All phenomena are non-self'... 'Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease'...
99:
Having known. 'Sato' (mindful) means being mindful through four causes: one who is mindful while practicing the foundation of mindfulness by contemplating the body in the body... such a person is called 'mindful.' 'Caranti' (wandering) means wandering, living, moving, proceeding, protecting, sustaining, and maintaining. Therefore, it means 'knowing which, one wanders mindful.'

In the phrase 'tarei loke visattikaṃ,' craving is called 'visattikā.' That which is lust, infatuation... covetousness, greed, the unwholesome root—this is craving. For what reason is it called 'visattikā'? It is called 'visattikā' because it is pervasive and widespread. 'Loke' (in the world) refers to the world of misery up to the world of the sense bases. 'Tarei loke visattikaṃ' means that one who is mindful should cross over, transcend, go beyond, overcome, surmount, and pass through this pervasive craving in the world. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Dhotaka, I will proclaim to you peace in this visible world, not based on hearsay, knowing which, wandering mindful, one may cross over the clinging in the world.'

'I rejoice in that, O Great Sage, the supreme peace, knowing which, wandering mindful, one may cross over the clinging in the world.' In the phrase 'tañcāhaṃ abhinandāမိ,' 'taṃ' refers to your word, speech, teaching, instruction, and advice. I delight in that word, I greatly rejoice in it, I am glad of it, I appreciate it, I desire it, I enjoy it, I long for it, I cherish it, and I speak of it with great longing.

In the phrase 'mahesi santimuttamaṃ,' 'mahesi' (Great Sage) means the Blessed One is called 'Mahesi' because he sought and searched for the great aggregate of virtue, the great aggregate of concentration, and so on. He is also called 'Mahesi' because he is sought after: 'Where is the Bull among men?' 'Santimuttamaṃ' (supreme peace) means the Deathless Nibbāna is called 'peace.' That which is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, and Nibbāna is called 'peace.' 'Uttamaṃ' means foremost, best, excellent, chief, supreme.

'Knowing which, one wanders mindful' means having known that Nibbāna... having seen, weighed, investigated, developed, and manifested that 'All formations are impermanent'; having seen, weighed, investigated, developed, and manifested that 'All formations are suffering,' 'All phenomena are non-self,' 'Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease'...
100:
Having developed and made manifest. "Mindful" (sato) means being mindful through four reasons—developing the foundation of mindfulness of the body (kāyānupassanā satipaṭṭhāna) in the body... such a person is called "mindful". "Faring" (caraṃ) means practicing... maintaining—knowing that Nibbāna, one should fare mindfully.

In the phrase "one should cross over the attachment (visattikā) in the world"—"visattikā" refers to craving (taṇhā). It is passion (rāga), intense passion... covetousness (abhijjhā), greed (lobha), the unwholesome root. For what reason is it called "visattikā"? Because it is widespread (visata) and extensive (vitthata), it is called "visattikā". "In the world" means in the world from the world of misery (apāya-loka) to the world of sense-bases (āyatana-loka). "One should cross over the attachment in the world" means one should cross over that attachment in the world mindfully, cross over completely... cross over once more—one should cross over the attachment in the world. Therefore, that Brahmin said:

"I greatly rejoice in the Blessed One, the Great Seer (Mahesi), who seeks the supreme peace (Nibbāna), and in that supreme peace itself;
Knowing which, faring mindfully, one may cross over the attachment in the world."

"Dhotaka, whatever you know—above, below, across, and in the middle—knowing this as an attachment in the world, do not create craving for becoming or non-becoming (bhavābhava)," said the Blessed One.

"Whatever you know" (yaṃ kiñci sampajānāsi) means you know everything, you know thoroughly, you know specifically, you penetrate—you know all things well. "Dhotaka, said the Blessed One" (dhotakāti bhagavā) means the Blessed One addresses that Brahmin by name. "Bhagavā" is a title of respect... a designation realized, this is the name "Bhagavā"—"Dhotaka," said the Blessed One.

In the phrase "above, below, across, and in the middle" (uddhaṃ adho tiriyañcāpi majjhe)—"above" (uddhaṃ) refers to the future; "below" (adho) refers to the past; "across and in the middle" (tiriyañcāpi majjhe) refers to the present. "Above" refers to the deva world; "below" refers to the world of misery; "across and in the middle" refers to the human world. Alternatively, "above" refers to wholesome states (kusala dhammā); "below" refers to unwholesome states (akusala dhammā); "across and in the middle" refers to indeterminate states (abyākata dhammā). "Above" refers to the formless realm (arūpa-dhātu); "below" refers to the sense realm (kāma-dhātu); "across and in the middle" refers to the form realm (rūpa-dhātu). "Above" refers to pleasant feeling; "below" refers to painful feeling; "across and in the middle" refers to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. "Above" means upwards from the soles of the feet...
101:
"Below" means downwards from the tips of the hair. "Across and in the middle" means the middle of the body. "Above, below, across, and in the middle" refers to the future, the past, and the present; to wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states; to pleasant, painful, and neutral feelings; to the deva world, the world of misery, and the human world; to the formless realm, the sense realm, and the form realm; and to the parts above the soles of the feet, below the tips of the hair, and the middle of the body.

Knowing this Dhamma as "this is attachment (saṅga) in the world, a clinging, a bond, an obstacle," having known, understood, weighed, investigated, developed, and made it manifest.

Craving (taṇhā) ranges from craving for forms (rūpa-taṇhā) to craving for mental objects (dhamma-taṇhā). For the sake of becoming and non-becoming (bhavābhava), for the sake of the round of kamma and the round of result (kamma-vaṭṭa and vipāka-vaṭṭa), for the sake of the round of kamma and result in the sense realm, form realm, and formless realm, for the sake of repeated destiny (gati), rebirth (upapatti), relinking (paṭisandhi), and the manifestation of individual existence (attabhāva)—do not create craving, do not produce it, do not let it arise. Abandon that craving, dispel it, eliminate it, and make it come to non-existence. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"Dhotaka, knowing all that you know—above, below, across, and in the middle—as attachment in this world, do not create craving for becoming or non-becoming."

At the end of the verse... "Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is my teacher, I am a disciple (sāvaka)," he said.

## 5. Exposition of the Questions of the Young Man Dhotaka (Dhotakamāṇavapucchāniddesa).

## 6. Exposition of the Questions of the Young Man Upasīva (Upasīvamāṇavapucchāniddesa).

The venerable young man Upasīva addressed the Buddha thus:
"O Sakyan, alone and without support, I am not able to cross the great flood (ogha).
O All-Seeing One (Samantacakkhu), tell me an object (ārammaṇa) depending on which I may cross this flood."

"Alone" means without a second person or a second Dhamma to help. Wishing to cross the great floods of sense-desire (kāmogha), becoming (bhavogha), views (diṭṭhogha), and ignorance (avijjogha) by means of the four paths (magga), depending on a person or the Dhamma. "Sakyan" (Sakka) is used because the Blessed One went forth from the Sakyan clan, and because he is endowed with the wealth of jhāna and Dhamma.
102:
I am alone, O Sakka, [wishing to cross] the great flood. 'Eko' (alone) means that I have no second person or second Dhamma as a companion; or it means having no companion to rely on a person or a Dhamma in order to cross, transcend, or overcome the great floods of sense-desire (kāmogha), existence (bhavogha), views (diṭṭhogha), and ignorance (avijjogha). 'Sakka' means the Blessed One is called Sakka because he went forth from the Sakyan clan. Alternatively, he is called Sakka because he is rich in the wealth of Dhamma. The Blessed One possesses these riches: the wealth of faith, virtue, shame, fear of wrongdoing, learning, generosity, wisdom, the foundations of mindfulness, and so on, up to the wealth of Nibbāna. Because he is rich and wealthy with these many jewels of wealth, he is called Sakka. Alternatively, he is called Sakka because he is capable, powerful, competent, heroic, valiant, energetic, fearless, unshakeable, undaunted, not fleeing, having abandoned fear and dread, and being free from horripilation. Thus: "I am alone, O Sakka, [wishing to cross] the great flood."

The venerable Upasīva spoke thus. 'Iccā' is a word-junction. 'Āyasmā' is a term of endearment. 'Upasīva' is the name of that Brahmin.

"Without support, I am unable to cross," he said. 'Anissito' (without support) means that without relying on a person or a Dhamma, one is unable to carry across, unable to strive, unable to manage, or unable to cross, transcend, or overcome the great floods of sense-desire, existence, views, and ignorance.

O All-Seeing One, tell me the support (object). 'Ārammaṇaṃ' means the support, the object, the basis, or the condition. 'Brūhi' means tell, show, teach, point out, establish, reveal, analyze, make plain, and manifest. 'Samantacakkhu' (All-Seeing Eye) refers to omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). The Blessed One is endowed with, possessed of, attained to, and gifted with that omniscience.

In this world, there is nothing unseen by that Blessed One; furthermore, there is nothing especially unknown among the things that should be known and are known.
He has fully known all the knowable things (ñeyya-dhamma) that exist; therefore, the Tathāgata is called the All-Seeing One.
Tell me the support, O All-Seeing One.
103:
Relying on which person or relying on which Dhamma I may cross, transcend, overcome, or go beyond the great floods of sense-desire, existence, views, and ignorance—this is the meaning of "Relying on which I may cross this flood." Therefore, that Brahmin spoke thus:

"I am alone, O Sakka, [wishing to cross] the great flood,
(The venerable Upasīva spoke thus)
Without support, I am unable to cross.
O Blessed One, who possesses the All-Seeing Eye (omniscience),
Tell me the support, relying on which I may cross this flood."

"Upasīva, mindful and observing the sphere of nothingness,
(The Blessed One spoke thus)
Mindfully contemplating 'there is nothing', relying on that, cross the flood.
Abandoning sense-pleasures, detached from talk,
Day and night, look intensely at the destruction of craving (Nibbāna)."

'Ākiñcaññaṃ pekkhamāno satimā' means: That Brahmin was naturally an attainer of the attainment of the sphere of nothingness, yet he did not know his support, thinking, "This is my support." To that Brahmin, the Blessed One tells the support and the higher path of escape from the round of suffering. Entering the attainment of the sphere of nothingness mindfully, and emerging from it while remaining mindful, he observes, sees, looks at, contemplates, and examines the mental states (citta-cetasika) arising therein as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a boil, as a dart, as a calamity, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, as a disaster, as a trouble, as a danger, as an obstacle, as shaky, as fragile, as non-lasting, as no protection, as no shelter, as no refuge, as not being a refuge, as empty, as vain, as void, as non-self, as a peril, as subject to change, as coreless, as the root of misery, as existence, as non-existence, as having taints, as conditioned, as Māra's bait, as subject to birth, as subject to aging, as subject to sickness, as subject to death, as subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, as subject to arising, as subject to passing away, as gratification (due to the power of lust), as a changing peril, and as an escape.
104:
One who is mindful refers to that mindfulness, recollection, repeated recollection... right mindfulness (sammā-sati). One endowed with this mindfulness is called 'one who is mindful.' Looking towards the sphere of nothingness, one should be mindful.

'O Upasīva,' thus the Blessed One addressed that brahmin by name. 'Bhagavā' is a term of respect... it is a designation realized by himself. This is the address, 'O Upasīva.'

'Depending on "there is nothing," cross the flood' refers to the attainment of the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana-samāpatti). Why is it said 'there is nothing'? Having mindfully entered the attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana-samāpatti) and emerging from it, one makes that very consciousness non-existent, specifically making it disappear, and sees that 'there is nothing.' For that reason, depending on, relying on, and making an object of the attainment of the sphere of nothingness, cross over, transcend, go beyond, and surmount the flood of sensuality (kāmogha), the flood of existence (bhavogha), the flood of views (diṭṭhogha), and the flood of ignorance (avijjogha).

In the phrase 'having abandoned sensual pleasures and refraining from talk,' there are two kinds of sensual pleasures: objective sensual pleasures (vatthu-kāma) and subjective sensual pleasures (kilesa-kāma). Abandoning sensual pleasures means fully understanding objective sensual pleasures and abandoning, removing, getting rid of, and bringing to non-existence the subjective sensual pleasures. 'Refraining from talk' refers to refraining from, being liberated from, and dwelling with a boundless mind away from doubt called 'kathaṃkathā,' [which is] uncertainty, doubt regarding the truth of suffering... the agitation of the mind, and the mental scratching. Alternatively, it also means refraining from, being liberated from, and dwelling with a boundless mind away from the thirty-two types of pointless talk (tiracchāna-kathā).

In the phrase 'look intensely at the destruction of craving day and night,' craving refers to craving for forms... craving for mental phenomena. 'Nattaṃ' is said to be night. 'Aho' is day. Day and night, [look at] the destruction of craving, the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion, the destruction of destiny, the destruction of rebirth, the destruction of relinking, the destruction of existence...
105:
...the destruction of the round of rebirth (saṃsāra), the destruction of the cycle (vaṭṭa). Look, look intensely, see, observe, contemplate, and examine. 'Look intensely at the destruction of craving day and night.' Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"Looking towards nothingness, being mindful, [O Upasīva, said the Blessed One,]
Depending on 'there is nothing,' cross the four floods;
Having abandoned sensual pleasures, refraining from talk,
Look intensely at the destruction of craving day and night."

The Venerable Upasīva spoke thus:
"One who is free from lust in all sensual pleasures,
Depending on nothingness, having abandoned others,
Supremely intent on the liberation of perception,
Would he remain there without departing?"

In the phrase "sabbesu kāmesu yo vītarāgo," "sabbesu" is a term that includes everything entirely, in every way, without exception or remainder. "Kāmesu" briefly refers to two kinds: objective sensual pleasures and subjective sensual pleasures... these are called objective sensual pleasures... these are called subjective sensual pleasures. "One who is free from lust in all sensual pleasures" refers to one who is without lust, whose lust has gone, who has relinquished lust, who has vomited out lust, who is freed from lust, who has abandoned lust, and who has further relinquished lust through the abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna) in all sensual pleasures.

In the phrase "iccāyasmā upasīvo," "iccā" is a word-conjunction... "āyasmā" is a term of endearment... "Upasīva" is the name and designation of that brahmin.

"Depending on nothingness, having abandoned others" means one who relies on, approaches, reaches, and is intent on the attainment of the sphere of nothingness, having abandoned, relinquished, given up, and transcended the six lower attainments.

In the phrase "saññāvimokkhe paramedhimutto," the seven attainments of perception are called 'liberations of perception' (saññā-vimokkha). Among those attainments of perception, the liberation of the attainment of the sphere of nothingness is the foremost, the best, the most excellent, the chief, the highest, and the most noble. It refers to one who is intent on that supreme liberation of resolve (adhimutti-vimokkha), who frequents that sphere of nothingness, who respects it, who leans towards it, and who dwells making that sphere of nothingness the priority.
106:
One who is especially resolved through the noble liberation of resolution (adhimutti-vimokkha), resolved therein, inclined towards that sphere of nothingness, frequenting it, abundant in it, valuing it, leaning towards it, sloping towards it, resolved upon it, and dwelling with it as the predominant factor, is one who is especially resolved in the noble liberation of perception (saññā-vimokkha).

In the phrase "Does he remain there in that sphere of nothingness without passing away?", the words "Does he remain?" (tiṭṭhe nu) constitute a question of doubt, a question of uncertainty, a question of indecision, and a non-categorical question. Asking "Will he remain thus? Will he not remain? How will he remain? In what way will he remain?" is the meaning of "Does he remain?". "There" (tattha) refers to the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana). "Without passing away" (anānuyāyī) refers to one who does not follow the sequence [of lower realms], who does not move, who does not disappear, who does not vanish, and who does not decline. Alternatively, it refers to one who is not lustful with passion, not corrupted by hatred, not deluded, and not defiled by mental impurities; such a person is meant by "Does he remain there in that sphere of nothingness without passing away?". Therefore, that brahmin said this:

"He who is free from passion in all sensual pleasures,
(Thus the venerable Upasīva spoke)
Having left other [lower attainments], relies on the sphere of nothingness;
Being especially resolved in the noble liberation of perception,
Does he remain there without passing away?"

"He who is free from passion in all sensual pleasures,
(Upasīva, said the Blessed One)
Having left other [lower attainments], relies on the sphere of nothingness;
Being especially resolved in the noble liberation of perception,
He would remain there without passing away."

In the phrase "He who is free from passion in all sensual pleasures," the word "all" (sabbesu) is a term encompassing everything in every way, entirely, without exception, and without remainder. Regarding "sensual pleasures" (kāmesu), there are two kinds in brief: sensual pleasures of objects (vatthu-kāma) and sensual pleasures of defilements (kilesa-kāma). ... These are called sensual pleasures of objects. ... These are called sensual pleasures of defilements. "He who is free from passion in all sensual pleasures" refers to one who is free from lust in all sensual pleasures, ... one who has abandoned passion through the abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna).

In the phrase "Upasīva, said the Blessed One," the Blessed One addresses that brahmin by name. "Bhagavā" (Blessed One) is a term of respect. ... The name designated by personal realization is "Bhagavā."
107:
"Having left other [lower attainments], relies on the sphere of nothingness" means having abandoned, given up, relinquished, transcended, well-transcended, and especially transcended the six lower attainments (samāpatti), one dwells relying on, adhering to, approaching, closely approaching, being intensely focused on, and being resolved upon the attainment of the sphere of nothingness.

In the phrase "Being especially resolved in the noble liberation of perception" (saññā-vimokkhe parame dhimutto), the seven attainments of perception are called the liberations of perception (saññā-vimokkha). Among those attainments of perception, the liberation of the attainment of the sphere of nothingness is the foremost, the best, the most excellent, the chief, the highest, and the most noble. One who is resolved through the liberation of resolution that is thus noble, foremost, best, most excellent, chief, highest, and most noble; resolved therein, thus resolved... (pe) ... making it the predominant factor, is called "especially resolved in the noble liberation of perception."

"He would remain there without passing away" means that person would remain for sixty thousand aeons (kappas). "There" (tattha) refers to the realm of the sphere of nothingness. "Without passing away" (anānuyāyī) means remaining without moving or shifting, without reaching disappearance, without vanishing, and without declining, rather than following the sequence [of lower realms]. Alternatively, remaining without being lustful with passion, without being corrupted by hatred, without being deluded by ignorance, and without being defiled by mental impurities is what is meant by "He would remain there without passing away." For that reason, the Blessed One said:

"Upasīva, he who is free from passion in all sensual pleasures, having left the lower jhānas, relies on the jhāna of the sphere of nothingness; he is resolved in the highest liberation of perception; that person would remain in that realm of the sphere of nothingness without declining."

"O Blessed One, the All-seeing One (Samantacakkhu) who can see all around, if that person remains in that realm of the sphere of nothingness without declining, does he remain there peacefully liberated from defilements for many years? Does the consciousness (viññāṇa) of such a person pass away?"

"If he remains there without passing away" means if that person should remain for sixty thousand aeons. "There" (tattha) refers to the realm of the sphere of nothingness. "Without passing away" (anānuyāyī) means remaining in the realm of the sphere of nothingness without shifting, without reaching disappearance, without reaching vanishing, and without reaching decline. Alternatively, remaining without being lustful with passion, without being corrupted by hatred, without being deluded by ignorance, and without being defiled by mental impurities is what is meant by "If he remains there without passing away."
108:
Regarding the phrase "pūgampi vassāni samantacakkhu": "pūgampi vassāni" means for many years, for many hundreds of years, for many thousands of years, for many hundreds of thousands of years, for many aeons (kappas), for many hundreds of aeons, for many thousands of aeons, and for many hundreds of thousands of aeons. "Samantacakkhu" refers to omniscient wisdom (sabbaññutañāṇa). Because the Blessed One is endowed with that wisdom, he is called the All-seeing One (Samantacakkhu). This is the meaning of the phrase "pūgampi vassāni samantacakkhu."

Regarding the phrase "tattheva so sītisiyā vimutto, cavetha viññāṇaṃ tathāvidhassa": Does that person reach a state of coolness in that very sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana) and remain there as long as an aeon, in a state that is permanent, stable, eternal, and unchanging? Or does that person's consciousness pass away, be cut off, perish, vanish, and cease to exist? Does the rebirth-consciousness arise again in the sense realm, the fine-material realm, or the immaterial realm? This is an inquiry into the permanence (sassata) and annihilation (uccheda) of one who has attained the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness. Or does he attain final liberation (parinibbāna) in that very realm through the Nibbāna element without remainder (anupādisesa nibbānadhātu)? Or does that person's consciousness pass away and a rebirth-consciousness arise again in the sense realm, the fine-material realm, or the immaterial realm? This is an inquiry into the parinibbāna and rebirth of one who has been reborn in the sphere of nothingness. "Tathāvidhassa" means of such a nature, of one who stays in that realm, of such a manner, of one who has been reborn in the sphere of nothingness. Therefore, that Brahmin addressed the Buddha thus:

"If he should remain there without moving,
O All-seeing One, for many years,
Would he be cooled and liberated from defilements in that very place,
Or would the consciousness of such a person pass away?"

The Blessed One replied thus:
"Upasīva, just as a flame blown by the force of the wind,
Reaches its end and cannot be designated,
Even so, the sage, liberated from the mental body,
Reaches his end and can no longer be designated."

Regarding the phrase "acci yathā vātavegena khittā": "acci" is called a flame. "vāta" (wind) refers to the east wind, west wind, north wind, south wind, dusty wind, dustless wind, cold wind, hot wind, gentle wind, strong wind, harsh wind, high wind in the sky, all winds, winds like the swoop of a garuda, winds that blow with dry leaves, and winds produced by fanning. "vātavegena khittā" means blown by the force of the wind.
109:
Intense winds include kāḷavāta, verambhavāta, pakkhavāta, supaṇṇavāta, tālapannavāta, and vidhūpanavāta. "Blown by the force of the wind" means thrown by the force of the wind, lifted up, scattered, repeatedly scattered, obstructed, or removed. "Just as a flame blown by the force of the wind" is the same. "Upasīva," the Blessed One said, addressing that Brahmin by name. "Bhagavā" (the Blessed One) is a term of respect... (detailed)... This name "Bhagavā" is a manifest designation. Thus, the Blessed One said, "Upasīva."

"Reaches its end, cannot be designated" means: "reaches its end" means reaches destruction, reaches disappearance, ceases, is calmed, is completely stilled. "Cannot be designated" means it does not reach the state of being named, does not reach description, does not reach counting, does not reach conceptualization. There is no cause, no support, no reason by which it could be designated as "gone to the east, gone to the west, gone to the north, gone to the south, gone upwards, gone downwards, gone across, or gone to an intermediate direction." Therefore, it is said to reach its end and not be designated.

In the sentence "Even so, the sage, liberated from the mental body": "evaṃ" (even so) is a comparison. "muni" (sage): knowledge is called "mona"... (detailed)... Because he has transcended the net of attachment, he is called a sage. "Liberated from the mental body" means that the sage is naturally already liberated from the physical body. He has abandoned defilements through temporary abandonment (tadaṅgapahāna) and abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhanapahāna). That sage, having reached the end of existence, has attained the four Noble Paths. Because of attaining the four Noble Paths, the mental body and the physical body are fully understood (pariññāta). Because the mental body and the physical body are fully understood, he is released, liberated, and well-liberated from both the mental body and the physical body through the ultimate liberation without clinging (accanta-anupādā-vimokkha). Thus, it is said that the sage is liberated from the mental body.

"Reaches its end, cannot be designated" means: "reaches its end" means attaining parinibbāna through the Nibbāna element without remainder (anupādisesa nibbānadhātu), which is absolute cessation. "Cannot be designated" means that an Arahant who has attained parinibbāna through the Nibbāna element without remainder does not reach the state of being designated, described, counted, or conceptualized as a khattiya, a brahmin, a vessa, a sudda, a householder, a monk, a deva, a human, one with form, one without form, one with perception, one without perception, or one with neither-perception-nor-non-perception. There is no cause, no support, no reason by which he could be so designated.
110:
There is no cause by which he could be reckoned; that cause (or support, or proximate cause) does not exist. He has gone to rest and does not come under reckoning (designation or conceptualization). Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“Upasīva, just as a flame tossed by a gust of wind
Goes to rest and cannot be reckoned,
Even so the sage, freed from the mental body,
Goes to rest and cannot be reckoned.”

Does that person (who has arisen in the sphere of nothingness) reach destruction, or does that person no longer exist, or is he indeed free from change due to being eternal? O Sage, who has completed the task of a monk, please explain this matter well to me, for this Dhamma is thus known by you.

“Atthaṅgato so uda vā so natthi” means: Does that person perish, or does that person not exist, or has he ceased, or is he annihilated, or is he destroyed?

“Udāhu ve sassatiyā arogo” means: Or is he permanent, stable, eternal, and unchanging, remaining just so like the eternal?

In the phrase “Taṃ me munī sādhu viyākarohi”, “taṃ” refers to that cause which I ask about, request, urge, and place faith in. “Munī” refers to the knowledge called mona... etc... he who has transcended the web of craving and views is called a sage (muni). “Sādhu viyākarohi” means: please tell, teach, prescribe, establish, open, analyze, make clear, and show it well.

“Tathā hi te vidito esa dhammo” means: This Dhamma has been known, weighed, investigated, manifested, and developed by you. Therefore, that Brahmin Upasīva said:

“Does that person reach destruction, or does that person no longer exist, or is he indeed free from change due to being eternal?
O Sage, who has completed the task of a monk, please explain this matter well to me, for this Dhamma is thus known by you.”

Upasīva, for one who has attained Parinibbāna, there is no measure for reckoning.
111:
(The Blessed One said thus:) Upasīva, for one who has gone to rest, there is no measure (for comparison). That cause (such as lust, etc.) by which they might speak of him (as such and such), that cause for him no longer exists. When all things (dhammas) are uprooted, all pathways of speech (vādapatha) are also uprooted.

“For one who has gone to rest, there is no measure” means: For one who has attained Parinibbāna through the Nibbāna element without residue, there is no measure of form, no measure of feeling, no measure of perception, no measure of mental formations, and no measure of consciousness. (Those measures) no longer exist, are truly not present, cannot be found, are abandoned, are cut off at the root, are stilled, are fully stilled, are not liable to arise again, and are burnt (crushed) by the fire of knowledge. Thus, for one who has gone to rest, there is no measure.

“Upasīvāti bhagavā” means: The Blessed One addressed that Brahmin by name. “Bhagavā” is a term of respect... it is a designation based on realization, thus he is called “Bhagavā”. Thus, the Blessed One said, “O Upasīva”.

“That cause by which they might speak of him, that cause for him no longer exists” means: The cause by which they might speak of him through lust, through hatred, through delusion, through conceit, through views, through restlessness, through doubt, or through underlying tendencies—as ‘one who is lustful’, ‘one who is hateful’, ‘one who is deluded’, ‘one who is fettered’, ‘one who is misapprehending’, ‘one who is distracted’, ‘one who is undecided’, or ‘one who is obsessed’—those volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra) have been abandoned. Because the volitional formations have been abandoned, there is no cause, no support, and no reason by which they might speak, tell, say, show, or designate him according to his destination (gati) as ‘a hell-being’, ‘an animal’, ‘a peta’, ‘a human’, ‘a deva’, ‘one with form’, ‘one who is formless’, ‘one with perception’, ‘one without perception’, or ‘one with neither-perception-nor-non-perception’. Thus, that cause by which they might speak of him no longer exists for him.

“When all things are uprooted” means: When all things (dhammas), all aggregates (khandha), all sense bases (āyatana), all elements (dhātu), all destinations (gati), all rebirths (upapatti), all relinkings (paṭisandhi), all existences (bhava), all rounds of rebirth (saṃsāra), and all cycles (vaṭṭa) are uprooted, well uprooted, pulled out, well pulled out, removed, well removed, abandoned, cut off at the root, stilled, fully stilled, not liable to arise again, and burnt (crushed) by the fire of knowledge. Thus, “when all things are uprooted”.
112:
In the phrase, "All pathways of speech (vādapathā) are also completely uprooted," the defilements (kilesā), the aggregates (khandhā), and the volitional formations (abhisaṅkhārā) are called pathways of speech. For such a person, his arguments and the pathways of speech, designations (adhivacana) and the pathways of designation, expressions (nirutti) and the pathways of expression, concepts (paññatti) and the pathways of concept, are pulled out, completely uprooted, removed, well removed, abandoned, well abandoned, relinquished, cut off at the root, calmed, fully tranquilized, incapable of arising again, and burnt by the fire of knowledge. Therefore, it is said, "All pathways of speech are also completely uprooted."

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"For one who has reached the end, O Upasīva, there is no measure. That by which one might speak of him, that for him does not exist. When all things (dhammā) are completely uprooted, all pathways of speech are also completely uprooted."

At the conclusion of the verse, together with that brahmin... the one sitting with hands joined in reverence says, "Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is my teacher, I am a disciple."

## 6. Upasīvamāဏavapucchāniddesa

## 7. Nandamāဏavapucchāniddesa

The Venerable Nanda asked this:
"People say that there are sages (munis) in the world. How is this? Do they call one a sage because he is endowed with knowledge, or because he is endowed with a [certain] way of life?"

In the phrase "Santi loke munayo," "santi" means they exist, they are found, they are present, they are obtained. "Loke" means in the world of suffering (apāya-loka)... in the world of the sense bases (āyatana-loka). "Munayo" refers to those named sages, such as the Ājīvakas, Nigaṇṭhas, matted-hair ascetics (jaṭilas), and hermits (tāpasas). (In the world, devas perceive them as sages, but they are not true sages.) This is the meaning of the phrase "Santi loke munayo."

In the phrase "Iccāyasmā nando," "iccā" is a word-junction (padasandhi)... "āyasmā" is a term of endearment... "nando" is the name of that brahmin... his designation.
113:
Regarding the phrase “So people say, how is this?”: “People” (janā) refers to khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, suddas, householders, renunciants, gods, and humans. “Say” (vadanti) means they preach, speak, show, or designate. “How is this?” (tayidaṃ kathaṃsu) is a question of doubt, a question of uncertainty, a question of indecision, or a question of lack of certain knowledge, such as “Is it thus? Is it not thus? What is it? How is it?” Thus: “So people say, how is this?”

Regarding the phrase “Do they call one a sage because of being endowed with knowledge?”: Do they call, preach, speak, show, or designate one as a sage who is endowed with, possessed of, attained to, reached by, or characterized by the knowledge of the eight attainments (samāpatti) or the knowledge of the five superknowledges (abhiññā)? Thus: “Do they call one a sage because of being endowed with knowledge?”

Regarding the phrase “Or because of being endowed with a way of life?”: Or do they call, preach, speak, show, or designate one as a sage who is endowed with, possessed of, attained to, reached by, or characterized by the effort of various and diverse extremely difficult practices and austere living? Thus: “Or because of being endowed with a way of life?” Therefore, that brahmin said:

“There are sages in the world,” [said the venerable Nanda,]
“So people say. How is this?
Do they call one a sage because of being endowed with knowledge,
Or because of being endowed with a way of life?”

[The Buddha replied:]
“Not by view, not by hearing, not by knowledge,
O Nanda, do the skilled ones in this world call one a sage;
Having disbanded the army (of defilements), being without suffering and without desire,
Those who wander are the ones I call sages.”

Regarding the phrase “Not by view, not by hearing, not by knowledge”: “Not by view” means not by purity of view. “Not by hearing” means not by purity of hearing. “Not by knowledge” means not by the knowledge of the eight attainments, nor by the knowledge of the five superknowledges, nor by wrong knowledge. Thus: “Not by view, not by hearing, not by knowledge.”

Regarding the phrase “O Nanda, do the skilled ones in this world call one a sage”: “Skilled ones” (kusalā) refers to those who are skilled in the aggregates (khandha), skilled in the elements (dhātu), skilled in the sense bases (āyatana), skilled in dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), skilled in the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), skilled in the right efforts (sammappadhāna), skilled in the bases of power (iddhipāda), skilled in the faculties (indriya), and skilled in the powers (bala).
114:
The wise who are skilled in the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), skilled in the path (magga), skilled in the fruition (phala), and skilled in Nibbāna, do not call, preach, recite, show, or designate a person as a 'Muni' (sage) merely because they are endowed with purity of view, purity of hearing, the knowledge of the eight attainments, the knowledge of the five superknowledges, or even wrong knowledge, or what is seen, heard, or sensed. Nanda, in this world, the wise do not call such a person a Muni.

In the statement, 'Those who, having dismantled the army, live without suffering and without craving, them I call Munis'—the 'army' refers to Māra's army. Bodily misconduct is Māra's army. Verbal misconduct is Māra's army. Mental misconduct is Māra's army. Passion, hatred, delusion, anger... (and so on)... resentment, ingratitude, rivalry, envy, stinginess, deceit, treachery, stubbornness, impetuosity, conceit, overbearing pride, intoxication, and negligence—all defilements, all misconduct, all distress, all fevers, all torments, and all unwholesome volitional formations are called Māra's army. Regarding this, the Blessed One taught:

'Sensual pleasures are your first army; the second is called discontent.
Hunger and thirst are your third; craving is called the fourth.
Sloth and torpor are your fifth; fear is called the sixth.
Doubt is your seventh; hypocrisy and stubbornness are your eighth.
Gain, renown, honor, and whatever fame is falsely obtained;
And whoever exalts oneself and disparages others.
Behold, Namuci (Māra), this is your army, the striker of the Dark One (Kaṇha).
One who is not a hero cannot conquer it; only the victor attains happiness.'

When all Māra's armies and all defilements that form opposing armies have been conquered, subdued, destroyed, scattered, and turned away by the four Noble Paths, they are called 'visenikatvā' (having dismantled the army). 'Anīghā' means: passion is suffering (nīgha), hatred is suffering, delusion is suffering, anger is suffering, resentment is suffering... (and so on)... all unwholesome volitional formations are suffering (nīgha). Those for whom these sufferings have been abandoned, cut off at the root, calmed, stilled, made incapable of arising again, and burnt by the fire of knowledge, are called 'anīghā' (those without suffering).

In the term 'nirāsā', 'ni' denotes absence. 'Āsā' refers to the craving of desire. Whatever craving of desire, intense lust... (and so on)... excessive greed, the greed that is an unwholesome root exists...
115:
In the term 'nirāsā', 'āsā' refers to craving (taṇhā). Whatever passion, intense lust... ignorance, and greed which is the unwholesome root exists. Those for whom this craving (āsā/taṇhā) has been abandoned, cut off at the root, calmed, stilled, made incapable of arising again, and burnt by the fire of knowledge, are called 'nirāsā' (without craving)—Arahants whose taints are destroyed. 'Visenikatvā anīghā nirāsā, caranti ye te munayoti brūmi' means: those who live, dwell, move, proceed, maintain, and sustain themselves having dismantled the army of defilements, being free from suffering and free from craving—them I call 'Munis' in this world; I declare, teach, describe, establish, reveal, analyze, clarify, and proclaim them. Thus the Blessed One said:

## Not by view, nor by hearing, nor by knowledge, Nanda, do the skilled call one a Muni here;
## Having dismantled the army, free from suffering and craving, those who wander, them I call Munis.

Venerable Nanda asked this:
'Whatever recluses and brahmins there are
Who say that purity comes through seeing and hearing,
Who say that purity comes through virtue and vows, or who say that purity comes through many other ways.
O Blessed One, free from danger, do they, living restrained in that view, cross over birth and old age?
Blessed One, please tell me this.'

In the phrase 'ye kecime samaṇabrāhmaṇāse', 'ye keci' is a term that includes everything without exception. 'Samaṇa' refers to those recluses who have gone forth outside this Dispensation. 'Brāhmaṇa' refers to those who are in the habit of saying 'bho'. In the phrase 'iccāyasmā nando', 'icca' is a word-junction... 'āyasmā' is a term of endearment... 'Nanda' is the name of that brahmin.

'Diṭṭhassutenāpi vadanti suddhiṃ' means they speak of, preach, recite, show, and designate purity, supreme purity, total purity, liberation, supreme liberation, and total liberation through seeing. They also speak of, preach, recite, show, and designate purity, supreme purity, total purity, liberation, supreme liberation, and total liberation through hearing.
116:
They manifest, they designate. They speak of, preach, recite, manifest, and designate purity, special purity, complete purity, liberation, special liberation, and complete liberation even through seeing and hearing. "They speak of purity even through what is seen and heard" means they speak of purity through seeing and hearing.

"They speak of purity even through virtue and vows" means they speak of, preach, recite, manifest, and designate purity, special purity, complete purity, liberation, special liberation, and complete liberation even through virtue (sīla). They speak of, preach, recite, manifest, and designate purity, special purity, complete purity, liberation, special liberation, and complete liberation even through vows (vata). They speak of, preach, recite, manifest, and designate purity, special purity, complete purity, liberation, special liberation, and complete liberation even through virtue and vows (sīlabbata). "They speak of purity even through virtue and vows" means they speak of purity through virtue and vows.

"They speak of purity in various ways" means they speak of, preach, recite, manifest, and designate purity, special purity, complete purity, liberation, special liberation, and complete liberation through various types of omens and auspicious signs. "They speak of purity in various ways" means they speak of purity through various ways.

In the phrase "O Blessed One, do they, practicing with restraint therein", "kaccissu" is a question of doubt, a question of uncertainty, a question of being in two minds, a question of indecision, asking "Is it thus? Is it not thus? What is it? How is it?". "Te" refers to those who hold such views. "Bhagavā" is a term of respect... a designation realized [by him], namely, the Blessed One. "Tattha" means in one's own view, one's own patience, one's own preference, one's own doctrine. "Yatā" means restrained, well-restrained, guarded, protected, watched over, controlled. "Carantā" means those who are practicing, dwelling, moving, proceeding, maintaining, sustaining. "O Blessed One, do they, practicing with restraint therein" means asking, "O Blessed One, do those people practice with restraint in their own views?"

"Have they crossed over birth and old age, dear sir?" means they have crossed over, gone beyond, transcended, surpassed birth, old age, and death. "Mārisa" is a term of endearment, a term of respect, a term of address with reverence and honor. "Have they crossed over birth and old age, dear sir?" means asking, "Friends, have those people crossed over birth and old age?"

In the phrase "I ask you, Blessed One, tell me this", "pုccāmi taṃ" means I ask about that matter, I entreat you, I urge you, please tell me. "Bhagavā" is a designation realized [by him]. "Tell me this" means please speak, declare, teach, point out, establish, reveal, analyze, make plain. Therefore, the brahmin said, "Those recluses and brahmins who speak of purity through seeing and hearing, through virtue and vows, and in various ways. O Blessed One, do they, practicing with restraint in their own views, cross over birth and old age? Friends, have they crossed over birth and old age? I ask the Blessed One about that matter; please tell me." Those recluses and brahmins who through seeing and hearing, through virtue and vows, and in various ways...
117:
Please point out, establish, reveal, analyze, make plain, and manifest. (I ask this.) Blessed One, I ask you about this matter; please tell me this matter. Therefore, that brahmin said:

The Venerable Nanda said:
"O Blessed One, there are these recluses and brahmins who say that purity is through seeing and hearing, who say that purity is through virtue and vows, and who say that purity is in various ways.
O Blessed One, do they, practicing with restraint in that view, cross over birth and old age?
I ask you, Blessed One, tell me this."

The Blessed One said:
"Nanda, there are these recluses and brahmins who say that purity is through seeing and hearing, who say that purity is through virtue and vows, and who say that purity is in various ways.
Even though they practice with restraint in that view, I say they have not crossed over birth and old age."

In the phrase "Whatever recluses and brahmins there are", "ye keci" is a term that includes everything, in every way, at all times, without exception, and entirely. "Samaṇā" refers to those who have gone forth and become wanderers outside this Dispensation. "Brāhmaṇā" refers to all those who are bhovādīs (brahmins). "Nanda, said the Blessed One" means the Blessed One addresses that brahmin by name. "Bhagavā" is a term of respect... a designation realized [by him].

"They speak of purity even through what is seen and heard" means they speak of, preach, recite, manifest, and designate purity, special purity, complete purity, liberation, special liberation, and complete liberation through seeing. They speak of... through hearing... (and so on) they speak of, preach, recite, manifest, and designate purity, special purity, complete purity, liberation, special liberation, and complete liberation through seeing and hearing.

"They speak of purity even through virtue and vows" means they speak of, preach, recite, manifest, and designate purity, special purity, complete purity, liberation, special liberation, and complete liberation through virtue (sīla). They speak of... through vows (vata)... (and so on) they designate. They speak of, preach, recite, manifest, and designate purity, special purity, complete purity, liberation, special liberation...
118:
They speak of, preach, recite, illustrate, and designate complete liberation. They also speak of purity through virtue and vows. They speak of purity through various ways, which means they speak of, preach, recite, illustrate, and designate purity through diverse and noisy superstitions (kotūhalamangala), special purity, complete purity, liberation, special liberation, and complete liberation.

In the phrase 'kiñcāpi te tattha yatā caranti': 'kiñcāpi' is a conjunction of words, a combination of words, a completion of a phrase, a union of letters, a smoothness of consonants, and a sequence of words. 'Te' refers to those who have fallen into views. 'Tattha' means in their own view, in their own patience, in their own preference, and in their own belief. 'Yatā' means they are restrained, constantly restrained, secure, guarded, and controlled. 'Caranti' means they practice, they dwell, they maintain their postures, they conduct themselves, they preserve, they subsist, and they live.

'Nātariṃsu jātijaranti brūmi' means they have not crossed over birth, aging, and death; they have not specially crossed over, they have not diversely crossed over, they have not well crossed over, and they have not specially crossed over. Without escaping from birth, aging, and death, without being able to abandon them, and without crossing over, they revolve repeatedly within birth, aging, and death; they revolve repeatedly within the path of saṃsāra. They are followed by birth, pursued by aging, overwhelmed by disease, and struck down by death. I say they are without protection, without shelter, without refuge, and have become helpless. I tell, teach, proclaim, establish, open, analyze, clarify, and manifest this. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"Nanda, whatever recluses and brahmins in this world
Speak of purity through what is seen and heard,
Speak of purity through virtue and vows, or speak of purity through various ways;
Though they practice with restraint in those views, I say they have not crossed over birth and aging."

The venerable Nanda asked thus:
"Whatever recluses and brahmins in this world
Speak of purity through what is seen and heard,
Speak of purity through virtue and vows, or speak of purity through various ways."
119:
"If, O Sage, you say that these people have not crossed over the flood, then who in this world of devas and humans has crossed over birth and aging? I ask you, Blessed One, please tell me this."

"Ye kecime samaṇabrāhmaṇāse": the words 'ye keci' mean all, in every way, in all aspects, without exception, and without remainder; it is an exhaustive term. 'Samaṇā' refers to any wanderers (paribbājaka) who have gone forth outside of this Dispensation. 'Brāhmaṇā' refers to all those who are 'bhovādī' (brahmins). This is the meaning of the phrase 'ye kecime samaṇabrāhmaṇāse'. The venerable Nanda asked in this way.

"Diṭṭhassutenāpi vadanti suddhiṃ" means they speak of, preach, recite, illustrate, and designate purity, special purity, complete purity, liberation, special liberation, and complete liberation through what is seen and through what is heard. This is the meaning of the phrase 'diṭṭhassutenāpi vadanti suddhiṃ'.

"Sīlabbatenāpi vadanti suddhiṃ" means they speak of, preach, recite, illustrate, and designate purity, special purity, complete purity, liberation, special liberation, and complete liberation through virtue (sīla) and through vows (vata). This is the meaning of the phrase 'sīlabbatenāpi vadanti suddhiṃ'.

"Anekarūpena vadanti suddhiṃ" means they speak of, preach, recite, illustrate, and designate purity, special purity, complete purity, liberation, special liberation, and complete liberation through various kinds of superstitions (kotūhalamangala). This is the meaning of the phrase 'anekarūpena vadanti suddhiṃ'.

In the phrase "te ce munī brūsi anoghatiṇṇe": 'te ce' refers to those with wrong views. 'Munī': knowledge is called 'mona'. Because he has crossed the net of attachment such as lust and is free from craving, he is called a 'muni' (sage). 'Brūsi anoghatiṇṇe' means you say they have not crossed the flood of sensuality (kāmogha), the flood of existence (bhavogha), the flood of views (diṭṭhogha), and the flood of ignorance (avijjāogha); they have not transcended them, they revolve repeatedly within birth, aging, and death; they revolve within the path of saṃsāra; they are followed by birth, pursued by aging, overwhelmed by disease, and struck down by death; they are without protection, without shelter, and without refuge. 'Brūsi' means you tell, teach, make known, establish, open, analyze, and clarify. This is the meaning of the phrase 'brūsi anoghatiṇṇe'.
120:
(You) open, analyze, make plain, and manifest; regarding those people, you say: “Though they are sages, they have not crossed the flood.”

“Venerable Sir, who then in this world of gods and humans has crossed birth and old age? Dear Sir (mārisa), who is he that, in this world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its recluses and brahmins, its gods and humans, has crossed, surmounted, transcended, passed beyond, and well-overcome birth and old age?” “Mārisa” is a term of endearment, a term of respect, a designation of reverence and deference. “Who then, dear sir, in this world of gods and humans has crossed birth and old age?”

“I ask you, Blessed One, tell me this.” “I ask you” means I entreat you, I urge you, I express my faith in you. “Blessed One” (bhagavā) is a designation of respect... [omission]... a realization-concept, namely “Blessed One.” “Tell me this” means speak, explain, teach, make known, establish, open, analyze, make plain, and manifest. “I ask you, Blessed One, tell me this.” Therefore, that brahmin said:

“Whatever recluses and brahmins there are, [so the venerable Nanda said]
Who say that purity comes by what is seen and heard,
Who say that purity comes by precepts and vows, or by various other ways;
Though you call them sages, you say they have not crossed the flood.
Who then, dear sir, in this world of gods and humans,
Has crossed birth and old age? I ask you, Blessed One, tell me this.”

“The Blessed One said thus:
Nanda, I do not say that all recluses and brahmins
Are shrouded by birth and old age;
Those here who have abandoned all that is seen, heard, or sensed,
And have abandoned all precepts and vows,
And have abandoned all various ways (such as omens), 
Who, having fully understood craving, are without taints (anāsava),
Those men, I say, have crossed the flood.”

I do not say that all recluses and brahmins are obstructed, entangled, overwhelmed, shrouded, covered, or overturned by birth and old age. Those for whom birth, old age, and death are abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, made non-existent, and are of a nature not to arise in the future—of those recluses and brahmins, I speak, I declare, I teach, I make known, I establish, I open, I analyze, I make plain, and I manifest.

Those here who have relinquished, strongly abandoned, destroyed, caused to vanish, and made non-existent all views that “purity comes through what is seen”... those who have relinquished all views that “purity comes through what is heard”... those who have relinquished all views that “purity comes through what is sensed”...
121:
Nanda, I do not say that all recluses and brahmins are obstructed, entangled, overwhelmed, shut in, covered, or overturned by birth and aging. There are those recluses and brahmins for whom birth, aging, and death are abandoned, uprooted like a palm stump, made non-existent, and are of a nature not to arise again in the future. I say that such recluses and brahmins exist; I declare, preach, make known, establish, reveal, analyze, clarify, and make it manifest. This is the meaning of the words: "Nanda, I do not say that all recluses and brahmins are enveloped by birth and aging."

Those here who have relinquished all views that "purity comes through what is seen," having abandoned, thoroughly abandoned, discarded, destroyed, and caused them to reach non-existence. Those who have relinquished all views that "purity comes through what is heard"... those who have relinquished all views that "purity comes through what is sensed"... those who have relinquished all views that "purity comes through what is seen, heard, and sensed"... those who have relinquished all views that "purity comes through virtue"... those who have relinquished all views that "purity comes through vows"... those who have relinquished all views that "purity comes through virtue and vows," having abandoned, thoroughly abandoned, discarded, destroyed, and caused them to reach non-existence. This is the meaning of the words: "Those here who have abandoned all that is seen, heard, or sensed, and have abandoned all virtue and vows."

Having abandoned purity, supreme purity, ultimate purity, liberation, supreme liberation, and ultimate liberation through various tumultuous omens, having abandoned, thoroughly abandoned, discarded, destroyed, and caused them to reach non-existence. This is the meaning of the words: "Who have abandoned all various other ways."

Those who, having fully understood craving, are without taints—those men alone, I say, have crossed the flood of saṃsāra. Craving (taṇhā) refers to craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for odors, craving for flavors, craving for tangibles, and craving for mind-objects. To fully understand craving (taṇhaṃ pariññāya) means to understand craving through the three kinds of full understanding: full understanding of the known (ñāta-pariññā), full understanding by investigation (tīraṇa-pariññā), and full understanding by abandoning (pahāna-pariññā).

What is full understanding of the known? One knows craving: "This is craving for forms, this is craving for sounds, this is craving for odors, this is craving for flavors, this is craving for tangibles, this is craving for mind-objects." Thus one knows and sees—this is full understanding of the known.

What is full understanding by investigation? Having thus known, one investigates craving as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a boil... as a way of escape. This is full understanding by investigation.
122:
What is full understanding as abandoning (pahānapariññā)? Having investigated in this way (through tīraṇapariññā), one abandons craving, dispels it, makes an end of it, and leads it to non-existence. Regarding this, the Blessed One said: "Monks, whatever desire and lust (chandarāga) there is in craving, abandon it. When it is thus abandoned, that craving will be cut off, destroyed at the root, made like a palm-stump, made non-existent, and of a nature not to arise again in the future." This is full understanding as abandoning. "By fully understanding craving" means knowing craving through these three types of full understanding. "Anāsavā" (taintless ones) refers to the four taints (āsava): the taint of sensuality (kāmāsava), the taint of existence (bhavāsava), the taint of views (diṭṭhāsava), and the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava). Those for whom these taints are abandoned, destroyed at the root, made like a palm-stump, made non-existent, and of a nature not to arise again in the future, are called the taintless ones, the Arahants, those whose taints are exhausted—thus, "by fully understanding craving, they are taintless."

"I say those men have crossed the flood" means: I say, declare, teach, establish, reveal, analyze, clarify, and proclaim that those who are taintless by fully understanding craving have crossed the flood of sensuality, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance; they have crossed over, gone beyond, surpassed, and fully transcended the entire path of saṃsāra. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"I do not say that all recluses and brahmins, [O Nanda, said the Blessed One]
Are shrouded by birth and old age;
But those here who have abandoned all that is seen, heard, or sensed, or even virtue and vows,
Who have abandoned all the various forms, and by fully understanding craving are taintless,
Those men, I say, have crossed the flood."

I greatly delight in these words of the Great Seer (Mahesi), the well-proclaimed Gotama who is free from acquisitions (anūpadhika). Those here who have abandoned all that is seen, heard, or sensed, or even virtue and vows, who have abandoned all the various forms, and by fully understanding craving are taintless—I also say that they have crossed the flood. Thus, I greatly delight in, rejoice in, desire, and take pleasure in the words of the Blessed One.
123:
“I greatly delight in these words of the Great Seer” means: I delight in, greatly delight in, rejoice in, greatly rejoice in, desire, take pleasure in, long for, cherish, and speak longingly of your word, utterance, teaching, instruction, and advice. In the term “Mahesino” (of the Great Seer), why is the Blessed One called “Mahesi”? He is called “Mahesi” because he sought, searched for, and pursued the great aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha)... He is also called “Mahesi” because he is sought after by those asking, “Where is the Great One among men (narāsabha), the Buddha?” Thus, it means “I greatly delight in these words of the Great Seer.”

“O Gotama, free from acquisitions, it is well proclaimed” means: “Sukittitaṃ” (well proclaimed) means well spoken, well taught, well prescribed, well established, well revealed, well analyzed, well clarified, and well manifested. In the term “Gotamanūpadhikaṃ,” defilements (kilesa), aggregates (khandha), and volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra) are called “acquisitions” (upadhi). Nibbāna, which is the abandoning of acquisitions, the stilling of acquisitions, the relinquishing of acquisitions, the complete tranquilizing of acquisitions, and the deathless, is what is meant by “Gotamanūpadhikaṃ.” Thus, it means “O Gotama, free from acquisitions, it is well proclaimed.”

“Those here who have abandoned all that is seen, heard, sensed (known), and all virtue and vows” means: Those who have abandoned, given up, strongly rejected, dispelled, made an end of, and led to non-existence all views that purity comes from what is seen. Those who have abandoned... all views that purity comes from what is heard... all views that purity comes from what is sensed... all views that purity comes from what is seen, heard, and sensed... all views that purity comes from virtue... all views that purity comes from vows... those who have abandoned, given up, strongly rejected, dispelled, made an end of, and led to non-existence all views that purity comes from virtue and vows. Thus, it means “Those here who have abandoned all that is seen, heard, sensed, and all virtue and vows.”

“Who have abandoned all the various forms” means: Those who have abandoned, given up, strongly rejected, dispelled, made an end of, and led to non-existence the belief in purity, supreme purity, ultimate purity, liberation, supreme liberation, and ultimate liberation through various kinds of superstitious omens (koṭūhalamangala). Thus, it means “Who have abandoned all the various forms.”

“Those who, by fully understanding craving, are taintless, I say they have crossed the four floods” means: “Craving” (taṇhā) refers to craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for smells, craving for tastes, craving for touches, and craving for mental objects. “By fully understanding craving” means knowing craving through the three types of full understanding: full understanding as the known (ñātapariññā), full understanding as investigating (tīraṇapariññā), and full understanding as abandoning (pahānapariññā).

What is full understanding as the known (ñātapariññā)? One knows craving: “This is craving for forms, this is craving for sounds, this is craving for smells, this is craving for tastes, this is craving for touches, this is craving for mental objects.” Such knowing and seeing is called full understanding as the known.

What is full understanding as investigating (tīraṇapariññā)? Having thus known it, one investigates craving as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a boil, as a dart, as a calamity, as an affliction...
124:
One understands (craving) by way of: as another, as crumbling, as a calamity, as a disaster, as a terror, as an affliction, as unstable, as disintegrating, as non-permanent, as no protection, as no shelter, as no refuge, as not a sanctuary, as empty, as vain, as void, as non-self, as a danger, as subject to change, as coreless, as the root of misery, as a killer, as non-existence, as accompanied by cankers, as conditioned, as Mara's bait, as subject to birth, as subject to aging, as subject to sickness, as subject to death, as subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, as subject to defilement, as the origin, as the disappearance, as the gratification, as the danger, and as the escape. This is called full understanding as investigation (tīraṇapariññā).

What is full understanding as abandonment (pahānapariññā)? Having investigated thus, one abandons craving, dispels it, eliminates it, and brings it to non-existence. This is called full understanding as abandonment.

"Taṇhaṃ pariññāya" means understanding craving through these three aforementioned types of full understanding. "Anāsavā" refers to the four cankers: the canker of sensuality (kāmāsava), the canker of existence (bhavāsava), the canker of views (diṭṭhāsava), and the canker of ignorance (avijjāsava). Those for whom these cankers are abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, brought to non-existence, and are of a nature not to arise again in the future, are called cankerless Arahants, those whose cankers are destroyed (khīṇāsava). "Taṇhaṃ pariññāya anāsavāse, ahampi te oghatiṇṇāti brūmi" means that those who, having understood craving through the three types of full understanding, become cankerless; I, the Buddha, say and declare that they have crossed the flood of sensuality, the flood of existence, the flood of views, the flood of ignorance, and have crossed over, ascended, passed beyond, and transcended the entire path of saṃsāra (through the four paths). This is the meaning of the words: "Taṇhaṃ pariññāya anāsavāse, ahampi te oghatiṇṇāti brūmi."

Therefore, that youth Nanda said this:
"I greatly rejoice in these words of the Great Sage; the venerable Gotama has well-proclaimed the Dhamma that is free from substrates (upadhi).
Those in this world who abandon the seen, the heard, the sensed, and all virtue and vows.
Having abandoned all things of various forms, and having understood craving through full understanding, they become cankerless; I say that they are the ones who have crossed the four floods."

## The Exposition of the Questions of the Youth Nanda, the Seventh, is finished.
125:
## 8. Hemakamāṇavapucchaniddesa

The venerable Hemaka addressed the Buddha thus:
"Those who explained to me before the teaching of the venerable Gotama said: 'It was thus, it will be thus.' All that talk was mere hearsay. All that talk only increased speculation; I did not find delight in their views."

"Ye me pubbe viyākaṃsu" means—the Brahmin Bāvarī and his other teachers explained, told, taught, prescribed, established, opened, analyzed, made clear, and revealed their own views, their own endurance, their own preference, their own creed, their own disposition, and their own intention. This is the meaning of "Ye me pubbe viyākaṃsu."

"Iccāyasmā hemako": "Iccā" is a word-junction... the sequence of words. "Āyasmā" is a term of endearment... "Hemako" is the name of that Brahmin... a designation. This is the meaning of "Iccāyasmā hemako."

"Huraṃ gotamasāsanā" means—before the teaching of the venerable Gotama, outside the teaching of the venerable Gotama, prior to the teaching of the venerable Gotama; before the teaching of the Buddha, the teaching of the Victor (Jina), the teaching of the Tathāgata, and the teaching of the Arahant. This is the meaning of "Huraṃ gotamasāsanā."

"Iccāsi iti bhavissati" means—it was thus, it will be thus. This is the meaning of "Iccāsi iti bhavissati."

"Sabbaṃ taṃ itihītihaṃ" means—all that talk was mere hearsay of "it was so, it was so," a traditional lineage, acceptance because it is in the scriptures, based on logic, based on method, based on reasoned reflection, and based on acceptance of a view after pondering. It was not a Dhamma personally realized by themselves, nor did they speak of a Dhamma directly experienced by themselves. This is the meaning of "Sabbaṃ taṃ itihītihaṃ."

"Sabbaṃ taṃ takkavaḍḍhanaṃ" means—all that talk increases speculation, increases various thoughts, increases wrong thoughts, increases thoughts of sensuality, increases thoughts of malice, increases thoughts of cruelty, increases thoughts of relatives, increases thoughts of the country, increases elusive thoughts like the 'amara' fish, increases thoughts connected to compassion for others, increases thoughts connected to gain, honor, and fame, and increases thoughts connected to making oneself known to others. This is the meaning of "Sabbaṃ taṃ takkavaḍḍhanaṃ."
126:
"I do not delight in that view" means I do not delight in their view, I do not find it, I do not attain it, and I do not acquire it. Therefore, the young man Hemaka said this:

"Venerable Hemaka said: Those of old who explained to me outside the teaching of Gautama the Buddha, said 'It has been thus, it will be thus.' All that is mere hearsay and only increases speculation; therefore, I do not delight in that view.

O Sage, tell me the Dhamma, the destruction of craving, knowing which, one wandering mindful, may cross over the entanglement in the world."

In the phrase "Tell me the Dhamma," "You" refers to the Blessed One. "Tell me the Dhamma" means to tell, teach, prescribe, establish, open, analyze, make plain, and manifest the Dhamma which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, complete in meaning and phrasing, the entirely perfect and pure holy life, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, Nibbāna, and the practice leading to Nibbāna.

In the phrase "O Sage, the destruction of craving," "craving" (taṇhā) refers to craving for forms and so on, up to craving for mental objects. "Destruction of craving" means the abandoning, the stilling, the relinquishing, and the complete tranquilizing of craving, which is the Deathless Nibbāna. "Sage" (muni) refers to the knowledge that knows... because he has crossed over the web of attachments, he is called a Sage.

"Knowing which, one wandering mindful" means having known, weighed, investigated, developed, and made manifest. It means having known, weighed, investigated, developed, and made manifest that "All conditioned things are impermanent"... "All conditioned things are suffering"... "All phenomena are non-self"... "Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease." "Mindful" (sato) means being mindful through four causes, such as being mindful while developing the foundation of mindfulness of contemplation of the body in the body. "Wandering" (caraṃ) means practicing, living, moving, proceeding, protecting, and maintaining.

In the phrase "May cross over the entanglement in the world," "visattikā" refers to craving. It refers to lust, intense lust... greed, avarice, and craving which is the unwholesome root. It is called "visattikā" because it spreads and permeates. "In the world" refers to the world of misery, the human world, the deva world, the world of aggregates, the world of elements, and the world of sense bases. One should cross over that craving in the world while being mindful.
127:
For what reason is it called "visattikā"? Because it spreads and because it is extensive, it is called "visattikā" (craving). "In the world" means in the world of misery, the human world, the deva world, the world of aggregates, the world of elements, and the world of sense bases. "May cross over the entanglement in the world" means that in the world, one should cross over, go beyond, cross through, transcend, and overcome this entanglement, this craving, while being mindful. Therefore, that brahmin said:

"Tell me the Dhamma, the destruction of craving, O Sage,
Knowing which, one wandering mindful, may cross over the entanglement in the world."

(The Buddha replied:)
"Here, in things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized, O Hemaka,
The removal of desire and lust in dear forms is the deathless state of Nibbāna."

In the phrase "In things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized," "seen" (diṭṭha) means seen with the eye; "heard" (suta) means heard with the ear; "sensed" (muta) means smelled with the nose, tasted with the tongue, or touched with the body; "cognized" (viññāta) means cognized with the mind.

In the phrase "O Hemaka, in dear forms," what in the world is of a dear nature and a pleasant nature? In the world, the eye is of a dear nature and a pleasant nature. The ear... the nose... the tongue... the body... the mind is of a dear nature and a pleasant nature in the world. Forms... sounds... smells... tastes... touches... mental objects are of a dear nature and a pleasant nature in the world. Eye-consciousness... ear-consciousness... nose-consciousness... tongue-consciousness... body-consciousness... mind-consciousness is of a dear nature and a pleasant nature in the world. Eye-contact... ear-contact... nose-contact... tongue-contact... body-contact... mind-contact is of a dear nature and a pleasant nature in the world. Feeling born of eye-contact... feeling born of ear-contact... feeling born of nose-contact... feeling born of tongue-contact... feeling born of body-contact... feeling born of mind-contact is of a dear nature and a pleasant nature in the world. Perception of forms... perception of sounds... perception of smells... perception of tastes... perception of touches... perception of mental objects is of a dear nature and a pleasant nature in the world.
128:
In the world, volition regarding forms (rūpasañcetanā), volition regarding sounds (saddasañcetanā), volition regarding smells (gandhasañcetanā), volition regarding tastes (rasasañcetanā), volition regarding touches (phoṭṭhabbasañcetanā), and volition regarding mental objects (dhammasañcetanā) are pleasant and agreeable in nature. In the world, craving for forms (rūpataṇhā), craving for sounds (saddataṇhā), craving for smells (gandhataṇhā), craving for tastes (rasataṇhā), craving for touches (phoṭṭhabbataṇhā), and craving for mental objects (dhammataṇhā) are pleasant and agreeable in nature. In the world, thought regarding forms (rūpavitakka), thought regarding sounds (saddavitakka), thought regarding smells (gandhavitakka), thought regarding tastes (rasavitakka), thought regarding touches (phoṭṭhabbavitakka), and thought regarding mental objects (dhammavitakka) are pleasant and agreeable in nature. In the world, sustained thought regarding forms (rūpavicāra), sustained thought regarding sounds (saddavicāra), sustained thought regarding smells (gandhavicāra), sustained thought regarding tastes (rasavicāra), sustained thought regarding touches (phoṭṭhabbavicāra), and sustained thought regarding mental objects (dhammavicāra) are pleasant and agreeable in nature. This is the meaning of the phrase 'piyarūpesu hemaka'.

In the phrase 'chandarāgavinodanaṃ', 'lust and desire' (chandarāga) refers to whatever sensual desire (kāmacchanda), sensual lust (kāmarāga), sensual delight (kāmanandī), sensual craving (kāmataṇhā), sensual affection (kāmasineha), sensual fever (kāmapariḷāha), sensual infatuation (kāmamucchā), sensual obsession (kāmajjhosāna), the flood of sensuality (kāmogha), the bond of sensuality (kāmayoga), sensual clinging (kāmupādāna), and the hindrance of sensual desire (kāmacchandanīvaraṇa) exist regarding the cords of sensual pleasure. 'Chandarāgavinodanaṃ' means the abandoning of lust and desire, the stilling of lust and desire, the relinquishing of lust and desire, the complete tranquility of lust and desire, which is the deathless Nibbāna itself.

'Nibbānapadamaccutaṃ' refers to the state of Nibbāna which is a place of protection (tāṇapada), a place of shelter (leṇapada), a place of refuge (saraṇapada), and a place of fearlessness (abhayapada). 'Accutaṃ' means permanent, stable, eternal, and of an unchanging nature. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

## "Hemaka, in this world, the removal of lust and desire for things seen, heard, sensed, and known, which are pleasant in nature, is the unchanging state of Nibbāna."
## "Those who are mindful, knowing this Nibbāna, are cooled in this very life; they, being always peaceful, have crossed over the craving that spreads in the world," so He said.

In the phrase 'etadaññāya ye satā', 'etadaṃ' refers to the deathless Nibbāna. It is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna. 'Aññāya' means having known, having weighed, having investigated, having developed, and having made manifest. Having known, weighed, investigated, developed, and made manifest that "all formations are impermanent". Having known, weighed, investigated, developed, and made manifest that "all formations are suffering", and "all things are non-self"... "whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease," having known, weighed, and investigated...
129:
'Vibhāvayitvā' means making manifest. 'Ye' refers to the Arahants whose taints are destroyed. 'Satā' means being mindful through four causes—because they have developed the foundation of mindfulness consisting of the contemplation of the body in the body (kāyānupassanā satipaṭṭhāna)... therefore they are called 'mindful'. Thus, it means 'those who, knowing this meaning, are mindful'.

In the phrase 'diṭṭhadhammābhinibbutā', 'diṭṭhadhammā' refers to things seen, things known, things weighed, things investigated, things made manifest, and things developed. Things seen as 'all formations are impermanent'... things seen, known, weighed, investigated, made manifest, and developed as 'whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease'. 'Abhinibbutā' refers to those who are cooled because lust has been extinguished, cooled because hatred has been extinguished, cooled because delusion has been extinguished; those who are peaceful, calmed, fully calmed, reflective, extinguished, departed, and tranquilized due to the stilling, calming, complete calming, investigation, cessation, disappearance, and cooling of anger... resentment... and all unwholesome formations (akusalābhisaṅkhāra). Thus, it means 'those who are cooled in this very life'.

In the phrase 'upasantā ca te sadā', 'upasantā' refers to those who are peaceful because lust, hatred, delusion, anger, resentment... and all unwholesome formations have been stilled.
