'Te' refers to the Arahants whose taints are destroyed. 'Sadā' means always, at all times, constantly, perpetually, continuously, without interval, like the succession of waves, before the meal, after the meal, in the first watch, the middle watch, the last watch, during the dark fortnight, the bright fortnight, the rainy season, the winter, the summer, in the first stage of life, the middle stage of life, and the last stage of life—meaning they are always peaceful at all times.

In the phrase 'tiṇṇā loke visattikaṃ', 'visattikā' refers to craving (taṇhā). It is whatever lust, intense passion... covetousness, greed, and unwholesome roots. Why is it called 'visattikā'? Because it spreads and expands. 'Loke' refers to the world of misery... the world of the sense bases. 'Tiṇṇā loke visattikaṃ' means they have crossed over this craving in the world, they have especially crossed over, emerged from, transcended, well transcended, and particularly transcended. Therefore, the Blessed One said this:

At the end of the verse, (the youth Hemaka said): "Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is my teacher, and I am the disciple."

## The Explanation of the Question of the Youth Hemaka is finished.

## The Explanation of the Question of the Youth Todeyya

The Venerable Todeyya asked this: "In whom desires do not dwell, in whom craving does not exist, and who has crossed over doubt—what is the liberation of such a person?"

'Yasmiṃ kāmā na vasanti' means in which person desires do not dwell, do not reside together, do not especially dwell, and do not dwell in any way.

'Iccāyasmā todeyyo' means thus the Venerable Todeyya (asked).

'Taṇhā yassa na vijjati' means in whom craving does not exist, is not found, is not obtained, and has been burnt by the fire of knowledge.
130:
“Knowing this instruction, being mindful, those who are quenched in this very life, and are always peaceful, have crossed over the entanglement of craving in the world.” (Thus he said).

At the end of the verse ... “Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is my teacher, I am the disciple.” (Thus he said).

## The Exposition of the Questions of the Young Man Hemaka, the eighth, is finished.

## 9. The Exposition of the Questions of the Young Man Todeyya

In whom sensual pleasures do not dwell, (thus asked the venerable Todeyya),
In whom craving is not found,
And who has crossed over doubt, what is his liberation (vimokkha) like?

'Yasmiṃ kāmā na vasanti' means: in whom sensual pleasures do not dwell, do not reside together, do not particularly dwell, do not dwell in any way—thus, 'in whom sensual pleasures do not dwell.' 'Iccāyasmā Todeyyo' means: 'Iccā' is a conjunction of words ... 'āyasmā' is a term of endearment ... 'Todeyyo' is the name of that brahmin ... thus, 'thus asked the venerable Todeyya'.

'Taṇhā yassa na vijjati' means: in whom craving does not exist, is not present, is not found, is not obtainable, having been burnt by the fire of knowledge—thus, 'in whom craving is not found'.

'Kathaṃkathā ca yo tiṇṇo' means: he who has crossed over doubt, has crossed beyond, has crossed over completely, has transcended, has well transcended, has gone beyond—thus, 'and who has crossed over doubt'.

'Vimokkho tassa kīdiso' means: what is his liberation like? How is it established? Of what kind is it? What is it like? What should be desired? Thus he asks about liberation—thus, 'what is his liberation like?' Therefore, that brahmin said:

“In whom sensual pleasures do not dwell, (thus asked the venerable Todeyya),
In whom craving is not found,
And who has crossed over doubt, what is his liberation like?”
131:
In whom sensual pleasures do not dwell, (O Todeyya, said the Blessed One),
Craving is not found in him,
And who has crossed over doubt, for him there is no other liberation.

'Yasmiṃ kāmā na vasanti' means: in that person who is an Arahant, one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava). 'Kāmā' means: in brief, there are two kinds of sensual pleasures—sensual pleasures as objects (vatthukāma) and sensual pleasures as defilements (kilesakāma) ... these are called vatthukāma ... these are called kilesakāma. 'Yasmiṃ kāmā na vasanti' means in that person sensual pleasures do not dwell, do not reside together, do not particularly dwell, do not dwell in every way.

'Todeyya'ti Bhagavā' means: the Blessed One addresses that brahmin by name. 'Bhagavā' is a term of respect ... it is a designation realized by oneself, therefore he is called 'Bhagavā'—thus, 'O Todeyya, said the Blessed One'.

'Taṇhā yassa na vijjati' means: craving refers to craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for smells, craving for tastes, craving for tangibles, and craving for mental objects. 'Yassa' refers to the Arahant whose taints are destroyed. 'Taṇhā yassa na vijjati' means in whom craving does not exist, is not present, is not found, is not obtainable; it is abandoned, cut off at the root, calmed, tranquilized, incapable of arising again, and burnt by the fire of knowledge.

'Kathaṃkathā ca yo tiṇṇo' means: 'Kathaṃkathā' is called doubt (vicikicchā). Doubt regarding suffering ... the trembling of the mind, the wavering of the mind. 'Yo' refers to that Arahant whose taints are destroyed. 'Kathaṃkathā ca yo tiṇṇo' means he who has crossed over doubt, has crossed beyond, has crossed over completely, has transcended, has well transcended, has gone beyond.

'Vimokkho tassa nāparo' means: for him there is no other liberation. If there were another liberation by which he should be liberated, he is already liberated. He has done what was to be done through liberation.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“In whom sensual pleasures do not dwell, (O Todeyya, said the Blessed One),
Craving is not found in him,
And who has crossed over doubt, for him there is no other liberation.”
132:
Is he without desire or is he full of desire? Is he wise or is he a conceptualizer through wisdom? O Sakka, so that I may know the Sage (Muni), please explain this to me, O All-Seeing One.

'Is he without desire or is he full of desire' (Nirāsaso so uda āsasāno) is a question asking: Is that person free from craving, or does he possess craving and thus desire, long for, delight in, and yearn for forms, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, family, groups, dwellings, gains, fame, praise, happiness, robes, alms-food, lodgings, medicinal requisites, the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, sense-existence, fine-material existence, immaterial existence, existence with perception, existence without perception, existence with neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one-constituent existence, four-constituent existence, five-constituent existence, the past, the future, the present, and things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized?

'Is he wise or is he a conceptualizer through wisdom' (Paññāṇavā so uda paññakappī) means: Is he a wise person, one who possesses wisdom, intellect, and knowledge, one who is discerning and sagacious? Or does he, through the knowledge of the eight attainments, the five superknowledges, or through wrong knowledge, conceptualize, produce, generate, and bring about the conceptualization of craving or the conceptualization of views?

'O Sakka, so that I may know the Sage' (Muniṃ ahaṃ sakka yathā vijaññaṃ): 'Sakka' refers to the Blessed One. He is called 'Sakka' because he went forth from the Sakyan clan. Alternatively, he is called 'Sakka' because he is rich and possesses great wealth. His wealth consists of: the wealth of faith, the wealth of virtue, the wealth of moral shame, the wealth of moral dread, the wealth of learning, the wealth of generosity, the wealth of wisdom, the wealth of the foundations of mindfulness, the wealth of the right efforts, the wealth of the bases of power, the wealth of the faculties, the wealth of the powers, the wealth of the factors of enlightenment, the wealth of the path, the wealth of the fruition, and the wealth of Nibbāna. Because he is rich and possesses such various kinds of precious wealth, he is called 'Sakka'. Alternatively, he is called 'Sakka' because he is capable, powerful, competent, brave, heroic, valiant, fearless, undaunted, unafraid, not fleeing, having abandoned fear and dread, and being free from hair-standing-on-end. 'Muniṃ ahaṃ sakka yathā vijaññaṃ' means: O Sakka, so that I may know, recognize, understand, fully understand, and penetrate the nature of the Sage.
133:
In the phrase 'Explain this to me, O All-Seeing One' (Taṃ me viyācikkha samantacakkhu), 'Taṃ' (this) refers to what I am asking, requesting, urging, and expressing devotion toward regarding the Sage. 'Viyācikkha' means: please tell, teach, prescribe, establish, reveal, analyze, clarify, and manifest. 'Samantacakkhu' (All-Seeing Eye) refers to the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa). Because he possesses such knowledge, the Blessed One is called the 'All-Seeing One'. Therefore, that brahmin Todeyya spoke thus:

'Is he without desire or is he full of desire? Is he wise or is he a conceptualizer through wisdom?
O Sakka, so that I may know the Sage,
Please explain this to me, O All-Seeing One.'

(The Buddha replied:)
'He is without desire and not full of desire; he is wise and not a conceptualizer through wisdom.
In this way, Todeyya, know the Sage,
Who is possessionless and unattached to sense-existence.'

'He is without desire and not full of desire' (Nirāsaso so na ca āsasāno) means he is free from craving. He does not have the nature of desire. He does not desire forms. He does not desire, want, delight in, long for, crave, or speak with craving regarding sounds, smells, and so forth, nor regarding things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized.

In the phrase 'He is wise and not a conceptualizer through wisdom' (Paññāṇavā so na ca paññakappī), 'Paññāṇavā' means being a wise person who is learned, endowed with wisdom, intelligent, knowledgeable, discerning, sagacious, and free from defilements. 'Na ca paññakappī' means he does not construct conceptualizations of craving (taṇhā-kappa) or conceptualizations of views (diṭṭhi-kappa) through the knowledge of the eight attainments, the five superknowledges, or wrong knowledge; he does not produce, generate, bring about, or excessively complete them.

In the phrase 'In this way, Todeyya, know the Sage' (Evaṃ pi todeyya muniṃ vijāna), 'Muni' refers to knowledge called 'mona'. One who has crossed over the net of attachment is called a Sage. 'In this way, Todeyya, know the Sage' means: Todeyya, in this way know, recognize, fully understand, and penetrate the nature of the Sage.

In the phrase 'Who is possessionless and unattached to sense-existence' (Akiñcanaṃ kāmabhave asattaṃ), 'Akiñcana' (possessionless/without impediments) means the absence of the oppressive things called 'impediments' (kiñcana), namely: lust, hatred, delusion, pride, views, defilements, and misconduct. For whomsoever these oppressive things are abandoned, cut off at the root, calmed, fully tranquilized, made unable to arise again, and burnt by the fire of knowledge, that person is called 'Akiñcana'. 'Kāma' (sensuality) is of two kinds: objective sensuality (vatthu-kāma) and defilement-based sensuality (kilesa-kāma). 'Bhava' (existence) is also of two kinds: kamma-existence (kamma-bhava) and rebirth-existence (upapatti-bhava).
134:
One who has abandoned, cut off, calmed, stilled, and made incapable of arising again the 'impediments' (kiñcana) such as lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, views, defilements, and misconduct, and who has burnt them with the fire of knowledge, is called 'akiñcana' (one without impediments). Sensuality (kāma) is of two kinds in brief: objective sensuality (vatthu-kāma) and subjective sensuality (kilesa-kāma). ... These are called objective sensuality. ... These are called subjective sensuality. Existence (bhava) is of two kinds: kamma-existence (kamma-bhava) and rebirth-existence (upapatti-bhava), which is called renewed existence. ... This is called rebirth-existence.

'Akiñcanaṃ kāmabhave asattaṃ' means a person without impediments who is not attached, not clinging, not entangled, and not bound by craving etc., in sensuality and existence, who has gone out, escaped, is particularly liberated, unassociated, and lives with a mind that has made no boundaries—this refers to 'akiñcanaṃ kāmabhave asattaṃ'. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"That sage is without longing, and is not one who longs;
He is wise, and not one who conjectures with wisdom;
Todeyya, know such a sage as one without impediments,
Unattached to sensuality and existence."

At the end of the verse ... "Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is my teacher, I am the disciple."

## 9. Todeyyamāṇavapucchāniddesa

## 10. Kappamāṇavapucchāniddesa

"O Venerable Sir, for the beings standing in the middle of the pool (the round of rebirths),
In the flood (ogha) where great fear has arisen,
Who are oppressed by old age and death,
Please tell me of an island of refuge.
Venerable Sir, declare that island to me,
So that this suffering may not occur again," thus requested the Venerable Kappa.

In the phrase 'majjhe sarasmiṃ tiṭṭhataṃ', 'sarasmiṃ' (in the pool) refers to the round of rebirths (saṃsāra). Coming, going, coming and going, the time of death, the five destinations (gati), small and large existences, passing away, rebirth, manifestation, destruction, birth, old age, and death are called 'the pool'. The prior end of the round of rebirths is not known, and the posterior end is not known. Beings are standing, staying, clinging, approaching, being deeply absorbed in, and being convinced by the middle of the round of rebirths.
135:
How is it that the prior end of the round of rebirths is not known? There is no such limit as "the round of rebirths revolves for this many births, and not beyond that"; thus, the prior end of the round of rebirths is not known. There is no such limit as "the round of rebirths revolves for this many hundreds of births, and not beyond that"; thus, the prior end of the round of rebirths is not known. There is no such limit as "the round of rebirths revolves for this many thousands of births, and not beyond that"; thus, the prior end of the round of rebirths is not known. There is no such limit as "the round of rebirths revolves for this many hundred thousands of births, and not beyond that"; thus, the prior end of the round of rebirths is not known. There is no such limit as "the round of rebirths revolves for this many crores (ten millions) of births, and not beyond that"; thus, the prior end of the round of rebirths is not known. There is no such limit as "the round of rebirths revolves for this many hundreds of crores of births, and not beyond that"; thus, the prior end of the round of rebirths is not known. There is no such limit as "the round of rebirths revolves for this many thousands of crores of births, and not beyond that"; thus, the prior end of the round of rebirths is not known. There is no such limit as "the round of rebirths revolves for this many hundred thousands of crores of births, and not beyond that"; thus, the prior end of the round of rebirths is not known.

There is no such limit as "the round of rebirths revolves for this many years, and not beyond that"; thus, the prior end of the round of rebirths is not known. There is no such limit as "the round of rebirths revolves for this many hundreds of years, and not beyond that"; thus, the prior end of the round of rebirths is not known. There is no such limit as "the round of rebirths revolves for this many thousands of years, and not beyond that"; thus, the prior end of the round of rebirths is not known. There is no such limit as "the round of rebirths revolves for this many hundred thousands of years, and not beyond that"; thus, the prior end of the round of rebirths is not known. There is no such limit as "the round of rebirths revolves for this many crores of years, and not beyond that"; thus, the prior end of the round of rebirths is not known. There is no such limit as "the round of rebirths revolves for this many hundreds of crores of years, and not beyond that"; thus, the prior end of the round of rebirths is not known. There is no such limit as "the round of rebirths revolves for this many thousands of crores of years, and not beyond that"; thus, the prior end of the round of rebirths is not known. There is no such limit as "the round of rebirths revolves for this many hundred thousands of crores of years, and not beyond that"; thus, the prior end of the round of rebirths is not known.

There is no such limit as "the round of rebirths revolves for this many aeons (kappa), and not beyond that"; thus, the prior end of the round of rebirths is not known. For this many hundreds of aeons...
136:
The round of suffering occurs; there is no such limit as 'beyond this it does not occur.' In this way, the first point of saṃsāra is not known. For as many as a thousand aeons, the round of suffering occurs; there is no such limit as 'beyond this it does not occur.' In this way, too, the first point of saṃsāra is not known. For as many as a hundred thousand aeons, the round of suffering occurs; there is no such limit as 'beyond this it does not occur.' In this way, too, the first point of saṃsāra is not known. For as many as ten million aeons, the round of suffering occurs; there is no such limit as 'beyond this it does not occur.' In this way, too, the first point of saṃsāra is not known. For as many as a billion aeons, the round of suffering occurs; there is no such limit as 'beyond this it does not occur.' In this way, too, the first point of saṃsāra is not known. For as many as ten billion aeons, the round of suffering occurs; there is no such limit as 'beyond this it does not occur.' In this way, too, the first point of saṃsāra is not known. For as many as a hundred billion aeons, the round of suffering occurs; there is no such limit as 'beyond this it does not occur.' In this way, too, the first point of saṃsāra is not known.

Thus it was said by the Blessed One: "Monks, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning. A first point is not discerned of beings roaming and wandering on, hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving. For such a long time, monks, you have experienced suffering, experienced agony, experienced disaster, and swelled the cemeteries. It is enough, monks, to be weary of all conditioned things, enough to become dispassionate, enough to be liberated." In this way, too, the first point of saṃsāra is not known.

How is the final point of saṃsāra not known? There is no such limit as 'the round of suffering will occur for this many lives, and after that it will not occur.' In this way, the final point of saṃsāra is not known. For as many as a hundred lives, for as many as a thousand lives, for as many as a hundred thousand lives, for as many as ten million lives, for as many as a billion lives, for as many as ten billion lives, for as many as a hundred billion lives, for as many as this many years, for as many as a hundred years, for as many as a thousand years, for as many as a hundred thousand years, for as many as ten million years, for as many as a billion years, for as many as ten billion years, for as many as a hundred billion years, for as many as this many aeons, for as many as a hundred aeons, for as many as a thousand aeons, for as many as a hundred thousand aeons, for as many as ten million aeons, for as many as...
137:
...for as many as a billion aeons, for as many as ten billion aeons, for as many as a hundred billion aeons, the round of suffering will occur; there is no such limit as 'beyond this it will not occur.' In this way, the final point of saṃsāra is not discerned. Thus, neither the first point of saṃsāra is discerned, nor is the final point discerned. Only in the middle of saṃsāra are beings standing, established, attached, reached, deeply involved, and fully committed. This is the meaning of the phrase 'majjhe sarasmiṃ tiṭṭhataṃ' (for those standing in the middle of the lake [of saṃsāra]). In the phrase 'iccāyasmā kappo', 'iccā' is a euphonic conjunction (padasandhi). 'Āyasmā' is a term of endearment. 'Kappo' is the name of that Brahmin. Because it is an expression of the name, it is said 'iccāyasmā kappo' (Thus said the venerable Kappa).

'Oghe jāte mahabbhaye' means when the flood of sensual desire, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance have arisen, have been produced, have been generated, and have appeared. 'Mahabbhaye' refers to the fear of birth, the fear of aging, the fear of sickness, and the fear of death. This is the meaning of the phrase 'oghe jāte mahabbhaye'.

'Jarāmaccuparetānaṃ' refers to those who are touched, oppressed, gathered, and possessed by aging; and to those who are touched, oppressed, gathered, and possessed by death; those followed by birth, permeated by aging, overwhelmed by sickness, and struck down by death; those without protection, without shelter, without refuge, and for whom no refuge exists. This is the meaning of the phrase 'jarāmaccuparetānaṃ'.

'Dīpaṃ pabrūhi mārisa' means: please tell, preach, make known, establish, open up, analyze, clarify, and reveal the island which is Nibbāna—the protection, the shelter, the refuge, the destination, and the support. 'Mārisa' is a term of endearment, a term of respect, and a form of address accompanied by reverence and deference. This is the meaning of the phrase 'dīpaṃ pabrūhi mārisa'.

In the phrase 'tvañca me dīpammakkhāhi', 'tvaṃ' refers to the Blessed One. 'Dīpammakkhāhi' means: please tell, preach, make known, establish, open up, analyze, clarify, and reveal the island which is Nibbāna—the protection, the shelter, the refuge, the destination, and the support. This is the meaning of the phrase 'tvañca me dīpammakkhāhi'.

'Yathāyidaṃ nāparaṃ siyā' means: in such a way that this suffering may cease in this very life, may be calmed, may come to an end, may be fully tranquilized; so that the suffering of rebirth may not arise again; so that it may not occur in the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, or the immaterial sphere; or in the sense-existence, fine-material existence, immaterial existence, percipient existence, non-percipient existence, neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient existence, one-constituent existence, four-constituent existence, or five-constituent existence; so that it may not arise again in destination, birth, rebirth, existence, saṃsāra, or the round of suffering; so that it may not cease [partially], may not be completed [partially], but may fully cease, be calmed, come to an end, and be fully tranquilized in this very life. This is the meaning of the phrase 'yathāyidaṃ nāparaṃ siyā'.
138:
Or in the formless realm, or in the percipient realm, or in the non-percipient realm, or in the neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient realm, or in the one-constituent existence, or in the four-constituent existence, or in the five-constituent existence, or in a future destination, or in rebirth, or in conception, or in existence, or in the round of rebirths, or in the cycle of suffering, one should not produce, should not cause to arise, should not bring into being, should not generate. Only in this very life should it cease, be calmed, come to an end, and be thoroughly stilled. This is the meaning of "so that this should not happen again." Therefore, that Brahmin addressed [the Buddha] thus:

"For those standing in the middle of the lake, [so said the venerable Kappa]
When the flood has arisen with great fear,
For those overwhelmed by old age and death, tell me of an island, O Venerable Sir,
And do you declare that island to me, so that this should not happen again."

The Blessed One [said thus]:
"Kappa, for those standing in the middle of the lake,
When the flood has arisen with great fear,
For those overwhelmed by old age and death, I tell you of an island."

"Majjhe sarasmiṃ tiṭṭhataṃ" means: the "lake" (sara) refers to the round of rebirths (saṃsāra), coming, going, coming and going, the time of death, destination, various existences, passing away and rebirth, manifestation, destruction, conception, old age, and death. Neither the beginning nor the end of the round of rebirths is known. Beings are standing, established, clinging, approaching, deeply involved, and committed right in the middle of the round of rebirths.

How is the beginning of the round of rebirths not known? ... (detailed) ... Thus the beginning of the round of rebirths is not known. How is the end of the round of rebirths not known? ... (detailed) ... Thus the end of the round of rebirths is not known. Thus neither the beginning nor the end of the round of rebirths is known. Beings are standing, established, clinging, approaching, deeply involved, and committed right in the middle of the round of rebirths. This is the meaning of "Majjhe sarasmiṃ tiṭṭhataṃ." "Kappāti bhagavā" means: the Blessed One addresses that Brahmin by name. "Bhagavā" is a term of respect... (detailed)... This very "Bhagavā" is a designation based on realization. This is the meaning of "Kappāti bhagavā."

"Oghé jāte mahabbhaye" means: when the flood of sensual desire, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance have arisen, been produced, been brought into being, been generated, and become manifest. "Mahabbhaye" means: in the fear of birth, the fear of old age, the fear of sickness, and the fear of death. This is the meaning of "Oghé jāte mahabbhaye."
139:
"Jarāmaccuparetānaṃ" means: for those touched, oppressed, surrounded, and filled by old age; and for those touched, oppressed, surrounded, and filled by death; for those followed by birth, permeated by old age, overwhelmed by sickness, struck down by death, without protection, without shelter, without refuge, and for whom there is no refuge for those who seek it.

"Dīpaṃ pabrūmi kappa te" means: I tell, declare, teach, point out, establish, open, analyze, clarify, and reveal the island (which is Nibbāna) that is a protection, a shelter, a refuge, a destination, and a support. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"Kappa, for those standing in the middle of the lake of saṃsāra, where the great floods (of sensual desire, existence, views, and ignorance) have arisen, and who are oppressed by old age and death, I shall tell you of a refuge-island."

"That island which has no impediments and no grasping, that is the island without another. I call it Nibbāna, the complete destruction of old age and death."

In the phrase "Akiñcanaṃ anādānaṃ": "Kiñcana" (impediment) refers to the impediment of lust, the impediment of hatred, the impediment of delusion, the impediment of pride, the impediment of views, the impediment of defilements, and the impediment of misconduct. The abandoning of these impediments, the calming of impediments, the relinquishing of impediments, the complete stilling of impediments, the deathless, the Nibbāna which is the escape from craving, is called "Akiñcana." In the phrase "Anādānaṃ": "Ādāna" (grasping) refers to craving (taṇhā). That lust, intense passion... (etc.)... greed, avarice, the unwholesome root—the abandoning of this craving, the calming of craving, the relinquishing of craving, the complete stilling of craving, the deathless, the Nibbāna which is the escape from craving, is called "Akiñcanaṃ anādānaṃ."

"Etaṃ dīpaṃ anāparaṃ" means: this island which is a protection, a shelter, a refuge, a destination, and a support. "Anāparaṃ" means: there is no other island superior to that Nibbāna. Indeed, that island alone is the highest, the best, the most excellent, the foremost, the supreme, and the most noble.

In the phrase "Nibbānaṃ iti naṃ brūmi": "Vāna" refers to craving (taṇhā). That lust, intense passion... (etc.)... greed, avarice, the unwholesome root—the abandoning of craving, the calming of craving, the relinquishing of craving, the complete stilling of craving, and the deathless is Nibbāna. The word "iti" is used for connecting words, combining words, completing words, the conjunction of letters, the smoothness of syllables, and the sequence of words. I tell, make known, establish, reveal, analyze, clarify, and manifest.
140:
"Brūmi" means telling, preaching, prescribing, establishing, revealing, analyzing, clarifying, and making manifest. In the phrase "Nibbānaṃ iti naṃ brūmi," craving is called "vāna." I call that island Nibbāna, which is the place where craving is abandoned, where craving is stilled, where craving is relinquished, the complete stilling of craving, the deathless, and the escape from craving.

"Jarāmaccuparikkhayaṃ" means the abandoning, stilling, relinquishing, and further stilling of old age and death, referring to the deathless Nibbāna. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"Having nothing, without attachment, there is no other island than this.
I call that island Nibbāna, the total destruction of old age and death.
Those who, knowing this, are mindful and have attained Nibbāna in this very life,
Do not follow the power of Māra; they are not the servants of Māra."

In the phrase "Etadaññāya ye satā," "etaṃ" refers to the deathless Nibbāna. It is the stilling of all formations (saṅkhāra), the relinquishing of all acquisitions (upadhi), the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna. "Aññāya" means having known, weighed, investigated, developed, and made manifest; knowing that "all formations are impermanent," etc., and "whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease," having known, weighed, investigated, developed, and made manifest. "Ye" refers to the Arahants whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava). "Satā" means being mindful through four causes, such as being mindful by practicing the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) by contemplating the body in the body, etc. Thus, the phrase "Etadaññāya ye satā" is explained.

In the phrase "Diṭṭhadhammābhinibbutā," "diṭṭhadhammā" refers to those who have seen, known, weighed, investigated, made manifest, and developed the Dhamma. "Abhinibbutā" means cooled (nibbuta) because of the extinguishing of lust, and because of the stilling, calming, ceasing, being consumed, cooling, and complete stilling of all unwholesome volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra). Thus, the phrase "Diṭṭhadhammābhinibbutā" is explained.

In the phrase "Na te māravasānugā," "Māro" refers to the Evil One, the Dark One, the Overlord, the Ender, Namuci, the Kinsman of the Heedless. "Na te māravasānugā" means they do not come under the power of Māra, nor does Māra exercise power over them. They live, dwell, move, proceed, protect, and maintain themselves by overcoming, conquering, overwhelming, exhausting, and crushing Māra, his partisans, his snare, his hook, his bait, his domain, his dwelling, his pasture, and his bonds. Thus, the phrase "Na te māravasānugā" is explained.
141:
"Na te mārassa paddhagū" means they are not the followers, attendants, or disciples at the feet of Māra. They are the followers, attendants, and disciples at the feet of the Blessed Buddha. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Those who, knowing this, are mindful and have attained Nibbāna in this very life, do not follow the power of Māra; they are not the servants of Māra." At the end of the verse... "Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is my teacher, I am the disciple."

## 10. The Exposition of the Questions of the Youth Kappa is finished.

## 11. The Exposition of the Questions of the Youth Jatukaṇṇī

The venerable Jatukaṇṇī asked this:
"O Hero, having heard of the Blessed One who does not desire sensual pleasures,
I have come to ask the one who has crossed the flood and is free from desire.
O One with the eye of universal wisdom, tell me of the state of peace, Nibbāna.
O Blessed One, tell me this as it really is."

"Sutvānahaṃ vīra akāmakāmiṃ" means having heard, listened, learned, upheld, and noted that "Thus is the Blessed One, an Arahant... the Buddha, the Blessed One." "Vīra" (Hero) means the Blessed One is energetic. He is called "Vīra" because he possesses energy, has great energy, arouses energy, has a mind capable of fulfilling desires, is brave, and conquers enemies. He is called "Vīra" because he is without fear, without trembling, without terror, does not flee, has abandoned fear and dread, and is free from horripilation.

Being free from all evils in this world, having crossed over the suffering of hell, he is energetic. Such a person who is energetic, possesses the energy of the path, and destroys defilements is called one endowed with energy.

"Sutvānahaṃ vīra." In the term "akāmakāmiṃ," "kāma" (sensual pleasure) is twofold in brief: objective sensuality (vatthu-kāma) and subjective sensuality (kilesa-kāma). ... These are called objective sensuality... these are called subjective sensuality. The Blessed One has fully understood objective sensuality and has abandoned subjective sensuality. Because of his full understanding of objective sensuality and his abandonment of subjective sensuality, the Blessed One does not desire, long for, or love sensual pleasures, nor does he speak with longing. Those who desire, long for, and love sensual pleasures, and speak with longing, are called those who desire sensual pleasure, those with lust, those with perception (of pleasure). Because the Blessed One does not desire, long for, or love sensual pleasures, nor speaks with longing, the Blessed One is one who does not desire sensual pleasure (akāma), is free from desire (nikkāma), has relinquished desire (vītakāma), and has vomited out desire.
142:
Sensual pleasures (kāma) are twofold in brief: objective sensuality (vatthukāma) and defilement sensuality (kilesakāma). Because the Blessed One has fully understood objective sensuality and has abandoned defilement sensuality, the Blessed One does not desire sensual pleasures, does not long for them, does not love them, and does not speak of them with longing. Those who desire, long for, love, and speak of sensual pleasures with longing are called seekers of sensuality, those lusting for passion, and those perceiving through perceptions. The Blessed One does not desire, long for, love, or speak of sensual pleasures with longing. Therefore, the Blessed One is one without desire (akāma), free from lust (nikkāma), one who has given up sensuality (cattakāma), one who has vomited out sensuality (vantakāma), one who is released from sensuality (muttakāma), one who has abandoned sensuality (pahīnakāma), one who has relinquished sensuality (paṭinissaṭṭhakāma), one free from passion (vītarāga), one whose passion has departed (vigatarāga), one who has given up passion (cattarāga), one who has vomited out passion (vantarāga), one who is released from passion (muttarāga), one who has abandoned passion (pahīnarāga), one who has relinquished passion (paṭinissaṭṭharāga), one who is hungerless (nicchāta), one who is extinguished (nibbuta), one who has become cooled (sītibhūta), and one who experiences happiness, dwelling with a self that has become sublime (brahmabhūta). This is the meaning of: 'Having heard [the words of] the Hero who is free from sensual desire.'

## Iccāyasmā jatukaṇṇīti.
The word 'Iccā' is a conjunction used in the sequence of words. 'Āyasmā' is a term of endearment, a respectful and deferential address. 'Jatukaṇṇī' is the lineage (gotta), name, designation, description, and common usage for that brahmin. This is the meaning of: 'Thus the venerable Jatukaṇṇī spoke.'

## Oghātigaṃ puṭṭhumakamamāgamanti.
'Oghātigaṃ' refers to one who has crossed the flood, who has fully crossed over, who has transcended it. 'Puṭṭhuṃ' means for the purpose of asking, requesting, urging, and gaining confidence. 'Akāmamāgamaṃ' means we have come to, approached, and met with you, the one who is without desire, free from lust, who has given up, vomited out, been released from, abandoned, and relinquished sensuality and passion. This is the meaning of: 'We have come to ask the one who has crossed the flood and is free from desire.'

## Santipadaṃ brūhi sahajanettāti.
'Santi' in one sense is peace and also the state of peace (santipada). That itself is the Deathless, Nirvana. It is the stilling of all formations (sabbasaṅkhārasamatha), the relinquishing of all acquisitions (sabbūpadhipaṭinissagga), the destruction of craving (taṇhakkhaya), dispassion (virāga), cessation (nirodha), Nirvana. For it was said by the Blessed One: 'This state is peaceful, this state is sublime, that is, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nirvana.' In another sense, those qualities that lead to the attainment of peace, the touching of peace, and the realization of peace are also called 'santipada'. They are: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment...
143:
The Noble Eightfold Path is called the state of peace (santipada). Please tell, explain, establish, open up, analyze, make clear, and reveal the state of peace, the state of protection (tāṇapada), the state of shelter (leṇapada), the state of refuge (saraṇapada), the state of fearlessness (abhayapada), the unmoving state (accutapada), the deathless state (amatapada), and the state of Nirvana. In the word 'Sahajanetta', 'netta' refers to omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa). Because the omniscience and the state of the Conqueror (jinabhāva) of the Blessed Buddha arose simultaneously (ekakkhaṇa) at the foot of the Bodhi tree, the Buddha is called 'Sahajanetta' (One with Co-arisen Vision). O Sahajanetta, please tell me the state of peace, Nirvana.

In the phrase 'Yathātacchaṃ bhagavā brūhi metanti', 'yathātacchaṃ' refers to the deathless Nirvana, ...pe... the cessation that is Nirvana. 'Bhagavā' is a title of respect, ...pe... a realized designation. 'Brūhi metaṃ' means 'Please tell me that Dhamma', ...pe... 'reveal it'. Therefore, that brahmin said:

'Having heard [the words of] the Hero who is free from sensual desire, [thus the venerable Jatukaṇṇī spoke]
I have come to ask the one who has crossed the flood and is free from desire.
Tell me the state of peace, O One with Co-arisen Vision; O Blessed One, tell me this as it really is.'

'The Blessed One dwells having overcome sensual pleasures, just as the powerful sun [overcomes] the earth with its radiance. To me of small wisdom, O One of vast wisdom, teach the Dhamma so that I may know the abandoning of birth and old age in this world.'

In the phrase 'Bhagavā hi kāme abhibhuyya iriyati', 'Bhagavā' is a word of respect, ...pe... a realized designation. 'Kāma' is twofold in brief: objective sensuality and defilement sensuality. ...pe... These are called objective sensuality, ...pe... these are called defilement sensuality. The Blessed One, having fully understood objective sensuality and abandoned defilement sensuality, dwells, lives, and proceeds having overcome and conquered them.

In the phrase 'Ādiccova pathaviṃ tejī tejasā', 'Ādicca' refers to the sun. 'Pathavī' refers to the earth. Just as the sun, endowed with power and radiance, overcomes the earth, taking it over completely and heating it, and dispels the darkness in the sky to show the light while traveling through the expanse of the sky; so too, the Blessed One, endowed with the power of omniscience, dispels the darkness of craving and defilements which are the causes of the three types of volitional formations (abhisankhāra), and the mass of darkness that is ignorance (avijjā), showing the light of knowledge and fully understanding objective sensuality.
144:
Just as the sun, being endowed with power and radiance, overcomes, masters, overwhelms, completely takes over, and heats the earth, destroying all darkness in the sky and space, dispelling the gloom and showing the light as it travels through the open expanse, the cloudless sky, the path of the gods; even so, the Blessed One, endowed with the power of the fire of knowledge, destroys the darkness of craving—the cause of all three types of volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra)—and the gloom of defilements, the darkness of ignorance. Showing the light of knowledge, fully understanding the objects of sensual pleasure (vatthukāma) and abandoning the defilements of sensual pleasure (kilesakāma), He dwells, lives, moves, proceeds, protects, and maintains Himself, having overcome and conquered them. With reference to this, it is said: "Just as the sun overcomes the earth with its power and radiance, so the Blessed One dwells having overcome sensual pleasures."

"To me of little wisdom, O One of vast wisdom like the earth" means: I am one of little wisdom, inferior wisdom, low wisdom, very meager wisdom. You, however, possess great wisdom, wide wisdom, joyous wisdom, swift wisdom, sharp wisdom, and penetrative wisdom. "Bhūri" refers to the earth. Because the Blessed One is endowed with wisdom that is vast, extensive, and spread out like the earth, it is said: "To me of little wisdom, O One of vast wisdom like the earth."

"Teach me the Dhamma that I may understand" means: Teach, preach, proclaim, establish, open up, analyze, clarify, and make manifest the Dhamma—which is beautiful in the beginning, beautiful in the middle, and beautiful in the end, with the correct meaning and phrasing, the entirely complete and pure holy life, the four foundations of mindfulness... Nibbāna and the practice leading to Nibbāna. "That I may understand" means that I may know, fully know, specially know, realize, penetrate, attain, touch, and witness that Dhamma. Thus it is said: "Teach me the Dhamma that I may understand."

"To abandon birth and aging in this life" means: The abandoning, calming, relinquishing, and complete tranquilizing of birth, aging, and death in this very life—referring to the deathless Nibbāna. Therefore, that Brahmin Jatukaṇṇī said:

"The Blessed One dwells having overcome sensual pleasures,
Just as the sun overcomes the earth with its power and radiance.
To me of little wisdom, O One of vast wisdom like the earth,
Teach me the Dhamma that I may understand,
To abandon birth and aging in this life."
145:
“Jatukaṇṇī, dispel the greed for sensual pleasures. Seeing renunciation (the practice leading to Nibbāna) as safety, let go of the things (such as the aggregates) that are grasped; let there be no perturbation (kiñcana) of the defilements in you.”

Regarding the phrase “Kāmesu vinaya gedhaṃ”: Sensual pleasures (kāma) are of two kinds in brief—objective sensual pleasures (vatthu-kāma) and subjective sensual pleasures (kilesa-kāma). ...pe... These are called objective sensual pleasures. ...pe... These are called subjective sensual pleasures. “Gedhaṃ” refers to craving (taṇhā). It is that lust, intense greed ...pe... covetousness, greed, and the unwholesome root. “Kāmesu vinaya gedhaṃ” means dispel the greed for sensual pleasures, dispel it repeatedly, relinquish it, remove it, eliminate it, and make it reach the state of non-existence.

Regarding the phrase “Jatukaṇṇīti bhagavā”: The Blessed One addresses that Brahmin by his clan name (gotta). “Bhagavā” is a term of respect. ...pe... Because it is a designation realized through direct experience, He is called “Bhagavā.”

Regarding the phrase “Nekkhammaṃ daṭṭhu khemato”: Renunciation (nekkhamma) refers to the right practice, the conforming practice, the non-contrary practice, the practice in accordance with the meaning, the practice in accordance with the Dhamma, the fulfillment of virtues, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, being possessed of mindfulness and clear comprehension, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the Noble Eightfold Path, Nibbāna, and the practice leading to Nibbāna. It means seeing, weighing, investigating, cultivating, and making manifest these as safety, as protection, as a cave, as a refuge, as being a refuge, as fearlessness, as the deathless, as the undying, and as Nibbāna.

Regarding the phrase “Uggahitaṃ nirattaṃ vā”: “Uggahita” refers to what is taken, handled, clung to, entered into, and misapprehended through the power of craving and views. “Nirattaṃ vā” refers to what should be relinquished, abandoned, removed, and made to reach the state of non-existence.

Regarding the phrase “Mā te vijjittha kiñcanaṃ”: This refers to the perturbation (kiñcana) of lust, the perturbation of hatred, delusion, conceit, views, defilements, and misconduct. It means: let these perturbations not be in you, let them not exist, let them not be present; relinquish them, dispel them, remove them, and make them reach the state of non-existence. Therefore, the Blessed One said:
146:
“Discard greed for sensual pleasures, [said the Blessed One to Jatukaṇṇī], and looking towards Nibbāna, which is safety, strive for renunciation (nekkhamma). Let there be nothing at all that is grasped by you or that is useless.”

Dry up the defilements of the past; let there be nothing for you in the future. If you do not grasp in the middle (the present), you will wander as one whose defilements are at peace.

'Yam pubbe tam visosehi' means: dry up, thoroughly dry up, wither, thoroughly wither, make seedless, abandon, dispel, eliminate, and bring to non-existence those defilements that would arise in relation to past formations (saṅkhāra). Thus is the meaning of 'Dry up what was before'. Alternatively, it means: dry up, thoroughly dry up, wither, thoroughly wither, make seedless, abandon, dispel, eliminate, and bring to non-existence those past kamma-formations (kammābhisaṅkhāra) whose results have not yet ripened. Thus also is the meaning of 'Dry up what was before'.

'Pacchā te māhu kiñcanaṃ' means: 'behind' (pacchā) refers to future formations. The 'perturbations' (kiñcana) of lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, views, defilements, and misconduct. May these perturbations (kiñcana) not be for you, do not let them be, do not produce them, do not generate them, do not bring them into existence; abandon, dispel, eliminate, and bring them to non-existence. This is the meaning of 'Let there be nothing for you behind'.

'Majjhe ce no gahessasi' means: 'middle' (majjhe) refers to the present form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. You shall not grasp the present formations through the power of craving or the power of views; you shall not hold onto them, not misapprehend them, not delight in them, not greatly delight in them, and not be deeply attached to them. You shall abandon, dispel, eliminate, and bring to non-existence great delighting, great praising, deep attachment, grasping, misapprehension, and deep obsession. This is the meaning of 'If you do not grasp in the middle'.

'Upasanto carissasi' means: because of the calming of lust, you will wander at peace. Because of the calming... (etc.) ...of all unwholesome kamma-formations; because they are stilled, calmed, fully calmed, extinguished, quenched, gone, and subsided, you will wander, you will dwell as one who is still, at peace, fully at peace, quenched, and subsided.
147:
You will move, exist, protect, sustain, and maintain your life—this is the meaning of 'you will wander at peace'. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

'Dry up what was before,
Let there be nothing for you behind;
If you do not grasp in the middle,
You will wander at peace.'

O Brahmin (Jatukaṇṇī), for one who is free from greed in name-and-form entirely, no taints exist for him by which one would go under the power of Death.

'O Brahmin, for one who is free from greed in name-and-form entirely' (Sabbaso nāmarūpasmiṃ vītagedhassa brāhmaṇa): 'Entirely' (sabbaso) is a term for all in every way, without remainder, without exception, completely. 'Name' (nāma) refers to the four immaterial aggregates. 'Form' (rūpa) refers to the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements (upādā-rūpa). 'Greed' (gedha) is called craving. It is lust, passion... (etc.) ...covetousness, greed, the unwholesome root. 'O Brahmin, for one who is free from greed in name-and-form entirely' means one who is free from greed, whose greed has gone, who has relinquished greed, vomited greed, is freed from greed, has abandoned greed, has renounced greed; one who is free from lust, whose lust has gone, who has relinquished lust, vomited lust, is freed from lust, has abandoned lust, has renounced lust in name-and-form entirely.

'No taints exist for him' (Āsavāssa na vijjanti): 'Taints' (āsava) are the four taints—the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava), the taint of existence (bhavāsava), the taint of views (diṭṭhāsava), and the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava). 'For him' (assa) refers to the Arahant whose taints are destroyed. 'Do not exist' (na vijjanti) means these taints do not exist for that Arahant, they are not present, they are not found, they are not obtainable; they are abandoned, cut off at the root, calmed, subsided, incapable of arising again, and burnt up by the fire of knowledge.

'By which one would go under the power of Death' (Yehi maccuvasaṃ vaje) means: those taints by which one would go under the power of Death (maccu), or under the power of dying, or under the power of the faction of Māra. Those taints do not exist for him, they are not present, they are not found, they are not obtainable; they are abandoned, cut off at the root, calmed, subsided, incapable of arising again, and burnt up by the fire of knowledge. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

'O Brahmin, for one who is free from greed in name-and-form entirely,
No taints exist for him by which one would go under the power of Death.'

At the end of the verse, [the young man Jatukaṇṇī] declared: “The Blessed One is my teacher, I am the disciple.” The question of the young man Jatukaṇṇī is finished.
148:
At the end of the verse (...) he said, "Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is my teacher, I am the disciple."

## The Exposition of the Question of the Youth Jatukaṇṇi, the Eleventh, is finished.

## 12. The Exposition of the Question of the Youth Bhadrāvudha

[The Venerable Bhadrāvudha spoke thus:]
"I entreat the One of great wisdom, who has abandoned the home (abode), who has cut off craving, who is unagitated,
Who has abandoned delight, who has crossed the flood, who is liberated,
Who has abandoned conceptualizations. Having heard the word of the Great One (Nāga), they will depart from here."

"Okañjahaṃ taṇhacchidaṃ anejaṃ": "Okañjahaṃ" means: whatever desire, lust, delight, craving, attachment, and the mind's staying, settling, and underlying tendency (anusaya) there is in the element of form (rūpadhātu), these have been abandoned by the Blessed Buddha, their roots have been cut, they have been made like a palm-tree stump, they have been rendered non-existent, and they are of a nature not to arise in the future. Therefore, the Buddha is called Okañjaha. In the element of feeling... (...) ...in the element of perception... in the element of mental formations... in the element of consciousness, whatever desire, lust, delight, craving, attachment, and the mind's staying, settling, and underlying tendency (anusaya) there is, these have been abandoned by the Blessed Buddha, their roots have been cut, they have been made like a palm-tree stump, they have been rendered non-existent, and they are of a nature not to arise in the future. Therefore, the Buddha is called Okañjaha.

"Taṇhacchidaṃ" means: craving refers to craving for forms... (...) ...craving for mental objects. That craving has been cut by the Blessed Buddha, specially cut, completely cut, calmed, fully calmed, is no longer capable of arising, and has been burnt by the fire of knowledge. Therefore, the Buddha is called Taṇhacchida.

"Anejo" means: "Ejā" refers to craving. Whatever lust, intense lust, (...) covetousness (abhijjhā), greed, and craving which is the root of the unwholesome there is—that ejā-craving has been abandoned by the Blessed Buddha, its roots have been cut, it has been made like a palm-tree stump, it has been rendered non-existent, and it is of a nature not to arise in the future. Therefore, the Buddha is called Aneja. Because he has abandoned ejā-craving, the Blessed One, called Aneja, does not shake in the face of gain, does not shake in the face of loss, does not shake in the face of fame, does not shake in the face of disrepute, does not shake in the face of praise, does not shake in the face of blame, does not shake in the face of happiness, does not shake in the face of pain; he does not move, does not tremble, does not shake violently, does not shake violently again and again. Therefore, the Buddha is called Aneja.
149:
Regarding the term "Anejo" in the verse "Okañjahaṃ taṇhacchidaṃ anejaṃ": "Taṇhacchidaṃ" means the Buddha is called Taṇhacchida (cutter of craving) because craving for forms and so forth has been burnt and cut by the fire of knowledge. "Anejo" means the Buddha is called Aneja (unagitated) because he has abandoned the craving called "ejā," and because he does not shake or move in the face of the worldly conditions of gain and loss, fame and disrepute, praise and blame, happiness and pain. Regarding the phrase "Iccāyasmā Bhadrāvudho": "Iccā" is a word-connection. "Āyasmā" is a term of endearment. "Bhadrāvudho" is the name of that brahmin. "Iccāyasmā Bhadrāvudho" is the expression (abhilāpa) used.

"Nandiñjahaṃ oghatiṇṇaṃ vimuttaṃ": "Nandī" refers to craving. Whatever lust, intense lust (sārāga)... covetousness (abhijjhā), greed, and craving which is the root of the unwholesome there is—that craving called delight (nandī) has been abandoned by the Blessed Buddha, its roots have been cut, it has been made like a palm-tree stump, it has been rendered non-existent, and it is of a nature not to arise in the future. Therefore, the Buddha is called Nandiñjaha (abandoner of delight). "Oghatiṇṇaṃ" means: the Blessed One has crossed the flood of sensuality, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance. He has crossed the entire path of saṃsāra, crossed over, crossed through, transcended, well transcended, and specially transcended. That Blessed One has lived the holy life (ariya-vāsa) and has completed the practice. For that Blessed One, the cycle of birth and death and further rebirth no longer exist. This is the meaning of "Nandiñjahaṃ oghatiṇṇaṃ." "Vimuttaṃ" means: the Blessed One's mind is liberated from lust, specially liberated, well liberated. From hatred... from delusion... from all unwholesome volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra), the mind is liberated, specially liberated, well liberated. This is the meaning of "Nandiñjahaṃ oghatiṇṇaṃ vimuttaṃ."

"Kappañjahaṃ abhiyāce sumedhaṃ": "Kappa" refers to two: craving-conceptualization (taṇhā-kappa) and view-conceptualization (diṭṭhi-kappa). This is called craving-kappa; this is called view-kappa. The Blessed One has abandoned craving-kappa and relinquished view-kappa. Because he has abandoned craving-kappa and relinquished view-kappa, the Buddha is called Kappañjaha. "Abhiyāce" means I entreat, I beseech, I invite, I welcome, I long for, I cherish, I speak, I speak out. "Sumedhā" refers to wisdom. It is the wisdom that knows, wisdom that discerns... non-delusion (amoha), investigation of states (dhamma-vicaya), and right view (sammā-diṭṭhi). The Blessed One is endowed with this wisdom called medhā, well endowed, attained, well attained, possessed, and fully possessed of it. Therefore, the Buddha is called Sumedha. This is the meaning of "Kappañjahaṃ abhiyāce sumedhaṃ."

"Sutvāna nāgassa apanamissanti ito": "Nāgassa" refers to the Nāga (the Buddha). The Blessed One is called Nāga because he does no evil (āguṃ na karoti). He is called Nāga because he does not go to (unwholesome states). He is called Nāga because he does not come back (to defilements). Thus, the Blessed One is called Nāga because he does not go (to what is improper). "Sutvāna nāgassa apanamissanti ito" means: having heard, listened to, learned, borne in mind, and well noted the word of the Venerable One, the spoken word, the Dhamma teaching, the repeated instruction, and the advice, they will depart from here, they will go, they will leave, they will go to various directions and intermediate directions. This is the meaning of "Sutvāna nāgassa apanamissanti ito." Therefore, that brahmin said: "Okañjahaṃ taṇhacchidaṃ anejaṃ, nandiñjahaṃ oghatiṇṇaṃ vimuttaṃ, kappañjahaṃ abhiyāce sumedhaṃ, sutvāna nāgassa apanamissanti ito."
150:
Venerable Sir, I entreat the Wise One who has abandoned the home (attachment), cut off craving, is unshakable, has abandoned delight, crossed the flood, and is liberated. Having heard the words of the Nāga (the Buddha), they will depart from here.

O Hero, many people gathered from various provinces are greatly longing for your words. Please explain well to them. For you have known this Dhamma in such a way.

The Buddha stands close (to the benefit), stands well, has arrived, has arrived fully, and has arrived completely. Therefore, the Buddha is called 'Sumedha'. This is the meaning of the phrase 'Kappañjahaṃ abhiyāce sumedhaṃ'. In the phrase 'Sutvāna nāgassa apanamissanti ito', 'Nāgassa' means the Buddha is called 'Nāga' because he does not do evil, because he does not go to places where one should not go, and because he does not return (to defilements). Thus, the Buddha is called 'Nāga' because he does not go (to evil). 'Sutvāna nāgassa apanamissanti ito' means that having heard, learned, borne in mind, and well-remembered the words of the Buddha, the spoken words, the Dhamma teaching, the repeated instructions, and the words of advice, they will depart from here and go to their respective directions. This is the meaning of the phrase 'Sutvāna nāgassa apanamissanti ito'. Therefore, that Brahmin addressed the Buddha with these words whose meanings have been explained: 'Okañjahaṃ taṇhacchidaṃ anejaṃ, nandijahaṃ oghatiṇṇaṃ vimuttaṃ, kappañjahaṃ abhiyāce sumedhaṃ, sutvāna nāgassa apanamissanti ito'. Being greatly longing for your words, they have come to this place in unison. Being entreated, please explain well to them. For you have known this Dhamma in such a way. Thus did the youth Bhadrāvudha entreat.

## Nānājanā janapadehi saṅgatāti.
In the phrase 'Nānājanā janapadehi saṅgatā', 'Nānājanā' refers to kings, brahmins, householders, commoners, laypeople, monastics, devas, and humans. 'Janapadehi saṅgatā' refers to those who have come from the Aṅga country, Magadha country, Kaliṅga country, Kāsi country, Kosala country, Vajji country, Malla country, Cetiya country, Vaṃsa country, Kuru country, Pañcāla country, Maccha country, Sūrasena country, Assaka country, Avanti country, Yona country, and Kamboja country. 'Saṅgatā' means those who have come together in unison, met, and assembled. This is the meaning of the phrase 'Nānājanā janapadehi saṅgatā'.

## Tava vīra vākyaṃ abhikaṅkhamānāti.
In the phrase 'Tava vīra vākyaṃ abhikaṅkhamānā', 'Vīrā' means the Hero (Vīra). The Buddha is called 'Vīra' because he is energetic, because he is endowed with power and majesty, because he is skilled, because he has a capable mind, and because he is free from horripilation. Having abstained from all evils in this world and having transcended the suffering of hell, he is energetic. One who has such effort, who destroys evil with the Path, and who possesses noble effort is called 'Vīra' because of such nature. 'Tava vīra vākyaṃ abhikaṅkhamānā' refers to your words, the manner of speaking, the teaching, the instruction, and the repeated instruction. 'Abhikaṅkhamānā' means those who are greatly longing, desiring, delighting in, yearning for, cherishing, and speaking with longing. This is the meaning of the phrase 'Vākyaṃ abhikaṅkhamānā'.

## Tesaṃ tuvaṃ sādhu viyākarohīti.
In the phrase 'Tesaṃ tuvaṃ sādhu viyākarohi', 'Tesaṃ' refers to those kings, brahmins, householders, commoners, laypeople, monastics, devas, and humans. 'Tuvaṃ' refers to the Buddha. 'Sādhu viyākarohi' is an entreaty meaning: please listen well, please preach, please make it known, please establish, please open up, and please analyze.
151:
Please preach, make known, establish, open up, analyze, make clear, and reveal (the Dhamma) to those (who entreat); please answer them well, Venerable Sir. For you have known, weighed, investigated, manifested, and developed this Dhamma as it is perceived by beings. Therefore, that Brahmin spoke thus:

'Many people gathered from various provinces, O Hero, are greatly longing for your words. Please explain well to them, for you have known this Dhamma.'

'O Bhadrāvudha,' (said the Buddha), 'one should remove all craving for grasping—above, below, and across in the middle. Whatever one grasps in the world, by that very grasping, Māra follows the being.'

In the phrase 'one should remove all craving for grasping (ādānatṇhā)', 'ādānatṇhā' refers to craving for form (rūpa-taṇhā) and so forth. Why is it called 'ādānatṇhā'? Because through that craving, they take up, grasp, seize, misapprehend, and adhere to form. They take up, grasp, seize, misapprehend, and adhere to feeling... perception... mental formations... consciousness... destiny... rebirth... relinking... existence... saṃsāra... and the round of rebirths. For that reason, it is called 'ādānatṇhā'. 'One should remove all craving for grasping' means one should remove, repeatedly remove, abandon, dispel, eliminate, and bring to a state of non-existence all craving for grasping. The Buddha addressed that Brahmin by name as 'Bhadrāvudha'. 'Bhagavā' is a term of respect... it is called 'Bhagavā' because it is a designation realized by himself.

In the phrase 'above, below, and across in the middle', 'above' (uddhaṃ) refers to the future, 'below' (adho) refers to the past, and 'across in the middle' (tiriyañcāpi majjhe) refers to the present. 'Above' means the celestial world, 'below' means the hell world, and 'middle' means the human world. Alternatively, 'above' means wholesome states (kusala dhamma), 'below' means unwholesome states (akusala dhamma), and 'middle' means indeterminate states (abyākata dhamma). 'Above' means the formless realm (arūpadhātu), 'below' means the sense realm (kāmadhātu), and 'middle' means the form realm (rūpadhātu). 'Above' means pleasant feeling (sukha vedanā), 'below' means painful feeling (dukkha vedanā), and 'middle' means neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (adukkhamasukha vedanā). 'Above' means upwards from the soles of the feet.
152:
'Adho' means the part below the tips of the hair. 'Tiriyañcāpi majjhe' means the center. It refers to above, below, across, and in the middle.

'Yaṃ yañhi lokasmimupādiyanti' means whatever form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness they take, cling to, grasp firmly, misapprehend, or focus upon in the world. 'Lokasmiṃ' refers to the world ranging from the woeful worlds to the world of the bases. This is the meaning of 'Yaṃ yañhi lokasmimupādiyanti'.

'Teneva māro anveti jantun' means that by the power of those kamma-formations caused by that clinging craving, the Mara of the aggregates, the Mara of the elements, the Mara of the bases, the Mara of the destinations, the Mara of rebirth, the Mara of conception, the Mara of existence, the Mara of saṃsāra, and the Mara of the round of rebirths follow, pursue, and accompany the being. 'Jantun' refers to a being, a person, a man, a youth, an individual, a soul, a creature, or a human. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"Bhadrāvudha, one should remove all clinging craving—above, below, across, and in the middle. Whatever one clings to in the world, by that very thing Māra follows the person."

Therefore, a monk, being mindful, should not cling to anything in the whole world, seeing these beings who are attached to clinging as entangled in the realm of Death.

In the phrase 'Tasmā pajānaṃ na upādiyetha', 'Tasmā' means for that reason, because of that cause, due to that condition, or by that origin—seeing this danger in clinging craving. 'Pajānaṃ' means knowing, understanding, perceiving, discerning, comprehending, and penetrating that "all formations are impermanent," and so on, up to "whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease." 'Na upādiyetha' means one should not take, cling to, grasp firmly, misapprehend, or focus upon form. One should not take, cling to, grasp firmly, misapprehend, or focus upon feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, destination, rebirth, conception, existence, saṃsāra, or the round of rebirths. This is the meaning of 'Tasmā pajānaṃ na upādiyetha'.
153:
Knowing that there is a thing of the nature to arise, and that all such things are of the nature to cease—knowing thus through discernment, through focus, through special knowledge, through repeated special knowledge, and through penetration—one should not cling. 'Na upādiyetha' means one should not take, cling to, grasp, misapprehend, or focus upon form. One should not take, cling to, grasp, misapprehend, or focus upon feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, destination, rebirth, conception, existence, saṃsāra, or the round of rebirths. This is the meaning of the phrase 'Tasmā pajānaṃ na upādiyetha'.

In the phrase 'Bhikkhu sato kiñcanaṃ sabbaloke', 'Bhikkhu' refers to either a virtuous worldling monk or a monk who is a trainee (sekha). 'Sato' means one who is mindful through four reasons: by developing the foundation of mindfulness consisting of the contemplation of the body in the body, and so on... such a person is called 'mindful'. This is the meaning of 'Bhikkhu sato'. 'Kiñcanaṃ' refers to anything consisting of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. 'Sabbaloke' means in the entire world of woeful states, the entire human world, the entire celestial world, the entire world of aggregates, the entire world of elements, and the entire world of bases. This is the meaning of the phrase 'Bhikkhu sato kiñcanaṃ sabbaloke'.

In the phrase 'Ādānasatte iti pekkhamāno', those beings who take, cling to, grasp firmly, misapprehend, or focus upon form are called 'those attached to clinging'. Those who take, cling to, grasp firmly, misapprehend, or focus upon feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, destination, rebirth, conception, existence, saṃsāra, or the round of rebirths are also called 'those attached to clinging'. 'Iti' refers to the connection of words or the sequence of words. 'Pekkhamāno' means observing, looking, seeing, viewing, or contemplating. This is the meaning of the phrase 'Ādānasatte iti pekkhamāno'.

In the phrase 'Pajaṃ imaṃ maccudheyye visattaṃ', 'Paja' is a synonym for beings. The defilements, the aggregates, and the kamma-formations are called 'maccudheyya' (the realm of Death). Beings are entangled, specially entangled, intensely entangled, stuck, specifically stuck, or obstructed in the round of rebirths connected with the Mara of Death, with Mara, and with death. Just as goods are hung, entangled, or stuck on a wall-peg or an ivory hook, in the same way, beings are entangled, specially entangled, intensely entangled, stuck, specifically stuck, or obstructed in the round of rebirths connected with the Mara of Death, with Mara, and with death. This is the meaning of the phrase 'Pajaṃ imaṃ maccudheyye visattaṃ'. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"Therefore, one should not cling to anything among beings; a monk, being mindful, should not cling to anything in the whole world.
Observing those attached to clinging in this way, one should see this generation entangled in the realm of Death."

At the conclusion of the verses... "Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is my teacher, I am the disciple."

## The Explanation of the Questions of the Young Man Bhadrāvudha, the Twelfth, is finished.

"I have come to ask a question of the one who is meditative, stainless, seated, who has done what was to be done, who is without taints, and who has reached the further shore of all things. Please teach me the liberation that destroys ignorance through knowledge," said the young man Udaya. In the phrase 'Jhāyī virajamāsīnaṃ', 'Jhāyī' means the Blessed One is accustomed to delighting in meditation. He is accustomed to delighting in the first jhāna.
154:
## 13. Exposition of the Questions of the Young Man Udaya

To the one who is meditative, free from the dust of defilements, and seated (seeking the welfare of beings), the Venerable Udaya spoke thus:
To the one who has completed what was to be done, who is free from taints (āsavas),
And who has reached the far shore of all dhammas, I have come with a question.
Please proclaim the liberation (vimokkha) through gnosis, which destroys ignorance.

Jhāyiṃ virajamāsīnanti. "Jhāyiṃ" means the Blessed One possesses jhāna. He meditates and delights in the first jhāna, the second jhāna, the third jhāna, and the fourth jhāna. He meditates and delights in the jhāna with initial and sustained application (vitakka and vicāra), in the jhāna without initial application and with sustained application only, and in the jhāna without both initial and sustained application. He meditates and delights in the jhāna accompanied by rapture (pīti), and in the jhāna without rapture. He meditates and delights in the jhāna accompanied by happiness (sukha), and in the jhāna accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā). He meditates and delights in the jhāna associated with the liberation of emptiness (suññata-vimokkha), in the jhāna associated with the signless liberation (animitta-vimokkha), and in the jhāna associated with the undirected liberation (appaṇihita-vimokkha). He meditates and delights in mundane jhāna and in supramundane jhāna. Because he delights in jhāna, is devoted to solitude, and values his own goal, he is called "Jhāyiṃ."

"Virajaṃ" means—lust is dust, hatred is dust, delusion is dust, anger is dust, malice is dust... all unwholesome formations (akusala-abhisaṅkhāra) are dust. These dusts have been abandoned by the Buddha, the Blessed One; they are uprooted, made like a palm stump, made non-existent, and made not liable to arise again in the future. Therefore, the Buddha is without dust, free from dust, departed from dust, removed from dust, has abandoned dust, is detached from dust, and has transcended all dust.

Lust is called dust, but actual dust (of the earth) is not called so. "Dust" is a designation for lust. Having abandoned and dispelled this dust of lust, the One with Vision (possessing the five eyes) remains. Therefore, the Conqueror (Jina) is called "one who has gone beyond dust."

Hatred is called dust, but actual dust (of the earth) is not called so. "Dust" is a designation for hatred. Having abandoned and dispelled this dust of hatred, the One with Vision (possessing the five eyes) remains. Therefore, the Conqueror (Jina) is called "one who has gone beyond dust."
155:
Delusion is called dust; however, mere soil is not called 'dust'. This word 'dust' is a designation for delusion. Because the Blessed One, who possesses the five eyes, has abandoned this dust of delusion, the Victorious Buddha is called 'one free from dust' (vigataraja). Regarding 'virajaṃ' (stainless) and so forth—the Blessed One has abandoned the dust of unwholesome formations (akusala-abhisaṅkhāra), cut them at the root, made them like a palm stump, rendered them non-existent, so that they are not subject to future arising. Therefore, the Blessed One is without dust, free from dust, emerged from dust, detached from dust, has abandoned dust, is separated from dust, and has transcended all dust. Lust (rāga) is called dust; mere soil is not called 'dust'. This 'dust' is a name for lust. The Blessed One, who possesses the five eyes, having abandoned and dispelled that dust of lust, remains [steadfast]. Therefore, the Victorious Buddha is called 'one free from dust'. Hatred (dosa) is called dust; mere soil is not called 'dust'. This 'dust' is a name for hatred. The Blessed One, who possesses the five eyes, having abandoned and dispelled that dust of hatred, remains [steadfast]. Therefore, the Victorious Buddha is called 'one free from dust'. Delusion (moha) is called dust; mere soil is not called 'dust'. This 'dust' is a name for delusion. The Blessed One, who possesses the five eyes, having abandoned and dispelled that dust of delusion, remains [steadfast]. Therefore, the Victorious Buddha is called 'one free from dust'. This is the meaning of the word 'virajaṃ'.

'Āsīnaṃ' (seated) means the Blessed One was seated on the stone slab at the Pāsāṇaka Cetiya, desiring the welfare of beings. Disciples who possess the three knowledges (tevijjā) and have abandoned death attend to the Sage who is seated on the side of the mountain [at Rājagaha], who has reached the further shore of all suffering, and who dwells desiring the welfare of beings. In this way also, the Blessed One is 'seated'. Alternatively, the Blessed One is 'seated' because all anxieties of the defilements have been stilled, and he dwells beholding the welfare of beings. Having lived the holy life, with conduct (caraṇa) practiced... the cycle of birth, aging, and death, as well as future rebirth, no longer exists for that Blessed One. In this way also, the Blessed One is 'seated'. This is the meaning of the phrase 'jhāyiṃ virajamasīnaṃ'.

'Iccāyasmā udayo'—'iccā' is a word-junction; 'āyasmā' (venerable) is a term of endearment; 'udaya' is the name of that brahmin. This is the meaning of the phrase 'iccāyasmā udayo'.

'Katakiccaṃ anāsavaṃ' (one who has done what was to be done, without taints) means the Blessed One has abandoned what should and should not be done by the mind, and what should and should not be done by the body; he has cut them at the root, made them like a palm stump, rendered them non-existent, and made them such that they are not subject to future arising. Therefore, the Buddha is one who has done what was to be done (katakicca). For the monk who has cut the stream of lust and other [defilements], who has abandoned what should and should not be done by the mind, and in whom the spreading craving does not exist, the fever of defilements is not found. In the phrase 'katakiccaṃ anāsavaṃ', the taints (āsava) are four: the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava), the taint of existence (bhavāsava), the taint of views (diṭṭhāsava), and the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava). The Blessed One has abandoned these taints, cut them at the root, made them like a palm stump, rendered them non-existent, and made them such that they are not subject to future arising. Therefore, the Buddha is free from taints (anāsava). This is the meaning of the phrase 'katakiccaṃ anāsavaṃ'.

'Pāragūṃ sabbadhammānaṃ' (gone to the further shore of all dhammas) means the Blessed One has reached the further shore of all things through higher knowledge (abhiññā), reached the further shore through full understanding (pariññā), reached the further shore through abandoning (pahāna), reached the further shore through development (bhāvanā), reached the further shore through realization (sacchikiriya), and reached the further shore through attainment (samāpatti). He has reached the further shore of all dhammas through higher knowledge; the further shore of all suffering through full understanding; the further shore of all defilements through abandoning; the further shore of the four paths through development; the further shore of cessation through realization; and the further shore of all attainments through attainment. He has attained mastery and perfection in noble virtue (sīla), attained mastery and perfection in noble concentration (samādhi), attained mastery and reached the noble state in noble wisdom (paññā), and attained mastery and reached the noble state in noble liberation (vimutti). That Blessed One has reached Nibbāna through the Path, reached Nibbāna through Fruition; reached the end of the world through the Path, reached the end of the world through Fruition; reached the summit through the Path, reached the summit through Fruition; reached the end of the aggregates through the Path, reached the end of the aggregates through Fruition; reached the end through the Path, reached the end through Fruition; reached protection through the Path, reached protection through Fruition; reached shelter through the Path, reached shelter through Fruition; reached refuge through the Path, reached refuge through Fruition; reached fearlessness through the Path, reached fearlessness through Fruition; reached the state free from falling through the Path, reached the state free from falling through Fruition; reached the deathless through the Path, reached the deathless through Fruition; reached liberation from defilements through the Path, and reached liberation from defilements through Fruition. That Blessed One dwells in the ten noble abodes (ariyavāsa). For that Blessed One, dwelling in future existence no longer exists. This is the meaning of the phrase 'pāragūṃ sabbadhammānaṃ'.
156:
That Blessed One has attained mastery in noble concentration, he has reached the further shore. He has attained mastery in noble wisdom, he has reached the further shore. He has attained mastery in noble liberation, he has reached the further shore. That Blessed One has gone to the far shore, reached the far shore; gone to the end, reached the end; gone to the summit, reached the summit; gone to the limit, reached the limit; gone to the conclusion, reached the conclusion; gone to the protection, reached the protection; gone to the shelter, reached the shelter; gone to the refuge, reached the refuge; gone to the fearless, reached the fearless; gone to the changeless, reached the changeless; gone to the deathless, reached the deathless; gone to Nibbāna, reached Nibbāna. That Blessed One has lived the holy life, practiced the conduct... for him, there is no more birth, death, or the suffering of the round of rebirths (saṃsāra), and there is no further becoming in a new life—thus, he has reached the far shore of all dhammas.

'I have come with a question' means: I have come because there is a question, I have come wishing to ask a question, I have come wishing to hear a question. In this way, it is said, 'I have come with a question.' Alternatively, it means there is the coming, the proceeding, the approaching, and the attending of those who desire a question, who wish to ask a question, or who wish to hear a question; in this way also, it is said, 'I have come with a question.' Alternatively, it means: 'The answer to the question exists with you; you are capable and competent to speak and answer what I have asked; please bear this burden.' In this way also, it is said, 'I have come with a question.'

'Proclaim the liberation of final knowledge' means: the liberation of Arahantship is called the liberation of final knowledge. Proclaim the liberation of Arahantship—tell it, teach it, declare it, establish it, open it, analyze it, make it clear, and manifest it.

'The shattering of ignorance' means: the shattering of ignorance, its breaking, its abandoning, its calming, its relinquishing, its total tranquility, the deathless Nibbāna. Therefore, that Brahmin addressed him thus:

[The Venerable Udaya said:]
'To the one who is meditating, sitting stainless,
Who has done what was to be done and is without taints,
Who has reached the far shore of all dhammas, I have come with a question.
Proclaim the liberation of final knowledge, the shattering of ignorance.'
157:
The abandoning of sensual desires, (so the Blessed One said to Udaya)
And of both kinds of distress,
The dispelling of sloth, and the warding off of remorse.
