'The abandoning of sensual desires' means: whatever sensual desire (kāmacchanda), sensual lust, sensual delight, sensual craving, sensual affection, sensual thirst, sensual fever, sensual infatuation, sensual obsession, the flood of sensuality, the yoke of sensuality, the clinging to sensuality, and the hindrance of sensual desire there is regarding sensual pleasures. 'The abandoning of sensual desires' refers to the abandoning, the calming, the relinquishing, the tranquility, the deathless Nibbāna of those sensual desires. 'Udaya, so the Blessed One said' means: the Blessed One addressed that Brahmin by name. 'Bhagavā' (Blessed One) is a designation of respect.

'Both kinds of distress' means: distress (domanassa) is whatever is mentally unpleasant, mental pain, unpleasant and painful experience born of mental contact, or unpleasant and painful feeling born of mental contact. 'Both kinds of distress' refers to the abandoning, the calming, the relinquishing, the tranquility, the deathless Nibbāna of both sensual desire and distress.

'The dispelling of sloth' means: sloth (thīna) is the unhealthiness of the mind, the unreadiness for work, the shrinking, the withdrawing, the sluggishness, the state of being stuck, the stiffness, and the mental rigidity. 'The dispelling of sloth' refers to the dispelling, the abandoning, the calming, the relinquishing, the tranquility, the deathless Nibbāna of that sloth.

'The warding off of remorse' means: remorse (kukkucca) includes fidgeting with the hands, fidgeting with the feet, or fidgeting with both hands and feet. It is perceiving what is not allowable as allowable, or perceiving what is allowable as not allowable... perceiving what is faultless as faulty, or perceiving what is faulty as faultless. Such remorse, the act of being remorseful, the state of being remorseful, mental regret, and mental scratching is called remorse. Furthermore, remorse, mental regret, and mental scratching arise from two causes: from what has been done and from what has not been done. How do they arise from what has been done and what has not been done? Remorse, mental regret, and mental scratching arise thinking, 'I have committed bodily misconduct; I have not performed bodily good conduct.'
158:
Scratches of the mind (manovilekha). "I have committed verbal misconduct, I have not committed verbal good conduct" ... "I have committed mental misconduct, I have not committed mental good conduct" ... "I have committed the taking of life, I have not practiced the restraint from taking life" ... "I have committed the taking of what is not given, I have not practiced the restraint from taking what is not given" ... "I have committed sexual misconduct, I have not practiced the restraint from sexual misconduct" ... "I have committed falsehood, I have not practiced the restraint from falsehood" ... "I have committed malicious speech, I have not practiced the restraint from malicious speech" ... "I have committed harsh speech, I have not practiced the restraint from harsh speech" ... "I have committed frivolous speech, I have not practiced the restraint from frivolous speech" ... "I have had covetousness, I have not practiced non-covetousness" ... "I have had a mind of ill-will, I have not had a mind of non-ill-will" ... "I have held wrong view, I have not held right view." Thus, remorse (kukkucca), mental agitation (vippaṭisāra), and scratches of the mind (manovilekha) arise. Due to such things done and not done, remorse, mental agitation, and scratches of the mind arise.

Alternatively, "I am not one who fulfills the virtues (sīla)," thus remorse, mental agitation, and scratches of the mind arise. "I am one who does not guard the doors of the sense faculties" ... "I am one who does not know moderation in eating" ... "I am one who is not devoted to wakefulness" ... "I am one who is not possessed of mindfulness and clear comprehension" ... "I have not developed the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path" ... "I have not fully understood the truth of suffering, I have not abandoned the truth of the origin, I have not developed the truth of the path, I have not realized the truth of cessation." Thus, remorse, mental agitation, and scratches of the mind arise.

"The hindrance of remorse" (kukkuccānaṃ nivāraṇaṃ) means the obstructing, the hindering, the abandoning, the calming, the complete calming, the relinquishing, the tranquility, the deathless, which is Nibbāna—this is the hindrance of remorse. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"The abandoning of sensual desires,
The abandoning of both types of sorrow,
The dispelling of sloth,
The hindering of remorse (is Nibbāna)."
159:
The scratching of the mind (kukkucca) occurs. "The hindrance of remorse" (kukkuccānaṃ nivāraṇaṃ) means the obstructing, the hindering, the abandoning, the calming, the complete calming, the relinquishing, the tranquility, the deathless, which is Nibbāna—this I, the Buddha, call "liberation" (mokkha). Thus, the meaning of the term "the hindrance of remorse" should be understood. Because of this, the Blessed One said: "The abandoning of sensual desires, the abandoning of both types of sorrow, the dispelling of sloth and torpor, the hindering of remorse."

Purified by equanimity and mindfulness,
Preceded by the thought of the Dhamma,
I proclaim liberation through final knowledge (arahatta-phala),
And the breaking of ignorance.

"Purified by equanimity and mindfulness" (upekkhā-sati-saṃsuddhaṃ): Equanimity is the neutrality, the looking on, the close looking on, the evenness of mind, the tranquility of mind, and the middle state of mind that occurs in the fourth jhāna. Mindfulness is the recollection, the constant recollection ... (and so on) ... right mindfulness that occurs in the fourth jhāna, taking equanimity as its object. "Purified by equanimity and mindfulness" means that in the fourth jhāna, both equanimity and mindfulness are pure, specially pure, extremely pure, completely pure, bright, without blemish, free from defilements, malleable, wieldy, steady, and have reached imperturbability. Therefore, it is called "purified by equanimity and mindfulness."

"Preceded by the thought of the Dhamma" (dhamma-takka-purejavaṃ): Thought of the Dhamma is called Right Intention (sammā-saṅkappa). It occurs at the beginning, at the front, and is the precursor to liberation through final knowledge. In this way also, it is "preceded by the thought of the Dhamma." Alternatively, thought of the Dhamma is called Right View (sammā-diṭṭhi). It also occurs at the beginning, at the front, and is the precursor to liberation through final knowledge. In this way also, it is "preceded by the thought of the Dhamma." Alternatively, thought of the Dhamma is called insight (vipassanā) that occurs in the preliminary stage of the four paths. It also occurs at the beginning, at the front, and is the precursor to liberation through final knowledge. In this way also, it is "preceded by the thought of the Dhamma."

"I proclaim liberation through final knowledge" (aññā-vimokkhaṃ pabrūmi): Liberation through final knowledge is called the liberation of the fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala). I proclaim, tell, teach, establish, open, analyze, make plain, and manifest the liberation of the fruit of Arahantship. Therefore, it is said, "I proclaim liberation through final knowledge."

"The breaking of ignorance" (avijjāya pabhedanaṃ): Ignorance is the non-knowing of the truth of suffering ... (and so on) ... ignorance, delusion, the root of the unwholesome. "Breaking" (pabhedanaṃ) means the breaking, the abandoning, the calming, the relinquishing, the complete calming of ignorance, which is the deathless Nibbāna. Therefore, it is said, "the breaking of ignorance." Because of this, the Blessed One said: "Purified by equanimity and mindfulness, preceded by the thought of the Dhamma, I proclaim liberation through final knowledge, the breaking of ignorance."

With what is the world fettered? What is its wandering? By the abandoning of what is it called Nibbāna?

In the phrase "With what fettered" (kiṃ-saṃyojano): What is the world's fetter, attachment, bond, and defilement? With what is the world joined, intensely joined, firmly joined, well joined, attached, and repeatedly hindered?
160:
“By what is the world fettered?” means the world’s fetter, attachment, bond, and defilement. By what is the world joined, engaged, bound, well-bound, attached, stuck, and obstructed? This is the meaning of “By what is the world fettered?”

“What is its wandering (vicāraṇa)?” means what is the world’s movement, its wandering here and there, its wandering towards various objects? By what does the world move, wander here and there, and wander towards various objects? This is the meaning of “What is its wandering?” “By the abandoning of what is it called Nibbāna?” means by the abandoning, the stilling, the relinquishing, and the complete tranquilizing of what is it called Nibbāna, is it termed, taught, recited, shown, and designated? Therefore, that Brahmin addressed this to the Buddha:

“By what is the world fettered? What is its wandering?
By the abandoning of what is it called Nibbāna?”

“The world is fettered by delight (nandī); thought (vitakka) is its wandering.
By the abandoning of craving (taṇhā), it is called Nibbāna.”

Regarding the phrase “Nandisaṃyojano loko”: Delight (nandī) refers to craving (taṇhā). That lust, intense greed ... covetousness, and greed which are unwholesome roots are called delight. That delight is the world’s fetter, attachment, bond, and defilement. Because the world is joined, engaged, bound, well-bound, attached, stuck, and obstructed by this delight, it is said, “The world is fettered by delight (nandī).”

Regarding the phrase “Vitakkassa vicāraṇā”: There are nine kinds of thoughts (vitakka). They are: sensual thought, thought of ill-will, thought of cruelty, thought of relatives, thought of country, thought of immortality, thought connected with compassion for others, thought connected with gain, honor, and fame, and thought connected with not being despised. These are called the nine thoughts. These nine thoughts are the world’s movement, its wandering here and there, and its wandering towards various objects. Because the world moves, wanders here and there, and wanders towards various objects by these nine thoughts, it is said, “Thought (vitakka) is its wandering.”

Regarding the phrase “Taṇhāya vippahānena nibbānaṃ iti vuccati”: Craving (taṇhā) refers to craving for forms ... craving for mental objects. Because of the abandoning, the stilling, the relinquishing, and the complete tranquilizing of craving, it is called Nibbāna, is it termed, taught, recited, shown, and designated. Therefore, the Blessed One said:
161:
"The world is fettered by delight; thought is its wandering; by the abandoning of craving, it is called Nibbāna."

"For one practicing in what way, being mindful, does consciousness cease? We have come to ask the Blessed One; let us hear your word."

"For one practicing in what way, being mindful" means for one who is mindful, clearly comprehending, practicing, dwelling, moving, maintaining, protecting, and sustaining. This is the meaning of "For one practicing in what way, being mindful."

"Consciousness ceases" means consciousness is extinguished, is stilled, goes to an end, and is completely tranquilized. This is the meaning of "Consciousness ceases."

"We have come to ask the Blessed One" means we have come, approached, and arrived to ask, to request, to invite, and to show devotion to the Buddha, the Blessed One; "We have come together with you." This is the meaning of "We have come to ask the Blessed One."

"Let us hear your word" means we shall hear, learn, bear in mind, reflect upon, and mark well your word, speech, teaching, instruction, and advice. This is the meaning of "Let us hear your word." Therefore, that Brahmin said:

"For one practicing in what way, being mindful, does consciousness cease? We have come to ask the Blessed One; let us hear your word."

"For one who does not delight in feeling, whether internal or external; for one practicing thus, being mindful, consciousness ceases."

"For one who does not delight in feeling, whether internal or external" means one who dwells contemplating feeling in feelings internally does not delight in, does not welcome, and does not remain attached to feeling. He abandons, dispels, eliminates, and brings to non-existence the delighting, welcoming, attachment, grasping, misapprehension, and dogmatic adherence. One who dwells contemplating feeling in feelings externally does not delight in, does not welcome, and does not remain attached to feeling. He abandons, dispels, eliminates, and brings to non-existence the delighting, welcoming, attachment, grasping, misapprehension, and dogmatic adherence. One who dwells contemplating feeling in feelings both internally and externally does not delight in, does not welcome, and does not remain attached to feeling. He abandons delighting...
162:
He abandons, dispels, makes an end of, and brings to non-existence delighting, welcoming, cleaving, grasping, misapprehending, and adherence. Contemplating the nature of arising in feelings internally, one who dwells contemplating feelings in feelings (this phrase is not in the Siamese edition) does not delight in, does not welcome, and does not cleave to feelings. He abandons, dispels, makes an end of, and brings to non-existence delighting, welcoming, cleaving, grasping, misapprehending, and adherence. Contemplating the nature of vanishing in feelings internally, one who dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... (Pe)... Contemplating the nature of both arising and vanishing in feelings internally, one who dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... (Pe)... Contemplating the nature of arising in feelings externally, one who dwells contemplating feelings in feelings does not delight in, does not welcome, and does not cleave to feelings. He abandons, dispels, makes an end of, and brings to non-existence delighting, welcoming, cleaving, grasping, misapprehending, and adherence. Contemplating the nature of vanishing in feelings externally, one who dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... (Pe)... Contemplating the nature of both arising and vanishing in feelings externally, one who dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... (Pe)... Contemplating the nature of arising in feelings both internally and externally, one who dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... (Pe)... Contemplating the nature of vanishing in feelings both internally and externally, one who dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... (Pe)... Contemplating the nature of both arising and vanishing in feelings both internally and externally, one who dwells contemplating feelings in feelings does not delight in, does not welcome, and does not cleave to feelings. He abandons, dispels, makes an end of, and brings to non-existence delighting, welcoming, cleaving, grasping, misapprehending, and adherence. One who dwells contemplating feelings in feelings in these twelve ways... (Pe)... brings to non-existence.

Alternatively, one who sees feelings as impermanent does not delight in, does not welcome, and does not cleave to feelings. He abandons, dispels, makes an end of, and brings to non-existence delighting, welcoming, cleaving, grasping, misapprehending, and adherence. One who sees feelings as suffering, as a disease, as a boil, as a dart, as a calamity, as an affliction... (Pe)... as an escape, does not delight in, does not welcome, and does not cleave to feelings. He abandons, dispels, makes an end of, and brings to non-existence delighting, welcoming, cleaving, grasping, misapprehending, and adherence. One who dwells contemplating feelings in feelings in these forty (forty-two in the Siamese edition) ways does not delight in, does not welcome, and does not cleave to feelings. He abandons, dispels, makes an end of, and brings to non-existence delighting, welcoming, cleaving, grasping, misapprehending, and adherence—this is the meaning of the phrase 'for one who does not delight in feelings both internally and externally'.
163: 'For one wandering thus mindful' means for one who is mindful, clearly comprehending, wandering, staying, proceeding, behaving, guarding, maintaining, and sustaining in this way—thus 'for one wandering thus mindful.' 'Consciousness is ceased' means consciousness accompanied by meritorious volitional formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra), consciousness accompanied by demeritorious volitional formations (apuññābhisaṅkhāra), and consciousness accompanied by imperturbable volitional formations (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra) ceases, is stilled, goes to destruction, and is calmed—thus 'consciousness is ceased.' Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'For one wandering thus mindful, not delighting in feelings both internally and externally, consciousness is ceased.' Immediately upon the conclusion of the verse... 'The Blessed One, Bhante, is my teacher; I am a disciple,' he said. ## The Exposition of the Questions of the Young Man Udaya, the thirteenth, is finished. ## 14. The Exposition of the Questions of the Young Man Posāla 'The one who points out the past (so said the venerable Posāla), who is free from craving, who has cut off doubt, who has reached the far shore of all dhammas, I have come with a question.' In the phrase 'The one who points out the past,' 'He' refers to the Blessed One, the Self-become (Swayambhū). Without a teacher, he himself fully awakened to the Four Noble Truths among dhammas not heard before, and therein reached omniscience and mastery of the powers. 'Points out the past' (atītaṃ ādisati) means the Blessed One points out the past, points out the future, and points out the present, both for himself and for others. How does the Blessed One point out his own past? The Blessed One points out one past birth of his own, points out two births, points out three births, points out four births, points out five births, points out ten births, points out twenty births, points out thirty births, points out forty births...
164:
(The Blessed One) points out; he points out fifty births, he points out a hundred births... [pe] ...a thousand births... a hundred thousand births... many aeons of world-contraction... many aeons of world-expansion... many aeons of world-contraction and expansion. "In such a place I was of such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such an experiencer of pleasure and pain, such was the end of my lifespan. Passing away from there, I was reborn in such a place. There too, I was of such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such an experiencer of pleasure and pain, such was the end of my lifespan. Passing away from there, I was reborn here." Thus, with their aspects and particulars, he points out his manifold past dwellings. In this way, the Blessed One points out his own past.

How does the Blessed One point out the past of others? The Blessed One points out one birth of others, he points out two births... [pe] ...he points out many aeons of world-contraction and expansion. "In such a place that person was of such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such an experiencer of pleasure and pain, such was the end of his lifespan. Passing away from there, he was reborn in such a place. There too, he was of such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such an experiencer of pleasure and pain, such was the end of his lifespan. Passing away from there, he was reborn in this present life." Thus, with their aspects and particulars, he points out the manifold past dwellings. In this way, the Blessed One points out the past of others.

While speaking the five hundred Jātakas, the Blessed One points out the past of himself and others. While speaking the Mahāpadāniya Suttanta, he points out the past of himself and others. While speaking the Mahāsudassaniya Suttanta, he points out the past of himself and others. While speaking the Mahāgovindiya Suttanta, he points out the past of himself and others. While speaking the Maghadeviya Suttanta, he points out the past of himself and others.

For this was said by the Blessed One: "Cunda, concerning the past duration, the Tathāgata has knowledge that follows memory. He recollects as far as he desires. Cunda, concerning the future... [pe] ...Cunda, concerning the present duration, the knowledge born of enlightenment arises in the Tathāgata: 'This is the last birth, now there is no more renewed existence.'"
165:
The knowledge of the degree of maturity of the faculties of beings (indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa) is a power of the Tathāgata. The knowledge of the inclinations and underlying tendencies of beings (āsayānusaya-ñāṇa) is a power of the Tathāgata. The knowledge of the twin miracle (yamaka-pāṭihīra-ñāṇa) is a power of the Tathāgata. The knowledge associated with the attainment of great compassion (mahākaruṇā-samāpatti-ñāṇa) is a power of the Tathāgata. The knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) is a power of the Tathāgata. Unobstructed knowledge (anāvaraṇa-ñāṇa) is a power of the Tathāgata. The unattached, unimpeded, and unobstructed knowledge in all things (assangamappaṭihatamanāvaraṇa-ñāṇa) is a power of the Tathāgata. In this way, the Blessed One points out the past of himself and others, points out the future, points out the present; he declares, teaches, describes, establishes, opens, analyzes, makes clear, and reveals. This is the meaning of "one who points out the past."

In the phrase "Iccāyasmā Posālo," "iccā" is a word-conjunction. "Āyasmā" is a term of endearment. "Posālo" is the name of that brahmin. The utterance is called "Iccāyasmā Posālo."

In the phrase "Anejo chinnasaṃsayo," "ejā" refers to craving (taṇhā). Lust, passion, covetousness, greed, and the unwholesome roots are called "ejā." That craving called "ejā" has been abandoned by the Buddha, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, and is of a nature not to arise again in the future. Therefore, the Buddha is called "aneja" (unagitated). Because of abandoning "ejā," he is "aneja." The Blessed One does not shake in the face of gain... [pe] ...he does not shake in the face of suffering, he does not move, does not tremble, does not shake violently, does not waver in any way; thus he is called "aneja." In the phrase "chinnasaṃsayo," "saṃsaya" refers to doubt (vicikicchā). Uncertainty regarding suffering, the trembling of the mind, and the scratching of the mind are called "saṃsaya." That doubt has been abandoned by the Buddha, cut off, completely cut off, utterly cut off, calmed, relinquished, fully subsided, is no longer liable to arise, and has been burnt by the fire of knowledge. Therefore, the Buddha is called "chinnasaṃsayo." This is the meaning of "Anejo chinnasaṃsayo."

"Pāraguṃ sabbadhammānaṃ" means the Blessed One has reached the further shore of all phenomena through higher knowledge (abhiññā), he has reached the further shore through full understanding (pariññā), he has reached the further shore through abandoning (pahāna), he has reached the further shore through development (bhāvanā), he has reached the further shore through realization (sacchikiriyā), he has reached the further shore through attainment (samāpatti). He has reached the further shore of all phenomena through higher knowledge. For that Blessed One, the round of birth and death does not exist; there is no more renewed existence. This is the meaning of "Pāragū sabbadhammānaṃ."

"Atthi pañhena āgamaṃ" means "I have come desiring [to ask] a question." With the meaning "Please bear this burden," it is said "Atthi pañhena āgamaṃ." Therefore, that brahmin said this:
166:
The Venerable Posāla spoke thus:

"To the one who points out the past,
Who is free from the trembling [of craving], who has cut off doubt,
Who has reached the far shore of all dhammas,
I have come with a desire for a question.
For one whose perception of form has disappeared, who has abandoned all bodies,
Who sees both internally and externally that 'there is nothing,'
I ask the Sakyan about his knowledge; how is such a person to be led [to the higher paths]?"

In the term "vibhūtarūpasaññissa," what is "perception of form" (rūpasaññā)? For one who has attained the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) attainments, or for one who is reborn there, or for one who dwells in happiness in the present life, there is the act of perceiving, the marking, the state of marking—this is called perception of form. Regarding "vibhūtarūpasaññissa," for one who has obtained the four immaterial attainments (arūpasamāpatti), the perceptions of form have disappeared, vanished, been transcended, well-transcended, and specially transcended. Therefore, it is said, "vibhūtarūpasaññissa."

Regarding "sabbakāyappahāyino," all of that person's rebirth-linking physical body has been abandoned. That person's physical body has been abandoned through transcendence by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga) and abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhana). Therefore, it is said, "sabbakāyappahāyino."

In the phrase "ajjhattañca bahiddhā ca natthi kiñcīti passato," the term "there is nothing" (natthi kiñci) refers to the attainment of the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana). Why is the attainment of the sphere of nothingness called "there is nothing"? Because one enters the attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana) with mindfulness, and after emerging from it, one makes that very consciousness disappear, vanish, and pass away, seeing that "there is nothing." For that reason, the attainment of the sphere of nothingness is called "there is nothing." This is the meaning of the person who sees both internally and externally that "there is nothing."

In the phrase "ñāṇaṃ sakkānupucchāmi," "Sakka" refers to the Blessed One who is a Sakyan prince. He is called Sakka because he went forth from the Sakyan clan... and because he has abandoned fear and dread and is free from hair-standing-on-end. "Ñāṇaṃ sakkānupucchāmi" means I ask about his knowledge, I ask about his wisdom, I ask about his perfect understanding. "What kind of knowledge, what form of knowledge, what variety of knowledge, what distinction of knowledge is desired?"—thus he asks about the knowledge.

Regarding "kathaṃ neyyo tathāvidho," how is that person who has attained the sphere of nothingness to be intensely known, known in various ways, repeatedly known, made to be known, made to be seen, looked upon, or made clear? How should that person produce higher knowledge? "Tathāvidho" refers to such a person, one who has that variety in the sphere of nothingness, one who has that portion in the sphere of nothingness.
167:
One who is of such nature, of such form, of such variety, of such a portion—that is, one who has obtained the attainment of the sphere of nothingness—how is he to be known, how is he to be led? Therefore, that brahmin said:

"For one whose perception of form has disappeared, who has abandoned all bodies,
Who sees both internally and externally that 'there is nothing,'
I ask the Sakyan about his knowledge; how is such a person to be known (led)?"

"Posāla," said the Blessed One, "the Tathāgata, knowing all the stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo),
Knows this person who is established [by way of volitional formations], who is devoted [to the sphere of nothingness], and has it as his destination."

Regarding "all the stations of consciousness," the Blessed One knows the four stations of consciousness by way of volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra), and He knows the seven stations of consciousness by way of rebirth (paṭisandhi). How does the Blessed One know the four stations of consciousness by way of volitional formations? For this was said by the Blessed One: "Monks, consciousness, while remaining, might remain attached to form; with form as its object, with form as its support, sprinkled with the water of delight, it might reach growth, increase, and abundance. Or, monks, consciousness... might remain attached to feeling... or attached to perception... or, monks, consciousness, while remaining, might remain attached to formations; with formations as its object, with formations as its support, sprinkled with the water of delight, it might reach growth, increase, and abundance." Thus, the Blessed One knows the four stations of consciousness by way of volitional formations.

How does the Blessed One know the seven stations of consciousness by way of rebirth? For this was said by the Blessed One: "Monks, there are beings with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions, such as human beings, some devas, and some beings in the states of deprivation (vinipātika). This is the first station of consciousness.

Monks, there are beings with diverse bodies and uniform perceptions, such as the devas of the Brahma-group (brahmakāyika) who are first reborn [in the first jhāna plane]. This is the second station of consciousness.

Monks, there are beings with uniform bodies and diverse perceptions, such as the Ābhassara devas. This is the third station of consciousness."
168:
Monks, there are beings with uniform bodies and uniform perceptions, such as the devas of Radiant Glory (Subhakiṇha). This is the fourth station of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti).

Monks, there are beings who, through the complete transcending of perceptions of form, the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and non-attention to perceptions of diversity, [perceiving] 'space is infinite,' have reached the base of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana). This is the fifth station of consciousness.

Monks, there are beings who, through the complete transcending of the base of infinite space, [perceiving] 'consciousness is infinite,' have reached the base of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana). This is the sixth station of consciousness.

Monks, there are beings who, through the complete transcending of the base of infinite consciousness, [perceiving] 'there is nothing,' have reached the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana). This is the seventh station of consciousness. Thus, the Blessed One knows the seven stations of consciousness by way of rebirth. This is the meaning of the phrase 'viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo sabbā'.

'Posāla,' the Blessed One addressed that brahmin by name. 'Bhagavā' (Blessed One) is a title of respect... (pe)... it is a designation realized by himself. 'Bhagavā' is how the Blessed One addressed Posāla.

Regarding 'abhijānaṃ tathāgato': 'abhijānaṃ' means knowing directly, knowing specially, knowing again specifically, and knowing through penetration—the Tathāgata. For the Blessed One said this: 'Cunda, regarding the past, if it is untrue, incorrect, and unbeneficial, the Tathāgata does not declare it. Cunda, regarding the past, if it is true and correct but unbeneficial, the Tathāgata does not declare it. Cunda, regarding the past, if it is true, correct, and beneficial, then the Tathāgata knows the proper time to answer that question. The same applies to the future... (pe)... Cunda, regarding the present, if it is untrue, incorrect, and unbeneficial, the Tathāgata does not declare it. Cunda, regarding the present, if it is true and correct but unbeneficial, the Tathāgata does not declare it. Cunda, regarding the present, if it is true, correct, and beneficial, then the Tathāgata knows the proper time to answer that question. Thus, Cunda, regarding things past, future, and present, the Tathāgata is one who speaks at the right time (kālavādī), one who speaks the truth (bhūtavādī), one who speaks what is beneficial (atthavādī), one who speaks the Dhamma (dhammavādī), and one who speaks the Vinaya (vinayavādī). Therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.'

Cunda, in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmas, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained...
169:
...sought after, and pondered by the mind, all that has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata with his superior knowledge. Therefore, he is called the Tathāgata. Cunda, from the night the Tathāgata fully awakens to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment until the night he passes away into the Nibbāna element with no residue of fuel remaining, whatever he speaks, utters, and explains in this interval, all that is just so and not otherwise. Therefore, he is called the Tathāgata. Cunda, as the Tathāgata speaks, so he acts; as he acts, so he speaks. Because he acts as he speaks and speaks as he acts, he is called the Tathāgata. Cunda, in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmas, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, the Tathāgata is the conqueror, unconquered, all-seeing, and wielder of power. Therefore, he is called the Tathāgata. This is the meaning of the phrase 'abhijānaṃ tathāgato'.

Regarding the words 'He knows this person who is currently existing': The Blessed One knows a person even while they are existing in this life, by the power of volitional formations (kammābhisaṅkhāra) of unwholesome kamma: 'This person, with the breakup of the body, after death, will be reborn in the plane of misery, the bad destination, the lower world, hell.' The Blessed One knows a person even while they are existing in this life, by the power of volitional formations of unwholesome kamma: 'This person, with the breakup of the body, after death, will be reborn in the animal realm.' The Blessed One knows a person even while they are existing in this life, by the power of volitional formations of unwholesome kamma: 'This person, with the breakup of the body, after death, will be reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts (peta).' The Blessed One knows a person even while they are existing in this life, by the power of volitional formations of wholesome kamma: 'This person, with the breakup of the body, after death, will be reborn among humans.' The Blessed One knows a person even while they are existing in this life, by the power of volitional formations of wholesome kamma: 'This person, having practiced well, with the breakup of the body, after death, will be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.'

This was said by the Blessed One: 'Sāriputta, here, having encompassed the mind of a certain person with my own mind, I know: "This person practices in such a way, behaves in such a way, and has entered upon such a path that, with the breakup of the body, after death, he will be reborn in the plane of misery, the bad destination, the lower world, hell."' 

'Sāriputta, here, having encompassed the mind of a certain person with my own mind, I know: "This person practices in such a way, behaves in such a way, and has entered upon such a path that, with the breakup of the body, after death, he will be reborn in the animal realm."'
170:
“Sāriputta, here in this world, I know a certain person by encompassing their mind with my own mind thus: ‘This person practices in such a way, behaves in such a way, and has entered upon such a path that, with the breakup of the body, after death, he will be reborn in the realm of the hungry ghosts (peta-loka).’

Sāriputta, here in this world, I know a certain person by encompassing their mind with my own mind thus: ‘This person practices in such a way, behaves in such a way, and has entered upon such a path that, with the breakup of the body, after death, he will be reborn among human beings.’

Sāriputta, here in this world, I know a certain person by encompassing their mind with my own mind thus: ‘This person practices in such a way, behaves in such a way, and has entered upon such a path that, with the breakup of the body, after death, he will be reborn in a happy destination, in the heavenly world.’

Sāriputta, here in this world, I know a certain person by encompassing their mind with my own mind thus: ‘This person practices in such a way, behaves in such a way, and has entered upon such a path that, through the destruction of the taints (āsavas), he will, in this very life, realize for himself with direct knowledge, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, dwell therein.’ Thus, I know that person as he stands.

Regarding the phrase ‘adhimuttaṃ tapparāyaṇaṃ’, ‘adhimuttaṃ’ means inclining towards the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana) through liberation (vimokkha); it is the mind’s inclination toward that state, making that state the predominant influence. Alternatively, the Blessed One knows: ‘This person is inclined towards forms, inclined towards sounds, inclined towards smells, inclined towards tastes, inclined towards tangibles, inclined towards family, inclined towards a group, inclined towards a dwelling, inclined towards gain, inclined towards fame, inclined towards praise, inclined towards pleasure, inclined towards robes, inclined towards alms-food, inclined towards lodging, inclined towards medicinal requisites for the sick, inclined towards the Suttanta, inclined towards the Vinaya, inclined towards the Abhidhamma, inclined towards forest-dwelling, inclined towards the practice of alms-round, inclined towards the practice of wearing rag-robes, inclined towards the practice of the three robes, inclined towards the practice of house-to-house alms-round, inclined towards the practice of not eating after time, inclined towards the practice of the sitter, inclined towards the practice of any-available-seat, inclined towards the first jhāna, inclined towards the second jhāna, inclined towards the third jhāna, inclined towards the fourth jhāna, inclined towards the attainment of the base of infinite space, inclined towards the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness, inclined towards the attainment of the base of nothingness, inclined towards the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.’ This is what is meant by ‘adhimuttaṃ’.
171:
‘Tapparāyaṇa’ means that which is completed by the base of nothingness, prioritizing that base of nothingness, having volitional formations (kamma) as the destination, having resultants (vipāka) as the destination, valuing kamma, and valuing rebirth. Alternatively, the Blessed One knows: “This person has forms as his destination... has the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as his destination.” This is the meaning of ‘adhimuttaṃ tapparāyaṇaṃ’. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“The Tathāgata knows all the stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti),
O Posāla, he knows this person as he stands,
Inclined and destined for that [base of nothingness].

Knowing the origin of the base of nothingness,
And knowing that delight is a fetter,
Having known this [base of nothingness] thus with direct knowledge,
He then meditates with insight therein.
This knowledge is true for that brahmin
Who has lived the life and whose taints are destroyed.”

‘Ākiñcaññasambhavaṃ ñatvā’ means that the volitional formation (kammābhisankhāra) of wholesome kamma that leads to the base of nothingness is called ‘ākiñcaññasambhava’. Knowing that wholesome volitional formation which leads to the base of nothingness as the origin of nothingness, knowing it as an attachment, knowing it as a bond, knowing it as an impediment; having known, weighed, investigated, developed, and made it clear—this is ‘ākiñcaññasambhavaṃ ñatvā’.

‘Nandisaṃyojanaṃ iti’ means that lust for the formless realm (arūparāga) is called the fetter of delight (nandisaṃyojana). Knowing that the kamma is attached by formless lust, knowing that formless lust which has reached attachment and impediment as the fetter of delight, knowing it as an attachment, knowing it as a bond, knowing it as an impediment; having known, weighed, investigated, developed, and made it clear. The word ‘iti’ is included for the purpose of connecting words, combining words, completing the sentence, harmony of syllables, euphony of consonants, and the sequence of words.

‘Evametaṃ abhiññāya’ means having known this base of nothingness thus with direct knowledge, having weighed, investigated, developed, and made it clear.

‘Tato tattha vipassati’: In the phrase ‘therein’ (tattha), it means having entered the attainment of the base of nothingness, and after emerging from it, one contemplates with insight the mental states (citta and cetasika) that arose in that attainment as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease... as an escape; he sees, looks at, reflects upon, and investigates them.

‘Etaṃ ñာṇaṃ tatham tassa’ means this knowledge is real, true, factual, and non-erroneous for that person of the base of nothingness.
172:
Regarding the phrase 'of the brahmin who has lived the life' (brāhmaṇassa vusīmato): He is called a brahmin because he has abandoned seven things... one who is free from taints (āsavas) and endowed with the quality of 'suchness' (tādi) is called a Brahma (brahmin). The phrase 'of the brahmin who has lived the life' means that, starting from the level of a virtuous worldling (puthujjana) up to the seven types of trainees (sekhas), they live (dwell) in order to reach what has not yet been reached, to attain what has not yet been attained, and to realize what has not yet been realized (through the dwelling of the Path). An Arahant, however, is one who has lived the life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through right knowledge. That Arahant is one who has practiced the conduct... for him, the round of birth and death, as well as future rebirth, no longer exists. Therefore, the Blessed One said this:

“Having known the origin of the sphere of nothingness,
And thus recognizing the fetter of delight,
Having understood it in this way, he then sees with insight into that sphere of nothingness.
This knowledge is true for that person of the sphere of nothingness,
For that brahmin who has lived the life (of the Path).”

At the end of the verse... (he said), “Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is my teacher, I am the disciple.”

## 14. Exposition of the Questions of the Young Man Posāla.

## 15. Exposition of the Questions of the Young Man Mogharāja

“Twice I have asked the Sakyan, [thus said the venerable Mogharāja]
But the One with Vision did not answer me;
I have heard that the Divine Seer answers on the third time.”

Regarding 'Twice I have asked the Sakyan' (dvāhaṃ sakkaṃ apucchissaṃ): That brahmin asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, the question twice. Although the brahmin asked, the Blessed One did not answer immediately, considering, “In the interval, the spiritual faculties (indriya) of this brahmin will reach maturity.” 'Sakka' means the Capable One. He is also called Sakka because he went forth from the Sakyan clan. Alternatively, he is called Sakka because he is wealthy and possesses great riches. The Blessed One possesses these riches of the Dhamma, namely: the wealth of faith, the wealth of virtue, the wealth of shame, the wealth of fear of wrongdoing, the wealth of learning, the wealth of generosity, the wealth of wisdom, the wealth of the foundations of mindfulness, the wealth of the right efforts, the wealth of the bases of power, the wealth of the faculties, the wealth of the powers, the wealth of the factors of enlightenment, the wealth of the path, the wealth of the fruit, and the wealth of Nibbāna. Because he is rich and endowed with these various kinds of precious wealth, he is called Sakka. Alternatively...
173:
The Blessed One, called Sakka, is capable, powerful, competent, brave, heroic, valiant, fearless, not trembling, not terrified, not fleeing, having abandoned fear and dread, and having hair that does not stand on end. Therefore, he is called Sakka. 'Twice I have asked the Sakyan' means I have asked, requested, invited, and propitiated the Blessed One who is Sakka.

Regarding 'Thus said the venerable Mogharāja': 'Thus' (iccha) is a conjunction... 'Venerable' (āyasmā) is a term of endearment... 'Mogharāja' is the name of that brahmin... 'said' (iti) refers to the speech—thus the venerable Mogharāja said.

Regarding 'The One with Vision did not answer me': 'Did not answer me' means he did not answer, did not tell, did not teach, did not make known, did not establish, did not open, did not analyze, did not make clear, and did not manifest. 'The One with Vision' (cakkhumā) means the Blessed One has vision through five eyes: the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the eye of wisdom, the Buddha-eye, and the universal eye.

How is the Blessed One endowed with vision through the fleshly eye (maṃsacakkhu)? In the Blessed One's fleshly eye, five colors exist: blue, yellow, red, black, and white. The place where the eyelashes are situated is blue, a beautiful blue, pleasing and lovely to behold, like the flax flower (ummā). Beyond that, it is yellow, a beautiful yellow, the color of gold, pleasing and lovely to behold, like the kaṇikāra flower. Both corners of the Blessed One's eyes are red, a beautiful red, pleasing and lovely to behold, like the indagopaka insect. In the center, it is black, a beautiful black, not coarse but smooth, pleasing and lovely to behold, like a black nut (aḍḍāriṭṭha). Beyond that, it is white, a beautiful white, pure and pale, pleasing and lovely to behold, like the morning star (osadhitārakā). With this natural fleshly eye, which is part of his physical body and produced by the meritorious deeds of past lives, the Blessed One sees for one league (yojana) all around, both by day and by night. Even when there is fourfold darkness—when the sun has set, on the Uposatha day of the dark fortnight, in a thick forest, and when a great dark cloud has arisen—in such fourfold darkness...
174:
He sees within a league all around. There is no wall, door, rampart, mountain, bush, or creeper that acts as an obstruction to the seeing of forms. Even if one were to mark a single sesame seed and place it in a cartload of sesame, He could pick out that very same sesame seed. Such is the purity of the Blessed One's natural physical eye (maṃsacakkhu). In this way, the Blessed One is 'possessed of vision' (cakkhumā) even by means of the physical eye.

How is the Blessed One 'possessed of vision' also by means of the divine eye (dibbacakkhu)? With the divine eye, purified and surpassing human sight, the Blessed One sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate. He understands how beings fare according to their karma: 'These worthy beings, indeed, were possessed of bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct; they were revilers of the noble ones, held wrong views, and undertook actions based on wrong views. With the breakup of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a state of ruin, even in hell. But these worthy beings were possessed of good bodily conduct, good verbal conduct, and good mental conduct; they were not revilers of the noble ones, held right views, and undertook actions based on right views. With the breakup of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a good destination, even in a heavenly world.' Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing human sight, He sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and He understands how beings fare according to their karma.

If the Blessed One wishes, He can see one world system (lokadhātu), two world systems, three world systems, four world systems, five world systems, ten world systems, twenty world systems, thirty world systems, forty world systems, fifty world systems, or a hundred world systems. He can see the thousandfold minor world system (cūḷanika-lokadhātu), the twice-thousandfold middle world system (majjhimika-lokadhātu), and the thrice-thousandfold great world system (mahāsahassī-lokadhātu). Or rather, He sees as many world systems as He wishes. Such is the purity of the Blessed One's divine eye. In this way, the Blessed One is 'possessed of vision' (cakkhumā) also by means of the divine eye.
175:
How is the Blessed One 'possessed of vision' also by means of the eye of wisdom (paññācakkhu)? The Blessed One is possessed of great wisdom, wide wisdom, swift wisdom, joyful wisdom, sharp wisdom, penetrative wisdom; He is skilled in the distinctions of wisdom, possessed of differentiated knowledge, has attained the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), reached the four intrepidities (vesārajja), bears the ten powers (dasabala), is a bull among men, a lion among men, an elephant among men, a noble thoroughbred among men, a leader among men. He is possessed of infinite knowledge, infinite majesty, infinite fame; He is rich, of great wealth, and possessed of the treasure of wisdom. He is the leader, the trainer, the guide, the teacher, the one who makes others contemplate, the observer, the one who looks upon, and the one who inspires confidence. For the Blessed One is the originator of the unarisen path, the producer of the unproduced path, the declarer of the undeclared path; He is the knower of the path, the discoverer of the path, the one skilled in the path. And now His disciples dwell following the path, becoming possessed of it afterwards.

For the Blessed One, knowing, He knows; seeing, He sees. He has become vision, become knowledge, become Dhamma, become Brahma. He is the speaker, the proclaimer, the bringer of meaning, the giver of the Deathless (Amata), the Lord of Dhamma, the Tathāgata. There is nothing unknown, unseen, unperceived, unrealized, or untouched by the Blessed One's wisdom. Taking into account the past, future, and present, all things in every aspect come within the range of the Blessed One's knowledge. Whatever is knowable (ñeyya)—whether it be one's own benefit, the benefit of others, or the benefit of both; benefit in the present life or benefit in the future life; manifest benefit, deep benefit, hidden benefit, concealed benefit, knowable benefit, inferred benefit, faultless benefit, stainless benefit, pure benefit, or the ultimate benefit—all that revolves within the Buddha's knowledge.

All bodily action of the Buddha, the Blessed One, follows knowledge; all verbal action follows knowledge; all mental action follows knowledge. The Buddha, the Blessed One, has unobstructed knowledge regarding the past, unobstructed knowledge regarding the future, and unobstructed knowledge regarding the present. As far as the knowable extends, so far does His knowledge extend. As far as His knowledge extends, so far does the knowable extend. Knowledge has the knowable as its boundary; the knowable has knowledge as its boundary. Knowledge does not proceed beyond the knowable, nor is there any path of the knowable beyond knowledge. These things stand within each other's limits. Just as with two well-fitting halves of a casket, the lower half...
176:
The upper lid does not exceed the lower lid, and the lower lid of a casket does not exceed the upper lid, but they stand meeting at the edges; even so, the knowable (neyya) and the knowledge (ñāṇa) of the Blessed Buddha stand meeting at the edges. As far as the knowable extends, so far does the knowledge extend; as far as the knowledge extends, so far does the knowable extend. Knowledge has the knowable as its limit; the knowable has knowledge as its limit. Knowledge does not proceed beyond the knowable, and there is no ground for the knowable beyond knowledge. These things stand meeting at the edges.

The knowledge of the Blessed Buddha proceeds in all things. All things are connected to the Blessed Buddha’s reflection, desire, attention, and thought-arising. The knowledge of the Blessed Buddha proceeds in all beings. The Blessed One knows the inclinations (āsaya) of all beings, knows their latent tendencies (anusaya), knows their temperaments (carita), and knows their dispositions (adhimutti). He knows beings with little dust in their eyes and those with much dust, those with sharp faculties and those with dull faculties, those with good qualities and those with bad qualities, those easy to teach and those hard to teach, and those capable and incapable of realization. The world with its devas, Maras, and Brahmas, this generation with its recluses and brahmins, with its devas and humans, revolves within the Buddha’s knowledge.

Just as whatever fish or turtles, including even the Timi and Timiṅgala, revolve within the great ocean; even so, the world with its devas, Maras, and Brahmas, this generation with its recluses and brahmins, with its devas and humans, revolves within the Buddha’s knowledge. Just as whatever birds, including even the Garuḍa, son of Vinatā, fly and revolve in a portion of the sky; even so, those who are endowed with wisdom like the Venerable Sāriputta revolve only in a portion of the Buddha’s knowledge. The Buddha’s knowledge stands pervading and surpassing the wisdom of devas and humans.

There are wise kshatriyas, wise brahmins, wise householders, and wise recluses who are subtle, skilled in the doctrines of others, like hair-splitting archers; they wander about, as it were, shattering the views of others with their wisdom. They prepare and formulate questions and approach the Tathāgata to ask about deep and hidden matters. Those questions are explained and answered by the Blessed One with their reasons pointed out. They then become disciples of the Blessed One. Thus, the Blessed One alone shines there with wisdom. In this way, the Blessed One is 'Cakkhumā' (One with Vision) through the Eye of Wisdom (Paññā-cakkhu).
177:
How is the Blessed One 'Cakkhumā' (One with Vision) through the Buddha-eye (Buddha-cakkhu)? When the Blessed One surveys the world with the Buddha-eye, he sees beings with little dust in their eyes and those with much dust, those with sharp faculties and those with dull faculties, those with good qualities and those with bad qualities, those easy to teach and those hard to teach, and some who live seeing the danger and fault in the next world.

Just as in a pond of blue, red, or white lotuses, some lotuses—born in the water, grown in the water, not having risen above the water—thrive submerged in the water; some lotuses—born in the water, grown in the water—stand at the water's level; and some lotuses—born in the water, grown in the water—stand having risen above the water, unsullied by the water; even so, when the Blessed One surveys the world with the Buddha-eye, he sees beings with little dust in their eyes and those with much dust, those with sharp faculties and those with dull faculties, those with good qualities and those with bad qualities, those easy to teach and those hard to teach, and some who live seeing the danger and fault in the next world.

The Blessed One knows: 'This person is of a lustful temperament, this person is of a hateful temperament, this person is of a deluded temperament, this person is of a discursive temperament, this person is of a faithful temperament, this person is of an intellectual temperament.' To a person of lustful temperament, the Blessed One speaks a discourse on foulness (asubha). To a person of hateful temperament, the Blessed One instructs in the meditation on loving-kindness (mettā-bhāvanā). To a person of deluded temperament, the Blessed One establishes them in the study of the texts, in questioning, in listening to the Dhamma at the proper time, in discussing the Dhamma at the proper time, and in living with teachers. To a person of discursive temperament, the Blessed One instructs in mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati). To a person of faithful temperament, the Blessed One instructs in the inspiring signs: the perfect enlightenment of the Buddha, the excellence of the Dhamma, the good practice of the Saṅgha, and the virtues (sīla). To a person of intellectual temperament, the Blessed One instructs in the signs of insight (vipassanā): the aspect of impermanence, the aspect of suffering, and the aspect of non-self.

'As one standing on a rocky mountain peak
Beholds the people all around,
Even so, O Wise One, O All-Seeing One,
Having ascended the palace made of Dhamma,
Free from sorrow, look down upon the people
Immersed in sorrow, overcome by birth and old age.' (Thus he spoke).
178:
Thus, the Blessed One is 'One with Vision' (Cakkhumā) also by means of the Buddha-eye (Buddha-cakkhu).

How is the Blessed One 'One with Vision' also by means of the All-seeing eye (Samanta-cakkhu)? The All-seeing eye is called Omniscient Knowledge (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). The Blessed One is endowed with, fully endowed with, attained to, fully attained to, possessed of, fully possessed of, and has arrived at the perfection of Omniscient Knowledge.

'There is nothing in this world unseen by Him, nor anything unknown that should be known; He has fully understood everything that can be known; therefore, the Tathāgata is the All-seeing One.'

Thus, because the Blessed One is 'One with Vision' by means of the All-seeing eye—the One with Vision (the Buddha) did not answer me.

'Up to the third time, O Divine Seer (Devīsi), I have heard that He answers' means: I have heard that up to the third time, the Buddha, the Divine Seer among devas, answers a question. When asked a question concerning the Dhamma (sahadhammika) up to the third time, the Buddha answers and does not cause delay (does not keep one in the round of rebirths)—thus have I learned, thus have I upheld, thus have I noted. 'Devīsi' means the Blessed One is both a deva and a seer (isi); hence, 'Devīsi'. Just as kings who have gone forth are called royal seers (rāji-isi), and brahmins who have gone forth are called brahmin seers (brāhmaṇi-isi), even so, the Blessed One is both a deva and a seer; hence, 'Devīsi'.

Alternatively, the Blessed One is a seer (isi) because He has gone forth. He is a seer because He sought, searched for, and repeatedly sought the great aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha). He is a seer because He sought... the great aggregate of concentration... the great aggregate of wisdom... the great aggregate of liberation... the great aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation. He is a seer because He sought the destruction of the great mass of darkness (ignorance). He is a seer because He sought the breaking of the great perversion (vipallāsa). He is a seer because He sought the pulling out of the great dart of craving... the untying of the great bond of views... the bringing down of the great banner of conceit... the stilling of the great volitional formations... the crossing over the great flood... the laying down of the great burden... the cutting off of the great round of rebirths... the quenching of the great fever... the allaying of the great heat... the raising of the great banner of Dhamma.

He is a seer because He sought the great foundations of mindfulness... the great right strivings... the great faculties... the great powers... the great factors of enlightenment... the great Noble Eightfold Path... the great ultimate Deathless Nibbāna. Or, He is sought, searched for, and repeatedly sought by beings of great power—
179:
—'Where is the Buddha? Where is the Blessed One? Where is the God of gods? Where is the Bull among men?'—thus He is a seer (isi). 'Up to the third time, O Divine Seer, I have heard that He answers.' Therefore, that brahmin said:

'Twice, O Sakka, I have asked, [thus said the Venerable Mogharāja]
The One with Vision did not answer me;
Up to the third time, O Divine Seer, I have heard that He answers.'

This world, the other world, and the Brahma world together with the devas, do not know the view of the glorious Gotama.

In the phrase 'Ayaṃ loko paro loko', 'Ayaṃ loko' refers to the human world. 'Paro loko' refers to all other worlds excluding the human world. This is the meaning of the phrase 'Ayaṃ loko paro loko'.

'Brahmaloko sadevako' refers to the six deva realms, the Vasavatti deva realm, the Brahma realm together with the world of space (okāsaloka), and the world of beings (sattaloka) including recluses, brahmins, devas, and humans. This is the meaning of the phrase 'Brahmaloko sadevako'.

'Diṭṭhiṃ te nābhijānāti' means the world of beings does not know Your view, preference, liking, doctrine, intention, or purpose. They do not know, do not see, do not perceive, do not reach, do not find, and cannot obtain the thought: 'This person has such a view, such a preference, such a liking, such a doctrine, such an intention, such a purpose.' This is the meaning of the phrase 'Diṭṭhiṃ te nābhijānāti'.

'Gotamassa yasassino' means the Blessed One is called 'Yasassī' because He has attained fame and a great following. Alternatively, the Blessed One is called 'Yasassī' because He is honored, revered, respected, worshipped, and esteemed, and is a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. This is the meaning of the phrase 'Gotamassa yasassino'. Therefore, that brahmin said:

'This world, the other world, and the Brahma world together with the devas, do not know the view of the glorious Gotama.'
180:
O Lord who sees so transcendently, I have come with a question. How should one look upon the world so that the King of Death does not see him?

"One who sees so transcendently" means one who sees in this way transcendently, sees the foremost, sees the best, sees the distinguished, sees the chief, sees the noble, sees the supreme.

"I have come with a question" means one who has a need for a question has come... it means "carry this burden which is a burden."

"How should one look upon the world" means in what manner one looks, reflects, weighs, investigates, develops, or makes manifest.

"The King of Death does not see" means the King of Death does not see, does not behold, does not find, does not encounter, does not obtain.

Therefore, that brahmin said:
"O Lord who sees so transcendently, I have come with a question. How should one look upon the world so that the King of Death does not see him?"

"Mogharāja, always mindful, look upon the world as empty. Having removed the view of self, one should thus be a crosser of death. The King of Death does not see one who looks upon the world in this way."

In the phrase "look upon the world as empty," "world" refers to the hell world, the animal world, the ghost world, the human world, the deva world, the world of aggregates, the world of elements, the world of sense bases, this world, the other world, the Brahma world, and the world with its devas.

A certain monk said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, it is said 'world, world.' To what extent, Venerable Sir, is it called 'world'?"

"Monk, it is called 'world' because it disintegrates. And what disintegrates? The eye, monk, disintegrates; forms disintegrate; eye-consciousness disintegrates; eye-contact disintegrates; whatever feeling—pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises with eye-contact as condition, that too disintegrates. The ear disintegrates; smells disintegrate... the body..."
181:
(The body) disintegrates; tangibles disintegrate. The mind disintegrates; mental objects disintegrate; mind-consciousness disintegrates; mind-contact disintegrates. Whatever feeling—pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises with mind-contact as condition, that too disintegrates. "Monk, it is called world because it disintegrates," (the Blessed One said).

"Look upon the world as empty" means looking upon the world as empty through two reasons: by way of noting the occurrence that does not follow one's will, or by way of rightly seeing formations as void. How does one look upon the world as empty by way of noting the occurrence that does not follow one's will? Control is not obtained over form; control is not obtained over feeling; control is not obtained over perception; control is not obtained over formations; control is not obtained over consciousness.

The Blessed One has said this: "Monks, form is non-self. For if, monks, this form were self, this form would not lead to affliction, and one could obtain (this) regarding form: 'Let my form be thus; let my form not be such.' But because, monks, form is non-self, therefore form leads to affliction, and one does not obtain (this) regarding form: 'Let my form be thus; let my form not be such.'"

"Feeling is non-self. For if, monks, this feeling were self, this feeling would not lead to affliction, and one could obtain (this) regarding feeling: 'Let my feeling be thus; let my feeling not be such.' But because, monks, feeling is non-self, therefore feeling leads to affliction, and one does not obtain (this) regarding feeling: 'Let my feeling be thus; let my feeling not be such.'"

"Perception is non-self. For if, monks, this perception were self, this perception would not lead to affliction, and one could obtain (this) regarding perception: 'Let my perception be thus; let my perception not be such.' But because, monks, perception is non-self, therefore perception leads to affliction, and one does not obtain (this) regarding perception: 'Let my perception be thus; let my perception not be such.'"

"Formations are non-self. For if, monks, these formations were self, these formations would not lead to affliction, and one could obtain (this) regarding formations: 'Let my formations be thus; let my formations not be such.' But because..."
182:
Bhikkhus, formations are non-self. Therefore, formations lead to affliction, and one cannot obtain [one's wish] regarding formations: 'Let my formations be thus; let my formations not be thus.'

Consciousness is non-self. Bhikkhus, if this consciousness were self, this consciousness would not lead to affliction, and one could obtain [one's wish] regarding consciousness: 'Let my consciousness be thus; let my consciousness not be thus.' Bhikkhus, because consciousness is non-self, therefore consciousness leads to affliction, and one cannot obtain [one's wish] regarding consciousness: 'Let my consciousness be thus; let my consciousness not be thus.'

For this was said by the Blessed One: 'Bhikkhus, this body is not yours, nor does it belong to others. Bhikkhus, this body should be seen as old kamma, conditioned, intended, and to be felt.' Bhikkhus, in that regard, the well-informed noble disciple attends closely and wisely to dependent origination itself: 'Thus, when this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases. That is to say: with ignorance as condition, formations come to be; with formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be. Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.'

'But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of formations; with the cessation of formations, the cessation of consciousness ...pe... with the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.' Thus, one looks upon the world as empty by way of noting the occurrence [of things] that do not follow one's will.

How does one look upon the world as empty by way of contemplating formations as hollow? No essence is found in form, no essence is found in feeling, no essence is found in perception, no essence is found in formations, no essence is found in consciousness. Form is without essence, void of essence, departed from essence, whether by way of the essence of permanence, or the essence of happiness, or the essence of self, or by way of being permanent, or stable, or eternal, or...
183:
...or by way of having an unchanging nature. Feeling is without essence, void of essence, departed from essence...pe... Perception is without essence, void of essence, departed from essence... Formations are without essence, void of essence, departed from essence... Consciousness is without essence, void of essence, departed from essence, whether by way of the essence of permanence, or the essence of happiness, or the essence of self, or by way of being permanent, or stable, or eternal, or by way of having an unchanging nature.

Just as a reed is without essence, void of essence, departed from essence; and just as a castor oil plant...pe... just as a fig tree is without essence, void of essence, departed from essence; just as a white wood tree is without essence, void of essence, departed from essence; just as a coral tree is without essence, void of essence, departed from essence; just as a mass of foam is without essence, void of essence, departed from essence; just as a water bubble is without essence, void of essence, departed from essence; just as a mirage is without essence, void of essence, departed from essence; just as a plantain trunk is without essence, void of essence, departed from essence; just as a magical illusion is without essence, void of essence, departed from essence—even so, form is without essence, void of essence, departed from essence, whether by way of the essence of permanence, or the essence of happiness, or the essence of self, or by way of being permanent, or stable, or eternal, or by way of having an unchanging nature. Feeling is without essence, void of essence, departed from essence...pe... Perception is without essence, void of essence, departed from essence... Formations are without essence, void of essence, departed from essence... Consciousness is without essence, void of essence, departed from essence, whether by way of the essence of permanence, or the essence of happiness, or the essence of self, or by way of being permanent, or stable, or eternal, or by way of having an unchanging nature. In this way, one looks upon the world as empty by way of contemplating formations as hollow. Through these two reasons, one looks upon the world as empty.

Furthermore, one looks upon the world as empty in six ways. The eye is empty of self, or of what belongs to self, or of permanence, or of stability, or of eternity, or of an unchanging nature. The ear is empty...pe... the nose is empty... the tongue is empty... the body is empty... the mind is empty of self, or of what belongs to self, or of permanence, or of stability, or of eternity, or of an unchanging nature. Forms are empty...pe... sounds are empty... smells are empty... tastes are empty... tactile objects are empty... mental phenomena are empty of self, or of what belongs to self, or of permanence, or of stability, or of eternity, or of an unchanging nature. Eye-consciousness is empty...pe... mind-consciousness is empty. Contact associated with eye-consciousness is...
184:
Mind-contact is empty. ... Feeling born of eye-contact is empty. ... Feeling born of mind-contact is empty. Perception of forms is empty. ... Perception of mental objects is empty. Volition regarding forms is empty. ... Volition regarding mental objects is empty. Craving for forms is empty. Initial thought regarding forms is empty. Sustained thought regarding forms is empty. ... Sustained thought regarding mental objects is empty—empty of self, or of what belongs to self, or of what is permanent, or stable, or eternal, or not subject to change. In these six ways, one regards the world as empty.

Furthermore, one regards the world as empty in ten ways. One regards form as hollow, as vain, as empty, as not-self, as pithless, as murderous, as destruction, as the root of suffering, as accompanied by taints, as conditioned. Feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness... passing away... reappearance... rebirth... existence... the round of saṃsāra as hollow, as vain, as empty, as not-self, as pithless, as murderous, as destruction, as the root of suffering, as accompanied by taints, as conditioned. In these ten ways, one regards the world as empty.

Furthermore, one regards the world as empty in twelve ways. Form is not a being, not a life-principle, not a person, not a youth, not a woman, not a man, not a self, not what belongs to self, not 'I', not 'mine', not anything, not belonging to anyone. Feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness is not a being, not a life-principle, not a person, not a youth, not a woman, not a man, not a self, not what belongs to self, not 'I', not 'mine', not anything, not belonging to anyone. In these twelve ways, one regards the world as empty.

The Blessed One said this: 'Bhikkhus, abandon what is not yours. Your abandoning of it will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time. And what, bhikkhus, is not yours? Form, bhikkhus, is not yours; abandon it. Your abandoning of it will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time. Feeling, bhikkhus, is not yours; abandon it. Your abandoning of it will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time. Perception, bhikkhus, is not yours; abandon it. Your abandoning of it will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time. Volitional formations, bhikkhus, are not yours; abandon them. Your abandoning of them will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time. Consciousness, bhikkhus, is not yours; abandon it. Your abandoning of it will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.'
185:
Bhikkhus, suppose people were to carry off the grass, sticks, branches, and leaves in this Jeta’s Grove, or burn them, or do with them as they wish. Would you think: ‘People are carrying us off, or burning us, or doing with us as they wish’? 'No, venerable sir.' 'Why is that?' 'Because, venerable sir, that grass, wood, etc., is neither our self nor what belongs to our self.'

In the same way, bhikkhus, abandon what is not yours. Your abandoning of it will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time. And what, bhikkhus, is not yours? Form, bhikkhus, is not yours; abandon it. Your abandoning of it will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time. Feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness is not yours; abandon it. Your abandoning of it will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time. In this way, one regards the world as empty.

The venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: 'Venerable sir, it is said, "The world is empty, the world is empty." In what respect, venerable sir, is it said that the world is empty?' 'Ānanda, because it is empty of self or of what belongs to self, it is said that the world is empty. And how, Ānanda, is it empty of self or of what belongs to self? The eye, Ānanda, is empty of self or of what belongs to self. Forms are empty... eye-consciousness is empty... eye-contact is empty... whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is empty of self or of what belongs to self. The ear is empty... sounds are empty... the nose is empty... odors are empty... the tongue is empty... tastes are empty... the body is empty... tactile objects are empty... the mind is empty... mental objects are empty... mind-consciousness is empty... mind-contact is empty... whatever feeling arises with mind-contact as condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is empty of self or of what belongs to self. Because it is empty of self or of what belongs to self, Ānanda, it is said that the world is empty.' In this way too, one regards the world as empty.

For one who sees as it really is
The pure arising of phenomena,
The pure succession of conditioned things,
There is no fear, Gāmaṇi.
186: 'When one sees the world as equal to grass and wood with wisdom, then one no longer desires anything else besides the cessation of rebirth.' In this way, one looks upon the world as empty. For this was said by the Blessed One: 'In the same way, monks, a monk thoroughly investigates form as far as the scope of form goes; he thoroughly investigates feeling as far as the scope of feeling goes; he thoroughly investigates perception as far as the scope of perception goes; he thoroughly investigates volitional formations as far as the scope of volitional formations goes; he thoroughly investigates consciousness as far as the scope of consciousness goes. For that monk who is thoroughly investigating form... feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness as far as the scope of consciousness goes, whatever notion of "I" or "mine" or "I am" he had, that no longer exists for him.' In this way, one looks upon the world as empty. 'Look upon the world as empty' means look upon the world as empty, reflect on it, see it, and make it clear through the investigations of weighing and defining—thus 'look upon the world as empty.' 'Mogharāja, always mindful' means the Blessed One addresses that brahmin by name as 'Mogharāja.' 'Always' means at all times... until the final stage of life. 'Mindful' means one who is mindful through four reasons... one who develops the foundation of mindfulness by repeatedly contemplating the body in the body is called 'mindful'—thus 'Mogharāja, always mindful.' 'Having removed the view of self' means the view of self (attānudiṭṭhi) refers to the twenty-fold personality view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi). Here, an uninstructed worldling (assutavā puthujjana), who has no regard for the noble ones, is unskilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, is undisciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones, who has no regard for the true men, is unskilled in the Dhamma of the true men, is undisciplined in the Dhamma of the true men, regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. He regards feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness. Such a view, a resort of views, a tangle of views, a jungle of views, a wilderness of views, a distortion of views, a vacillation of views, a fetter of views, a grip, a misapprehension, an adherence, a presumption, a wrong path, a false way, falsity, a sectarian landing-place, a distorted grasp, a contrary grasp, an inverted grasp, a wrong grasp, a baseless and erroneous grasp.
187:
grasping the untrue as true; as far as the sixty-two types of views go, this is the view of self (attānudiṭṭhi). 'Having uprooted the view of self' means: having uprooted the arisen view of self, having thoroughly eradicated it, extracted it, pulled it out, abandoned it, dispelled it, eliminated it, and brought it to a state of non-existence.

'Thus one may cross over death' means: in this way, one may cross over death, cross over old age, and cross over dying; one may transcend, go beyond, and completely surmount them.

'Thus regarding the world' means: one who thus contemplates the world, weighs it, and makes it clear.

'The King of Death does not see' means: death itself is the King of Death, Māra is the King of Death, and dying is the King of Death. It means that the King of Death does not see, does not look, does not find, and does not reach [him].

The Blessed One said this: 'Monks, for example, a forest deer roaming in the woods and groves goes, stands, sits, and lies down with confidence. Why is that? Monks, it is because that deer has not come within the range of the hunter.
