In the same way, monks, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. Monks, this monk is said to have blinded Māra, to have abolished Māra’s tracks, and to have gone where the Evil One cannot see.

'Furthermore, monks, with the subsiding of thought and examination, a monk enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration... [the third jhāna]... [the fourth jhāna]. Monks, this monk is said to have blinded Māra, to have abolished Māra’s tracks, and to have gone where the Evil One cannot see.

'Furthermore, monks, with the complete transcending of perceptions of form, with the passing away of perceptions of sensory reaction, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, [aware that] "space is infinite," a monk enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite space. Monks, this monk...'
188:
"The bhikkhu has blinded Māra; having destroyed the tracks of Māra, he has gone to a state where he cannot be seen by the Evil One."

Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and by not attending to perceptions of diversity, thinking 'space is infinite,' enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite space... (pe)...

Furthermore, bhikkhus, by completely transcending the sphere of infinite space, thinking 'consciousness is infinite,' he enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness... (pe)...

Furthermore, bhikkhus, by completely transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking 'there is nothing,' he enters and dwells in the sphere of nothingness... (pe)...

Furthermore, bhikkhus, by completely transcending the sphere of nothingness, he enters and dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception... (pe)...

Furthermore, bhikkhus, by completely transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling; and having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed. This bhikkhu, O bhikkhus, is said to have "blinded Māra; having destroyed the tracks of Māra, he has gone to a state where he cannot be seen by the Evil One, and has crossed the entanglement of craving in the world." He goes confidently, stands confidently, sits confidently, and sleeps confidently. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, the bhikkhu has gone out of the range of the Evil One—the King of Death does not see him. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"Look upon the world as empty, Mogharāja, always mindful;
Having uprooted the view of self, one may thus overcome death;
The King of Death does not see one who looks upon the world in this way."

At the conclusion of the verses... (pe)... "Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is my teacher, I am the disciple," he addressed.

## 15. Exposition of the Questions of the Young Man Mogharāja ends.

## 16. Exposition of the Questions of the Young Man Piṅgiya

I am old, weak, and my complexion has faded (thus the venerable Piṅgiya addressed),
My eyes are not clear, and my hearing is not easy;
May I not perish while deluded in the interval; teach me the Dhamma that I may know,
The abandoning of birth and decay in this very life.
189:
"I am old, weak, and my complexion has faded" means: "Jiṇṇohamasmi" refers to being old, aged, advanced in years, having reached the end of one's life span, having reached old age, being one hundred and twenty years of age. "Abalo" means being weak, having little strength, being powerless. "Vītavaṇṇo" means being without complexion, having a faded complexion, having a vanished complexion. It means that the former beautiful complexion and radiance have disappeared, and the fault of old age has become manifest; thus, it is said, "I am old, weak, and my complexion has faded."

"The venerable Piṅgiya (addressed) thus" means: "Iccā" is a conjunction of words (padasandhi). "Āyasmā" is a term of endearment and respect. "Piṅgiyo" is the name and designation of that Brahmin. Thus, it is said, "The venerable Piṅgiya (addressed) thus."

"My eyes are not clear, and my hearing is not easy" means: "Nettā asuddhā" means the eyes are not clear, especially not clear, not pure all around, not bright. It means one does not see forms with the eyes as before; thus, it is said, "My eyes are not clear." "Savanaṃ na phāsu" means the hearing is not clear, especially not clear, not pure all around, not bright. It means one does not hear sounds with the ears as before; thus, it is said, "My eyes are not clear, and my hearing is not easy."

"May I not perish while deluded in the interval" means: "Māhaṃ nassaṃ" means may I not perish, especially may I not perish, may I not perish severely. "Momuho" means being deluded, fallen into ignorance, being without knowledge, being unclear, being of little wisdom. "Antarāva" means without knowing, without attaining, especially without knowing, without obtaining, without touching, without realizing your Dhamma, view, practice, and path, may I not pass away (die) in the interval; thus, it is said, "May I not perish while deluded in the interval."

"Teach me the Dhamma that I may know" means: "Dhammaṃ" refers to the holy life (brahmacariya) which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, complete in meaning and phrasing, entirely perfect and pure; the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, Nibbāna, and the practice leading to Nibbāna. Teach, show, prescribe, establish, open, analyze, make plain, and make manifest these things; thus, it is said, "Teach the Dhamma." "Yamahaṃ vijaññaṃ" means that Dhamma which I may know, know by way of object, know specially, know repeatedly and specially, know by penetration, reach, touch, and realize; thus, it is said, "Teach me the Dhamma that I may know."

"The abandoning of birth and decay in this very life" means: The abandoning, the stilling, the relinquishing, the subsiding of birth, decay, and death in this very dispensation, referring to the deathless Nibbāna; thus, it is said, "The abandoning of birth and decay in this very life." Therefore, that Brahmin (addressed thus):
190:
“I am old, worn out, and my complexion has faded. My eyes are not clear, and my hearing is not good. May I not perish in confusion in the meantime. Please teach me the Dhamma that I may understand—the pure and noble practice, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, Nibbāna, and the practice leading to Nibbāna. Please teach me the Nibbāna that is the abandoning of rebirth and aging in this life, the cessation, the cooling, and the deathless.” (Thus the Brahmin Piṅgiya addressed.)

“Seeing people suffering because of forms, Piṅgiya, heedless people suffer in forms. Therefore, Piṅgiya, being heedful, abandon form for the sake of non-rebirth,” said the Blessed One.

Regarding the phrase 'Seeing them suffering because of forms' (disvāna rūpesu vihaññamāne): Form (rūpa) refers to the four great elements and the derived form dependent on the four great elements. Beings are harmed, suffer, and are oppressed because of form, on account of form, and by reason of form. Because there is form, various punishments (kammakaraṇa) are inflicted. They are beaten with whips, they are beaten with canes, and they are beaten with short sticks. Hands are cut off, feet are cut off, and both hands and feet are cut off. Ears are cut off, noses are cut off, and both ears and noses are cut off. They are subjected to the 'vinegar-pot' torture (bilangathālika), the 'shell-shave' torture (saṅkhamuṇḍika), the 'Rāhu's mouth' torture (rāhumukha), the 'fire-garland' torture (jotimālika), the 'hand-torch' torture (hatthapajjotika), the 'grass-wrap' torture (erakavattika), the 'bark-dress' torture (cīrakavāsika), the 'antelope' torture (eṇeyyaka), the 'flesh-hook' torture (baḷisamaṃsika), the 'coin-cut' torture (kahāpaṇika), the 'alkali-drip' torture (khārāpatacchika), the 'pivot-turn' torture (palighaparivattika), and the 'straw-mat' torture (palālapīṭhaka). They are splashed with boiling oil, they are made to be devoured by dogs, they are impaled alive on stakes, and their heads are cut off with swords. Thus, beings are harmed, suffer, and are oppressed because of form, on account of form, and by reason of form. Seeing, observing, weighing, judging, and making clear these sufferings is the meaning of 'Seeing them suffering because of forms'.

'Piṅgiya, said the Blessed One' (piṅgiyāti bhagavā): The Blessed One addresses that Brahmin by name. 'Bhagavā' (Blessed One) is a term of respect... it is a designation realized through direct experience; this is the name 'Bhagavā'.
191:
"Heedless people suffer in forms" means: "Ruppanti" means they are afflicted, they are disturbed, they are oppressed, they are harassed, they become diseased, and they become dejected. They are afflicted, disturbed, oppressed, and harassed by eye-disease; they become diseased and dejected. By ear-disease... (and so on). By body-disease... (and so on). By the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, creeping things, and lice, they are afflicted, disturbed, oppressed, and harassed; they become diseased and dejected. Thus, they suffer in forms.

Alternatively, when the eye is failing, declining, disappearing, or vanishing, they are afflicted, disturbed, oppressed, and harassed; they become diseased and dejected. When the ear, nose, tongue, body, visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, family, group, monastery, gain, fame, praise, happiness, robes, alms-food, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick are failing, declining, or vanishing, they are afflicted, disturbed, oppressed, and harassed; they become diseased and dejected. In this way also, they suffer in forms.

"People" (janā) refers to khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, suddas, householders, monastics, devas, and humans. "Heedless" (pamattā) refers to heedlessness (pamāda) through bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, or mental misconduct, or the letting go of the mind in the five cords of sensual pleasure, following that letting go, lack of respect in the development of wholesome states, lack of perseverance, lack of steadiness, sluggishness, lack of desire, laying down the burden, lack of practice, lack of development, lack of frequenting, lack of determination, and lack of application. Such heedlessness, being heedless, and the state of being heedless is called heedlessness. People endowed with this heedlessness are "heedless people." Thus, heedless people suffer in forms.

"Therefore, Piṅgiya, you should be heedful" means: "Tasmā" (therefore) means for that reason, because of seeing that danger. "Appamatto" (heedful) means acting with respect, acting with perseverance... (and so on) being heedful in wholesome states. Thus, Piṅgiya, therefore you should be heedful.

"Abandon form for the sake of non-rebirth" means: "Form" (rūpa) refers to the four great elements and the derived form dependent on the four great elements. "Abandon form" means abandon form, give up form, dispel form, eliminate form, and bring form to non-existence. For the sake of non-rebirth...
192:
In the sense that your form (rūpa) should cease in this very life, and that a renewed existence (paṭisandhika bhava) should not arise in the sense sphere (kāmadhātu), the fine-material sphere (rūpadhātu), or the immaterial sphere (arūpadhātu); nor in the sense existence (kāmabhava), fine-material existence (rūpabhava), or immaterial existence (arūpabhava); nor in the existence with perception (saññābhava), existence without perception (asaññābhava), or existence with neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññābhava); nor in the one-constituent existence (ekavokārabhava), four-constituent existence (catuvokārabhava), or five-constituent existence (pañcavokārabhava); and that it should not be produced, should not be generated, should not arise, and should not be manifested again in any destination (gati), rebirth (upapatti), relinking (paṭisandhi), existence (bhava), saṃsāra, or the cycle (vaṭṭa); but should cease, be stilled, come to an end, and be subsided in this very life—this is the meaning of "Abandon form for the sake of no more rebirth." Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"Seeing [beings] being afflicted in forms, [O Piṅgiya, said the Blessed One]
Negligent people suffer in forms.
Therefore, Piṅgiya, being diligent,
Abandon form for the sake of no more rebirth."

The four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below—these are the ten directions.
In this world, there is nothing unseen, unheard, unsensed, or unknown by You, even in the slightest.
Tell me the Dhamma that I may know, which is the abandoning of birth and old age in this very life.

"The four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below—these are the ten directions" means in all ten directions.

"In this world, there is nothing unseen, unheard, unsensed, or unknown by You, even in the slightest" means that for You, there is nothing unseen, unheard, unsensed, or unknown, whether it be one's own benefit (attattha), the benefit of others (parattha), the benefit of both (ubhayattha), the benefit in the present life (diṭṭhadhammika), the benefit in the future life (samparāyika), an evident meaning (uttāna), a deep meaning (gambhīra), a hidden meaning (gūḷha), a concealed meaning (paṭicchanna), a meaning to be inferred (neyya), an explicit meaning (nīta), a blameless benefit (anavajja), a defilement-free benefit (nikkilesa), a pure benefit (vodāna), or the ultimate benefit (paramattha)—it is not that these do not exist, are not present, or are not found [in Your knowledge]. (It means there is nothing You do not know).

In the phrase "Tell me the Dhamma that I may know," "Dhamma" refers to that which is good in the beginning... (in detail) tell, teach, describe, establish, reveal, analyze, make clear, and manifest the Nibbāna and the practice leading to Nibbāna.
193:
Make the Dhamma clear; reveal it. "That I may know" means that I may know, understand, fully comprehend, repeatedly know, penetrate, attain, encounter, and realize—this is the meaning of "Tell me the Dhamma that I may know."

"Abandoning birth and old age here" (jātijarāya idha vippahānaṃ) means the abandoning, the stilling, the relinquishing, the subsiding of birth, old age, and death in this very Dispensation (sāsana), which is the Deathless Nibbāna—thus it is the abandoning of birth and old age in this Dispensation. Therefore, that brahmin said:

"The four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below—these are the ten directions.
In this world, there is nothing unseen, unheard, unsensed, or unknown by You, even in the slightest.
Tell me the Dhamma that I may know, so that I may abandon birth and old age in this very Dispensation."

(The Blessed One said:)
"O Piṅgiya, seeing humans overcome by craving, afflicted by old age and thus reaching torment,
Therefore, Piṅgiya, being diligent, abandon craving for the sake of no more rebirth."

"Seeing humans overcome by craving" (taṇhā-dhipanne manuje pekkhamāno)—craving (taṇhā) ranges from craving for forms (rūpa-taṇhā) to craving for mental objects (dhamma-taṇhā). "Overcome by craving" (taṇhā-dhipanne) refers to those who are overwhelmed by craving, who follow craving, who are pursued by craving, who are pervaded by craving, who are immersed in craving, who are conquered by craving, who are oppressed by it, and whose minds are completely seized by it. "Humans" (manuje) is a designation for beings. "Seeing" (pekkhamāno) means observing, seeing, looking at, contemplating, and examining—thus it is "seeing humans overcome by craving." "O Piṅgiya, said the Blessed One" means the Blessed One addresses that brahmin by name. "Blessed One" (Bhagavā) is a title of respect... it is a designation realized [by Him], namely "Bhagavā"—thus the Blessed One [called him] "Piṅgiya."

"Born of torment, afflicted by old age" (santāpajāte jarasa parete)—"Born of torment" (santāpajāte) means those who have the torment caused by birth, the torment caused by old age, the torment caused by sickness, the torment caused by death, the torment caused by sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, the torment caused by the suffering of hell... the torment caused by the suffering of the ruin of views (diṭṭhibyasana).
194:
Being beset by danger, being beset by affliction, means being beset by distress. 'Overcome by old age' means touched by old age, overcome, encountered, and possessed by it. Those followed by birth, pursued by old age, overwhelmed by disease, struck down by death, without protection, without shelter, without refuge, having become refuge-less—these are called 'beset by distress, overcome by old age'.

'Therefore, Piṅgiya, be heedful' means for that reason, for that cause, due to that condition, because of that source, seeing the danger in this way, Piṅgiya, you should act with respect and not be heedless regarding wholesome states.

'Abandon craving for the sake of non-becoming' means abandon craving, starting from craving for forms up to craving for mental phenomena; abandon it, dispel it, eliminate it, and make it non-existent. 'For the sake of non-becoming' means so that your rebirth-linking existence does not arise again in the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere, or the immaterial sphere; in the sense-existence, fine-material existence, immaterial existence, percipient existence, non-percipient existence, or neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient existence; in the one-constituent existence, four-constituent existence, or five-constituent existence; so that it is not generated, not produced, does not arise, and does not manifest again in any destination, rebirth, rebirth-linking, existence, saṃsāra, or the round of suffering; but rather ceases right here, is calmed, reaches its end, and is stilled. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"Seeing people overcome by craving, [O Piṅgiya, said the Blessed One,]
beset by distress, overcome by old age;
therefore, Piṅgiya, be heedful, abandon craving for the sake of non-becoming."

At the conclusion of the verse, for many thousands of beings who shared the same desire, effort, intention, and disposition as that brahmin, the dust-free, stainless Eye of Dhamma arose: "Whatever is subject to origination is all subject to cessation." And for that brahmin, the dust-free, stainless Eye of Dhamma [the path of non-returning] arose: "Whatever is subject to origination is all subject to cessation." Simultaneously with the attainment of the Eye of Dhamma, the antelope skin, matted hair, bark garments, triple staff, water pot, hair, and beard disappeared.
195:
(Piṅgiya) sat wearing dyed robes, carrying the double-layered robe and alms bowl, with hands joined in respectful salutation according to the practice, paying homage to the Blessed One, saying: "Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is my teacher, I am the disciple."

## Exposition of the Questions of the Youth Piṅgiya (Piṅgiya-māṇava-pucchā-niddesa), the Sixteenth.

## 17. Exposition of the Verses in Praise of the Way to the Beyond (Pārāyanatthuti-gāthā-niddesa)

The Blessed One, while dwelling at the Pāsāṇaka Shrine in the Magadhan country, being requested and asked by the sixteen attendant brahmins, answered the questions.

"The Blessed One said this" (Idamavoca bhagavā) means he spoke this Pārāyana. "Blessed One" (Bhagavā) is a term of respect... it is a designation realized by himself; thus, "the Blessed One said this". "Dwelling in the Magadhan country" means staying, moving about, proceeding, maintaining, and living in the district named Magadha. "At the Pāsāṇaka Shrine" means at the seat of the Buddha called the Pāsāṇaka Shrine. "Of the sixteen attendant brahmins" means the brahmin Piṅgiya was a devoted follower, attendant, and disciple of the brahmin Bāvarī. Together with Piṅgiya, there were sixteen brahmins. Alternatively, those sixteen brahmins were devoted followers, attendants, and disciples of the Buddha, the Blessed One.

In the phrase "Being requested, he answered the questions as they were asked," "requested" (ajjhiṭṭho) means urged or invited. "Asked and asked" (puṭṭho puṭṭho) means as they were asked, questioned, requested, urged, and entreated. "Answered the questions" (pañhaṃ vyākāsi) means he answered the questions, taught, pointed out, established, opened up, analyzed, made clear, and explained. Thus, "Being requested, he answered the questions as they were asked." Therefore, the ancient teachers said:

"The Blessed One, while dwelling at the Pāsāṇaka Shrine in the Magadhan country, being requested and asked by the sixteen attendant brahmins, answered the questions."
196:
If one practices the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, having understood the meaning and the Dhamma of each and every question, one will surely go to the far shore of aging and death. These teachings are those that lead to the far shore. Therefore, the name for this Dhamma-discourse is 'Pārāyana' (The Way to the Far Shore).

'Of each and every question' refers to the question of Ajita, the question of Tissa Metteyya, the question of Puṇṇaka, the question of Mettagū, the question of Dhotaka, the question of Upasīva, the question of Nanda, the question of Hemaka, the question of Todeyya, the question of Kappa, the question of Jatukaṇṇī, the question of Bhadrāvudha, the question of Udaya, the question of Posāla, the question of Mogharāja, and the question of Piṅgiya.

In the phrase 'having understood the meaning and the Dhamma,' the question itself is the Dhamma (the text), and the explanation is the meaning (attha). To understand the meaning means to know, weigh, investigate, cultivate, and make it clear. To understand the Dhamma also means to know, weigh, investigate, cultivate, and make the Pali text clear.

'One should practice the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma' means practicing the right practice, the conforming practice, the non-opposing practice, the practice in accordance with the purpose, and the practice in accordance with the supramundane Dhamma. In the phrase 'one will surely go to the far shore of aging and death,' the far shore of aging and death refers to the Deathless Nibbāna. It is Nibbāna, which is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, fading away, and cessation. 'One will surely go to the far shore of aging and death' means one will reach, attain, touch, and realize Nibbāna, which is the end of aging and death. 'These teachings lead to the far shore' means these teachings cause one to reach the shore of Nibbāna, to reach it well, to reach it successively, and they lead to the transcending of aging and death.

In the phrase 'Therefore, of this Dhamma-discourse,' 'therefore' means because of that reason, because of that cause, because of that condition, because of that origin. 'Of this Dhamma-discourse' means...
197:
Of this Pārāyana: This is the name of this Dhamma-discourse because it leads to the shore of Nibbāna, because it is the cause for reaching Nibbāna, because it arises based on the benefit of Nibbāna, and because it points to the benefit of Nibbāna. 'Pārāyana' is just a name. The Deathless Nibbāna is called 'Pāra' (the shore). ... Nibbāna, which is the cessation of lust and the escape from defilements, is called 'Pāra'. Because the journey to Nibbāna is attained, it is called 'Ayana'. That journey is the Noble Eightfold Path, namely: Right View ... Right Concentration. 'Adhivacana' (designation) means a term, a name, a concept, a common usage, a label, a naming, a nomenclature, an expression, a phrasing, and a designation. Therefore, Pārāyana is a name.

Therefore, the Elders of the Council said:
'If one practices the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, having understood the meaning and the Dhamma of each and every question, one will surely go to the far shore of aging and death. These teachings are those that lead to the far shore. Therefore, the name for this Dhamma-discourse is Pārāyana.'

Ajita, Tissa Metteyya, Puṇṇaka, and Mettagū,
Dhotaka, Upasīva, Nanda, and Hemaka,
The two, Todeyya and Kappa, and the wise Jatukaṇṇī,
Bhadrāvudha, Udaya, and the Brahmin named Posāla,
The wise Mogharāja, and the great seer Piṅgiya.

These approached the Buddha, the Seer of perfect conduct. They approached the Buddha, the most excellent of all, to ask subtle questions.

'Ete Buddhaṃ upāgacchuṃ' refers to those sixteen Pārāyanika Brahmins. 'Buddha' refers to the Blessed One who is self-become, who without a teacher realized the truths by himself among teachings not heard before, and in those truths attained omniscience and mastery over the powers.

For what reason is he called 'Buddha'? He is the Buddha because he realized the Four Noble Truths. He is the Buddha because he makes the generation of beings realize them. He is the Buddha because of his omniscience. He is the Buddha because of his all-seeing nature. He is the Buddha because he knows what is to be known. He is the Buddha because he makes various qualities blossom like a blooming lotus. He is the Buddha because his taints are destroyed. He is the Buddha because he is free from the smearing of defilements. He is the Buddha because he is absolutely free from lust. He is the Buddha because he is absolutely free from hatred. He is the Buddha because he is absolutely free from delusion. He is the Buddha because he is absolutely free from defilements. He is the Buddha because he has gone on the unique path to Nibbāna. He is the Buddha because he alone realized the unsurpassed supreme enlightenment. He is the Buddha because he destroyed ignorance and attained wisdom.

This name 'Buddha' was not given by his mother, father, brother, sister, friends, companions, relatives, or by ascetics, brahmins, or devas. This name of the Blessed Buddhas, which occurs at the end of the path of liberation, was realized at the foot of the Bodhi tree together with the attainment of omniscience.
198:
The name 'Buddha' is the name attained at the end of the Path of Arahantship. It is a designation realized by the Blessed Buddhas upon attaining Omniscience at the foot of the Bodhi tree. Those sixteen Brahmins approached the Buddha, attended upon him, served him, asked questions, and compared their inquiries. This is the meaning of 'ete buddhaṃ upāgacchuṃ'.

In the phrase 'sampannacaraṇaṃ isiṃ', 'caraṇa' refers to the practice of virtue. Restraint of virtue is caraṇa, restraint of the senses is caraṇa, moderation in eating is caraṇa, and devotion to wakefulness is caraṇa. The seven noble qualities (saddhamma) and the four jhanas are also taught as caraṇa by the Blessed One. 'Sampannacaraṇa' means having conduct that is complete, well-accomplished, specially accomplished, foremost, noble, and most excellent. 'Isi': The Blessed One is called 'Isi' because he seeks, searches for, and pursues the great mass of virtue (collection of attributes). Alternatively, he is called 'Isi' because he is sought, searched for, and pursued by beings of great power [asking], 'Where is the Buddha? Where is the Blessed One? Where is the God of gods? Where is the Bull among men?' This is the meaning of 'sampannacaraṇaṃ isiṃ'.

In the phrase 'pucchantā nipuṇe pañhe', 'pucchantā' means wishing to ask, requesting, urging, and inspiring faith. 'Nipuṇe pañhe' refers to questions that are deep, hard to see, hard to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of mere reasoning, subtle, and to be experienced by the wise.

In the phrase 'buddhasetthaṃ upāgamuṃ', 'Buddha' is the designation realized by that Blessed One. 'Settha' means the foremost, the most praised, the specially praised, the chief, the noble, and the most excellent. They approached, attended upon, respectfully served, reflected on the questions, and investigated the most excellent Buddha. Therefore, it is said:

## "These [Brahmins] approached the Buddha, the Sage of perfect conduct;
## Asking subtle questions, they approached the most excellent Buddha."

## When asked the questions, the Buddha answered them as they truly are;
## By answering the questions, the Sage delighted the Brahmins.

In the phrase 'tesaṃ buddho pabyākāsi', 'tesaṃ' refers to the sixteen Pārāyana Brahmins. 'Pabyākāsi' means the Buddha told, taught, designated, established, revealed, analyzed, clarified, and made manifest to those Brahmins.

In the phrase 'pañhaṃ puṭṭho yathātathaṃ', 'puṭṭho' means being asked, requested, urged, and inspired. 'Yathātathaṃ' means telling, teaching, designating, establishing, revealing, analyzing, clarifying, and making manifest exactly as it should be told, taught, designated, established, revealed, analyzed, clarified, and made manifest. This is the meaning of the phrase 'pañhaṃ yathātathaṃ'.

'Pañhānaṃ veyyākaraṇena' means by answering, teaching, designating, establishing, revealing, analyzing, clarifying, and making manifest the questions.

In the phrase 'tosesi brāhmaṇe muni', 'tosesi' means caused delight, specially delighted, inspired faith, satisfied, and made joyful. 'Brāhmaṇa' refers to the sixteen Pārāyana Brahmins. 'Muni': Wisdom is called 'muni'. That Arahant [who has crossed] all the entanglements of defilements and bonds...
199:
The Blessed One told [the answer to the problem]; he taught it as it should be taught, designated it as it should be designated, established it as it should be established, revealed it as it should be revealed, analyzed it as it should be analyzed, clarified it as it should be clarified, and made it manifest as it should be made manifest. Thus, he answered the asked question as it truly is. 'By answering the questions' means answering by telling, teaching, designating, establishing, revealing, analyzing, clarifying, and making manifest the questions. In 'The Sage delighted the Brahmins', 'delighted' means causing delight, specially delighting, inspiring faith, satisfying, and making joyful. 'Brahmins' refers to the sixteen Pārāyana Brahmins. 'Muni' refers to wisdom... because he has transcended the entanglement and bond of defilements, he is called a Sage (Muni). Referring to that matter, it is said: 'The Buddha answered the questions asked by them as they truly are. By answering the questions, the Sage delighted the Brahmins.'

'The Buddha, the Visionary, the kinsman of the Sun, delighted them. They practiced the holy life in the presence of the Buddha, who possesses supreme wisdom.' In 'delighted those who have the five eyes', 'those' refers to the sixteen Pārāyana Brahmins. 'Delighted' means being delighted, specially delighted, inspired with faith, satisfied, and made joyful. 'The Visionary' (Cakkhumā) is because the Blessed One is endowed with five eyes: the fleshly eye (maṃsa-cakkhu), the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), the eye of wisdom (paññā-cakkhu), the Buddha-eye (buddha-cakkhu), and the all-seeing eye (samanta-cakkhu). The Blessed One has vision through the fleshly eye... and thus he has vision through the all-seeing eye. In 'The Buddha, kinsman of the Sun', 'Buddha' is the name designated by the Blessed One himself through realization. In 'kinsman of the Sun', the sun is called 'Ādicca'. Just as the sun is of the Gotama lineage, the Blessed One is also of the Gotama lineage. Because the Blessed One is a relative of the sun by lineage, he is called 'Kinsman of the Sun' (Ādiccabandhu).
200:
In the phrase "brahmacariyamacariṃsu," brahmacariya (the holy life) means the special abstinence, refraining, further refraining, avoidance, non-doing, the state of not doing, non-transgression by mind, not overstepping the bounds of the Dhamma of the virtuous, and the destruction [of defilements] by the Path from the attainment of the ignoble practice (sexual intercourse). Alternatively, in a direct sense, the Noble Eightfold Path is called brahmacariya. These are: Right View, Right Intention, Right Speech, Right Action, Right Livelihood, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, and Right Concentration. "Brahmacariyamacariṃsu" means they lived the holy life, they lived it repeatedly, they undertook and practiced it in various ways.

"Varapaññassa santike" means in the presence of the one of excellent wisdom, supreme wisdom, best wisdom, distinguished wisdom, foremost wisdom, highest wisdom, noble wisdom (the Buddha). "Santike" means near, in the vicinity, close by, not far, in the suitable proximity. Therefore, the Elders who recited the council said: 

"Satisfied by the Visionary, the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun, they lived the holy life in the presence of the one of excellent wisdom."

If one should practice each and every question as taught by the Buddha, one would go to the further shore from the hither shore.

"Ekamekassa pañhassa" means each and every question of Ajita, each and every question of Tissa Metteyya... (and so on) each and every question of Piṅgiya.

In the phrase "yathā buddhena desitaṃ," "Buddha" means the Blessed One who is self-enlightened... (and so on) the name "Buddha" is a designation based on realization. "Yathā buddhena desitaṃ" means as pointed out, taught, made known, established, opened up, analyzed, made plain, and proclaimed by the Buddha.

"Tathā yo paṭipajjeya" means one should practice the right practice, the practice in accordance [with the Dhamma], the non-hostile practice, the practice following the goal, the practice of the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma.

In the phrase "gacche pāraṃ apārato," "pāra" (the further shore) means the deathless Nibbāna... (and so on) cessation, Nibbāna. "Apāra" (the hither shore) means the defilements, the aggregates, and the volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra). One would go to the further shore...
201:
"Apārato" means from the non-shore (hither shore) one should go to the further shore, one should reach the further shore, one should touch the further shore, one should realize the further shore; for this reason, it is said "one would go to the further shore from the hither shore." Therefore, it is said:

"If one should practice each and every question as taught by the Buddha, one would go to the further shore from the hither shore."

One would go from the hither shore to the further shore, developing the supreme path; that path is for going to the further shore, therefore it is called "Pārāyana."

In the phrase "from the hither shore to the further shore," the defilements, the aggregates, and the volitional formations are called "the hither shore (apāra)." The deathless Nibbāna... (pe)... the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna is called "the further shore (pāra)." "One would go from the hither shore to the further shore" means one would go from the hither shore to the further shore, reach the further shore, touch the further shore, and realize the further shore.

In the phrase "developing the supreme path," the Noble Eightfold Path is called the "supreme path." What is that path? It is: Right View... (pe)... Right Concentration. "Supreme path" means the path that is noble, excellent, distinguished, foremost, highest, and supreme. "Developing" means cultivating, associating with, and practicing frequently.

In the phrase "that path is for going to the further shore":
The path is the way, the track, the road, the path, the path, the path, the boat, the bridge for crossing, the raft, the raft, the bridge.
"For going to the further shore" means for going to Nibbāna, for reaching Nibbāna, for attaining Nibbāna in due order, for crossing over old age and death.

In the phrase "therefore it is called 'Pārāyana'," "therefore" means for that reason, because of that, due to that, on account of that, by that cause. The deathless Nibbāna... (pe)... cessation, Nibbāna is called "the further shore (pāra)." The path is called "the way (ayana)." "Iti" is a particle for connecting words... (pe)... the sequence of words. Therefore, it is said "therefore it is called 'Pārāyana'." Therefore, it is said:

"One would go from the hither shore to the further shore, developing the supreme path; that path is for going to the further shore, therefore it is called 'Pārāyana'."

## 17. Exposition of the Verses in Praise of the Pārāyana.
202:
## 18. Pārāyanānugītigāthāniddesa

The Venerable Piṅgiya said this:
"I will chant the Way to the Beyond (Pārāyana) just as the Blessed One saw it and just as he declared it. Why would the Blessed One—who is stainless, of vast wisdom like the earth, free from sensual desire, without the forest of defilements, and known as the Nāga—speak a lie? I will continuously chant (proclaim) that Pārāyana."

"Pārāyanamanugāyissaṃ" means I will continuously chant the practice chanted by the Blessed One, I will continuously speak the practice spoken, I will continuously recite the practice recited, I will continuously utter the practice uttered, and I will continuously teach the practice taught—thus, "Pārāyanamanugāyissaṃ."

In the phrase "iccāyasmā piṅgiyo," "iccā" is a conjunction of words... it follows the sequence of words—thus, "iccā." "Āyasmā" is a term of endearment, a term of respect, and a designation conveying reverence and deference—thus, "āyasmā." "Piṅgiyo" is the name of that Elder, his designation, appellation, common usage, name-giving, name, speaking, making, and utterance—thus, "iccāyasmā piṅgiyo."

"Yathādakkhi tathākkhāsi" means just as he saw, so he taught, informed, showed, prescribed, established, revealed, analyzed, clarified, and manifested. Just as he saw that "all formations are impermanent," so he taught, informed, showed, prescribed, established, revealed, analyzed, clarified, and manifested. "All formations are suffering"... "All phenomena are non-self"... "Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease"—just as he saw, so he taught, informed, showed, prescribed, established, revealed, analyzed, clarified, and manifested—thus, "yathādakkhi tathākkhāsi."

In the phrase "vimalo bhūrimedhaso," "vimalo" means lust is a stain, hatred is a stain, delusion is a stain, anger... resentment... all unwholesome volitional formations are stains. Those stains have been abandoned by the Buddha, the Blessed One, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, and are of a nature not to arise again in the future. The Buddha is without stain, stainless, pure, departed from stains, rid of stains, released from stains, and has transcended all stains. "Bhūri" refers to the earth. The Blessed One is endowed with wisdom that is vast and expansive like the earth. "Medhā" refers to wisdom. That wisdom which is discernment... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view. The Blessed One is endowed with this wisdom called medhā.
203:
The Blessed One is endowed with wisdom, has approached it, has well approached it, is not without it, and has attained full endowment. Therefore, the Buddha is called "Sumedhasa" (one of good wisdom)—thus, "vimalo bhūrimedhaso."

Regarding "nikkāmo nibbano nāgo": Sensual desires (kāma), in brief, are of two kinds—objective sensuality (vatthukāma) and subjective sensuality (kilesakāma)... (Pe)... These are called objective sensuality... (Pe)... These are called subjective sensuality. The Blessed One has fully understood objective sensuality and has abandoned subjective sensuality. Because of his full understanding of objective sensuality and his abandonment of subjective sensuality, the Blessed One does not desire, long for, cherish, or speak with longing for sensual pleasures. Those who desire, long for, crave, cherish, and speak of sensual pleasures are called seekers of sensuality, those possessed of lust, and those possessed of perception. The Blessed One does not delight in, desire, long for, cherish, or speak of sensuality. Therefore, the Buddha is called "Nikkāma," being free from desire. He is one who has relinquished, vomited, been freed from, abandoned, and forever renounced desire. Because he is free from lust, is cooled, has attained peace, experiences happiness, and dwells with a self that has become sublime, he is called "Nikkāma."

"Nibbano" means lust is a forest (vana), hatred is a forest, delusion is a forest, anger is a forest, resentment is a forest... all unwholesome volitional formations are forests. Those forests have been abandoned by the Buddha, the Blessed One, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, and are of a nature not to arise again in the future. Therefore, the Buddha is called "Nibbana," being free from those forests, having emerged from them. "Nāgo" means the Blessed One is called "Nāga" because he does not commit (na karoti) evil (āguṃ). He is called "Nāga" because he does not go to where one should not go, and because he does not come from where one should not come. (Pe). Thus, because the Blessed One does not come (to rebirth), he is called "Nāga." This is the meaning of the phrase "nikkāmo nibbano nāgo."

"Kissa hetu musā bhaṇe" means for what reason, for what cause, on what account, or due to what condition would he speak a lie? "Musā bhaṇe" means he would speak, show, or utter a false word, a lie, an untruth, or a word not spoken by the Noble Ones. In this world, some person, having gone to an assembly, a gathering, among relatives, among a group, or into the royal court, is brought forth and questioned as a witness: "Come, good man, tell what you know." That person, not knowing, says (thus):
204:
Speaking 'I know' while knowing, speaking 'I do not know' while not knowing, speaking 'I see' while not seeing, and speaking 'I do not see' while seeing; thus, for one's own sake, for the sake of another, or for the sake of some small material gain, deliberately speaking what is not true is called lying (mosavajja).

Furthermore, false speech occurs through three factors. Before speaking, the thought 'I will speak a lie' arises; while speaking, the knowledge 'I am speaking a lie' arises; after speaking, the knowledge 'I have spoken a lie' arises. Through these three factors, false speech occurs. Furthermore, false speech occurs through four factors. Before speaking, the thought 'I will speak a lie' arises; while speaking, the knowledge 'I am speaking a lie' arises; after speaking, the knowledge 'I have spoken a lie' arises; and by concealing one's view (diṭṭhi). Through these four factors, false speech occurs. Furthermore, false speech occurs through five... six... seven... eight factors. Before speaking, the thought 'I will speak a lie' arises; while speaking, the knowledge 'I am speaking a lie' arises; after speaking, the knowledge 'I have spoken a lie' arises; and by concealing one's view (diṭṭhi), concealing one's preference (khanti), concealing one's liking (ruci), concealing one's perception (saññā), and concealing one's intention (bhāva). Through these eight factors, false speech (mosavajja) occurs. For what reason would he speak, preach, show, or declare a lie? This means 'For what reason would he speak a lie?' Therefore, the Elder Piṅgiya said this:

'I will chant the Pārāyana,
As he saw it, so he declared it, the Stainless One of vast wisdom;
Free from desire, without craving, the Naga; for what reason would he speak a lie?'

Now I shall praise the words endowed with the virtues of the Buddha, who has abandoned stains and delusion, and has abandoned conceit and disparagement (makkha).

'Pahīnamalamohassa' means: Stains (mala) are—lust is a stain, hatred is a stain, delusion is a stain, conceit is a stain, views are a stain, defilements are a stain, all misconduct is a stain, and all kamma leading to rebirth is a stain.

Delusion (moha) means ignorance regarding the truth of suffering ... (and so on) ... it refers to the bolt of ignorance, bewilderment, and the root of unwholesomeness called delusion. This is called delusion. These stains and delusion have been abandoned by the Blessed Buddha, cut at the root, made like a palm stump, and made non-existent.
205:
They are of the nature to not arise again in the future. Therefore, the Buddha has abandoned stains and delusion; this is the meaning of the term 'pahīnamalamohassa'.

In the term 'mānamakkhappahāyino', conceit (māna) is, in one way, the elevation of the mind. In two ways, conceit is the conceit of self-exaltation and the conceit of disparaging others. In three ways, conceit is the pride 'I am better', 'I am equal', and 'I am inferior'. In four ways, conceit is generated because of gain, because of fame, because of praise, and because of happiness. In five ways, conceit is generated because of obtaining pleasant sights, pleasant sounds, smells, tastes, and touches. In six ways, conceit is generated because of the perfection of the eye, the perfection of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. In seven ways, conceit is māna (conceit), atimāna (superiority conceit), mānātimāna (excessive conceit), omāna (inferiority conceit), avamāna (depreciation conceit), asmimāna (the 'I am' conceit), and micchāmāna (wrong conceit). In eight ways, conceit is generated because of gain, inferiority is generated because of loss, conceit is generated because of fame, inferiority is generated because of lack of fame, conceit is generated because of praise, inferiority is generated because of blame, conceit is generated because of happiness, and inferiority is generated because of suffering. In nine ways, conceit is: towards one superior, 'I am better', 'I am equal', 'I am inferior'; towards one equal, 'I am better', 'I am equal', 'I am inferior'; towards one inferior, 'I am better', 'I am equal', 'I am inferior'. In ten ways, conceit is: here, someone generates conceit because of birth, lineage, being a son of a good family, beauty, wealth, study, work, craft, science, learning, intelligence, or any other ground. Such conceit, thinking, the state of thinking, elevation, haughtiness, banner-like pride, grasping, and the mind's desire for a banner—this is called conceit.

Disparagement (makkha) is the smearing of others' virtues, the act of smearing, the state of smearing, harshness, and harsh actions; this is called disparagement. Conceit and disparagement have been abandoned by the Blessed Buddha, cut at the root, made like a palm stump, and made non-existent.
206: With roots cut off, made like a palm-stump, reached the state of non-existence, they are of a nature not to arise in the future. Therefore, the Buddha is one who has abandoned pride and hypocrisy—one who has abandoned pride and hypocrisy. The word "Handāhaṃ" is a term characterized by the conjunction of words, the blending of words, the completion of words, the harmony of syllables, the smoothness of consonants, and the sequence of words—"Handāhaṃ". "I shall praise with words endowed with qualities" (kittayissāmi giraṃ vaṇṇūpasaṃhitaṃ) means I shall praise, preach, designate, establish, open, analyze, clarify, and manifest the speech, words, utterance, and proclamation that are endowed with, fully endowed with, approached by, fully approached by, not separate from, associated with, and have reached fulfillment in qualities—"Now I shall praise with words endowed with qualities." Therefore, the Elder Piṅgiya said: "Of the one who has abandoned the stain of delusion, who has abandoned pride and hypocrisy, now I shall praise with words endowed with qualities." The Buddha, the dispeller of darkness, the all-seeing eye, the one who has gone to the end of the world, who has transcended all existences, free from taints, who has abandoned all suffering, whose name is Truth—O Brahmin, he has been attended by me. "Tamonudo" (Dispeller of darkness) means he has dispelled, driven away, abandoned, dispelled, eliminated, brought to non-existence, and caused to never arise again the darkness of lust, the darkness of hatred, the darkness of delusion, the darkness of pride, the darkness of views, the darkness of defilements, and the darkness of misconduct, which cause blindness, cause ignorance, obstruct wisdom, belong to the side of distress, and do not lead to Nibbāna. "Buddho" is the realized designation and name of that Blessed One... "Samantacakkhu" (All-seeing eye) refers to the knowledge of omniscience... thus the Tathāgata is the all-seeing eye—the Buddha, the dispeller of darkness, the all-seeing eye. In the phrase "The one who has gone to the end of the world, who has transcended all existences," "world" (loka) as one world is the world of existence (the round of rebirth in the three planes). As two worlds, it is the world of existence (rebirth) and the world of origin (kamma); or the world of existence in a happy state and the world of origin in a happy state; or the world of existence in a miserable state and the world of origin in a miserable state. Three worlds are the three feelings. Four worlds are the four nutriments. Five worlds are the five aggregates of clinging. Six worlds are the six internal bases. Seven worlds...
207: ...are the seven stations of consciousness. Eight worlds are the eight worldly conditions. Nine worlds are the nine abodes of beings. Ten worlds are the ten (coarse) bases. Twelve worlds are the twelve bases. Eighteen worlds are the eighteen elements. "Lokantagū" (Gone to the end of the world) means the Blessed One has gone to the end of the world, reached the end, gone to the peak, reached the peak... gone to Nibbāna, reached Nibbāna. He has lived the life, fulfilled the conduct... for him, the round of birth and death does not exist, there is no renewed existence (punabbhava)—thus, he is the one who has gone to the end of the world. "Sabbabhavātivatto" (Transcended all existences) means: there are two kinds of existence—kamma-existence (kamma-bhava) and renewed existence through rebirth (upapatti-bhava). What is kamma-existence? Meritorious formations, non-meritorious formations, and imperturbable formations—these are kamma-existence. What is renewed existence through rebirth? The matter, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness that arise through rebirth—these are renewed existence through rebirth. The Blessed One has especially surpassed and transcended both kamma-existence and renewed existence through rebirth. Therefore, he is the one who has gone to the end of the world and transcended all existences. "Anāsavo sabbadukkhappahīno" (Free from taints, one who has abandoned all suffering) means: "Anāsavo" refers to the four taints—the taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, the taint of views, and the taint of ignorance. These taints have been abandoned by the Buddha, the Blessed One, with roots cut off, made like a palm-stump, brought to non-existence, and are of a nature not to arise in the future. Therefore, the Buddha is free from taints. "One who has abandoned all suffering" means that for the Blessed One, all suffering of birth, suffering of aging, suffering of sickness, suffering of death, suffering of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair... the suffering of the ruin of views, associated with rebirth, has been abandoned, completely cut off, calmed, stilled, made incapable of arising, and burned by the fire of knowledge. Therefore, the Buddha is "one who has abandoned all suffering"—free from taints, one who has abandoned all suffering. "Saccavhyayo brahme upāsito me" (O Brahmin, the one whose name is Truth has been attended by me) means: "Saccavhyayo" is having a name that is consistent with the truth (the name "Buddha"). The Blessed Vipassī, the Blessed Sikhī, the Blessed Vessabhū, the Blessed Kakusandha, the Blessed Koṇāgamana, and the Blessed Kassapa—these Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have similar names and similar titles. The Blessed Sakyamuni also has a name and title similar to those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones—therefore, the Buddha is "Saccavhyaya". "Brahme upāsito me" means that Blessed One has been served by me, attended by me, repeatedly attended by me, questioned by me, and repeatedly cross-examined by me. Therefore, the Elder Piṅgiya said: Just as a bird leaves a tree with little fruit and resorts to a tree full of flowers and fruit, even so, I now fly like a swan to the one who is like the ocean, leaving those of limited vision. A bird leaves a tree with little fruit and resorts to a tree with much fruit; even so, I leave those of limited vision and attend to the one of great wisdom. In this verse, a bird is called "dija".
208:
“The Buddha, who dispels the darkness, who possesses the Samantacakkhu (the all-seeing eye of wisdom), who has reached the end of the world, who has transcended all states of existence, who is free from taints (āsavas), who has abandoned all suffering, and who is named Truth—I have come to attend upon Him,” (so said the Elder Piṅgiya).

Just as a bird, leaving a small forest with little fruit, would resort to a large forest with much fruit; even so, I, leaving those of limited vision, have arrived (at the Buddha), just as a king of swans reaches the great ocean.

In the phrase “Just as a bird, leaving a small forest with little fruit, would resort to a large forest with much fruit”: A bird is called “dija” (twice-born). Why is a bird called “dija”? Because it is born twice: once from the mother's womb and once from the eggshell. For that reason, a bird is called “dija.” “Leaving a small forest with little fruit” means: just as a bird, having abandoned, surpassed, and transcended a small forest with little fruit, little food, and little water, would reach, find, and obtain another large forest or woodland with much fruit, much food, and much water, and would make its dwelling in that woodland. This is the meaning of the words “Just as a bird, leaving a small forest with little fruit, would resort to a large forest with much fruit.”

In the words “Even so, I, leaving those of limited vision, have arrived (at the Buddha), just as a king of swans reaches the great ocean”: “Even so” is the application of the simile. “Leaving those of limited vision” means: the Brahmin Bāvarī and his other teachers, when compared to the Blessed Buddha, are only those of limited vision, small vision, slight vision, inferior vision, low vision, or insignificant vision. Having abandoned, forsaken, surpassed, and transcended those of limited vision, I have found, reached, and obtained the Blessed Buddha, who has infinite vision, supreme vision, excellent vision, distinguished vision, foremost vision, highest vision, noble vision, who is peerless, equal to the unequaled, matchless, incomparable, the unique person, the God above gods, the bull among men, the lion among men, the elephant among men, the noble breed among men, the leader among men, the bearer of the great burden, and the possessor of the ten powers. Just as a king of swans, heading towards the great ocean...
209:
...would reach, find, and obtain a great lake, or Lake Anotatta, or the great ocean which is unshakable and has an immeasurable mass of water; even so, I have found that Teacher, the noble Conqueror, the Great Seer, who is the teacher of gods and men, who is unshakable, of immeasurable majesty, of analytical knowledge, with eyes wide open, skilled in the divisions of wisdom, who has attained the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), who has reached the four intrepidities (vesārajja), whose mind is purely inclined, whose self is pure due to the absence of latent tendencies, who is free from double-speaking, who is the same in the face of the desired and the undesired, who acknowledges things as they truly are, who has no small virtues, who has reached greatness beyond limits, who is profound, immeasurable, difficult to fathom, who possesses the jewels of faith and so on, who has vast virtues like the ocean, who is endowed with six-factored equanimity (chaḷaṅgupekkhā), who is peerless, of great abundance, of incomparable virtue and concentration, who is endowed with such qualities, who speaks the most excellent Dhamma, who is like Mount Meru among mountains, like the king of Garudas among birds, like the king of lions among beasts, and like the ocean among rivers and streams. I have very surely attended upon and found Him. Thus, I, leaving those of limited vision, have arrived (at the Buddha), just as a king of swans reaches the great ocean. Therefore, the Elder Piṅgiya said:

“Just as a bird, leaving a small tree with little fruit,
Would resort to a forest with much fruit;
Even so, I, leaving those of limited vision,
Have arrived (at the Buddha), just as a king of swans reaches the great ocean.”

Those who previously explained to me, outside the Dispensation of Gotama, saying, “It was thus, it will be thus”—all that was mere hearsay, all that only increased speculation.

“Those who previously explained to me” means the Brahmin Bāvarī and others who were his teachers; they explained, told, taught, prescribed, established, opened, analyzed, clarified, and made known their own views, their own endurance, their own preferences, their own doctrines, their own desires, and their own intentions.

“Outside the Dispensation of Gotama” means outside the Dispensation of the Lord Gotama, the Dispensation of the Buddha who first knew the Four Noble Truths, the Dispensation of the Conqueror (Jina) who conquered the five Maras, the Dispensation of the Tathāgata who came truly as it is, the Dispensation of the gods, and the Dispensation of the Arahant who is worthy of special offerings.

“It was thus, it will be thus” means “It is said to have been so, it is said it will be so.”
210:
All that talk is merely 'so it has been heard, so it has been heard.' It is by way of such things as hearsay, tradition, scriptural authority, logical reasoning, inference, reflective thought, and acceptance of a view after deliberation. It is not something known by oneself through direct realization; they do not speak of a Dhamma that is personally witnessed. Therefore, it is said: 'All that is hearsay' (Sabbaṃ taṃ itihītihaṃ).

'All that increases speculation' (Sabbaṃ taṃ takkavaḍḍhanaṃ) means all that increases thought, increases discursive thought, increases intention, increases thoughts of sensual desire, increases thoughts of ill will, increases thoughts of cruelty, increases thoughts of relatives, increases thoughts of the country, increases thoughts of immortality (unstable like the amarā fish), increases thoughts connected with sympathy for others, increases thoughts connected with gain, honor, and fame, and increases thoughts connected with not being despised by others. Therefore, it is said: 'All that increases speculation.' Thus, the Elder Piṅgiya said:

"Those who explained to me in the past, outside the teaching of Gotama,
Saying, 'It was so, it will be so,'
All that was merely hearsay, all that was just increasing speculation."

Alone, the dispeller of darkness, the radiant one, the light-maker, that Gotama of vast wisdom, Gotama of vast intelligence.

In the phrase 'Alone, the dispeller of darkness' (Eko tamonudāsīno), 'Alone' (Eko) means: The Blessed One is alone by way of his renunciation; he is alone in the sense of being without a companion; he is alone in the sense of having abandoned craving; he is alone because he is absolutely free from lust; he is alone because he is absolutely free from hatred; he is alone because he is absolutely free from delusion; he is alone because he is absolutely free from defilements; he is alone because he has gone on the one-way path (ekāyana-magga); he is alone because he alone has fully awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.

How is the Blessed One alone by way of his renunciation? The Blessed One, while still young, with black hair, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the prime of life, against the wishes of his weeping and lamenting parents, cut off all the burdens of household life, cut off the burdens of wife and children, cut off the burdens of relatives, cut off the burdens of friends and ministers, shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and went forth from the home life into homelessness. Having reached the state of having nothing, he wanders alone, dwells alone, maintains his postures, practices, protects, sustains himself, and lives. Thus, the Blessed One is alone by way of his renunciation.

How is the Blessed One alone in the sense of being without a companion? Having thus gone forth, he resorts alone to forest dwellings, remote lodgings, with little noise...
211:
(The Blessed One resorts to lodgings) with little sound, free from the wind of people, suitable for human privacy, and appropriate for seclusion. He walks alone, stands alone, sits alone, lies down alone, enters the village for alms alone, goes forward alone, returns alone, sits in private alone, undertakes the walking meditation alone, wanders alone, dwells alone, maintains his postures, practices, protects, sustains himself, and lives. Thus, the Blessed One is alone in the sense of being without a companion.

How is the Blessed One alone in the sense of having abandoned craving? While dwelling thus alone, without a companion, diligent, ardent, and resolute, at the foot of the Bodhi tree on the bank of the Nerañjarā River, exerting great effort, he defeated Māra the Evil One, the Namuci, the kinsman of the negligent, along with his army. He abandoned, dispelled, eliminated, and brought to non-existence the net of craving that spreads and clings to objects.

"A man with craving as his companion, wanders for a long time in Saṃsāra,
He does not transcend Saṃsāra, this state of being or another.
Knowing this danger, that craving is the origin of suffering,
A bhikkhu, free from craving, without grasping, mindful, should wander."

Thus, the Blessed One is alone in the sense of having abandoned craving.

How is the Blessed One alone because he is absolutely free from lust? Because lust has been abandoned, he is the unique noble one who is absolutely free from lust. Because hatred has been abandoned, he is the unique noble one who is absolutely free from hatred. Because delusion has been abandoned, he is the unique noble one who is absolutely free from delusion. Because defilements have been abandoned, he is the unique noble one who is absolutely free from defilements.

How is the Blessed One alone because he has reached the one-way noble path? The one-way noble path refers to the four foundations of mindfulness... [and so on]... the Noble Eightfold Path.
212:
The Blessed One, who constantly cares for welfare and sees the end of birth (Nibbāna), knows the one-way path (leading to Nibbāna). In the past, they crossed the flood by this path; those who will cross and those who are crossing now [also do so].

Thus, the Blessed One is called 'Eka' (The One) because he has reached the one-way path.

How is it that the Blessed One alone has fully realized the unsurpassed supreme enlightenment? Knowledge, wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor, examination, insight, and right view occurring in the four paths are called 'Bodhi' (Enlightenment). With that enlightenment-knowledge, the Blessed One realized: 'All formations are impermanent'; he realized: 'All formations are suffering'; he realized: 'All phenomena are non-self'... he realized: 'Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease.' Alternatively, whatever should be known, should be understood, should be fully known, should be perfectly known, should be attained, should be touched, and should be realized—all that he knew, understood, fully knew, perfectly knew, attained, touched, and realized with that enlightenment-knowledge. Thus, the Blessed One is called 'Eka' because he alone has fully realized the unsurpassed supreme enlightenment.

'Tamonuda' (Dispeller of darkness) means the Blessed One dispelled, drove away, abandoned, dispelled, removed, and brought to non-existence the darkness of lust, the darkness of hatred, the darkness of delusion, the darkness of views, the darkness of defilements, and the darkness of misconduct—which cause blindness, lack of vision, and ignorance, which cease wisdom, which are on the side of distress, and which do not lead to Nibbāna. 'Āsīna' (Seated) means the Blessed One was seated at the Pāsāṇaka Shrine, contemplating the welfare of beings.

The disciples with the three knowledges, who have abandoned death, attend upon the Sage, the Buddha, who is seated by the side of the mountain and has reached the far shore of suffering.

In this way also, the Blessed One is called 'Āsīna'... Alternatively, the Blessed One is called 'Āsīna' because all anxieties of defilements have been stilled. That Blessed One has lived the holy life, has completed the practice... the round of birth and death and further rebirth no longer exist for him. In this way also, the Blessed One is called 'Āsīna'; thus he is called 'Eko tamonudāsīno' (The One, the dispeller of darkness, the seated one).

'Jutimā so pabhaṅkaro' means: 'Jutimā' is one who is radiant, wise, learned, endowed with wisdom, intelligent, knowledgeable, discerning, and sagacious. 'Pabhaṅkaro' is one who makes radiance, makes light, makes brilliance, makes a lamp, makes a manifest lamp, especially makes brilliance, and makes manifest light. This is the meaning of 'Jutimā so pabhaṅkaro'.
213:
## Gotamo Bhūripaññāṇo
The Blessed One Gotama possesses wisdom as vast as the earth. He is very famous for his knowledge. He has wisdom as his banner. He has wisdom as his pinnacle. He has mastery over wisdom. He frequently investigates the Dhamma. He frequently and specifically investigates the Four Noble Truths. He sees without leaving even an atom. He has the nature of seeing with balance. He has a manifest dwelling. He constantly practices that very wisdom. He frequently develops that very wisdom. He honors that very wisdom. He inclines towards that wisdom. He leans towards that wisdom. He slides towards that wisdom. He dwells having entered into that wisdom. He makes that wisdom his authority.

A banner is the sign of a chariot;
Smoke is the sign of fire;
A king is the sign of a country;
A husband is the sign of a woman.

In the same way, the Blessed One Gotama possesses much wisdom like the earth. He is very famous for his knowledge. He has wisdom as his banner. He has wisdom as his pinnacle. He has mastery over wisdom. He frequently investigates the Dhamma. He frequently and specifically investigates the Four Noble Truths. He sees without leaving even an atom. He has the nature of comparing and seeing with balance. He has a manifest dwelling. He constantly practices that very wisdom. He frequently develops that very wisdom. He honors that very wisdom. He inclines towards that wisdom. He leans towards that wisdom. He slides towards that wisdom. He dwells having entered into that wisdom. He makes that wisdom his authority. This is the meaning of the term 'Gotamo Bhūripaññāṇo'.

In the term 'Gotamo Bhūrimedhaso', 'Bhūri' refers to the earth. The Blessed One is endowed with wisdom as vast and wide as the earth. 'Medhā' refers to wisdom. It is the wisdom of knowing in various ways, knowing by aspects, the absence of delusion, the investigation of the Dhamma, and Right View which sees well. The Blessed One is endowed with this wisdom. He is perfectly endowed with it. He is established in it. He is well-established in it. He is not without it. He is associated with it. He has reached fulfillment in it. Therefore, the Blessed One is called 'Sumedhasa' (The Wise One). This is the meaning of the term 'Gotamo Bhūrimedhaso'. Therefore, the Elder Piṅgiya said:

"Alone, dispelling the darkness of defilements, the seated one,
The radiant one, the light-maker,
The Blessed One Gotama of vast wisdom,
The Blessed One Gotama of vast intelligence."

The Blessed One taught me the Dhamma, which is visible here and now, timeless, the destruction of craving, free from calamity, and to which there is no comparison anywhere.

In the phrase 'Yo me dhammaṃ adesi', 'Yo' refers to that Blessed One who is self-become (Sayam-bhū). Without a teacher, he himself fully realized the Four Noble Truths among the teachings not heard before. In those Four Noble Truths, he reached omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) and attained mastery over the powers (Bala). In the phrase 'dhammaṃ adesi', 'Dhamma' refers to the holy life that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, complete in meaning and phrasing, entirely perfect and pure; starting from the four foundations of mindfulness... up to the Noble Eightfold Path, Nibbāna, and the practice leading to Nibbāna, which he pointed out, taught, and prescribed...
214:
The Blessed One who taught me the Dhamma, opened it, analyzed it, made it clear, and proclaimed it.

"Sandiṭṭhika-akālika" means: the Dhamma that is visible here and now, to be seen by oneself, immediate in its results, inviting one to come and see, worthy of being applied to oneself, and to be personally realized by the wise. Thus it is called "sandiṭṭhika". Alternatively, when a person develops the Noble Eightfold Path in this very life, they attain, experience, and realize the fruit immediately following that path. In this way also, it is called "sandiṭṭhika". "Akālika" means: unlike worldly wealth which people give and do not receive the results immediately but must wait for time, this Dhamma is not like that. When a person develops the Noble Eightfold Path in this very life, they attain, experience, and realize the fruit immediately following that path; it is not received in another existence or in the next world. Thus it is called "akālika". This is "sandiṭṭhika-akālika".

"Taṇhakkhaya-anītika" means: craving (taṇhā) refers to craving for forms and so on, up to craving for mental objects. "Taṇhakkhaya" is the destruction of craving, the destruction of greed, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion, the destruction of destinations, the destruction of arising, the destruction of rebirth, the destruction of existence, the destruction of saṃsāra, and the destruction of the round of suffering. "Anītika" means: defilements, aggregates, and volitional formations are called "īti" (afflictions/dangers). Nibbāna, the deathless, which is the abandoning of those afflictions, the stilling of those afflictions, the relinquishing of those afflictions, and the complete tranquilizing of those afflictions, is called "taṇhakkhaya-anītika".

"Yassa natthi upamā kvaci" means: for that Nibbāna, there is no comparison, no likeness, no counterpart; it does not exist, is not manifest, and is not obtainable. "Kvaci" means it does not exist anywhere—whether internally, externally, or both internally and externally. Therefore, the Elder Piṅgiya said:

"He who taught me the Dhamma, visible here and now, immediate,
The destruction of craving, free from affliction, for which there is no comparison anywhere."

O Piṅgiya, why do you stay away even for a moment from that Gotama of vast wisdom, from that Gotama of great intelligence?

"Kiṃ nu tamhā vippavasi" means: why do you stay away, depart, or remain separate from the Buddha? "Muhuttamapi Piṅgiya" means: even for a moment, even for a split second, even for a brief instant, even for a short duration. The teacher Bāvarī addresses his nephew Piṅgiya by name.
216:
This Dhamma does not wait for time. Whoever develops the Noble Eightfold Path in this very life, for that person, the attainment of the fruit (phala) occurs immediately after the path (magga); they reach the fruit, they obtain it. It is not in another existence, nor in the world beyond; thus, in this very life, it gives results without delay. This is the meaning of the terms 'sandiṭṭhika' and 'akālika'.

In the term 'taṇhakkhaya-anītikaṃ'—'taṇhā' refers to craving for forms... up to craving for mental objects. 'Taṇhakkhaya' refers to Nibbāna, which is the destruction of craving, the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion, the destruction of destiny (gati), the destruction of rebirth, the destruction of conception, the destruction of existence, the destruction of saṃsāra, and the destruction of the round of suffering. In the term 'anītika'—defilements, the aggregates, and the three types of volitional formations are called 'īti' (calamities/afflictions). The deathless Nibbāna, which is the abandoning of those calamities, the subsiding of those calamities, the relinquishing of those calamities, and the tranquilizing of those calamities, is called 'taṇhakkhaya-anītika'.

In the phrase 'yassa natthi upamā kvaci'—'yassa' refers to Nibbāna. 'Natthi upamā' means there is no comparison, no basis for comparison, no similar thing, no counterpart; it simply does not exist, is not found, and cannot be obtained. 'Kvaci' means it does not exist anywhere—whether internally, externally, or both internally and externally. Therefore, that Brahmin Bāvarī said:

"That Blessed One has taught you the Dhamma that is visible here and now, timeless, the destruction of craving, free from calamity, and for which there is no comparison anywhere."

"Brahmin, I do not stay away even for a moment from that Gotama of vast wisdom, from that Gotama of broad intelligence."

'Nāhaṃ tamhā vippavasāmi' means I do not stay away from the Blessed One, I do not leave, I do not depart, I am not without Him.

'Muhuttamapi brāhmaṇa' means not staying away even for a moment, for a laya, for a vaya, or for a brief instant. 'Brāhmaṇa' is an address to his uncle out of respect.

'Gotamā bhūripaññāṇā' refers to the Buddha of the Gotama lineage, who possesses wisdom as vast as the earth, who has the mark of knowledge, the banner of wisdom, the established standard of wisdom, the sovereignty of wisdom; who is abundant in investigation, abundant in thorough investigation, abundant in scrutiny, whose nature is thorough scrutiny, who dwells in clarity, who practices based on that wisdom, who abounds in it, who honors it, who leans towards it, who inclines towards it, who tends towards it, who enters into it, and who makes that wisdom supreme.

In the term 'Gotamā bhūrimedhasā'—'bhūri' refers to the earth. The Blessed One is endowed with wisdom that is vast and wide like the earth. 'Medhā' refers to wisdom. That wisdom which is understanding... up to... non-delusion, investigation of states, and right view. The Blessed One is endowed with, fully endowed with, possessed of, fully possessed of, attained to, and fully attained to this medhā-wisdom. Therefore, the Buddha is of excellent wisdom (sumedhasa). Thus, the Elder Piṅgiya said:
217:
“Brahmin, I do not stay away even for a moment from that Gotama of vast wisdom, from that Gotama of broad intelligence.

That Blessed One has taught me the Dhamma that is visible here and now, timeless, the destruction of craving, free from the calamity of defilements, and for which there is no comparison anywhere.”

In the phrase “Who taught the Dhamma to me,” “Yo” refers to that Blessed One who is self-awakened (sayambhū), without a teacher, and who personally realized the Four Noble Truths among things unheard of before. Therein, He attained omniscience (sabbaññutā) and mastery over the powers (balas). “He taught the Dhamma” means: He declared, taught, described, established, opened, analyzed, made clear, and manifested the holy life (brahmacariya) that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, entirely complete and pure; as well as the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the Noble Eightfold Path, Nibbāna, and the practice leading to Nibbāna. This is the meaning of the phrase “Who taught the Dhamma to me.”

“Visible here and now, and timeless” means: It is called the Dhamma visible here and now because it is endowed with the qualities of being visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see (ehipassika), leading onwards (opanayika), and to be personally realized by the wise (paccattaṃ veditabbo viññūhi). Alternatively, whoever develops the Noble Eightfold Path in this very life, for that person, the attainment of the fruit occurs immediately after the path; they reach it, they obtain it. In this way too, it is called the Dhamma visible here and now. “Timeless” means: Unlike people who, after giving wealth that is subject to time, do not receive the benefit immediately but must wait for time, this Dhamma is not like that. Whoever develops the Noble Eightfold Path in this very life, for that person, the attainment of the fruit occurs immediately after the path; they reach it, they obtain it, not in another existence or another world. Thus, it is called the timeless Dhamma. This is the meaning of the phrase “visible here and now, and timeless.”

In the phrase “the destruction of craving, free from calamity,” craving refers to craving for forms and so on, up to craving for mental objects. “Destruction of craving” refers to Nibbāna, which is the destruction of craving, the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion, the destruction of destiny, the destruction of rebirth (upapatti), the destruction of conception, the destruction of existence, the destruction of saṃsāra, and the destruction of the round of suffering. In the phrase “free from calamity,” defilements, aggregates, and volitional formations are called “īti” (calamities/thorns). The deathless Nibbāna, which is the abandoning, the tranquilizing, and the further tranquilizing of those “īti,” is called “free from calamity.” This is the meaning of the phrase “the destruction of craving, free from calamity.”

In the phrase “for which there is no comparison anywhere,” “yassa” refers to Nibbāna. “No comparison” means there is no comparison, no basis for comparison, no similar thing, no counterpart; it simply does not exist and is not found. “Anywhere” means it does not exist in any place—whether internally, externally, or both internally and externally. This is the meaning of the phrase “for which there is no comparison anywhere.” Therefore, the Elder Piṅgiya said:
218:
"The Blessed One has taught me the Dhamma which is visible here and now, immediate in its results, the destruction of craving, free from danger, and for which there is no comparison anywhere."

Being diligent, I see Him with my mind as if with my eyes, day and night, O Brahmin. I spend the night in worship; because of that constant mindfulness, I do not consider myself to be dwelling apart from the Blessed One.

'I see Him with my mind as if with my eyes' means that just as a man with sight would see, perceive, look at, contemplate, and examine forms in the light, in the same way, I see, perceive, look at, contemplate, and examine the Blessed Buddha with my mind.

'O Brahmin, day and night, being diligent' means being diligent while developing the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānussati) in the mind both day and night.

In the phrase 'I spend the night in worship,' worship means spending and passing the time day and night while performing acts of worship, respect, honor, veneration, and homage through body, speech, mind, practice in accordance with the benefit, or practice in accordance with the Dhamma.

'Because of that, I do not consider myself to be dwelling apart' means that because of developing that recollection of the Buddha, I consider myself as not being apart from the Blessed One; I know it as not dwelling apart.
