Furthermore, some venerable recluses and brahmins, having eaten the food given in faith, remain devoted to watching spectacles which are like thorns to the Dispensation (visūkadassana), such as: dancing, singing, music, theatrical shows, storytelling, hand-clapping, cymbals, kettle-drums, artful displays, acrobatic shows, flute playing, bone-washing ceremonies, elephant fights, horse fights, buffalo fights, bull fights, goat fights, ram fights, cock fights, quail fights, stick-fighting, boxing, wrestling, sham-fights, roll-calls, battle-arrays, and seeing troops. He is devoted to such spectacles which are thorns to the Dispensation. In this way too, one is of distracted eyes.

How is one of "eyes cast down" (okkhittacakkhu)? Here, a certain monk is not frivolous of eye and is not possessed of eye-frivolity. He is not devoted to wandering long distances and aimlessly from fruit orchard to flower garden, garden to garden, village to village, town to town, city to city, country to country, and province to province for the sake of seeing forms, thinking he must see what has not been seen or move past what has been seen. In this way, one is of eyes cast down.

Alternatively, when a monk has entered the village and is walking on the street, he walks with restraint. He walks without looking at elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, boys, girls, women, men, shops, house doors, without looking up, without looking down, and without looking about in all directions. In this way too, one is of eyes cast down.

Alternatively, a monk, having seen a form with the eye, does not grasp at its signs or features. Since evil unwholesome states of covetousness and grief might flow in upon him if he dwells with the eye-faculty unrestrained, he practices for its restraint, he guards the eye-faculty, and he achieves restraint over the eye-faculty. In this way too, one is of eyes cast down.
286:
Furthermore, some recluses and brahmins, having consumed food offered out of faith, remain addicted to watching such spectacles which are like thorns and obstacles to the Dispensation, such as dancing, singing, music... [and so on]... and military arrays. He refrains from such spectacles which are like thorns and obstacles to the Dispensation. In this way, he is one with downcast eyes.

"And not foot-loose"—how is one foot-loose? Here, a certain monk is foot-loose, possessed of foot-looseness: he is addicted to long wandering, to unsettled wandering, from monastery to monastery, from park to park, from village to village, from town to town, from city to city, from country to country, from district to district. In this way, he is foot-loose.

Alternatively, a monk is foot-loose within the Saṅghārāma (monastic residence). Not for any purpose, not for any reason, but with a restless and unpeaceful mind, he goes from precinct to precinct, from dwelling to dwelling, from lean-to to lean-to, from mansion to mansion, from flat-roofed house to flat-roofed house, from cave to cave, from grotto to grotto, from hut to hut, from peaked house to peaked house, from watchtower to watchtower, from hall to hall, from wood-shed to wood-shed, from assembly hall to assembly hall, from pavilion to pavilion, from the foot of one tree to the foot of another. Or, where monks are sitting or walking, if there is one, he becomes the second; if there are two, he becomes the third; if there are three, he becomes the fourth. There, he indulges in much idle chatter, such as talk about kings, thieves... [and so on]... talk about existence and non-existence. In this way, he is foot-loose.

"And not foot-loose" means that the Paccekabuddha is far removed from foot-looseness, he refrains from it, he is completely abstinent, he has departed from it, he has relinquished it, he is liberated, he is detached, and with a mind made boundless, he delights in solitude, finds joy in solitude, is devoted to internal tranquility of mind, does not neglect meditation, is endowed with insight, cultivates empty places, is a meditator, delights in meditation, is devoted to singleness of mind, and regards his own welfare as paramount. Thus, he is one with downcast eyes and is not foot-loose.
287:
One with guarded senses and a protected mind—'One with guarded senses' means that the Paccekabuddha, having seen a form with the eye, does not grasp at its signs (such as male or female) nor its details (such as hands or feet). Since evil, unwholesome states of covetousness and grief might follow and overwhelm one who dwells with the eye-faculty unguarded, he practices for its restraint, he protects the eye-faculty, and he achieves restraint over the eye-faculty. Having heard a sound with the ear... smelled an odor with the nose... tasted a flavor with the tongue... felt a tangible object with the body... cognized a mental object with the mind, he does not grasp at its signs nor its details. Since evil, unwholesome states of covetousness and grief might follow and overwhelm this person who dwells with the mind-faculty unguarded, he practices for the restraint of that mind-faculty, he protects the mind-faculty, and he achieves restraint over the mind-faculty. Thus, he is called 'guttindriyo' (one with guarded senses). 'Rakkhitamānasāno' means one with a well-protected mind. Thus, he is 'guttindriyo rakkhitamānasāno' (one with guarded senses and a protected mind).

Regarding the phrase 'unmoistened and not burning,' the Venerable Mahā Moggallāna said this: "Friends, I will teach you the way of being moistened (avassuta) by defilements and the way of being unmoistened (anavassuta). Listen to that, pay close attention, and I will speak." Those monks replied to the Venerable Mahā Moggallāna, "Yes, friend." The Venerable Mahā Moggallāna said this:

"Friends, how is one moistened by defilements? Here, friends, a monk, having seen a form with the eye, is attracted to a pleasant form and is repelled by an unpleasant form. He dwells without mindfulness of the body established and with a limited mind. He does not understand as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those evil, unwholesome states that have arisen cease without remainder. Having heard a sound with the ear... cognized a mental object with the mind, he is attracted to a pleasant mental object and is repelled by an unpleasant mental object. He dwells without mindfulness of the body established and with a limited mind. He does not understand as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those evil, unwholesome states that have arisen cease without remainder. Friends, this person is called one who is moistened by defilements regarding forms cognizable by the eye... regarding mental objects cognizable by the mind. Friends, if Māra approaches a monk who dwells in such a way, even through the eye, Māra would surely gain an opportunity..."
288:
Māra would gain an entry, he would gain an object. If Māra approaches that monk through the ear... or through the mind, Māra would indeed gain an entry, Māra would indeed gain an object.

Friends, suppose there were a reed-house or a grass-house that had been dry and withered for three years. If a man were to approach it from the east with a blazing grass torch, the fire would indeed gain an entry, the fire would indeed gain an object. If he were to approach it from the west... from the north... from the south... from below... from above... from whatever direction a man were to approach it with a blazing grass torch, the fire would indeed gain an entry, the fire would indeed gain an object. In the same way, friends, if Māra approaches a monk who dwells in such a way through the eye, Māra would indeed gain an entry, Māra would indeed gain an object. If he approaches through the ear... or through the mind, Māra would indeed gain an entry, Māra would indeed gain an object.

Friends, forms overpower a monk who dwells in such a way; the monk does not overpower forms. Sounds overpower the monk; the monk does not overpower sounds. Odours overpower the monk; the monk does not overpower odours. Tastes overpower the monk; the monk does not overpower tastes. Tactile objects overpower the monk; the monk does not overpower tactile objects. Mental phenomena overpower the monk; the monk does not overpower mental phenomena. Friends, this monk is called one overpowered by forms, overpowered by sounds, overpowered by odours, overpowered by tastes, overpowered by tactile objects, and overpowered by mental phenomena. Being one who is overpowered rather than one who overpowers, he is overpowered by evil unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and leading to future birth, aging, and death. In this way, friends, one is corrupted (avassuta).

And how, friends, is one uncorrupted (anavassuta)? Here, friends, a monk, having seen a form with the eye, is not attracted to a pleasing form and is not repelled by a displeasing form. He dwells having established mindfulness of the body, with an immeasurable mind. He understands as it really is that liberation of mind...
289:
...and he understands as it really is the liberation by wisdom (paññāvimutti) through the path-knowledge. For the monk who knows thus, those evil unwholesome states that have arisen cease without remainder. Having heard a sound with the ear... (pe) ... Having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he is not attracted to a pleasing mental phenomenon and is not repelled by a displeasing mental phenomenon. He dwells having established mindfulness of the body (kāyagatāsati), with an immeasurable mind. That monk understands as it really is the liberation of mind (cetovimutti) and the liberation by wisdom (paññāvimutti). For the monk who knows thus, those evil unwholesome states that have arisen cease without remainder. Friends, this monk is called one who is uncorrupted by forms cognizable by the eye... (pe) ... uncorrupted by mental phenomena cognizable by the mind. Friends, if Māra (the Māra of defilements) approaches a monk who dwells in such a way through the door of the eye, Māra would not gain an entry, nor would he gain an object. If he approaches through the door of the ear... (pe) ... through the door of the mind, Māra would not gain an entry, nor would he gain an object.

Friends, suppose there were a gabled house or a gabled hall with thick walls and plastered with fresh plaster. If a man were to approach that house from the east with a blazing grass torch, the fire would not gain an entry, nor would it gain an object to catch fire. If he were to approach from the west... from the north... from the south... from below... from above... from whatever direction a man were to approach it with a blazing grass torch, the fire would not gain an entry, nor would it gain an object. In the same way, friends, if Māra approaches a monk who dwells in such a way through the door of the eye, Māra would not gain an entry, nor would he gain an object. If he approaches through the door of the ear... (pe) ... through the door of the mind, Māra would not gain an entry, nor would he gain an object.

Friends, a monk who dwells in such a way overpowers (conquers) forms; forms do not overpower the monk. The monk overpowers sounds; sounds do not overpower the monk. The monk overpowers odours; odours do not overpower the monk. The monk overpowers tastes; tastes do not overpower the monk. The monk overpowers tactile objects; tactile objects do not overpower the monk. The monk overpowers mental phenomena; mental phenomena do not overpower the monk. This monk...
290:
Friends, a monk overcomes visible forms; visible forms cannot overcome the monk. He also overcomes sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects; those objects cannot overcome the monk. Friends, this monk is called one who overcomes visible forms and so on, one who greatly overcomes, one who cannot be overcome by any defilements. He is called one who overcomes evil unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and leading to future birth, aging, and death. Friends, thus he is 'unstained' (anavassuto) by defilements. This is the meaning of the word 'anavassuto'.

'Not burning' (aparidahamāno) means not burning with the fever born of lust, not burning with the fever born of hatred, and not burning with the fever born of delusion. This is the meaning of the phrase 'unstained and not burning' (anavassuto aparidahamāno). One should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn. Therefore, that Paccekabuddha said—

"With downcast eyes and not restless of foot,
With guarded senses and a protected mind,
Unstained and not burning,
One should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn."

"Having discarded the marks of a layman,
Like a Pārichattaka tree with well-covered leaves,
Donning saffron robes and having gone forth,
One should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn."

In the phrase 'having discarded the marks of a layman' (ohārayitvā gihibyañjanāni), the marks of a layman mean hair, beard, and clothes with long fringes, and so on. 'Having discarded the marks of a layman' means having removed, having completely cast off, having laid down, and having relinquished the marks of a layman.

'Like a Pārichattaka tree with well-covered leaves' (sañchannapatto yathā pārichattako) means just as that Pārichattaka tree (Kovila) has dense foliage and flowers providing thick shade, even so, that Paccekabuddha carries a complete set of bowl and robes. This is the meaning of the phrase 'like a Pārichattaka tree with well-covered leaves'.
291:
'Having gone forth wearing saffron robes' (kāsāyavattho abhinikkhamitvā) means that Paccekabuddha, having cut off all impediments of household life, having cut off the impediment of wife and children, having cut off the impediment of relatives, having cut off the impediment of friends and companions, and having cut off the impediment of accumulation; having shaved off hair and beard, having donned saffron-dyed robes, having gone forth from the home life into homelessness, and having reached the state of being possessionless, wanders alone, dwells, moves, proceeds, maintains, sustains, and keeps himself going. Therefore, it is said: 'Donning saffron robes and having gone forth, one should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.' That Paccekabuddha said—

"Having discarded the marks of a layman,
Like a Pārichattaka tree with well-covered leaves,
Donning saffron robes and having gone forth,
One should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn."

## The Third Chapter.

## The Fourth Chapter

"Not being greedy for tastes, not being fickle,
Not supporting others, wandering for alms in order,
With a mind not attached to families,
One should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn."

"Not being greedy for tastes, not being fickle" means: Tastes are the taste of roots, the taste of trunks, the taste of bark, the taste of leaves, the taste of flowers, and the taste of fruits. Furthermore, they are sour, sweet, bitter, pungent, salty, alkaline, acidic, astringent, pleasant, unpleasant, cold, and hot. In this world, there are some recluses and brahmins who are greedy for tastes. They wander about seeking excellent tastes with the tip of their tongue. When they obtain something sour, they seek what is not sour; when they obtain what is not sour, they seek something sour. When they obtain something sweet, they seek what is not sweet; when they obtain what is not sweet, they seek something sweet. When they obtain something bitter, they seek what is not bitter; when they obtain what is not bitter, they seek something bitter. When they obtain something pungent, they seek what is not pungent; when they obtain what is not pungent, they seek something pungent. When they obtain something salty, they seek what is not salty; when they obtain what is not salty, they seek something salty. When they obtain something alkaline, they seek what is not alkaline; when they obtain what is not alkaline, they seek something alkaline. When they obtain something astringent, they seek what is not astringent; when they obtain what is not astringent, they seek something astringent. When they obtain something acidic, they seek what is not acidic; when they obtain what is not acidic, they seek something acidic. When they obtain a pleasant taste, they seek what is unpleasant; when they obtain what is unpleasant...
292:
Having obtained a delicious taste, they seek another; having obtained cold, they seek heat; having obtained heat, they seek cold. Not being satisfied with whatever taste they obtain, they seek here and there repeatedly. They are attached, greedy, tied, infatuated, obsessed, fastened, clung, and obstructed by pleasant tastes. That craving for tastes (rasataṇhā) has been abandoned by that Paccekabuddha, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, and is of a nature not to arise again in the future. Therefore, that Paccekabuddha, reflecting wisely, partakes of food: "Not for fun, not for intoxication, not for beautification, not for adornment, but only for the maintenance and endurance of this body, for ending discomfort, and for assisting the holy life. Thus, I shall terminate the old feeling and not produce a new feeling, and there will be for me maintenance, blamelessness, and living at ease."

Just as one would apply ointment to a wound only for the sake of healing; or just as one would grease an axle only for the sake of carrying a load; or just as one would eat the flesh of one's son only for the sake of crossing a desert; in the same way, that Paccekabuddha, reflecting wisely, partakes of food: "Not for fun, not for intoxication, not for beautification, not for adornment, but only for the maintenance and endurance of this body, for ending discomfort, and for assisting the holy life. Thus, I shall terminate the old feeling and not produce a new feeling, and there will be for me maintenance, blamelessness, and living at ease." He dwells abstaining, refraining, and recoiling from craving for tastes, having emerged, escaped, and being liberated and detached with a mind that has no boundaries. This is the meaning of "not being greedy for tastes."

"Alolo" (not fickle/greedy) refers to the craving called fickleness (loluppa). Whatever passion, intense lust... covetousness, greed, and unwholesome root exists; that fickle craving has been abandoned by that Paccekabuddha, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, and is of a nature not to arise again in the future. Therefore, the Paccekabuddha is called "alolo." This is the meaning of "not being greedy for tastes, not being fickle."

Regarding "Ananyaposī sapadānacārī," "ananyaposī" means that the Paccekabuddha supports only himself and does not support others.
293:
One who does not support others, who is unknown, tamed, established in the essence, whose taints are exhausted, and who has vomited out faults—him I call a Brahmin.

"Ananyaposī sapadānacārī" means that the Paccekabuddha, having dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and robes, enters a village or town for alms with a guarded body, guarded speech, and guarded mind, with established mindfulness and restrained faculties. With downcast eyes and perfect deportment, he wanders for alms from house to house without skipping any. Therefore, he is called "ananyaposī sapadānacārī."

"Having a mind not attached to every family" means that an attached mind arises through two reasons. An attached mind arises either by placing oneself low and exalting others, or by placing oneself high and humbling others. How does an attached mind arise by placing oneself low and exalting others? It is when one thinks: "You are of great help to me; depending on you, I receive robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites. Even when others think of giving to me or serving me, it is because they depend on you and see you. Even my former name and lineage given by my parents have disappeared; because of you, I am known as 'the family monk (kulūpaka) of such-and-such a male lay follower' or 'the family monk of such-and-such a female lay follower'." In this way, by placing oneself low and exalting others, an attached mind arises.

How does an attached mind arise by placing oneself high and humbling others? It is when one thinks: "I am of great help to you; because of me, you have gone to the Buddha for refuge, to the Dhamma for refuge, and to the Saṅgha for refuge. You refrain from taking life, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, and from fermented and distilled intoxicants which are the basis for negligence. I give you recitations, I give you explanations, I inform you of the Uposatha day, and I supervise new constructions. Yet, you neglect me and show respect, honor, esteem, and veneration to others." In this way, by placing oneself high and humbling others, an attached mind arises.

"Having a mind not attached to every family" means that the Paccekabuddha has a mind not attached through concern for families, not attached through concern for a group, not attached through concern for a dwelling, not attached through concern for robes, and not attached through concern for alms-food.
294:
He has a mind unattached to the impediment of lodging; he has a mind unattached to the impediment of medicinal requisites for the sick. This is the meaning of: "With a mind unattached to families, one should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn." Therefore, that Paccekabuddha said:

"Not being greedy for tastes, not being gluttonous, not supporting others, wandering for alms from house to house, with a mind unattached to families, one should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn."

"Having abandoned the five hindrances of the mind, having driven out all mental defilements by means of the path of insight, being independent, having cut through the fault of affection, one should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn."

"Having abandoned the five hindrances of the mind" means that Paccekabuddha, having abandoned, given up, dispelled, eliminated, and brought to non-existence the hindrance of sensual desire; having abandoned, given up, dispelled, eliminated, and brought to non-existence the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt; secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. This is the meaning of: "Having abandoned the five hindrances of the mind."

"Having driven out all mental defilements" means: Lust is a defilement of the mind, hatred is a defilement of the mind, delusion is a defilement of the mind, anger, enmity, and all unwholesome volitional formations are defilements of the mind. "Having driven out all mental defilements" means having driven out, pushed away, abandoned, dispelled, eliminated, and brought to non-existence all defilements of the mind. This is the meaning of: "Having driven out all mental defilements."
295:
Having abandoned, eliminated, and brought to non-existence the hindrance of restlessness and remorse and the hindrance of doubt, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. This is the meaning of: "Having abandoned the five hindrances of the mind." "Having driven out all mental defilements" means lust, hatred, delusion, anger, enmity, and so forth, adhere to and defile the mind. All unwholesome volitional formations adhere to and defile the mind. Driving out, abandoning, eliminating, and bringing to non-existence these impurities of the mind such as lust is the meaning of: "Having driven out all mental defilements."

In the verse "Being independent, having cut through affection and anger," "being independent" refers to two kinds of dependence: dependence on craving and dependence on views. This is dependence on craving; this is dependence on views. "Affection" refers to two kinds of affection: affection of craving and affection of views. This is affection of craving; this is affection of views. "Anger" refers to resentment of the mind, impact, repulsion, hostility, anger, irritation, intense irritation, hatred, ill will, intense ill will, the mind's malevolence, mental corruption, wrath, being angry, the state of being angry, hatred, hating, the state of being hated, malevolence, being malevolent, the state of being malevolent, ferocity, abusive speech, and dissatisfaction of the mind.

That Paccekabuddha, having cut through, severed, completely cut off, abandoned, dispelled, eliminated, and brought to non-existence the affection of craving, the affection of views, and anger, is independent of the eye, independent of the ear... independent of things to be seen, heard, sensed, and cognized; he is unattached, not approaching, not entering into, not attending to, but emerged, released, liberated, and detached, dwelling with a mind that has made no boundaries. Therefore, that Paccekabuddha said:

"Having abandoned the five hindrances of the mind, which are impurities, and having driven out all mental defilements, being independent, having cut through affection and anger, one should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn."

"Having turned one's back on pleasure and pain, and having previously extinguished joy and grief, having attained pure equanimity and tranquility, one should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn."

"Having turned one's back on pleasure and pain, and having previously extinguished joy and grief" means that Paccekabuddha, through the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and through the previous disappearance of joy and grief, enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and the purity of mindfulness through equanimity. This is the meaning of that phrase. In the phrase "having attained pure equanimity and tranquility," "equanimity" refers to the equanimity in the fourth jhāna, the mode of equanimity, the balance of mind, the non-distraction of mind, the state of equanimity. "Tranquility" refers to the steadiness of mind, well-established, firmly established, non-distraction, non-wavering, the state of having a non-distracted mind, tranquility, the faculty of tranquility, the power of tranquility, right concentration. All equanimity and tranquility in that jhāna are pure, exceptionally pure, radiant, free from the impurities of defilements, and free from mental defilements.
296:
Having attained pure equanimity and tranquility. Equanimity means the equanimity occurring in the fourth jhāna, looking on, looking on closely, mental evenness, mental serenity, mental non-distraction, and mental neutrality. Tranquility means the stability of mind, steadfastness, firmness, non-wavering, non-fluttering, the state of having a non-distracted mind, tranquility, the faculty of concentration, the power of concentration, and right concentration. In the fourth jhāna, equanimity and tranquility are pure, exceedingly pure, radiant, free from defilements, free from impurities, malleable, wieldy, stable, and have reached imperturbability. 'Having attained pure equanimity and tranquility' means having attained, reached, realized, and acquired the equanimity and tranquility of the fourth jhāna. Therefore, that Paccekabuddha said: 'Having attained pure equanimity and tranquility, a Paccekabuddha, like a rhinoceros horn, should wander alone.'

'Having left behind pleasure and pain,
And having previously extinguished joy and grief,
Having attained pure equanimity and tranquility,
A Paccekabuddha, like a rhinoceros horn, should wander alone.'

'With energy aroused for the attainment of the supreme goal,
With a mind that is not sluggish, not of lazy conduct,
With firm exertion, endowed with strength and power,
A Paccekabuddha, like a rhinoceros horn, should wander alone.'

In the phrase 'with energy aroused for the attainment of the supreme goal,' the supreme goal refers to Nibbāna, the deathless. It is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna. For the sake of attaining, reaching, penetrating, touching, and realizing that supreme goal, for the sake of abandoning unwholesome states and fulfilling wholesome states, he dwells with energy aroused, possessing strength, with firm exertion, not laying down the burden, and with energy applied to wholesome states.

'One with a mind that is not sluggish and not of lazy conduct' means that Paccekabuddha generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts the mind, and strives for the non-arising of evil unwholesome states that have not yet arisen. For the abandoning of evil unwholesome states that have arisen... For the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen... For those that have arisen...
297:
...for the persistence, non-disappearance, increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of wholesome states, he generates desire, strives, initiates energy, upholds the mind, and exerts effort firmly. Thus, he is one with an unshrinking mind and not given to laziness.

Alternatively: "Let only skin, sinews, and bones remain; let the flesh and blood in the body dry up; as long as that which is attainable by manly strength, manly power, manly energy, and manly endeavor has not been attained, there shall be no relaxing of energy." Thus he upholds the mind and exerts effort firmly. In this way too, he is one with an unshrinking mind and not given to laziness.

"As long as the thorn of craving is not pulled out,
I shall not eat, I shall not drink,
I shall not leave the monastery,
Nor shall I even lie down on my side."
Thus he upholds the mind and exerts effort firmly. In this way too, he is one with an unshrinking mind and not given to laziness.

"As long as my mind is not liberated from the taints through non-clinging, I shall not break this cross-legged sitting posture." Thus he upholds the mind and exerts effort firmly. In this way too, he is one with an unshrinking mind and not given to laziness.

"As long as my mind is not liberated from the taints through non-clinging, I shall not rise from this seat." Thus he upholds the mind and exerts effort firmly. In this way too, he is one with an unshrinking mind and not given to laziness.

"As long as my mind is not liberated from the taints through non-clinging, I shall not descend from this walking path ...pe... I shall not leave the monastery ... I shall not leave the dwelling compound ... I shall not leave the mansion ... I shall not leave the upper floor ... I shall not leave the cave ... I shall not leave the mountain cave ... I shall not leave the cell ... I shall not leave the gabled house ... I shall not leave the corridor house ... I shall not leave the single-pillared house ... I shall not leave the service hall ... I shall not leave the pavilion ... I shall not leave the foot of the tree." Thus he upholds the mind and exerts effort firmly. In this way too, he is one with an unshrinking mind and not given to laziness.

"In this very morning, I shall bring, fully bring, reach, touch, and realize the Noble Dhamma." Thus he upholds the mind and exerts effort firmly. In this way too, he is one with an unshrinking mind and not given to laziness. "In this very midday ...pe..."
298:
In the evening ... (pe) ... before the meal, after the meal, in the first watch, the middle watch, the last watch, during the dark fortnight, the bright fortnight, the rainy season, the winter, the summer, in the first stage of life, the middle stage, and the last stage, he exerts the mind and strives, thinking: 'I will bring the Dhamma of the Noble Ones near to my mind, I will bring it well, I will reach it through the path, I will touch the path of peaceful bliss, I will realize the fruit.' In this way, he is one with a mind that is not sluggish and not of lazy conduct. 'One with firm exertion and endowed with strength and power' means that Paccekabuddha is established in wholesome states. Because he is firmly established in good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind; in sharing gifts, undertaking virtue, observing the Uposatha, being dutiful to his mother, being dutiful to his father, respecting recluses, respecting brahmins, honoring elders in the family, and in other exceedingly wholesome states, he is called 'one with firm exertion.' 'Endowed with strength and power' means that Paccekabuddha is endowed with, fully endowed with, approached by, fully approached by, possessed of, and fully possessed of strength, power, energy, exertion, and wisdom. Therefore, it is said: 'One with firm exertion, endowed with strength and power, that Paccekabuddha, like a rhinoceros horn, should wander alone.' Therefore, that Paccekabuddha said:

'With energy aroused for the attainment of the supreme goal, with a mind that is not sluggish, not of lazy conduct, with firm exertion, endowed with strength and power, a Paccekabuddha, like a rhinoceros horn, should wander alone.'

'Not abandoning jhāna in seclusion, always practicing in accordance with the Dhamma among all things, contemplating the danger in existences, a Paccekabuddha, like a rhinoceros horn, should wander alone.'

'Not abandoning jhāna in seclusion' means that Paccekabuddha has the habit of delighting in seclusion, delights in seclusion, repeatedly practices the tranquility of mind (samatha) within himself, possesses jhāna that is not abandoned, is endowed with insight (vipassanā), cultivates secluded places, meditates, delights in jhāna, is devoted to one-pointedness, and regards his own welfare as important. This is the meaning of 'seclusion.' 'Not abandoning jhāna' means that Paccekabuddha does not abandon jhāna for two reasons: he is devoted and fully devoted to the arising of the first jhāna that has not yet arisen...
299:
...he is engaged, intensely engaged, specially engaged, repeatedly engaged, and well engaged for the arising of the unarisen second jhāna ... (pe) ... the unarisen third jhāna ... the unarisen fourth jhāna. In this way, too, he does not abandon jhāna.

Alternatively, he frequents, develops, and makes much of the arisen first jhāna; he frequents, develops, and makes much of the arisen second jhāna ... (pe) ... the arisen third jhāna ... the arisen fourth jhāna. In this way, too, he does not abandon jhāna; thus he is called "one not abandoning jhāna in seclusion."

In the phrase "always practicing in accordance with the Dhamma among the dhammas," the "dhammas" refer to the four foundations of mindfulness ... (pe) ... up to the Noble Eightfold Path. What are the "secondary dhammas" (anudhammas)? They are right practice, non-hostile practice, practice in accordance with the meaning, practice in accordance with the Dhamma, fulfilling virtue, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, and mindfulness and clear comprehension. These are called the "secondary dhammas." "Always practicing in accordance with the Dhamma among the dhammas" means that he practices, dwells, moves, carries on, protects, maintains, and keeps himself going in the dhammas daily, for a permanent duration, constantly, continuously, without interruption, in succession, like the waves of the water, with an unbroken continuity, being in contact with them before the meal, after the meal, in the first watch, the middle watch, the last watch, during the dark fortnight, the bright fortnight, during the rainy season, the winter season, the summer season, in the first stage of life, the middle stage of life, and the last stage of life. Thus, he is called "one who always practices in accordance with the Dhamma among the dhammas."

"Contemplating the faults in existences" means contemplating the faults in existences as "all formations are impermanent"; contemplating the faults in existences as "all formations are suffering" ... (pe) ... "all dhammas are non-self" ... (pe) ... "whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease." Contemplating the faults in existences in this way, like the horn of a rhinoceros, he should wander alone. Therefore, that Paccekabuddha said:

"Not abandoning jhāna in seclusion, always practicing in accordance with the Dhamma,
Contemplating the faults in existences, like the horn of a rhinoceros, one should wander alone."
300:
Desiring the destruction of craving, being diligent, not a deaf-mute (being wise), learned, mindful, having discerned the Dhamma, certain by the Path, and energetic, the Paccekasambuddha should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.

Regarding "Taṇhakkhayaṃ patthayamappamatto": Craving (taṇhā) refers to craving for forms... up to craving for mental objects. The destruction of craving (taṇhakkhaya) refers to the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion, the destruction of destiny, the destruction of rebirth, the destruction of conception, the destruction of existence, the destruction of saṃsāra, and the destruction of the round of suffering (Nibbāna). Desiring, wishing for, delighting in, longing for, and aspiring for this is called "taṇhakkhayaṃ patthayaṃ." "Appamatto" means that the Paccekasambuddha is one who acts with care, acts with perseverance... and is endowed with diligence in wholesome states. Thus, it is said: "taṇhakkhayaṃ patthayamappamatto."

Regarding "Aneḷamūgo sutavā satīmā": "Aneḷamūgo" means that the Paccekasambuddha is wise, intelligent, sagacious, possessed of knowledge, discerning, and prudent. "Sutavā" means that the Paccekasambuddha is very learned, a retainer of what is heard, and a storer of what is heard. He has heard much of those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, which, with the meaning and the letter, proclaim the entirely complete and pure holy life; he has retained them, recited them, mentally examined them, and well-penetrated them with wisdom. "Satīmā" means that the Paccekasambuddha is mindful. Being endowed with supreme mindfulness and prudence, he is one who remembers and recollects what was done long ago and what was said long ago. Thus, it is said: "aneḷamūgo sutavā satīmā."

Regarding "Saṅkhātadhammo niyato padhānavā": "Saṅkhātadhammo" refers to knowledge (ñāṇa). It is the wisdom that understands... non-delusion, investigation of states, and right view. "Saṅkhātadhammo" means that the Paccekasambuddha is one who has discerned the Dhamma, known the Dhamma, weighed the Dhamma, investigated the Dhamma, clarified the Dhamma, and developed the Dhamma. He is one who has discerned the Dhamma as "all formations are impermanent"... and as "whatever is subject to origination, all that is subject to cessation." He is one who has discerned, known, weighed, investigated, clarified, and developed the Dhamma. Alternatively, the aggregates of that Paccekasambuddha have been discerned, the elements have been discerned, the sense bases have been discerned, the destinies have been discerned, the births have been discerned, the conceptions have been discerned, the existences have been discerned, the saṃsāra has been discerned, and the round of suffering has been discerned. Alternatively, that Paccekasambuddha stands at the end of the aggregates...
301:
The Paccekabuddha stands at the end of the elements, stands at the end of the sense bases, stands at the end of the destinies, stands at the end of rebirths, stands at the end of conceptions, stands at the end of existences, stands at the end of saṃsāra, stands at the end of the round of suffering, stands at the end of formations, stands in the final existence, stands in the final individual form (attabhāva), and is a Paccekabuddha who bears the final body.

For that Paccekabuddha, this existence is the last, this individual form is the final one; for him, there is no more rebirth in the cycle of birth and death.

For that reason, the Paccekabuddha is called 'saṅkhātadhammo' (one who has discerned the Dhamma). 'Niyato' means the four Noble Paths are called 'niyāma' (certainty). Because he is endowed with these four Noble Paths, he is called 'niyato' (certain). One who has reached, well-reached, attained, touched, and realized the certainty of the Noble Path is called one who has reached certainty. In the term 'padhānavā', 'padhāna' refers to energy (vīriya). The exertion of energy of the mind, the effort to escape from defilements, the effort to subdue the enemy (defilements), striving, exertion, intense effort, persistence, capability, stability, unshaken effort, unflagging desire, unrelaxed responsibility, the upholding of effort, energy, the faculty of energy, the power of energy, and right effort are called 'padhāna'. That Paccekabuddha is endowed with, well-endowed with, possessed of, well-possessed of, not separate from, well-not separate from, and has reached fulfillment of this 'padhāna' energy. Therefore, that Paccekabuddha is called 'padhānavā' (energetic). The Paccekabuddha who has discerned the Dhamma, who is certain, and who is energetic should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn. Therefore, that Paccekabuddha said:

'Desiring Nibbāna, the destruction of craving, being diligent and mindful, without being mute (in defilements), being very learned and mindful, having discerned the Dhamma, being certain in the Path, being energetic, one should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.'

Like a lion not trembling at sounds, like the wind not caught in a net, like a lotus not smeared by water, one should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.

'Like a lion not trembling at sounds' means: Just as a lion, the king of beasts, is not startled by sounds, does not tremble due to danger, is not terrified, has no fear, has no doubt, does not dread, does not shake, and does not flee; in the same way, the Paccekabuddha is not startled by sounds, does not tremble due to danger, is not terrified, has no fear, has no doubt, does not dread, does not shake, and does not flee, but dwells with fear abandoned and with hair-standing-on-end removed. This is the meaning of the phrase 'like a lion not trembling at sounds'. In the phrase 'like the wind not caught in a net', the wind refers to the east wind, west wind, north wind, south wind, and winds with faults...
302:
Being free from terror, fearless, unshakable, not terrified, and not fleeing, a Paccekabuddha also is not startled by sounds, not terrified by danger, not greatly terrified, without fear or trembling, without doubt, not afraid, without bodily shaking, and without fleeing; having abandoned fear, he dwells with his hair not standing on end. This is the meaning of 'Like a lion not startled by sounds.'

In the phrase 'Like the wind not caught in a net,' wind refers to the east wind, west wind, north wind, south wind, dusty wind, dustless wind, cold wind, hot wind, slight wind, strong wind, Veramba wind, wing-born wind, Garuda-born wind, palm-leaf wind, and fan-born wind. A net refers to a thread net. Just as the wind is not caught, not held, not bound, and not repeatedly bound in a net, even so, there are two nets: the net of craving (taṇhā-jāla) and the net of views (diṭṭhi-jāla). ... This is the net of craving, ... this is the net of views. That Paccekabuddha has abandoned the net of craving and relinquished the net of views. Because of abandoning the net of craving and relinquishing the net of views, that Paccekabuddha is not caught in forms, not caught in sounds ... not caught, not held, not bound, and not repeatedly bound in things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized; he dwells as one who has emerged, escaped, is particularly liberated, and detached, with a mind free from boundaries. This is the meaning of 'Like the wind not caught in a net.'

In the phrase 'Like a lotus unsmeared by water,' 'paduma' refers to a lotus flower. 'Toya' refers to water. Just as a lotus flower is not smeared, not smeared all over, not smeared closely, is unsmeared, entirely unsmeared, and particularly unsmeared by water, even so, there are two smearings: the smearing of craving (taṇhā-lepa) and the smearing of views (diṭṭhi-lepa). ... This is the smearing of craving, ... this is the smearing of views. That Paccekabuddha has abandoned the smearing of craving and relinquished the smearing of views. Because of abandoning the smearing of craving and relinquishing the smearing of views, that Paccekabuddha is not smeared by forms, not smeared by sounds ... not smeared, not smeared all over, not smeared closely in things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized; he is one who is unsmeared, entirely unsmeared, particularly unsmeared, one who has emerged, escaped, is particularly liberated, and detached, dwelling with a mind free from boundaries. This is the meaning of 'Like a lotus unsmeared by water, one should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.' Therefore, that Paccekabuddha said—

Like a lion not startled by sounds,
Like the wind not caught in a net,
Like a lotus unsmeared by water,
One should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn—

Thus he spoke. Just as a lion, the king of beasts, strong in fangs, wanders having subdued and overcome others by power, even so, the Buddha-like one, who has the strength of wisdom as fangs, wanders having subdued all things by the power of wisdom and by the power of intense virtue. One should resort to remote lodgings. One should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn. Just as a lion, the king of beasts, strong in fangs, lives and wanders having subdued, overcome, and mastered all animals, even so, a Paccekabuddha, who has the strength of wisdom, wanders having subdued, overcome, and mastered all persons by the power of wisdom.
303:
Like a lion not startled by sounds, like the wind not caught in a net, like a lotus unsmeared by water, even so, a Paccekabuddha with the practice like a rhinoceros horn should wander alone.

Like a lion, strong in fangs, the king of beasts, wandering having subdued and overcome [others], even so, one should resort to remote lodgings, wandering alone like a rhinoceros horn.

'Like a lion, strong in fangs, the king of beasts, wandering having subdued and overcome [others]' means: Just as the lion, the king of beasts, strong in fangs, having fangs as a weapon, wanders, dwells, moves, proceeds, protects, maintains, and supports his life having subdued, overcome, overwhelmed, mastered, and crushed all animals, even so, a Paccekabuddha, having the strength of wisdom as a weapon, wanders, dwells, moves, proceeds, protects, maintains, and supports his life having subdued, overcome, overwhelmed, mastered, and crushed all beings and persons by wisdom.

'One should resort to remote lodgings' means: Just as the lion, the king of beasts, enters the middle of the forest and wanders, dwells, moves, proceeds, protects, maintains, and supports his life, even so, a Paccekabuddha resorts to remote lodgings in the middle of the forest, which are quiet, free from noise, free from the breath of people, secluded from people, and suitable for solitary retreat. That venerable one goes alone, stands alone, sits alone, lies down alone, enters the village for alms alone, returns alone, sits in private alone, undertakes walking meditation alone, and wanders, dwells, moves, proceeds, protects, maintains, and supports his life alone. Therefore, that Paccekabuddha said: 'Like a lion, strong in fangs, the king of beasts, wandering having subdued and overcome [others], one should resort to remote lodgings, wandering alone like a rhinoceros horn.'
304: At the proper time, practicing the liberation of mind (cetovimutti) known as loving-kindness (mettā), equanimity (upekkhā), compassion (karuṇā), and appreciative joy (muditā), not conflicting with the entire world of beings, that Paccekabuddha should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn. "At the proper time, practicing the liberation of mind known as loving-kindness, equanimity, compassion, and appreciative joy" means that the Paccekabuddha dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness. Likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus, above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility, and without ill-will. With a mind imbued with compassion... (pe)... With a mind imbued with appreciative joy... (pe)... With a mind imbued with equanimity—abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility, and without ill-will, he dwells pervading [the world]. This is the meaning of the phrase "At the proper time, practicing the liberation of mind known as loving-kindness, equanimity, compassion, and appreciative joy." "Not conflicting with the entire world" means that because of the development of loving-kindness, those beings in the eastern direction are not repulsive. Beings in the western direction... (pe)... beings in the northern direction... beings in the southern direction... beings in the south-eastern intermediate direction... beings in the south-western intermediate direction... beings in the north-western intermediate direction... beings in the north-eastern intermediate direction... beings in the lower direction... beings in the upper direction... those beings in the ten directions are not repulsive. Because of the development of compassion... because of the development of appreciative joy... because of the development of equanimity, those beings in the eastern direction... (pe)... those beings in the ten directions are not repulsive. "Not conflicting with the entire world" means dwelling without conflict, without opposition, without malice, and without being struck by the entire world of beings. Therefore, that Paccekabuddha said: "At the proper time, practicing the liberation of mind known as mettā, upekkhā, karuṇā, and muditā, not conflicting with the entire world of beings, one should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn."
305:
Having abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion, having shattered the fetters, and being without trembling at the end of life, the Paccekabuddha should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.

Regarding "Rāgañca dosañca pahāya mohaṃ": Lust (rāga) is the unwholesome root of greed, characterized by attachment, repeated attachment, and excessive longing. Hatred (dosa) is the resentment of the mind, harshness, ferocity, displeasure, and unhappiness of the mind. Delusion (moha) is ignorance regarding the truth of suffering, the bond of ignorance, and the unwholesome root of bewilderment. That Paccekabuddha has abandoned, dispelled, eliminated, and brought to non-existence lust, hatred, and delusion; thus, it is said: "rāgañca dosañca pahāya mohaṃ."

Regarding "Sandālayitvāna saṃyojanāni": There are ten fetters—the fetter of sensual lust, the fetter of aversion, and so on, up to the fetter of ignorance. Having shattered, broken, thoroughly destroyed, abandoned, dispelled, eliminated, and brought to non-existence these ten fetters; thus, it is said: "sandālayitvāna saṃyojanāni."

Regarding "Asantasaṃ jīvitasaṅkhayamhi": That Paccekabuddha, at the end of life, is not trembling with craving, not terrified, not anxious, not suspicious, not afraid, not quaking, not fearful, not fleeing, having abandoned fear and dread, and with hair no longer standing on end. Therefore, that Paccekabuddha said: "Having abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion, having shattered the fetters, and being without trembling at the end of life, one should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn."

## They associate and serve for a motive; friends without a motive are rare today.
## People are wise in their own interest and are impure; one should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.
306:
They associate with and serve others for the sake of a cause: for the sake of their own benefit, for the sake of another's benefit, for the sake of both, for the sake of benefit in the present life, for the sake of benefit in the future life, or for the sake of the ultimate benefit. Because they associate, thoroughly associate, serve, repeatedly serve, frequent, and repeatedly frequent, it is said: 'They associate and serve for the sake of a cause.'

'Friends without motive are rare today': there are two kinds of friends—the lay friend and the homeless friend. ...p... This person is a lay friend, ...p... this person is a homeless friend. 'Friends without motive are rare today' means these two kinds of friends are rare without a cause, without a motive, without a reason, without a condition (they are very difficult to obtain). Therefore, it is said: 'Friends without motive are rare today.'

'Impure humans wise for their own benefit': 'Wise for their own benefit' (attatthapaññā) means they associate, thoroughly associate, serve, repeatedly serve, frequent, repeatedly frequent, practice, thoroughly practice, attend, inquire, and investigate for the sake of their own benefit, for their own reason, for their own condition, for their own cause. Therefore, it is said: 'Wise for their own benefit.' 'Impure humans' (asuci manussā) means those possessed of impure bodily action, therefore they are called impure humans; those possessed of impure verbal action, therefore they are called impure humans; those possessed of impure mental action, therefore they are called impure humans. Those possessed of impure taking of life ...p... impure stealing ... impure sexual misconduct ... impure false speech ... those possessed of impure malicious speech ... those possessed of impure harsh speech ... those possessed of impure frivolous chatter ... those possessed of impure covetousness ... those possessed of impure ill-will, therefore they are called impure humans. Those possessed of impure wrong view, therefore they are called impure humans; those possessed of impure intention, therefore they are called impure humans; those possessed of impure aspiration, therefore they are called impure humans; those possessed of impure resolution, therefore they are called impure humans. Because they are impure, low, base, inferior, vile, wretched, and of little merit, it is said: 'Impure humans wise for their own benefit.'

'One should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn': 'Alone' (eko) means that Paccekabuddha is alone by way of renunciation ...p... 'Should wander' (care) refers to the eight modes of conduct ...p... 'Like a rhinoceros horn' (khaggavisāṇakappo) means just as the horn of a rhinoceros is single and without a second ...p... one should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn. Therefore, that Paccekabuddha said:
